233:
## Vinaya Piṭaka
## Mahāvagga Commentary
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## 1. Mahākhandhaka
## Bodhikathā
After the recitation of the two Vibhaṅgas, which are the detailed expositions of the two Pātimokkhas (for monks and nuns),
the Great Elders, who were experts in the Khandhakas, recited the Khandhaka.
Since the sequence of the commentary on that Khandhaka has now arrived,
this explanation of its obscure meanings will be given.
If we were to repeat the meanings of the terms already explained in the Padabhājanīya (word-by-word commentary) by those same methods,
when would the commentary ever reach its end?
What is the use of explaining meanings that are already clear
through their intention and context, or through the words themselves?
Because meanings that are not clear through intention, context, or words
cannot be understood if they are not explained,
this method of commentary is for those obscure meanings alone.

"At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Uruvelā on the bank of the river Nerañjarā at the foot of the Bodhi tree, having just attained supreme enlightenment." In this passage, although there is no special reason for using the instrumental case "tena samayena" (at that time) as in passages such as "At that time the Blessed One was at Verañjā," it should be understood that this expression is traditionally established in the Vinaya teaching from the very beginning. This same method should be understood for other similar introductions that follow this one.

What is the purpose of making this statement? The purpose is to show the origin (nidāna) of Vinaya acts, such as the going forth (pabbajjā), from the beginning. For there are the going forth and higher ordination (upasampadā) allowed by the Blessed One thus: "Monks, I allow the going forth and higher ordination by these three refuges," and there are the duties toward preceptors (upajjhāya) and teachers (ācariya) allowed by the Blessed One in Rājagaha and other places. It should be understood that the purpose of this statement is to show the origin of these acts—such as the going forth, higher ordination, and the duties toward preceptors and teachers—by explaining how the Buddha, after attaining the knowledge of the path of Arahatship and omniscience, spent seven weeks (49 days) at the Bodhi tree, set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion at Vārāṇasī, and then, traveling from place to place in this sequence, prescribed them for various reasons.
234:
"I allow the going forth and higher ordination by the three refuges." Thus, the going forth and higher ordination, as well as the duties toward preceptors and teachers allowed in Rājagaha and elsewhere, were prescribed in various places and for various reasons as the Buddha traveled in sequence after attaining enlightenment, staying for seven weeks (49 days) at the great site of enlightenment (Bodhimanda), and setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion at Vārāṇasī. It should be understood that showing the origin of these Vinaya acts, such as the going forth, from the beginning is the purpose of making this statement.

In that passage, "Uruvelāyam" means at the great bank of sand or at the great heap of sand. Alternatively, "Uru" means sand and "Velā" means a limit or boundary; thus, "Uruvelā" is to be understood as the sand that was brought there because a limit was exceeded. It is said that in the past, before a Buddha had arisen, ten thousand young men of good family went forth as ascetics and lived in that region. One day, they gathered and made a pact: "Bodily and vocal actions are obvious to others, but mental actions are not. Therefore, if anyone thinks a sensual thought, a malicious thought, or a harmful thought, since there is no other accuser, he must accuse himself, bring sand in a leaf-cup, and pour it in this place; let this be his penalty." From then on, whoever had such a thought would pour sand there with a leaf-cup. In due course, a great heap of sand was formed, and later people enclosed that heap and made it a shrine. With reference to that, it is said: "Uruvelāyam means at the great bank of sand or at the great heap of sand." With reference to that same story, it is also said: "Alternatively, Uru means sand and Velā means a limit; thus, Uruvelā is the sand brought because a limit was exceeded."

In the phrase "Bodhirukkhamūle," "Bodhi" refers to the knowledge (ñāṇa) of the four paths. Because the Blessed One attained that Bodhi at this place, the tree also received the name "Bodhi tree." Because he was near that Bodhi tree, it is said "at the foot of the Bodhi tree" (Bodhirukkhamūle). "Paṭhamābhisambuddho" means having just attained supreme enlightenment; it means the very first time after becoming a Buddha. "Ekapallaṅkena" means in a single cross-legged posture, without rising even once from the position in which he sat down. "Vimuttisukhapaṭisaṃvedī" means experiencing the bliss of liberation, which is the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti).
235:
"Paṭiccasamuppāda" (Dependent Origination) refers to the mode of conditions (paccayākāra). This is because the mode of conditions causes phenomena that arise together by depending on one another; thus, it is called "Paṭiccasamuppāda." This is merely a summary here. One who desires a detailed decision complete in all aspects should take it from the Visuddhimagga.

"Anuloma-paṭiloma" means forward and reverse order. Among these, the mode of conditions starting with ignorance, stated in the manner of "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]," is called "anuloma" (forward order) because it performs its own required function. That same mode of conditions, stated in the manner of "With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease," is called "paṭiloma" (reverse order) because it ceases by way of non-arising and does not perform that function; thus, it is called reverse due to that non-performance. Alternatively, the mode of conditions stated in the first manner is called forward because it conforms to the occurrence (pavatti) of the round of rebirth, and the other is called reverse because it is contrary to that occurrence. This is how the meaning should be understood. Since it is not stated by proceeding from the beginning to the end and from the end to the beginning, the forward and reverse nature is not suitable in any sense other than what has been stated.

"Manasākāsi" means he attended in his mind. Therein, to show how he attended in his mind in forward order, "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [arise]" etc., is stated. In that phrase, ignorance is both [the state] and the condition; therefore, it is called "avijjāpaccaya" (ignorance-condition). By this method, the meaning in all terms should be understood: "With ignorance as the condition, volitional formations come to be." This is the summary here. The detailed explanation complete in all aspects should be taken only from the Visuddhimagga by one who desires it.

To show how he attended in his mind in reverse order, "With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease" etc., is stated. In that phrase, "avijjāya tveva" means only of ignorance (due to its cessation). "Asesavirāganirodhā" means due to the remainderless cessation by the Path known as fading away (virāga). "SaṄkhāranirodho" means the cessation of volitional formations by way of non-arising. To show that due to the cessation of volitional formations thus ceased, consciousness ceases, and due to the cessation of consciousness etc., name-and-form etc. indeed cease, it is stated "With the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases" etc., and then "Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering." In that phrase, "kevalassa" means the whole, or purely, meaning devoid of a being. "Dukkha-kkhandhassa" means of the mass of suffering. "Nirodho hoti" means non-arising occurs.
236:
"Having understood this matter" means having understood in every aspect this matter stated as: "Through the power of ignorance etc., the arising of the mass of suffering such as volitional formations etc. occurs; and through the power of the cessation of ignorance etc., the cessation of the mass of suffering occurs." "At that time" means at the time of understanding that matter. "Uttered this inspired utterance" means that when that matter was understood, he uttered this inspired utterance starting with "Yadā have pātubhavanti dhammā," which arises from knowledge accompanied by joy and demonstrates the power of fully knowing the cause and the phenomena arisen from the cause; it means he emitted a joyful speech.

The meaning of that inspired utterance is: "Yadā have" means at which time. "Pātubhavanti" means they appear or arise. "Dhammā" means the 37 factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhammā) that accomplish the penetration of the forward and reverse dependent origination. Alternatively, "pātubhavanti" means they become manifest; they become clear and evident by way of realization through the Path. "Dhammā" means the truths of the Four Noble Truths. Ardor (ātāpa) is called energy (vģriya) in the sense of burning away defilements; "ātāpino" means of one who possesses the energy of right effort (sammappadhāna). "Jhāyato" means of one who meditates with jhāna characterized by both attending to the object (ārammaṇũpanijjhāna) and attending to the characteristics (lakkhaṇũpanijjhāna). "Brāhmaṇassa" means of the Arahant who has discarded evil. "Atha-ssa kaṄkhā vapayanti" means then the doubts of that Arahant, for whom the truths have thus appeared, vanish. "Sabbā" means all the doubts stated regarding the mode of conditions in the manner of: "'Venerable Sir, who touches?' 'The question is not fit,' the Blessed One said," etc., and likewise: "'Venerable Sir, what is aging and death? And for whom is this aging and death?' 'The question is not fit,' the Blessed One said," etc. Also, the sixteen types of doubt such as "Was I in the past?" etc., which arise due to not penetrating the mode of conditions itself—all those vanish, go away, and cease. Why? As it is stated, "Yato pajānāti sahetudhammaṁ"—because he fully knows, understands, and penetrates this phenomenon which is purely a mass of suffering, such as volitional formations, together with its cause such as ignorance.

In the second instance, "uttered this inspired utterance" means that when that matter was understood, he uttered the inspired utterance of the aforementioned kind, which demonstrates the power of realizing the destruction of conditions known as Nibbāna, which is manifested as: "With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease." The summary meaning there is: because he understood, knew, and penetrated Nibbāna, known as the destruction of conditions, therefore, when to that Arahant who has ardor and meditates with jhāna...
237:
To that brahmin (arahant) who is ardent and meditative, the aforementioned states become manifest. Then, all doubts that might arise due to not knowing Nibbāna vanish.

Regarding the phrase "uttered this inspired utterance" on the third occasion: it means that he understood the meaning known as the arising and ceasing of the mass of suffering through the Noble Path, both by way of function and by way of making it an object; he uttered the aforementioned inspired utterance which illustrates the power of that Noble Path. The summary meaning of that inspired utterance is: when the states become manifest to the brahmin who is ardent and meditative, then that brahmin stands dispelling the army of Māra—described in such ways as "Sensual pleasures are your first army"—either by those bodhipakkhiya-dhammas (requisites of enlightenment) that have arisen, or by that Noble Path through which the four Truths have become manifest. How? Just like the sun illuminating the sky. Just as the sun, having risen, stands illuminating the sky with its own radiance and dispelling the darkness, so too that brahmin stands dispelling the army of Māra while penetrating the Truths through those states or through that Path.

Thus, it should be understood that here the first inspired utterance arose by way of contemplating dependent origination, the second by way of contemplating Nibbāna, and the third by way of contemplating the Path. However, in the Udāna Pali, it is stated: "In the first watch of the night, he contemplated dependent origination in forward order; in the second watch, in reverse order; in the third watch, in both forward and reverse order." This statement refers to the reflection that occurred during the night after seven days had passed, thinking, "Tomorrow I shall rise from this seat." At that time, the Blessed One meditated in his mind on each section during the first and middle watches, by virtue of the preceding two verses which illustrate the power of knowing dependent origination and the attainment of the end of causes (Nibbāna). In this Khandhaka Pali, however, he reflected in this manner on the night of the first day of the waning moon.

The Blessed One attained the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa) in the first watch of the night of the full moon of Vesākha; in the middle watch, he purified the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu); in the last watch, having reflected on dependent origination in forward and reverse order, he attained omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) at the moment when it was said, "Now the dawn will rise." Immediately after attaining omniscience, the dawn rose. Thereafter, having spent that day in that same cross-legged posture, he reflected in this manner during the three watches of the night of the first day of the waning moon and uttered these inspired utterances.
238:
Thus, having reflected in this manner on the night of the first day of the waning moon, he spent those seven days at the foot of the Bodhi tree, as it is said, "He sat for seven days in a single cross-legged posture at the foot of the Bodhi tree."

## The Discussion on the Bodhi Tree is finished.

## The Discussion on the Ajapāla Tree

"Then, at the end of seven days, the Blessed One emerged from that concentration and went from the foot of the Bodhi tree to the Ajapāla banyan tree." In this statement, it does not mean that the Blessed One went to the Ajapāla banyan tree immediately after emerging from that concentration. For example, when it is said, "He sleeps after eating," it does not mean that he sleeps without washing his hands, without rinsing his mouth, without going near the bed, or without saying anything else; rather, the intended meaning is that he sleeps after eating, not that he does not sleep. Similarly, here too, it does not mean that he departed immediately after emerging from that concentration; rather, the intended meaning is that he departed after emerging, not that he did not depart.

What did the Blessed One do instead of departing immediately? He spent another three weeks (21 days) in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree. In this regard, this is the sequential account: While the Blessed One, having attained Buddhahood, sat for seven days in a single cross-legged posture, doubt arose in some deities, thinking, "The Blessed One has not yet arisen; are there perhaps other states that bring about Buddhahood?" Then, on the eighth day, the Blessed One, having emerged from the attainment and knowing the doubt of the deities, ascended into the sky to dispel their doubt and performed the Twin Miracle (yamaka-pāṭihāriya). Having dispelled the doubt of those deities, he stood a little to the northeast of the throne (pallaṅka) and spent seven days gazing with unblinking eyes at the throne and the Bodhi tree, which were obtained through the power of the perfections (pāramīs) accumulated over four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons. That place became known as the Animisa Cetiya.

Thereafter, in the jeweled walkway (ratana-caṅkama) extending from east to west between the throne and the place where he had stood, he spent seven days walking to and fro. That place became known as the Ratanacaṅkama Cetiya. Furthermore, in the western direction, the deities created a jeweled house (ratanaghara). Sitting there in a cross-legged posture, he spent [seven days] contemplating the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, especially the Samantapaṭṭhāna with its infinite methods within this Abhidhamma Piṭaka...
239:
Contemplating the Samantapaṭṭhāna (the Book of Relations) with its infinite methods, He spent seven days there; that place came to be known as the Ratanagharacetiya (the Jewel House Shrine).

In this manner, having spent four weeks (four sattāhas) in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree, in the fifth week, He proceeded from the foot of the Bodhi tree to the Ajapāla Nigrodha (Goatherds' Banyan tree). It is said that goatherds used to go and sit in the shade of that banyan tree; for that reason, the name "Ajapāla Nigrodha" arose for that banyan tree. Regarding the phrase "He experienced the bliss of liberation for seven days," it means that even at the foot of that Ajapāla Banyan tree, while contemplating the Dhamma, He sat experiencing the bliss of the attainment of the fruition of Arahatship (arahattaphalasamāpatti) repeatedly. This Ajapāla Banyan tree is located to the east of the Bodhi tree. While the Blessed One was sitting there in this manner, a certain Brahmin came and asked a question. Because of that questioning, the Elder Upāli recited the words beginning with "Atha kho aññataro."

In that passage, "huṃhuṅkajātika" means that the Brahmin was one known as a Diṭṭhamaṅgalika (one who believes in auspicious sights), and he used to wander about making the sound "huṃ huṃ" out of pride and anger; therefore, he is called "huṃhuṅkajātika." Some also read it as "huhukkajātika."

"Having understood this matter" means having understood the highest meaning of the words spoken by that Brahmin, He uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) at that time. The meaning of that inspired utterance is: A person is called a Brāhmaṇa because he has discarded evil qualities (bāhitapāpadhamma), not because he holds the view of a Diṭṭhamaṅgalika. One who claims to be a Brahmin merely by birth while being possessed of evil qualities such as making the "huṃ huṃ" sound out of pride and anger, or being stained with lust and so on, is not a true Brahmin. That Arahat is called a Brāhmaṇa because he has discarded evil qualities; he is called nihuṃhuṅka because of the abandonment of making the "huṃ huṃ" sound; he is called nikkasāva because of the absence of the stains (kasāva) of lust and so on; he is called yatatta because he has a mind associated with the practice of meditation (bhāvanā) or because he has a mind restrained by the restraint of virtue (sīlasaṃvara); he is called vedantagū because he has reached Nibbāna, which is the end of formations (saṅkhāra), through the Vedas known as the fourfold Path-knowledge (maggañāṇa), or because he has reached the end of the Vedas (the fruition of Arahatship); he is called vusitabrahmacariya because he has lived the holy life of the Path. He may rightly say, "I am a Brahmin." For that Arahat, there are no protuberances (ussada)—namely the protuberances of lust, hatred, delusion, pride, and wrong view—towards any single object anywhere in the entire world of beings. Such an Arahat may rightly say, "I am a Brahmin."

## The Story of Ajapāla is finished.

## The Story of Mucalinda

"Akālamegha" refers to a cloud that arises before the arrival of the rainy season. This occurred in the month of Jeṭṭha, the last month of the summer. "Sattāhavaddalikā" means that when that cloud arose, there was continuous rain for seven days. "Sītavātaduddinī" means that the rain...
240:
Because the continuous seven-day rain was accompanied by cold winds mixed with water droplets blowing all around the four directions, spoiling the days, it was called a gloomy day with cold winds (sītavātaduddinī). At that time, there was a powerful Naga King named Mucalinda, who was born in the pond near that very Mucalinda tree. "Having encircled [the Blessed One] seven times with his coils" means that while he stood having thus encircled Him with his coils and having made a large hood over the top of His head, the space inside his coils was equal to the size of a treasury chamber in the Brazen Palace (Lohapāsāda). Therefore, it was as if the Blessed One were sitting in a gabled house (kūṭāgāra) where the wind was still and the doors and windows were closed.

"May the Blessed One not be afflicted by cold," and so on, is an explanation of the reason why the Naga King acted and stood in that way. Indeed, he stood having acted thus, thinking, "May the Blessed One not be afflicted by cold, may He not be afflicted by heat, may He not be afflicted by the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, or creeping things." In that context, although there is actually no heat during a seven-day continuous rain, if the clouds were to clear occasionally, heat might occur; it is appropriate to think that the Naga King intended that even such heat should not afflict the Blessed One. "Viddhaṃ" means high, or far away due to the disappearance of clouds. "Vigatavalāhakaṃ" means free from clouds; "devaṃ" means the sky; "sakavaṇṇaṃ" means his own Naga form.

Seclusion is happiness for one who is content, for one who has heard the Dhamma, and for one who sees.
Non-affliction and restraint towards beings in the world is happiness.
Transcending sense pleasures and being free from lust in the world is happiness.
The removal of the conceit "I am" is indeed the highest happiness.

"Sukho viveko" means that the seclusion from the bases of existence (upadhiviveka) known as Nibbāna is happiness. "Tuṭṭhassa" means for one who is content with the satisfaction of the fourfold Path-knowledge. "Sutadhammassa" means for one who has the Dhamma clearly revealed. "Passato" means for one who sees that seclusion, or whatever is to be seen, with the eye of knowledge obtained through the power of one's own energy. "Abyāpajjaṃ" means the state of non-anger; by this word, the preliminary stage of loving-kindness (mettā) is shown. "Pāṇabhūtesu saṃyamo" means restraint towards living beings; the meaning is that the state of non-violence is happiness. By this word, the preliminary stage of compassion (karuṇā) is shown. By the words "sukhā virāgatā loke," it is shown that being free from lust is also happiness. "Kāmānaṃ samatikkamo" means that which is called "transcending sense pleasures"; the meaning is that such freedom from lust is also happiness. By this word, the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga) is spoken of. By the words "asmimānassa yo vinayo," the fruition of Arahatship (arahattaphala) is spoken of. Indeed, the fruition of Arahatship is called "the peaceful removal of the conceit 'I am'." There is no happiness superior to this fruition of Arahatship; therefore, He said, "This is indeed the highest happiness."

## The Story of Mucalinda is finished.

## The Story of Rājāyatana

"Mucalindamūlā" means from the foot of the Mucalinda tree located in the southeast corner from the Great Bodhi tree. "Rājāyatanaṃ" means [He approached] the Rājāyatana (Buchanania latifolia) tree located in the southern direction.
241:
Non-harming is happiness. This is the meaning of the word restraint (saṃyama). By this statement, he shows the compassion that existed previously. In this world, the absence of passion is happiness; by this statement, he shows that the absence of passion is also a cause of happiness. The absence of passion, which is called the transcending of sensual desires, is happiness. By this statement, he speaks of the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmi-magga). The removal of the conceit 'I am'—by this statement, he speaks of the Fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala). In truth, the Fruit of Arahantship is called the stilling of the conceit 'I am'. There is no happiness superior to this Fruit of Arahantship. Therefore, the Blessed One taught: 'This Fruit of Arahantship alone is the supreme happiness.'

The Account of Mucalinda ends.

The Blessed One proceeded from the foot of the Mucalinda tree, situated at the southeast corner of the Great Bodhi tree, to the Rājāyatana tree, situated to the south of the Great Bodhi tree. At what time was that? On the day the Blessed One rose from the concentration of the Fruit of Arahantship, after sitting for seven days in a single posture at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree. At the very time of dawn, knowing that there should be the act of taking food, Sakka, the king of devas, offered the medicinal yellow myrobalan (harītakī). The Blessed One partook of that myrobalan. As soon as he had partaken of it, there was the need for bodily functions (evacuation). Sakka offered water for washing the face. The Blessed One washed his face and sat at the foot of that very Rājāyatana tree. Thus, when the dawn had risen and the Blessed One was seated:

At that time, the merchants named Tapussa and Bhallika were traveling on a long journey from the Ukkala region to that place. 'Tapussa-Bhallikā vāṇijā' refers to the two brothers who were merchants, named Tapussa and Bhallika. 'Ukkalā' means from the Ukkala region. 'Taṃ desaṃ' refers to the place where the Blessed One was staying (the Middle Country). Therefore, it means they were traveling on the long-distance road to go to the Middle Country.

A deity who had been a former relative of those merchants spoke these words. That deity prevented all the merchants' carts from moving. Then, the merchants, wondering why the carts were not moving, made offerings to the road-protecting deities. While they were making the offerings, that deity appeared in visible form and said: 'Serve (the Blessed One) with parched grain and honey balls. Such service will be for your long-term welfare and happiness. May the Blessed One's acceptance also be for our long-term welfare and happiness.'

This thought occurred to the Blessed One: The bowl that he had during the time of his great exertion had disappeared even as the merchant's daughter Sujātā was coming to offer the milk-rice. Therefore, the Blessed One thought: 'I have no bowl. Moreover, the Tathāgatas of the past did not receive (food) with their hands. In what, then, shall I receive the parched grain and honey balls?'

Knowing the thought of the Blessed One—even before those merchants made their offering, the food offered by Sujātā had remained as a continuous flow of essence (ojā); during these forty-nine days, there had been no hunger, no thirst, and no physical weakness. But now, because he wished to receive food, he reflected in the manner beginning with 'The Tathāgatas do not...' Knowing that thought of the Blessed One with their own minds, the Four Great Kings offered stone bowls the color of mung beans from the four directions. (The Elder Upāli spoke referring to the stone bowls the color of mung beans.) At first, the Four Great Kings offered bowls made of blue gems (sapphire), but the Blessed One did not accept them. Thereafter, when they offered the four stone bowls the color of mung beans, the Blessed One accepted them out of consideration for the devotion of the Four Great Kings, and not because of great desire. Having accepted them, he resolved: 'Let them become one by my determination,' and the four bowls became a single bowl. It also resulted in equal merit for all Four Great Kings. In this way, with the precious stone bowl that had been resolved into one, the Blessed One received the parched grain and honey balls. 'Paccagghe' means...
242:
(The thought) arose. Knowing the thought that had thus arisen in the Blessed One's mind with their own minds, (the four Great Kings came) from the four directions. 'Catuddisā' means from the four directions. 'Selamaye patte' refers to the stone bowls having the color of mung beans. The Blessed One accepted only these (stone bowls); it was with reference to these (stone bowls) that (the Elder Upāli) spoke. In fact, the four Great Kings first offered bowls made of sapphire, but the Blessed One did not accept them. Then they offered these four stone bowls the color of mung beans, and the Blessed One accepted all four bowls out of consideration for the faith of the four Great Kings, not out of great desire. Having accepted them, he resolved that the four bowls should become a single bowl; the merit for the four Great Kings was equal. With the stone bowl thus resolved to be one, which was of great value, the Blessed One accepted the coarse cake and the honey ball. 'Paccagghe' means each one was of great value. Alternatively, 'paccagghe' means new, or having appeared at that very moment. Because those merchants had only two words (the Buddha and the Dhamma), they are called 'devācika' (lay followers of the two words). Or it means they attained the status of lay followers through two words. Having declared their status as lay followers in this way, they said to the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, from this day forward, to whom should we pay homage and rise to greet?" Then the Blessed One rubbed his head, and hairs came off into his hand. The Blessed One gave them to the merchants, saying, "Carry these hairs with you." Having received the hair relics, they were as joyful as if sprinkled with the nectar of immortality, and after paying homage to the Blessed One, they departed.

## The Account of the Rājāyatana Tree is finished.

## The Account of the Request by Brahma

Then, at the end of seven days, the Blessed One emerged from that concentration, and having completed all the aforementioned tasks, he went from the foot of the Rājāyatana tree back to the Ajapāla Banyan tree. 'Parivitakko udapādi' means that as soon as he sat at the foot of that banyan tree, this thought of the mind arose, which is the constant practice of all Buddhas. Why does this thought arise for all Buddhas? It is because of reflecting on the greatness, depth, and difficulty of the Dhamma, and because of the desire to teach when requested by a Brahma. For the Buddhas know: "When such a thought is reflected upon, a Brahma will come and request to teach the Dhamma; because of that request, beings will develop respect for the Dhamma, for the world of beings holds the Brahma in high esteem." Thus, for these two reasons, this thought arises.
243:
In that (reflection), "Adhigato kho myāyaṃ" means "I have indeed attained this Dhamma." "Ālayarāmā" means that beings indulge in the five cords of sensual pleasure; therefore, those sensual pleasures are called "ālaya" (attachments). Because they delight in those attachments, they are called "ālayarāmā." Because they are devoted to attachments, they are "ālayaratā." Because they greatly rejoice in attachments, they are "ālayasammuditā." "Yadidṃ" is a particle. Its meaning should be understood with reference to the context as "that which is this," or with reference to dependent origination as "that which is this dependent origination." "Idappaccayatā-paṭiccasamuppādo" means: the causes (such as ignorance) of these effects (such as formations) are called "idappaccaya"; the state of these causes is "idappaccayatā"; and because it is both the state of these causes and the arising of effects depending on causes, it is called "idappaccayatā-paṭiccasamuppādo." "So mamassa kilamatho" means that teaching the Dhamma to those who do not understand would be wearying for me, it would be troublesome for me. "Bhagavantaṃ" means to the Blessed One (Bhagavato). "Anacchariyā" means repeatedly wonderful. "Paṭibhaṃsu" means they became the objects of the knowledge called intuition (paṭibhāna); they reached the state of being reflected upon.

In the word "halaṃ," the letter "ha" is merely a particle; it means "alaṃ" (not suitable/no use). It means "It is not suitable for me now to teach this Dhamma which I have attained with difficulty." "Paṭisotagāmiṃ" means Nibbāna is called "paṭisota" (against the current); it means leading to Nibbāna. "Rāgarattā" refers to those who are infatuated with sensual lust, lust for existence, and lust for views. "Na dakkhanti" means they will not see. "Tamokhandhena āvuṭā" refers to those who are overwhelmed and covered by the mass of ignorance. "Appossukkatāya" means with a state of being unconcerned, with a lack of desire to teach.

"Yatra hi nāma" means in which world. "Bhagavato purato pāturahosi" means that for the purpose of requesting the teaching of the Dhamma, he brought the Mahābrahmās from the ten thousand world systems and appeared before the Blessed One. "Apparajakkhajātikā" refers to those who have little dust of lust, hatred, and delusion in their eye of wisdom. "Bhavissanti dhammassa aññātāro" means there will be those who will penetrate and understand the Dhamma.

"Pāturahosi" means he appeared. "Samalehi cintito" means (the doctrine) thought out by the six teachers who have stains such as lust. "Apāpuretaṃ" means open that (door). "Amatassa dvāraṃ" refers to the Noble Path which is like the door to the Deathless (Nibbāna). "Suṇantu dhammaṃ" means let them hear the Dhamma of the Four Truths understood in due order by the Blessed One, who is free from stains such as lust.

Just as a man with sight standing on a solid mountain peak made of stone might look down upon the people all around, so too, O Blessed One of great wisdom, who has the eye of omniscience that sees all around, please ascend the palace of Dhamma. Being yourself free from sorrow, look down upon the assembly of beings who are immersed in sorrow and oppressed by birth and old age.
244:
"Vimalenānubuddhaṃ" means: May these beings hear the Four Noble Truths realized in sequence by the Stainless Fully Enlightened One, who is pure due to the absence of stains such as passion (rāga).

"Sele yathā pabbatamuddhaniṭṭhito" means: Just as a man with sight standing on a solid rocky mountain peak would see the people all around, so too, O Wise One, O All-Seeing One who sees all around with the eye of omniscience, ascend the palace of Dhamma made of wisdom. Being yourself free from sorrow, look upon and contemplate the people immersed in sorrow, overcome by birth and old age.

"Uṭṭhehi" (Arise) is said as a request for the Blessed One to wander on a journey for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma. Among the words such as "Vīra" (Hero), the Blessed One is called Vīra because he possesses effort. He is called Vijitasaṅgāma (Victorious in Battle) because he has conquered Devaputta Māra, Maccu Māra, Kilesa Māra, and Abhisaṅkhāra Māra. He is called Satthavāha (Caravan Leader) because he is able to cross the wilderness of birth (jāti), etc. He is called Aṇaṇa (Debtless) because of the absence of the debt of sensual desire (kāmacchanda).

"Ajjhesana" means a request. "Buddhacakkhu" (Buddha-eye) refers to the knowledge of the degrees of the faculties of beings (indriyaparopariyattañāṇa) and the knowledge of their inclinations and latent tendencies (āsayānusayañāṇa). These two kinds of knowledge are called the Buddha-eye. Those beings with little dust such as passion in their eye of wisdom are called Apparajakkha. Those with much dust are called Mahārajakkha. Those whose faculties such as faith are keen are called Tikkhindriya. Those whose faculties are dull are called Mudindriya. Those with good dispositions in faith, etc., are called Svākāra. Those with bad dispositions are called Dvākāra. Those who can note the matters taught and can be easily made to understand are called Suviññāpaya. Those who are accustomed to seeing danger in the next world and in faults are called Paralokavajjabhayadassāvī.

"Uppaliniya" means in a pond of blue lotuses. In the remaining words, it should be understood in the same way. "Antonimuggaposīni" refers to lotuses that grow while remaining submerged within the water. "Samodakaṃ ṭhitāni" refers to lotuses that stand level with the water. "Udakaṃ accuggamma ṭhitāni" refers to lotuses that stand having risen above the water.

"Apārutā" means they are opened. "Amatassa dvārā" (Doors to the Deathless) refers to the Noble Path (Ariya Magga). That Noble Path is the door to Nibbāna, which is called the Deathless. "Pamuñcantu saddhaṃ" means let all beings release their faith. In the last two words, this is the meaning: "I, though having well-practiced and well-mastered..."
245:
"I, though having well-practiced and well-mastered [the Dhamma], did not wish to teach this sublime and supreme Four Noble Truths to gods and humans, perceiving it as wearisome for my body and speech."

## The Discussion on the Request of Brahma is finished.

## The Discussion on the Group of Five Monks

"Paṇḍito" means one who is endowed with wisdom. "Byatto" means one who is endowed with skill and proficiency. "Medhāvī" means one who is endowed with sagacity (wisdom arising according to the situation). "Apparajakkhajātiko" means a pure being of a nature without defilements, as the defilements have been removed by meditative attainment (samāpatti). "Ājānissati" means he will be able to note and penetrate [the Dhamma]. To the Blessed One also, the omniscient knowledge arose: "The ascetic Āḷāra died on the seventh day from today and was reborn in the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana)." "Mahājāniyo" means one who has a great loss, both because of falling away from the Path and Fruit that could have been attained within seven days, and because of being reborn in the sphere of nothingness, which is not an opportune time [for practice]. "Abhidosakālaṅkato" means having died yesterday. He saw that the ascetic Uddaka also had been reborn in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana). "Bahūkārā" means they are of great help. "Padhānapahitattaṃ upaṭṭhahiṃsū" means they served me, who was dedicated to striving, by providing water for washing the face and so forth.

Upaka saw the Blessed One between the Bodhi seat and Gayā. "Addhānamaggappaṭipannaṃ" refers to one who has set out on a long journey.

"Sabbābhibhū" means one who stands having overcome all things belonging to the three realms. "Sabbavidူ" means one who knows all things belonging to the four realms. "Sabbesu dhammesu anūpalitto" means one who is not smeared by defilements in all things belonging to the three realms. "Sabbañjaho" means one who stands having abandoned all things belonging to the three realms. "Taṇhakkhaye vimutto" means one who is liberated by taking Nibbāna, the destruction of craving, as the object. "Sayaṃ abhiññāyā" means having known all things belonging to the four realms by oneself. "Kamuddiseyyaṃ" means "Whom should I point out, saying 'This is my teacher'?"

"Na me ācariyo atthi" means "I have no teacher in the supramundane Dhamma." "Natthi me paṭipuggalo" means "I have no person who is my equal." "Sītibhūto" means one who has reached coolness by extinguishing all fires of defilements. He is "Nibbuto" (Peaceful/Extinguished) because the defilements have been extinguished.
246:
"Kāsīnaṃ puraṃ" refers to the city in the Kāsī kingdom (the city of Vārāṇasī). "I shall beat the drum of the Deathless" means he set out with the intention: "I shall beat the great drum of the Deathless Dhamma in order to cause the attainment of the Wheel of Dhamma."

"Worthy of being an Anantajina" means he is fit to be a Buddha who has infinite victories. "It may be so, friend" means "Friend, it could indeed be such a name." "Nodding the head" means moving or nodding the head.

12. "Saṇṭhapesun" means they made a pact. "Bāhullika" refers to one who practices for the sake of an abundance of robes and so forth. "Padhānavibbhanta" refers to one who has fallen away or declined from the exertion of meditation. "Āvatto bāhullāya" refers to one who has turned back to the abundance of robes and so forth. "O monks, lend your ears" means "O monks, apply your ears; direct the faculty of hearing (sotindriya) for the purpose of listening to the Dhamma." "I have attained the Deathless" shows that "I have attained the Deathless Nibbāna." "Iriyāya" means by means of a difficult posture. "Paṭipadāya" means by means of a difficult practice. "Do you recognize me?" is a question asking, "Have you known me before? Have you seen me before?" "Have I ever spoken such words?" means "Have I ever spoken words of such a nature?" That the Blessed One was able to convince the group of five monks means he was able to make them understand, "I have become a Buddha."

13. The words "Cakkhukaraṇī" (making the eye) are spoken with reference to the eye of wisdom (paññā-cakkhu). After this (Cakkhukaraṇī), all the words are quite clear in terms of their literal meaning. However, regarding the distinctions of intention (adhippāya), sequence (anusandhi), grammatical connection (yojanā), and so forth, they should be understood according to the method stated in the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary named Papañcasūdanī. This is because, from here on, out of concern for the minds of the many who might fear excessive detail, I shall explain only the Vinaya matters without explaining the Suttanta matters.

10. "That venerable one's state of being a monk occurred" means that for the Venerable Koṇḍañña, who was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) along with 180 million deities and Brahmās on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, that very "Ehi Bhikkhu" ordination was accomplished by the Blessed One's words, "Come, monk."

19. In the words "Then to the Venerable Vappa also," and so forth, the eye of Dhamma (dhamma-cakkhu) arose for the Elder Vappa on the first day of the fortnight, for the Elder Bhaddiya on the second day, for the Elder Mahānāma on the third day, and for the Elder Assaji on the fourth day. Of these monks...
247:
Furthermore, the Blessed One stayed only inside the monastery for the purpose of cleansing the impurities that arose in the monks' meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna). Whenever an impurity arose in a meditation subject, he would travel through the air and dispel that impurity. On the fifth day of the fortnight of Āsāḷha, he gathered all those monks together and exhorted them with the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta. Therefore, the words "Then the Blessed One addressed the group of five," and so forth, were spoken.

"At that time, there were six Arahants in the world" means that on the fifth day of the fortnight of Āsāḷha, there were six human Arahants in the world of beings.

## The Discussion on the Group of Five is finished.

## Discussion on Ordination

"Pubbānupubbaka" means those who existed in the past in successive order. "At that time, there were sixty-one Arahants in the world" means that when the first six and these fifty-five are combined, there were sixty-one human Arahants during the very period of the rainy season retreat (vassa).

Among those Arahants, this is the past connection (pubbayoga) of the young men of good family such as Yasa: It is said that in the past, fifty-five friends, forming a group, performed meritorious deeds and went about disposing of unclaimed corpses. One day, seeing a pregnant woman who had died, they took her to the cemetery, saying, "We shall cremate her." Among them, they left five men at the cemetery, saying, "You cremate her," and the rest entered the village. While the youth Yasa was cremating that body by piercing it with a stake and turning it over, he gained the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā). He showed it to the other four men, saying, "Look, sirs, at this impure and loathsome corpse." They too gained the perception of foulness there. Those five men then went to the village and told the remaining friends. The youth Yasa, however, went home and told his parents and his wife. They all developed the meditation on foulness. This was their past connection. Because of that, for the Venerable Yasa, only the perception of a cemetery arose regarding the troupe of dancers; and through that very perfection of the supporting condition (upanissaya-sampatti), the attainment of the distinction (the Dhamma) arose for all of them.

"Then the Blessed One addressed the monks" means that the Blessed One, while residing in Vārāṇasī until the final full moon of Kattika, one day addressed those sixty monks who had destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava) and spoke to them.
248:
"Dibba" refers to the snares of greed that arise in the divine spheres. "Mānusa" refers to the snares of greed that arise in the human spheres. "Mā ekena dve" means do not travel two together on a single path. "Assavanatā" is due to not hearing the Dhamma. "Parihāyantī" means they decline from the attainment of distinction because they do not attain the special Dhamma of the Paths and Fruits which they have not yet attained.

"Antakā" refers to lowly and inferior beings. The phrase "antalikkhasaro" was spoken with reference to the snare of lust (rāgapāsa). For that Māra, thinking of that snare of lust as a "snare that moves in the sky," spoke thus.

"Nānādisā nānājanapadā" means from various directions and various regions. In the passage beginning with, "Monks, you yourselves now ordain [them] in those various directions and in those various regions," the monk who ordains a noble son desiring ordination must exclude those persons prohibited by the passages starting from, "Monks, one afflicted with the five diseases should not be ordained," up to, "The blind, the mute, and the deaf should not be ordained." Only a person free from the faults regarding ordination should be ordained. Furthermore, that person must be one who has been permitted by his parents. The characteristic of such permission will be explained in the Sutta: "Monks, a son who is not permitted by his parents should not be ordained; for him who ordains [such a one], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."

When ordaining such a person who is free from faults regarding ordination and has been permitted by his parents, if he has not yet had his hair shaved and there are other monks within the same boundary (sīmā), permission must be requested for the shaving (bhaṇḍukamma). The manner of requesting that permission will be explained in the passage: "Monks, I allow you to ask the Saṅgha for permission for the shaving (bhaṇḍukamma)." If the opportunity is available, one should ordain him oneself. If one is busy with teaching, questioning, and so forth, and does not get the opportunity, a junior monk should be told, "Ordain this person." Even if not told, if a junior monk ordains him on behalf of the preceptor (upajjhāya), it is valid. If there is no junior monk, even a novice (sāmaṇera) should be told, "Take this person to the small boundary (khaṇḍasīmā), ordain him, clothe him in saffron robes, and return." However, the Refuges (saraṇagamana) must be given by oneself. Only in this way is he considered ordained by a monk. This is because no one other than a monk is allowed to ordain a man, and no one other than a bhikkhunī is allowed to ordain a woman. A novice (sāmaṇera) or a female novice (sāmaṇerī) is only allowed to give the robes by order. As for the shaving of the hair, it is well done regardless of who performs it.
249:
However, if the candidate is a noble son who is capable [of attainment], endowed with the necessary causes, well-known, and famous, one should make the opportunity and ordain him personally. He should not be sent away with the words, "Take a handful of clay, bathe, wet your hair, and come back." For those desiring ordination, there is strong enthusiasm at first, but later, upon seeing the saffron robes and the razor for shaving the hair, they become terrified and flee from that very place. Therefore, one should personally take him to the bathing place and, if he is not too young, tell him, "Bathe." His hair should be washed by oneself, taking the clay. If he is a young boy, one should personally enter the water and bathe him by rubbing him with cow dung and clay. Even if he has scabies or boils, just as a mother is not repulsed by her son, one should bathe him without repulsion, thoroughly rubbing his hands, feet, and head. Why? Because through such assistance, noble sons develop strong affection and deep respect for their teachers and preceptors and for the Sasana, and they become those who do not turn back. They dispel any dissatisfaction (anabhirati) that arises, reach the status of an Elder (thera), and become grateful and appreciative.

At the time of bathing or at the time of shaving the hair and beard, one should not say, "You are well-known and famous; now we shall not struggle for the requisites by relying on you." Nor should any other talk that does not lead out [of suffering] (aniyyānika-kathā) be spoken. Instead, one should say to him, "Friend, reflect well, establish mindfulness," and teach him the meditation on the five parts ending in skin (tacapañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna). When teaching it, one should teach by making clear its nature as impure, loathsome, and repulsive, or its nature as non-soul and non-being, by way of color, shape, smell, location, and space. If that person is one who has processed the formations (saṅkhāra) with insight and has developed meditation under previous Buddhas, like a ripe boil awaiting the prick of a needle, or like a mature lotus awaiting the rising of the sun, then while merely applying his mind to the meditation subject, his knowledge proceeds, crushing the mountain of defilements like a thunderbolt hitting a mountain, and he reaches Arahantship at the very tip of the razor (khuragga). All those who reached Arahantship at the tip of the razor did so by obtaining such a hearing and by relying on the method given by a teacher who is a noble friend (kalyāṇamitta), and not without such reliance. Therefore, such talk should be spoken to him from the very beginning.

After the hair has been shaved, having rubbed the head and body with turmeric powder or scented powder to remove the lay scent, [one gives] the saffron robes three times or...
250:
It should be accepted twice or once. Furthermore, if the teacher or the preceptor dresses him personally without giving the robes into his hands, it is allowable. If he commands another young monk, a novice, or a lay devotee, saying, "Friend, take these saffron robes and dress this person," or if he commands that person himself, saying, "Take these and dress yourself," it is all allowable. All the robes are considered as being given by that monk.

If he wears the inner robe or the outer robe without being commanded, those robes should be removed and given again. For a monk, only the saffron robes given by his own hand or by command are allowable; wearing them without being given is not allowable. Even if the robes belong to that person himself, it is still not allowable; what more need be said regarding robes originating from the preceptor! This is the decision regarding the passage: "Having first had the hair and beard shaved, having had him clothed in saffron robes, and having had him arrange his upper robe over one shoulder."

Regarding the phrase "having him pay homage to the feet of the monks," it means having him pay homage to the feet of the monks who have assembled there. After having him pay homage, he should be told to sit in a squatting position for the purpose of taking the refuges, and having him raise his joined palms in salutation, he should be told, "Say this." He should be told, "Say exactly what I say." Then, the preceptor or the teacher should administer the refuges to him in the manner beginning with "Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi," following the prescribed order and not out of order. If he gives them out of order by even a single word or a single syllable, or if he gives "Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ" three times and then gives the other refuges three times each, the refuges are considered not given.

Having set aside this ordination by taking the refuges, the ordination permitted [later] is allowable by the purity of one side [the teacher]. However, the novice ordination (pabbajjā) is allowable only by the purity of both sides, not by the purity of one side. Therefore, in the higher ordination (upasampadā), if the teacher performs the act avoiding defects in the motion (ñatti) and defects in the ritual procedure (kammavācā), it is considered well-performed. In the novice ordination, however, these three refuges must be recited by both the teacher and the pupil without failing in the perfection of the phonetical articulation (ṭhāna-karaṇa) of the consonants such as the letters 'bu' and 'dha'. If the teacher can recite but the pupil cannot, or if the pupil can recite but the teacher cannot, or if both cannot, it is not allowable. If both can recite, it is allowable.
251:
The teacher giving these refuges should give them either by connecting them as one, such as "Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi," ending with the nasal sound (niggahīta), or by separating them, such as "Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi," ending with the letter 'm'. In the Andhaka Commentary, it is said that after announcing the name, one should say, "Venerable Sir, I, Buddharakkhita, go to the Buddha as my refuge for as long as life lasts." That statement is not found in any other commentary, nor is it spoken in the Pāli Canon. Since it is merely the preference of the teachers of the Andhaka Commentary, it should not be accepted. Indeed, it should be noted that the refuges of one who does not speak in that way are not broken.

"Monks, I allow the going forth (pabbajjā) and the higher ordination (upasampadā) by these three refuges" means that He allows the going forth and the higher ordination by these three refuges recited three times with the purity of both sides in the manner beginning with "Buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi." Among those two, since the higher ordination (upasampadā) was later prohibited [by this method], it is no longer attained by the mere refuges at present. As for the going forth (pabbajjā), since it was later permitted by the words, "Monks, I allow the novice ordination (sāmaṇera-pabbajjā) by these three refuges," it is still attained by the mere refuges even now. By this much, one is established in the stage of a novice.

If this novice is of an intelligent nature and wise, then the training rules (sikkhāpada) should be pointed out to him in that very place. How should they be pointed out? They should be pointed out just as the Blessed One pointed them out. For this was said:

"Monks, I allow ten training rules for novices, and for the novices to train in them: Abstaining from taking life; abstaining from taking what is not given; abstaining from unchastity; abstaining from false speech; abstaining from wines, liquors, and intoxicants which are the cause of negligence; abstaining from eating at the wrong time; abstaining from dancing, singing, music, and watching shows which are like thorns [to the Dispensation]; abstaining from wearing garlands, perfumes, and cosmetics, and from finery and adornments; abstaining from high and large beds; and abstaining from accepting gold and silver."

## In the Andhaka Commentary, however, it is said that the training rules should be given just like the giving of the refuges, saying, "Venerable Sir, I, named so-and-so, undertake the training rule of abstaining from taking life for as long as life lasts."

That statement is neither in the Pāli Canon nor in the commentaries. Therefore, they should be pointed out only according to the Pāli Canon. Indeed, the novicehood is accomplished by the refuges alone. As for the training rules, they are merely...
252:
One should know [these things] for the purpose of fulfilling the training rules. Therefore, for a novice (sāmaṇera) who is unable to learn those training rules according to the method found in the Pali texts, it is permissible to explain them by means of the meaning in any language. As long as he does not yet know the training rules he must practice, and as long as he is not yet skillful in the procedures such as carrying the double robe (saṅghāṭi), the bowl, and the robes, or in standing and sitting, etc., and in the methods of drinking and eating, etc., he should not be sent to the dining hall, the place for distributing food-tickets (salākabhājanatthāna), or any other such place. He should be kept only in one's own presence and should be looked after like an unskilled child. All that is allowable and unallowable (kappiya and akappiya) should be explained to that novice, and he should be disciplined in the minor rules of conduct (abhisamācārika) such as dressing and robing. That novice, too, must carefully practice the ten precepts while fulfilling the minor rules of conduct and keeping far away from the ten grounds for expulsion (nāsananga) which will be mentioned later, thus: "Monks, I allow you to expel a novice endowed with ten factors."

## The Discussion on Going Forth (Pabbajjākathā) is finished.

## The Second Discussion on Māra (Dutiya Mārakathā)

"Mayhaṃ kho bhikkhave" means "by me." Or it means "because of that wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) of mine." Furthermore, in the word "anuppattā," the case ending should be changed and read as "mayā" (by me).

## The Second Discussion on Māra is finished.

## The Discussion on the Bhaddavaggiya Group (Bhaddavaggiyakathā)

Regarding "Bhaddavaggiyā": those princes were excellent (bhadda) both in appearance and in mind, and they wandered as a group (vagga); therefore, they are called "Bhaddavaggiyā." In the phrase "tena hi vo," the word "vo" is a mere particle (nipāta). "The eye of Dhamma (dhammacakkhu) arose" means that for some, the path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga) arose, for some the path of Once-returning (sakadāgāmimagga), and for some the path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga). All these three paths are called the "eye of Dhamma." It is said that in the Tuṇḍila Jātaka, they were thirty drunkards (dhutta); at that time, having heard the advice of the Great Pig Tuṇḍila, they kept the five precepts. This was their previous wholesome deed.

## The Discussion on the Bhaddavaggiya Group is finished.

## The Discussion on the Uruvela Miracles (Uruvelapāṭihāriyakathā)

"Pamukho" means the leader. "Pāmokkho" means the noble one who possesses pure wisdom.
253:
"Anupahacca" means without destroying. "Tejasā tejaṃ" means [subduing] the power of the dragon (nāga) with one's own power. "Pariyādiyeyyaṃ" means "if I were to overcome" or "if I were to destroy." "Makkha" refers to anger (kodha). An Arahant does not speak by thinking of himself as "I am an Arahant," in the way that I [the Buddha] do.

The verses beginning with "Nerañjarāyaṃ Bhagavā" were inserted later [by the elders who conducted the Council].

44-9. "Vissajjeyyaṃ" means that one would spread out [the robes] to dry. The tree is called "āharahattho" because it bent down as if saying, "Venerable Sir, take my hand." "Uyyojetvā" means having released. "Mandāmukhiyo" refers to fire-pots.

"Cirapaṭikā" means starting from a long time ago [from the time the dragon king was subdued].

In the words such as "kesamissaṃ," the hair itself is called "kesamissaṃ." This method is the same in all places. "Khārikājaṃ" is the shoulder-yoke (burden) on which the requisites of the ascetics are carried.

## The Discussion on the Uruvela Miracles is finished.

## The Discussion on the Meeting with King Bimbisāra

"Laṭṭhivane" means in the Palm Grove. "Suppatiṭṭha cetiye" means at a certain banyan tree, and it is said that this is the name of that tree. In the phrase "dvādasanahutehi," one "nahuta" is ten thousand. "Ajjhabhāsi" means he spoke in order to cut off their doubts.

"Kisakovādāno" means he was the teacher and instructor of the ascetics who were named "Kisaka" (the Lean) because their bodies were emaciated due to ascetic practices. Alternatively, it means that he himself, being an emaciated ascetic, was one who advised and instructed others. "Kathaṃ pahīnaṃ" is a question asking for what reason it was abandoned. The meaning of this statement is: "You, Kassapa, who were yourself the teaching master of the fire-worshipping ascetics living in Uruvela, what did you see that you abandoned the fire-sacrifice? I ask you this matter: for what reason has your fire-offering been abandoned?"

In the second verse, the meaning is: Sacrifices (yañña) praise these sensual pleasures such as forms, etc., and women. I, having known all these varieties of sensual pleasures such as forms, etc., as a stain (mala) in the aggregates (khandha) which are the basis of suffering (upadhi), and because these sacrifices consisting of offerings and oblations only indicate a stain, therefore, I no longer delight in the sacrifice (yiṭṭha) or in the oblation (huta).
254:
"Kisakovadāno" refers to the teacher who admonishes those known as "Kisaka" because they have lean bodies due to the practices of ascetics. Alternatively, it means one who is himself a lean ascetic due to his practices and also admonishes other ascetics. "Kathaṃ pahīnaṃ" is a question asking for what reason it was abandoned. The meaning of the sentence is: "Kassapa, who dwells in Uruvelā, you were a teacher of fire-worshipping ascetics; having seen what did you abandon fire sacrifice? I ask for what reason your fire sacrifice was abandoned." The meaning of the second verse is: Sacrifices (yaññā) are what people call the enjoyment of sensual pleasures such as visual forms, and women. I, seeing all these varieties of sensual pleasures as impurities (mala) in the aggregates (khandhas) which are the basis of suffering, no longer delight in those sacrifices, because great sacrifices and daily fire sacrifices only mean impurity. In the third verse, "Atha koca rahīti" means "Atha kva carahi" (If you do not delight in that, then where do you go?). The remaining words have clear meanings. In the fourth verse, "Padaṃ" refers to Nibbāna. It is called "Santa" (peaceful) because of its peaceful nature. It is called "Anupadhika" (without substrates) because of the absence of the substrates of sensuality, the aggregates, the defilements, and volitional formations. It is called "Akiñcana" (possessionless) because of the absence of anxieties such as lust. Because of not being attached to the three realms of existence, he is not attached even to that realm of sensual existence which is spoken of by sacrifices. It is called "Ananyathābhāvī" (unchanging) because of the absence of birth, aging, and death, not becoming otherwise. It is called "Ananyaneyya" (not to be led by another) because it is to be realized only through the Path one has developed oneself, and not through any other means. "Because I saw such a state (Nibbāna), I no longer delight in great sacrifices (yiṭṭha) or daily fire sacrifices (huta)." What is shown by these words? It means to show: "If I do not delight even in sacrifices that accomplish the prosperity of the worlds of devas and humans, how could I say that my mind delights in this world of devas and humans?"

After thus making clear his lack of delight in the whole world, the Venerable Uruvela Kassapa declared his status as a disciple of the Blessed One, saying, "I am a disciple." In declaring his discipleship, he displayed various miracles in the sky to make it clear. "Dhamma-cakkhu" (the Eye of Dhamma) refers to the knowledge of the Path of Stream-entry. "Assāsakā" means aspiration or prayer (patthanā). In the phrase "Eso'haṃ bhante," although the attainment of the refuges is accomplished by the penetration of the Path, he now performs the verbal act of self-dedication. Having reached the state of fixed refuge by the power of the Path, he speaks thus to make it clear to others through speech and to show great reverence. "Siṅgīnikkhasavaṇṇa" means having a complexion like a nugget of pure Siṅgī gold. "Dasavāsa" means one who has lived in the ten noble dwellings (ariya-vāsa). "Dasadhammavidū" means one who knows the ten courses of action (kamma-patha). "Dasabhi cupeto" means endowed with the ten qualities of an adept (asekha). "Sabbadhidanto" means tamed in all respects; for the Blessed One, there is nothing untamed in the faculties such as the eye. Having noted that the Blessed One had finished his meal and removed his hand from the bowl, he sat to one side. This meaning is very clear.
255:
"Sat" (Nisīdi) is the meaning. "Atthikānaṃ" refers to those who desire to go to see the Blessed One and to hear the Dhamma. "Abhikkamanīyaṃ" means worthy of approaching. "Appākiṇṇaṃ" means not crowded with people. "Appasaddaṃ" means quiet, with few voices of speech. "Appanigghosaṃ" means having little noise from the shouting of city-dwellers. "Vijanavātaṃ" means a place free from the bodily heat and breath of wandering people. There is also a variant reading "Vijanavādaṃ," meaning free from the sound of people's talk within. There is also a variant reading "Vijanapātaṃ," meaning free from the movement of people. "Manussarāhaseyyakaṃ" means a place suitable for the private acts of humans. "Paṭisallānasāruppaṃ" means a place suitable for solitary retreat.

## The Discussion on the Meeting with King Bimbisāra is Finished.

## The Discussion on the Going Forth of Sāriputta and Moggallāna

Sāriputta and Moggallāna refers to Sāriputta and Moggallāna. They had made an agreement: "Whoever first attains the Deathless (Amata), let him inform the other." It is said that when they were laymen, known by the names Upatissa and Kolita, they went to the mountain-top festival (Giraggasamajja) with a retinue of two hundred and fifty youths. Seeing the great crowd of people there, the thought occurred to them: "This great assembly of beings, before a hundred years have passed, will fall into the jaws of death." Then, when the assembly had departed, they questioned each other and, having the same desire and the perception of death having arisen, they consulted together: "Friend, since there is death, there must also be a state free from death. Come, let us seek the Deathless." To seek the Deathless, they went forth in the presence of the wanderer named Sañjaya with their retinue. Within a few days, they reached the limit of that teacher's knowledge, but not seeing the Deathless, they asked: "Teacher, is there any other essence in this doctrine?" Hearing the reply, "Friends, there is only this much; there is no other essence," they thought, "Friend, this is empty and without essence. Now, whoever among us first attains the Deathless, let him inform the other." Thus they made an agreement. Therefore, it was said, "They made an agreement," and so on.

In the phrases such as "Pāsādikena abhikkantena," the instrumental case should be understood in the sense of marking a characteristic. The phrase "Atthikehi upaññātaṃ maggaṃ" (the path recognized by those in need) is the statement of the reason for following. This is what is meant: "What if I were to follow this monk closely from behind..."
256:
Why? Because this so-called following behind is the path (magga) closely known by us who desire the deathless (amata). It means the path that is both known and reached. Alternatively, it should be understood here that there is Nibbāna, which is known by us who desire the deathless through inference, thinking, "If there is death, there must also be the deathless," and it is for the sake of realizing that Nibbāna while searching for it.

"Taking the alms-food, he withdrew" means that he approached the foot of a certain wall and sat down, as described in the Sudinna-kaṇḍa. Sāriputta also stood to one side, waiting for the right time, thinking, "It is not yet the time to ask a question." Then, in order to fulfill the duties, he gave water from his own water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) to the Elder who had finished his meal. After the Elder had washed his hands and feet, Sāriputta engaged in pleasant conversation with him and then asked the question. Therefore, it was said (by the Elder Upāli), "Then the wanderer Sāriputta..." and so on. "I am not able" means "I am not able to preach to you [at length]." Here, it is not that the Elder, who had attained the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), was unable to preach this much Dhamma in detail; he was indeed able. However, thinking, "I will inspire respect for the Dhamma in this wanderer," he spoke thus, taking the position that it was not his domain but entirely the domain of the Buddha (buddhavisaya).

"Those things which proceed from a cause" refers to the five aggregates which arise depending on a cause; by this, he showed the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca) to that wanderer. "Their cause the Tathāgata has told" means he showed that the Tathāgata has preached the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca), which is the cause of those things. "And also their cessation" means the Tathāgata has also preached the cessation of both those truths through non-occurrence (nirodha-sacca). By this, he showed the Truth of Cessation to that wanderer. Although the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca) is not shown here in its own form, it is shown by way of implication; for when cessation is mentioned, the path that leads to that cessation is also mentioned. Alternatively, in the phrase "and also their cessation," both truths—the Truth of Cessation and the Truth of the Path, which is the means to cessation—are shown. Now, wishing to conclude the meaning of these Four Noble Truths, he said, "The Great Ascetic is of such a doctrine."

"This itself is the Dhamma, even if it were only this much" means that even if there were no higher Dhamma than this fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) attained by me, and even if only this much fruit of Stream-entry were to be reached, this fruit of Stream-entry itself is indeed the Dhamma I have been searching for. "The sorrowless state (asoka) has been realized" means that the sorrowless Nibbāna, which we have been wandering in search of, has been penetrated and realized by you; it has been reached by you. "Unseen, it has passed by for many hundreds of thousands of aeons (nahuta)" means that we have passed by this Nibbāna for many hundreds of thousands of aeons without seeing it. By this statement, he showed his great loss over a long period of time due to not seeing that Nibbāna.
257:
By the phrase, "Unseen, it has passed by for many hundreds of thousands of aeons (nahuta)," he showed his great loss over a long period of time due to the fact that that state (Nibbāna) was unseen.

"In the profound domain of knowledge" (gambhīre ñāṇavisaye) means in that which is both profound and the object of profound knowledge (Nibbāna). "In the unsurpassed end of acquisitions" (anuttare upadhisaṅkhaye) means in Nibbāna, where there is no Dhamma more excellent than itself and where the four kinds of acquisitions (upadhi) end. "Liberated" (vimutte) means liberated from defilements by the liberation of the fruit of Stream-entry which has that Nibbāna as its object. "He declared" (vyākāsī) means that while saying, "These two will be my pair of disciples, the chief and excellent pair," he made the declaration regarding the knowledge of the perfection of a disciple (sāvakapāramī-ñāṇa). For those venerable ones, that very 'Come, Bhikkhu' (ehibhikkhu) ordination became their higher ordination (upasampadā). Among those who had thus reached the state of a monk, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna was established in Arahantship in seven days, and the Elder Sāriputta was established in Arahantship in half a month (fifteen days).

In the past, it is said, a Buddha named Anomadassī appeared in the world. In the presence of that Buddha, an ascetic named Sarada built a pavilion with various flowers in his own hermitage. Having invited the Blessed One to sit on a seat of flowers, and having likewise built a pavilion and prepared flower-seats for the Saṅgha of monks, he made a wish for the station of a Chief Disciple. After making the wish, he sent word to a merchant named Siriwaḍḍha, saying, "I have made a wish for the station of a Chief Disciple; you also come and make a wish for a certain station." The merchant then built a pavilion covered with blue lotuses and, having fed the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha in that pavilion, he made a wish for the station of the Second Disciple. Among them, the ascetic Sarada became the Elder Sāriputta, and Siriwaḍḍha became the Elder Mahāmoggallāna. This was their past deed (pubbakamma).

In the words beginning with "aputtakatāya" (childlessness): they were envious because the sons of certain families went forth, resulting in the childlessness of those families; because the husbands of certain women went forth, resulting in their widowhood; and because of the termination of the lineage by both these means. "Sañcayānī" means the disciples of Sañcaya. "Giribbaja of the Magadhans" means the city of Giribbaja (Rājagaha) in the country of Magadha. "Great Heroes" (mahāvīrā) means those possessing great energy. "Of those who are leading away" (nayamānānaṃ) refers to those who are leading [disciples]. "What envy is there for those who know?" means what envy can there be for those who know thus: "They are leading away according to the Dhamma"?

## The Account of the Going Forth of Sāriputta and Moggallāna is finished.

## Discussion on the Duties towards the Preceptor (Upajjhāyavatta-kathā)

64-5. "Those without preceptors" (anupajjhāyakā) means those who are devoid of a teacher (guru) who closely observes faults and non-faults. "Those not endowed with proper conduct" (anākappasampannā) means those who are not endowed with proper behavior, being devoid of the conduct suitable for recluses.
258:
The meaning is: 'Upari-bhojane' means above the food. 'Uttiṭṭha-patta' refers to the bowl used for wandering for alms. Because people tend to perceive it as containing leftovers (ucchiṭṭha), it is called 'uttiṭṭha-patta'. Alternatively, it is so called because people stand up (uṭṭhahitvā) to offer the bowl; this is also how the meaning should be understood. 'I allow you, monks, to take a preceptor' means the permission to take an Upajjhāya. 'He will establish the mind of a son' means he should maintain the thought, 'This is my son,' through the power of household-based affection (gehassita-pema). The same method applies to the second term. 'With respect and deference' (sagāravā sappatissā) means practicing with the sense of the preceptor's gravity and seniority. 'Of similar livelihood' (sabhāgavuttino) means having a shared way of living. The five words beginning with 'Sāhu' (It is well) are synonyms for accepting the status of a preceptor. When the co-resident (saddhivihārika) says three times, 'Venerable, please be my preceptor,' and the preceptor signifies the acceptance of the preceptor-role through any of those five words—by body, by speech, or by both body and speech—saying 'The preceptor is taken by you,' then the preceptor is taken. Indeed, the taking of a preceptor here means the preceptor's vocalizing of any of these five words or making the meaning known through the body. Some teachers say this refers to the acceptance using the word 'Sādhu'. That statement is not authoritative. This is because the taking of a preceptor is accomplished merely by the request and the granting; here, the formal acceptance is not an essential factor. The co-resident should not merely know, 'I have taken the preceptor with this word.' He should also know this: 'From this day forward, the Elder is my responsibility, and I am the Elder's responsibility.'

'In that, this is the proper conduct' means: in the statement 'one should practice properly,' this duty is the proper conduct. 'Rising early, he should remove his sandals' means: if sandals are worn for walking on the cloister or for moving about after washing the feet at dawn, he should rise early and remove those sandals. 'Tooth-wood should be given' means: after offering three types of tooth-wood—large, medium, and small—whichever type the preceptor takes for three consecutive days, that same type should be given from the fourth day onwards. If he takes whatever is available without a fixed preference, then whatever tooth-wood is obtained should be given.

'Face-washing water should be given' means: after offering both cold and hot water, whichever water he uses for three days, that same type of water should be given as face-washing water from the fourth day onwards.
259:
...he gives the face-washing water. If he takes whatever is available without a fixed preference, then whatever water is obtained should be given. If he uses both types, both types should be brought. Having placed the water at the place for washing the face, the area should be swept starting from the toilet (vaccakuṭi). When the Elder goes to the toilet, the courtyard (pariveṇa) should be swept; by sweeping in this way, the courtyard becomes 'not empty' (clean). The seat (āsana) should be prepared even before the Elder comes out of the toilet. When he returns after attending to his bodily needs, the duties mentioned in the method beginning with 'If there is gruel (yāgu)' should be performed. 'Uklāpo' means being cluttered with some kind of rubbish; however, if there is no other rubbish and there are only water drops, they should be wiped away even with the hand.

'Sagunaṃ katvā' means making the two robes into one (layering them); both robes made into one should be given (as the Saṅghāṭi). Because all robes are folded together, they are called 'Saṅghāṭi'. Therefore, it is said, 'The Saṅghāṭi robes should be given.' In the phrase 'He should walk neither too far nor too near,' it should be understood that if the preceptor turns and looks, and the student can reach him in one or two steps, this much distance constitutes walking neither too far nor too near. 'He should receive what is included in the bowl' means if the preceptor, while wandering for alms, receives gruel or food and the bowl is hot or heavy, the student should give his own bowl to the preceptor and take that bowl; this is the meaning. While the preceptor is speaking, one should not interrupt with other talk before he has finished; whether in the village or elsewhere, while he is speaking, one should not start another conversation before his speech is finished. From this point onwards, wherever a prohibition is made with the word 'na' (not), it should be understood as a Dukkaṭa offense. This is the nature of the Khandhakas. 'Speaking words close to an offense' means speaking words that border on an offense through the way of teaching word-by-word (padasodhamma) or coarse speech (duṭṭhullā), etc. 'He should be restrained' means he should be restrained like one asking, 'Venerable, is it proper to say such a thing? Does it not constitute an offense?' He should not be told, 'Old man, do not speak thus,' with the intent of 'I will restrain him.'

'Having arrived earlier' means: if the village is nearby, or if there is a sick monk in the monastery, he should return from the village earlier. If the village is far and there is no one else coming with the preceptor, he should leave the village together with him, wrap the bowl with the robe, and then from the middle of the path, [go] earlier...
260:
One must arrive before (the preceptor). The student (saddhivihārika) returning in this manner must arrive first and perform all duties such as preparing the seat. "Sinnam hoti" means being wet with sweat or soaked with sweat. "Moving the edge by four finger-breadths" means that the robe should be folded by extending the edge by about four finger-breadths.

Why is this? It is to prevent a crease from forming in the middle. A robe folded with edges aligned tends to develop a crease in the middle. If a crease is always formed there, the robe breaks and wears out easily at that spot. This instruction is given to prevent that. Therefore, to avoid breaking again tomorrow at the same place where it was folded today, one should fold it by shifting it about four finger-breadths every day. "The belt should be placed inside the robe" means the belt should be folded and placed within the fold (coil) of the robe.
