Regarding the phrase "If there is alms-food," if a preceptor returns after eating in the village, inside a house, or at a refectory, or if he did not receive any alms-food, it should be said that the preceptor has no alms-food. If the preceptor has not yet eaten in the village or has received alms-food, it should be said that he has alms-food. Therefore, the instruction beginning with "If there is alms-food" was given. Even if the preceptor has no alms-food but wishes to eat, one should offer water and also offer alms-food from what one has received oneself. "One should ask with drinking water" means that one should ask the preceptor who is eating three times, "Venerable Sir, shall I bring drinking water?" If there is still time, one should eat only after the preceptor has finished eating. If the time for noon is approaching, one should place the drinking water near the preceptor and eat oneself.

"Anantarahitāya" means that the alms-bowl should not be placed on the ground mixed with dust and gravel where nothing such as a mat or a piece of leather is spread. However, if the ground is blackened or smoothed with plaster and is free of dust, it is permissible to place the bowl on such ground. It is also permissible to place it on clean sand. It is not proper to place it where there is soil, dust, or gravel. In such places, one should spread a leaf or a bowl-stand and place the bowl on that leaf or bowl-stand. "The edge should be placed on the far side and the fold on one's own side" is said so that one may place it down gently with the hand facing oneself, having inserted the hand under the robe-rail or similar object. If one holds the robe by the edge and places the fold over the robe-rail, the fold may hit the wall. Therefore, one should not do that.

"The powder should be kneaded" means that the bathing powder should be sprinkled with water and made into a ball. "It should be placed on one side" means it should be placed in a suitable spot where there is no smoke. Service (parikamma) in the sweat-house (jantāghara) refers to all duties such as providing charcoal, fine clay, and hot water. Service in water (udakaparikamma) refers to all duties such as massaging the limbs. Because thirst often occurs in the sweat-house due to the heat, one should ask with drinking water.

"If he is capable" means if he is healthy and not oppressed by any illness. Indeed, a healthy student (saddhivihārika), even if he has sixty years of seniority (vassa), must personally perform the major and minor duties for the preceptor. A student who does not perform the duties out of disrespect commits an offense of wrongdoing (dukkhaṭa) for the breach of duty. Furthermore, regarding the words connected with the negative particle "na" (prohibitions)...
261:
Service (parikamma) in the sweat-house or fire-room means all tasks such as providing charcoal, fine clay, and hot water. Service in water (udakaparikamma) also means all tasks such as massaging the limbs. It is said, "One should ask with drinking water," because thirst often occurs in the sweat-house due to the intense heat.

"If he is capable" means if he is able and not overcome by any illness. A healthy student (saddhivihārika), even if he has sixty years of seniority (vassa), must personally perform all duties for the preceptor. If he does not perform them out of disrespect, he commits an offense of wrongdoing (dukkhaṭa) for the breach of duty. However, regarding the terms associated with the negative particle "na" (prohibitions), even if one is ill, if one performs a prohibited action, it is still an offense of wrongdoing. "Without scratching" means without scratching the ground. "The door-leaf and the door-frame" means without hitting the door-leaf and the door-frame. "Impurity (santānaka)" refers to anything such as insect nests or cobwebs. "First bring down from the ceiling" means that one should start from the ceiling and bring it down from top to bottom. "The windows and corner parts" means that the parts of the windows, the corner parts, the small window shutters inside and outside, and the four corners of the room should be wiped and cleaned.

"It should be spread as it was spread" means it should be spread exactly as it was originally spread. It is for the purpose of being able to spread it as it was that the previous duty was laid down: "One should note how it was spread, remove it, and place it on one side." However, if it was spread by someone who did not know the proper way, it should be spread by keeping it about two or three finger-breadths away from the wall all around. This is the duty regarding spreading. If the mat is very large, one should cut it, fold the edge, tie it, and then spread it. If one does not know how to fold and tie the edge, it should not be cut. "The eastern windows should be closed" means that the windows in the eastern direction should be closed. Likewise, the remaining windows should also be closed.

"Should be removed" means should be taken to another place. "Should cause to be removed" means telling another monk, "Take the elder and go elsewhere." "Should be abandoned" means causing to give up. "Should cause to be abandoned" means telling another person, "Make the elder give up his wrong view." "Effort should be made" means that one should approach and request various monks for the purpose of granting probation (parivāsa). If one is capable oneself, one should grant it oneself. If one is not capable, one should have another grant it. "In what way?" means by what means or method. This method is the same in all places. Light body...
262:
"Vā pariṇāmeyyā" means that instead of performing the act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma), one should perform the act of censure (tajjaniyākamma) or the act of subordination (niyassakamma). Therefore, if one knows that "the Saṅgha wishes to perform the act of suspension on the preceptor," one should approach each monk individually and plead, "Venerable sirs, please do not perform the legal act on our preceptor." If they still proceed, one should plead, "Please perform only the act of censure or the act of subordination." If they still proceed, one should plead with the preceptor, "Venerable sir, please conduct yourself properly." Having thus caused the preceptor to conduct himself properly, one should plead with the monks, "Venerable sirs, please settle the legal act."

"Samparivattakaṃ samparivattakaṃ" means turning over and over (to let the dye soak in). "Na ca acchinne theve pakkamitabbaṃ" means that if even a small amount of dye is still dripping, one should not yet depart. "Na upajjhāyaṃ anāpucchā ekaccassa patto dātabbo" and so forth—all these are spoken with reference to a person who is incompatible with the preceptor. "Na upajjhāyaṃ anāpucchā gāmo pavisitabbo" means that if one wishes to enter the village for the sake of alms or for any other business, one should enter only after asking permission from the preceptor. If the preceptor rises early and wishes to go for alms to a distant place, he should depart after instructing, "Let the junior monks enter for alms." If he departs without giving instructions, and the pupil goes to the precinct and does not see the preceptor, it is allowable to enter the village. If he sees the preceptor while entering the village, it is allowable only after asking permission from the place where he is seen.

"Na susānaṃ gantabbaṃ" means one should not go to a cemetery either for the purpose of staying or for viewing a corpse. Regarding "Na disā pakkamitabbā," a pupil who wishes to depart for another direction should inform the preceptor of the reason and plead up to three times. If he grants permission, it is well. If he does not grant permission, yet while living in dependence on that preceptor, one's recitation (uddesa), questioning (paripucchā), or meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) is not fulfilled; or if the preceptor is foolish and incompetent, and refuses permission to go merely because he wants the pupil to stay near him—in such cases, it is allowable to go even if he prohibits it. "Vuṭṭhānamassa āgametabbaṃ" means one should wait for the preceptor's recovery from illness; one should not go anywhere. If there is another monk to attend to him, one should search for medicine, hand it over to that monk, and say, "Venerable sir, this monk will attend to you," and then one may depart.

## The Discussion on the Duties towards the Preceptor is finished.
263:
## Discussion on the Duties towards the Co-resident Pupil (Saddhivihārika)

In the proper conduct of a preceptor towards a co-resident pupil (saddhivihārika)—he should support and favor that pupil through recitation (uddesa) and so forth. Among those (uddesa etc.), "uddesa" means teaching the Pali text. "Paripucchā" means explaining the meaning of the Pali text. "Ovāda" means admonishing before a matter has arisen, saying, "Do this; do not do that." "Anusāsanī" means instructing after a matter has arisen. Alternatively, the first speaking, whether a matter has arisen or not, is called "ovāda"; repeated speaking is called "anusāsanī."

If the preceptor has an extra bowl, (he should give it to that pupil). In this same manner, it should be understood for all requisites. "Parikkhāra" means other monastic requisites as well. Here, "striving" (ussukka) means searching for requisites by a righteous means that will bring them about. After this (searching for requisites), the duties beginning with providing a tooth-stick and ending with pouring water into the rinsing-pot should be performed only for a sick co-resident pupil. However, things such as dispelling dissatisfaction (anabhirati) should be performed even for a pupil who is not sick. A pupil who is dyeing a robe should dye it after receiving the method from the preceptor, saying, "It should be dyed in this way." The remaining points should be understood in the same manner as stated (in the duties towards the preceptor).

## The Discussion on the Duties towards the Co-resident Pupil is finished.

## Discussion on Improper Conduct and So Forth

"Na sammā vattantī" means not fulfilling the duties towards the preceptor as prescribed. If a pupil does not fulfill the duties as prescribed, it means he incurs an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). "Paṇāmetabbo" means he should be dismissed or expelled. There is no excessive worldly affection (gehassitapema) or excessive development of loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā) towards the preceptor. The "white side" (sukkapakkha) should be understood by the method opposite to the "black side" (kaṇhapakkha) already mentioned. "Alaṃ paṇāmetunti" means it is proper to dismiss him.

A preceptor who does not dismiss (a misbehaving pupil) is at fault (sātisāra) and incurs an offense. Therefore, a pupil who does not conduct himself properly must indeed be dismissed. In the case of improper conduct, if the duties up to the dyeing of robes are not performed, it is a loss for the preceptor. Therefore, an offense is incurred by the co-resident pupil who does not perform those duties, whether he is free from dependence (nissaya) or not. Starting from giving a bowl to a monk who is compatible with some preceptors... an offense is incurred by a co-resident pupil who is not yet free from dependence. If the co-resident pupils conduct themselves properly but the preceptor does not, the preceptor incurs an offense. If the preceptor conducts himself properly but the co-resident pupils do not, those pupils incur an offense. If the preceptor enjoys the duties performed by many co-resident pupils (without fulfilling his own), all those pupils incur an offense. If the preceptor says, "I have someone to attend to me; you all should strive only in your own studies, reflection, and so forth," no offense is incurred by the co-resident pupils. Whether the preceptor enjoys...
264:
There is a decline for the preceptor. Therefore, for one who does not perform that duty, whether they are released from dependence or not, an offence is indeed incurred. For some, starting from the giving of the bowl, an offence is incurred only for those not yet released from dependence.

If the co-residents conduct themselves properly but the preceptor does not, the preceptor incurs an offence. If the preceptor conducts himself properly but the co-residents do not, those students incur an offence. If the preceptor consents to the service being performed, even if there are many co-residents, all of them incur an offence. If the preceptor says, "I have an attendant; you all apply yourselves to your own recitation, reflection, and so forth," then the co-residents do not incur an offence. If the preceptor is a fool and does not know whether he consents or not, and there are many co-residents, if among them one monk who is perfect in his duties says, "I will perform the preceptor's duties; you all remain unconcerned," and thus takes the responsibility upon himself and releases the others, then from the time he takes the responsibility, the others do not incur an offence.

## The Discussion on Improper Conduct etc. is Finished.

## The Story of the Brahmin Rādha

In the story of the Brahmin Rādha—although the Venerable Sāriputta knew the going-forth (pabbajjā) and the higher ordination (upasampadā) authorized by the Blessed One in Bārāṇasī by means of the three refuges, the Blessed One, wishing to reject that light form of ordination and make it a serious one by means of the formal act with a motion and three proclamations (ñatticatuttha-kammavācā), authorized the higher ordination. Then the Elder, knowing His intention, said, "Venerable Sir, how shall I give the going-forth and the higher ordination to that Brahmin?" Indeed, the assemblies of the Buddhas are skilled in knowing the intention, and this Elder is the foremost among the Buddha's assembly.

In the phrase "by a competent and capable monk" (vyattena bhikkhuna paṭibalena), "competent" (vyatta) means one who has mastered the Vinaya Piṭaka along with its commentaries. In the absence of such a person, even if one has well-learned and mastered at least this much—the text of the formal act with a motion and three proclamations—he is also called "competent" in this context. If a person, due to illness such as coughing or phlegm, or due to a defect in lips, teeth, or tongue, or due to lack of practice in the scriptures (pariyatti), is unable to recite the kammavācā with complete syllables and phrases, and omits a syllable or a phrase, or recites a syllable or phrase differently from how it should be said, that monk is "incapable" (appaṭibala).
265:
...due to illness, or due to a defect in lips, teeth, tongue, etc., or due to lack of practice in the scriptures, if one is unable to recite the kammavācā with complete syllables and phrases, and omits a syllable or a phrase, or says what should be said in a different way, this monk is called "incapable" (appaṭibala). The monk who is the opposite of that should be known as "capable" (paṭibala) in this context. "The Saṅgha should be informed" means the Saṅgha should be made to know. After that, to show the manner in which the Saṅgha is to be informed, He said "Let the Saṅgha hear me, Venerable Sir" (suṇātu me bhante) and so forth.

"Immediately after being ordained" (upasampannasamanantarā) means immediately after having become a monk. "He practices misconduct" (anācāraṃ ācarati) means he commits a transgression of the regulations or a transgression of the training rules. "May he uplift me" (ullumpatu maṃ) means may he raise me up; may he lift me out of unwholesome states and establish me in wholesome states; or it means may he lift me out of the state of a novice (sāmaṇera) and establish me in the state of a monk (bhikkhu). "Out of compassion" (anukampaṃ upādāya) means based on sympathy; the meaning is "having shown compassion towards me".

"It is established" (aṭṭhitā hoti) means it occurs constantly. "The four supports" (cattāro nissaye) means the four requisites. Because the individual existence (attabhāva) arises and persists depending on the four requisites, therefore those four requisites are called "supports" (nissaya).

## The Story of the Brahmin Rādha is Finished.

## The Discussion on the Duties towards a Teacher

"What is this monk to you?" (kintāyaṃ bhikkhu hoti) is a question asking how this monk is related to you. It means he is still to be exhorted and instructed by others. "He has turned to worldliness, that is, cliquishness" (bāhullāya āvatto yadidaṃ gaṇabandhikaṃ)—"cliquishness" (gaṇabandhika) means having the bond of a group for the sake of that worldliness (bāhulla). It refers to the state of being many. It means "for the sake of that worldliness which is called cliquishness, you have arrived very quickly".

"Incompetent" (avyattā) means those who are devoid of the sharpness of wisdom. "Another who was formerly a member of another sect" (aññattaropi aññatitthiyapubbo) refers to the wanderer named Pasūra. It is said that he thought, "I will steal the Dhamma," and after ordaining in the presence of the Elder Udāyī, when he was exhorted by the Elder Udāyī with the training rules to be practiced by the five classes of co-religionists, he attempted to refute the Elder Udāyī's doctrine. In the passage beginning with "I allow, O monks, by a competent monk...", "competent" (vyatto) means a wise monk. Previously...
266:
Thinking, "I will steal the Dhamma," he ordained under the Elder Udāyi. When he was instructed by the Elder Udāyi with the sahadhammika (training rules to be practiced by fellow Dhamma-practitioners), he subjected the Elder's view to refutation (niggaha). In the passage beginning with "Monks, I allow a competent monk (to give dependence)," the term "competent" (byatta) refers to one who has the characteristics previously mentioned in the explanation of the exhorter of nuns (bhikkhunovādaka). However, one who is capable of performing duties such as attending to a resident pupil (antevāsika) or a co-resident (saddhivihārika) when they are ill is intended here as "capable" (paṭibala). It is also said: "Upāli, a monk endowed with five factors may confer higher ordination, give dependence, and look after a novice. What are the five? He is capable of attending to or causing others to attend to a resident pupil or a co-resident when ill; he is capable of dispelling or causing others to dispel dissatisfaction; he is capable of dispelling according to the Dhamma any remorse (kukkucca) that has arisen; he is capable of training them in the Abhidhamma; and he is capable of training them in the Abhivinaya" (from the Parivāra).

"Pakkhasankantesu" means when they have gone over to the side of the sectarians (titthiyas). "Monks, I allow a teacher" refers to allowing a teacher who teaches the training of proper conduct (abhisamācārika-sīla). The entire passage beginning with "Monks, a teacher should [regard] a resident pupil [as a son]" should be understood in the same manner as the method stated in "Monks, a preceptor should [regard] a co-resident [as a son]." There is only a difference in name here between ācariya/antevāsika and upajjhāya/saddhivihārika.

## Conclusion of the Discussion on the Duties towards a Teacher (Ācariya-vatta-kathā).

## Discussion on Dismissal and Forgiveness (Paṇāmanā-khama-nā-kathā).

Regarding the statement "Resident pupils do not conduct themselves properly towards their teachers," the following characteristic was previously mentioned: "Because of improper conduct, if the duties are not performed up to the dyeing of robes, there is a loss for the preceptor; therefore, for the one who does not perform those duties, whether he is one released from dependence or not, an offense is indeed incurred." Also, "For some, starting from the giving of the bowl, an offense is incurred only for the one not yet released from dependence." By that characteristic alone, the offense of a resident pupil taking dependence should be understood. This is because as long as a resident pupil lives in dependence on a teacher, he must perform all the duties towards the teacher. However, for those who are pupils through going forth (pabbajjā), through higher ordination (upasampadā), or through the Dhamma...
267:
Even those released from dependence must perform the duties from the beginning until the dyeing of the robes. However, in matters such as giving the bowl without asking permission, no offense is incurred by these resident pupils, pupils through going forth, or pupils through higher ordination. Among these—pupils through going forth, pupils through higher ordination, resident pupils, and pupils through the Dhamma—the pupils through going forth and pupils through higher ordination are the teacher's responsibility for life. As for resident pupils and pupils through the Dhamma, they are a responsibility only as long as they live near the teacher. Therefore, the teacher must also conduct himself properly towards those pupils. For if any teacher does not conduct himself properly towards his pupils (ācariyantevāsika), that teacher incurs an offense.

## The Discussion on Dismissal and Forgiveness is finished.

## Discussion on the Cessation of Dependence (Nissaya-paṭippassaddhi-kathā).

Regarding the cessation of dependence from a preceptor, in the passages beginning with "The preceptor has departed (upajjhāyo pakkanto vā)," there is this decision: "Departed" (pakkanto) means having gone to another direction with the desire to live away from that monastery. When the preceptor has thus departed, if there is a teacher in that monastery who can give dependence, or if there is a teacher from whom dependence was previously taken, or if there is a teacher who shares the same use of requisites (sambhoga) and the same Dhamma (pari-bhoga) with oneself or the preceptor, then dependence should be taken from that teacher. If it is taken in this way, it is not that there is no exemption (parihāra) from offense even for a single day; there is indeed such an exemption. If such a teacher is not available, but there is another monk who is shame-fearing (lajjī) and virtuous (pesala), one who knows his shame-fearing and virtuous nature should request dependence on the very day the preceptor departs. If he grants it, that is good.

Otherwise, if he asks, "Will your preceptor return soon?" and the preceptor had said so, one should reply, "Yes, venerable sir." If he says, "In that case, wait for the preceptor's return," then waiting is proper. However, if one does not know the naturally virtuous (pesala) nature of that monk, one should observe his behavior for four or five days, and after obtaining permission, take dependence.

If there is no one in the monastery to give dependence, and the preceptor departed saying, "I will return in a few days, do not be anxious," then an exemption (parihāra) from offense is obtained until his return. Even if people in that place make him stay for five or ten days beyond the specified time, he should send word to the monastery: "Let the young monks not be anxious; I, on such and such a day..."
268:
If he says, "I will return," the exemption (from tutelage) can be obtained. If, while returning, there is danger on the way due to a flood in the river or because of robbers, etc., and the elder is waiting for the water to recede or is searching for a companion, and if the young monks hear this news, the exemption is obtained until the elder returns. However, if that elder sends word, "I will stay right here," the exemption is no longer obtained. One must go to a place where tutelage (nissaya) can be obtained.

If the preceptor (upajjhāya) disrobes, passes away, or changes sides, the exemption is not obtained even for a single day. One must go to a place where tutelage can be obtained. "Āṇatti" (order) refers to the dismissal of tutelage (nissayapaṇāmanā). Therefore, whether by the Pali method such as, "I dismiss you," or "Do not enter here," or "Take your bowl and robes and go," or "I do not wish to be attended by you," or by methods not directly in the Pali such as, "Do not ask me for permission to enter the village," etc., the student who has been dismissed from tutelage must apologize to the preceptor.

If he does not forgive at first, one should perform a penalty (daṇḍakamma) and apologize three times by oneself. If he still does not forgive, one should bring the elder monks (mahattheras) in that monastery to apologize. If he still does not forgive, one should bring monks from a nearby monastery to apologize. If, despite doing so, he still does not forgive, one should go elsewhere and stay with monks who are associates (sabhāga) of the preceptor. (One should stay there with the intention that) "Knowing that I am staying with his associates, he might forgive me." If he still does not forgive while staying thus, one should continue to stay there. If it is not possible to stay there due to dangers such as famine, etc., it is proper to return to the original monastery and stay after taking tutelage from another teacher. This is the decision regarding dismissal (āṇatti).

Regarding the cessation of tutelage from a teacher (ācariya), in the statement "the teacher has departed," some teachers depart after informing (the student), while some depart without informing. The student is the same. In that regard, if the student informs the teacher, "Venerable sir, I wish to go to such a place for some business," and the teacher asks, "When will you go?" and he replies, "I will depart in the evening or after waking up at night," and the teacher accepts, saying, "Very well," the tutelage ceases at that very moment.
269:
If, when it is said, "Venerable sir, I wish to go to such a place," the teacher says, "After wandering for alms in such a village, we shall know later," and that student accepts, saying, "Very well," and if he goes after that, it is a proper departure. If he does not go, the tutelage does not cease.

Otherwise, if it is said, "I shall go," and the teacher says, "Do not go yet, we shall know after consulting at night," and he goes after consulting, it is a proper departure. If he does not go, the tutelage does not cease. For a student who departs without informing the teacher, the tutelage ceases upon crossing the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā). For a student who returns from within the precinct boundary, the tutelage does not cease.

If the teacher asks the student, "Friend, I will go to such a place," and the student asks, "When will you go?" and he says, "In the evening or during the night," and the student accepts, saying, "Very well," the tutelage ceases at that very moment.

If the teacher says, "I will go tomorrow after wandering for alms," and the other (student) accepts, saying, "Very well," the tutelage does not cease for the first whole day; it is only on the next day that the tutelage is ceased. If he says, "After wandering for alms in such a village, I shall know whether I go or not," and if he does not go, the tutelage does not cease. Otherwise, if it is said, "I shall go," and the student says, "Venerable sirs, do not go yet, please know after consulting at night," and even after consulting he does not go, the tutelage does not cease.

If both the teacher and the student go outside the precinct boundary for some business, and while outside that precinct boundary, the teacher develops the intention to travel and goes without informing, but returns within two stone-throws (leḍḍupāta), the tutelage does not cease. If he returns after crossing beyond two stone-throws, the tutelage is ceased. If the teacher and preceptor stay in another monastery beyond two stone-throws, the tutelage ceases.

If the teacher disrobes, passes away, or changes sides (to another sect), the tutelage ceases at that very moment. In the case of dismissal, however, if the teacher dismisses the student with the dismissal of tutelage while only wishing to release him, and the student, thinking, "Although the teacher dismisses me, he is soft-hearted," remains attached to the teacher, the tutelage does not cease. If the teacher remains attached...
270:
Even if the student, without attachment to the teacher, relinquishes the burden thinking, "I will no longer live depending on this teacher," the nissaya (dependence) does not cease. If both parties still have attachment, the nissaya certainly does not cease. Only when both relinquish the burden does the nissaya cease. A student who has been expelled must perform a penalty (daṇḍakamma) and then apologize (ask for forgiveness) to the teacher three times. If the teacher does not forgive, one should proceed according to the method already mentioned regarding the preceptor (upajjhāya).

In the phrase "meeting with the preceptor," meeting should be understood by way of seeing and hearing. Indeed, if a student living in dependence on a teacher sees the preceptor paying homage to a cetiya in the same monastery, or sees the preceptor wandering for alms in the same village, the nissaya ceases. If the preceptor sees the student but the student does not see the preceptor, the nissaya does not cease. If the student sees the preceptor walking on the road or traveling through the air, but because of the distance only knows him as "a monk" and does not know him as "the preceptor," the nissaya does not cease. If he knows, the nissaya ceases. If the preceptor lives on the upper floor of a pavilion and the student lives below, and the student departs after drinking gruel without seeing the preceptor; or if the student departs after eating in one place without seeing the preceptor sitting in the assembly hall; or if the student departs after listening to the Dhamma without seeing the preceptor sitting in the Dhamma-preaching pavilion, the nissaya does not cease. Thus, meeting should be understood by way of seeing.

By way of hearing: if the student hears the voice of the preceptor while he is preaching the Dhamma or giving a blessing (anumodanā) in the monastery or in the village, and recognizes it as "the voice of my preceptor," the nissaya ceases. If he does not recognize it, it does not cease. This is the decision regarding meeting.

## The discussion on the cessation of dependence is finished.

## The discussion on the five factors for giving ordination

Now, to explain in detail the characteristics of preceptors and teachers which were previously stated in brief: "Monks, I allow a monk who is competent and able, who has ten years or more than ten years of standing, to give ordination and to give nissaya," the Buddha said, "Monks, possessed of five factors..." and so on. Therein, "five factors" refers to five factors of lack of quality. For that monk, because he is not possessed of the aggregate of virtue and so on, is indeed possessed of factors lacking quality. He should not give ordination (should not act as a preceptor).
271:
One should not give ordination by being a preceptor. "Nissaya should not be given" means one should not give nissaya by being a teacher. Here, in the three sets of five (pañcaka) beginning with "not being possessed of the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training (asekha)," "not being himself an asekha," and "being faithless," the prohibition is made by way of unsuitability, not by way of the factors of an offense. For if a person who is not possessed of the aggregate of virtue of an asekha and so on, and is unable to establish others in those virtues, governs a following while being possessed of faults such as faithlessness, his following will only decline in virtue and so on, and will not grow. Therefore, it is said that such a person should not give ordination and so on by way of unsuitability, not by way of the factors of an offense. Indeed, the Blessed One did not allow the status of preceptor or teacher only to those whose taints are destroyed (Arahants). If it were allowed only to such a person, He would not have said, "If dissatisfaction (anabhirati) arises in the preceptor," and so on. But because the following of one whose taints are destroyed does not decline in virtue and so on, it is said, "Monks, a monk possessed of five factors should give ordination," and so on.

In the phrases such as "one who has failed in virtue regarding the higher virtue (adhisīla-sīlavipanna)," one who has committed a Pārājika or a Saṅghādisesa offense is called "one who has failed in virtue regarding the higher virtue." One who has committed any of the remaining five classes of offenses is called "one who has failed in conduct regarding behavior (ācāra-vipanna)." One who has abandoned right view and is possessed of a view that takes an extreme (eternalism or annihilationism) is called "one who has failed in view (diṭṭhi-vipanna)." One who is devoid of the learning that should be possessed by one governing a following is called "one of little learning (appassuta)." One who does not know what should be known, such as offenses, is called "unwise (duppañña)." In this set of five, the first three terms are spoken by way of unsuitability, and the last two by way of the factors of an offense.

"Does not know an offense" means that even when it is said, "I have done such and such an act," he does not know, "This person has committed such and such an offense." "Does not know rehabilitation (vuṭṭhāna)" means he does not know that rehabilitation (purification) from an offense occurs in such a way, whether from an offense requiring rehabilitation (vuṭṭhānagāminī) or an offense requiring confession (desanāgāminī). In this set of five, the first two terms are spoken by way of unsuitability, and the last three by way of the factors of an offense.

"In the training of higher conduct (abhisamācārika-sikkhā)" means he is not competent to train others in the duties of the Khandhakas. "In the training of the fundamental holy life (ādibrahmacariyaka-sikkhā)" means he is not competent to train others in the Sekha rules (Pātimokkha). "In the Abhidhamma" means he is not competent to train others in the discernment of mind and matter (Abhidhamma). "In the Abhivinaya" means he is not competent to train others in the entire Vinaya Piṭaka. "Not competent to train" means, in all instances, not being able to teach.
272:
It means being able to. 'Dhammato vivecetum' means to cause to be dismissed (resolved) by means of the Dhamma. In this group of five (pañcaka), there is an offense in all terms. In the group of five beginning with 'He does not know the offense' (āpattiṃ na jānāti), there is also an offense in all terms. In the group of five ending with not having completed ten years (vassa), it is the same way.

Thus, the first three groups of five, three terms from the fourth group of five, and two terms from the fifth group of five (a total of four groups of five) are spoken of by way of being improper. Two terms from the fourth group of five, three terms from the fifth group of five, and the sixth, seventh, and eighth groups of five (a total of four groups of five) are spoken of by way of the factors of an offense. On the bright side (sukkapakkha), in all eight groups of five, there is certainly no offense.

## The Discussion on the Group of Five to be Ordained is finished.

## Discussion on the Group of Six to be Ordained

In the groups of six (chakka), the term 'having less than ten years' is the distinction; that term causes an offense in every instance. The rest should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. In those groups of six, 'the two Pātimokkhas have not come to that monk in detail (not well-recited)' means they have not come well by way of the two Vibhaṅgas. 'Not well-analyzed' means by way of the Mātikā and the Vibhaṅga. 'Not well-maintained' means by way of oral recitation. 'Not well-decided according to the Suttas and according to the syllables' means not well-decided from both the Mātikā and the Vibhaṅga.

## The Discussion on the Group of Six to be Ordained is finished.

## Discussion on the Story of Those Formerly Belonging to Other Sects

In the story of those formerly belonging to other sects—the one named Pasūra, because he has gone over to another sect (titthiyapakkantaka), should not be ordained. To show what should be done for another person who comes without having been previously ordained in this Dispensation, the Buddha said, 'Monks, whatever other person also,' and so on. To that person, a four-month probation (parivāsa) should be given; this is called the 'titthiya-probation' (titthiyaparivāsa), and it is also called 'unconcealed probation' (appaṭicchannaparivāsa). This probation is only for naked wanderers or Ājīvakas...
273:
Or it is given to a naked ascetic (acelaka). If that person comes wearing a garment or any emblem (banner) of another sect, such as a woolen blanket, probation should not be given to him. However, for ascetics (tāpasa) or white-clad wanderers (paṇḍaraṅga) other than naked ascetics, probation is certainly not to be given.

With the words "First, the hair and beard" (paṭhamaṃ kesamassuṃ), the Buddha shows the novice ordination (sāmaṇerapabbajjā) of that former member of another sect from the very beginning. When monks are ordaining him in this way, while he is sitting in the midst of the Saṅgha, they should not say to the elder monks, "Venerable Sir, please ordain him; Venerable Sir, please be the teacher (ācariya); Venerable Sir, please be the preceptor (upajjhāya)." This is because if the elders spoken to in this way do not accept out of reluctance for the role of teacher or preceptor for that person, he might depart in anger, thinking, "These monks do not trust me." Therefore, after leading him to a suitable place, the teacher and preceptor should be sought for him.

"Monks, in this way a former member of another sect is one who fulfills the duties; in this way he is one who does not fulfill the duties"—this statement is the Mātikā (summary) set forth to show the probation duties to be practiced by him. "Monks, how is it?" and so on is the Vibhaṅga (detailed explanation) of that same Mātikā. In that Vibhaṅga, "entering the village too early" means entering the village for alms (piṇḍāya) at the very time when the monks should be performing their duties. "Returning late in the day" means speaking household talk with men, women, boys, and girls in the houses of families, eating there, and returning only when the monks have already put away their bowls and robes and are engaged in study or are in seclusion. He does not perform the duties toward the preceptor or the teacher, but instead enters his living quarters and sleeps. "Monks, in this way a former member of another sect is one who does not fulfill the duties" means that a former member of another sect acting in this way is not one who practices or completes the probation duties.

In the terms beginning with "Or having a prostitute as a resort" (vesiyāgocaro vā), "prostitute" (vesiyā) refers to women who live by their beauty and are easy to approach for misconduct by giving a small amount of material gain. "Widow" (vidhavā) refers to women whose husbands are dead or who are separated from their husbands; such women desire friendship (intimacy) with any man. "Mature virgin" (thullakumārikā) refers to young women who have reached or passed the age of puberty; they wander about desiring men and seek intimacy with any man. "Paṇḍaka" refers to those of indeterminate sex whose defilements are thick and whose fever of passion is not calmed; being overcome by the force of the fever of passion, they seek intimacy with any man. "Nuns" (bhikkhuniyo) refers to women who have the same ordination; intimacy with these nuns occurs quickly, and from that, virtue (sīla) is destroyed.
274:
Among those such as *vesiyāgocara* (resort of prostitutes), one is said to have a 'resort of prostitutes' when, being a frequent visitor to the families of prostitutes, or using alms-round as an excuse, one approaches them with a heart bound by affection and a constant desire to see and converse with them. Such a person will soon be spoken of as 'going about with such-and-such a prostitute.' This same principle applies to all other cases, such as the resort of widows (*vidhavāgocara*). However, if prostitutes and others offer food by tickets (*salākabhatta*) and so on, it is proper to go with other monks and eat together or to return after receiving the alms. It is also proper to go with monks who are going to advise sick bhikkhunīs, to preach the Dhamma, or to provide instruction and inquiry (*uddesaparipucchā*). But if one goes not in such a proper manner, but out of a desire for friendship and intimacy, he is one who fails to satisfy the requirements (*anārādhaka*).

'Various duties' (*uccāvacāni karaṇīyāni*) refers to great and small tasks. Among them, tasks such as repairing *cetiyas* and great mansions, which are to be done by the Saṅgha assembling in harmony after the bell is struck, are called 'high' (*uccā*). Tasks such as washing and dyeing robes, which are included in the *Khandhaka*, and duties pertaining to the fire-room (*aggisālavatta*) and other such customary duties (*ābhisamācārika*), are called 'low' (*avacā*). In those tasks, 'not skilled' (*na dakkho*) means not being clever or well-trained in those duties. 'Not energetic' (*na analaso*) means not being endowed with rousing effort; upon hearing that 'there is work for the Bhikkhu Saṅgha,' he quickly finishes his meal, enters his inner chamber, sleeps as much as he likes, and only comes out in the evening. 'For the means therein' (*tatrupāyāya*) means for the means in those tasks. 'For investigation' (*vīmaṃsāya*) means investigation arising on the spot. He is not endowed with the wisdom that arises at that very moment, thinking, 'This should be done this way; this should not be done that way.' 'Not fit to act, not fit to arrange' (*na alaṃ kātuṃ na alaṃ saṃvidhātuṃ*) means he is not capable of doing it with his own hands, nor is he capable of managing and encouraging others to work together, saying, 'Venerable sirs, please take this; young monk, take this; novice, take this; if you or we do not do it, who will do it now?' When monks say, 'Let us do the work,' he makes some illness an excuse; he wanders around near the monks who are working, merely showing his head; such a person is also one who fails to satisfy the requirements.

'Not having intense desire' (*na tibbachando*) means not having strong desire. 'In instruction' (*uddese*) means in learning the Pali text. 'In inquiry' (*paripucchāya*) means in hearing the meaning. 'In higher virtue' (*adhisīle*) means in the *Pātimokkha* virtue. 'In higher mind' (*adhicitte*) means in the development of mundane concentration. 'In higher wisdom' (*adhipaññāya*) means in the development of the supramundane path.
275:
One who has 'crossed over' (*saṅkanto*) means one who has arrived in this Dispensation (*sāsana*). 'His teacher' (*tassa satthuno*) means the master of the source of that sect's doctrine. 'His view' (*tassa diṭṭhiyā*) means the doctrine received from that teacher. Now, since that teacher of that sect likes and approves of that very doctrine, and holds it with a firm grasp, thinking, 'This alone is the truth,' it is called his preference (*khanti*), liking (*ruci*), and clinging (*ādāya*). Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'By his preference, by his liking, by his clinging.' 'When dispraise is spoken' (*avaṇṇe bhaññamāne*) means when blame is spoken. 'Dissatisfied' (*anabhiraddho*) means one whose intention is not fulfilled, whose mind is not uplifted. 'Elated' (*udaggo*) means one with an extremely uplifted body and mind.

'Monks, this is a cause for dissatisfaction (*saṅghātanika*) in one formerly of another sect' means: Monks, when dispraise is spoken of that teacher and of that doctrine, the dissatisfaction that produces physical and vocal alteration, thinking, 'Why do these monks blame others?'; when dispraise is spoken of the Buddha and others, the satisfaction; when praise is spoken of that same teacher and that same doctrine, the satisfaction; and when praise is spoken of the Buddha and others, the dissatisfaction—these are the causes for dissatisfaction in one formerly of another sect. In the matter of not fulfilling the duties to be lived, this is the sign (*liṅga*), this is the mark (*lakkhaṇa*), this is the unwavering standard (*acalappamāṇa*). 'Monks, such a person formerly of another sect who has come and fails to satisfy the requirements should not be ordained' means that if he is endowed with even one of these aforementioned factors, he should not be ordained. In the 'bright side' (*sukkapakkha*), everything should be understood as the opposite of what has been stated.

'Monks, such a person who satisfies the requirements' means: one who does not enter the village at an improper time, returns to the monastery before noon, does not go to improper places such as the resort of prostitutes, is skilled in the duties of fellow celibates, has intense desire in instruction and so on, is satisfied when dispraise of sectarians is spoken, is dissatisfied when dispraise of the Buddha and others is spoken, is dissatisfied when praise of sectarians is spoken, and is satisfied when praise of the Buddha and others is spoken. By fulfilling these eight duties of a sectarian (*titthiyavatta*), a person formerly of another sect who has come and satisfies and pleases the monks should be ordained.

If, however, he breaks even one duty at the ordination platform (*upasaṃpadāmāḷaka*), he must undergo probation (*parivāsa*) for another four months. Just as a *sikkhamānā* who has broken her training is given the training rules and the agreement of training (*sikkhāsammuti*) again, there is nothing further to be given to this person. This is because the probation previously given is his only probation. Therefore, he must undergo probation for another four months. If, while undergoing probation, he attains the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*)...
276:
Mundane states are of a nature to be disturbed (unstable); therefore, ordination should not be granted based on them alone. Ordination should only be granted after one has fulfilled the duties for the full four months of probation. However, if while undergoing probation (parivāsa), one comprehends the four great elements, distinguishes the derived materiality, defines mind and matter, and begins to practice insight (vipassanā) by applying the three characteristics—even then, because mundane states are of a nature to be disturbed, ordination should not yet be granted. But if, through the development of insight, one attains the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), then the duties are considered fully completed. All wrong views have been well-uprooted, and the thorn of doubt (vicikicchā) has been extracted; thus, ordination should be granted on that very day. Even if one becomes a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) while still in the guise of another sect, there is no need for the probationary period; one should be ordained as a novice and then granted full ordination on that very day.

Regarding the phrase 'the robe should be sought with the preceptor as the source,' it means the robe should be sought by making the preceptor (upajjhāya) the authority. The bowl should also be sought in the same manner. Therefore, if the preceptor has a bowl and robe, one should say, 'Please give these to this person.' If the preceptor does not have them, and others wish to give, they should give them to the preceptor, saying, 'Having made this bowl and robe your own, please give them to this person.' Why is this? Those from other sects are often contrary by nature; they might say, 'The Saṅgha gave me this bowl and robe, what does it have to do with you?' and thus might not follow advice and instruction. However, if one's livelihood depends on the preceptor, one will be obedient to the preceptor's words. For this reason, it was said, 'the robe should be sought with the preceptor as the source.' The term 'bhaṇḍu-kamma' refers to the act of shaving the hair. The explanation of 'bhaṇḍu-kamma' will appear later.

'Aggika' refers to those who tend the sacrificial fire. 'Jaṭilaka' refers to matted-hair ascetics. 'Monks, these people are kiriyavādins' means they do not reject the efficacy of action; they hold the view that 'there is action (kamma), and there is the result of action (kamma-vipāka).' All Buddhas, while fulfilling the perfection of renunciation (nekkhamma-pāramī), fulfilled it by entering this very type of renunciation; I, too, have fulfilled it in the same way. Ordination in their tradition is not contrary to this Dispensation (Sāsana); therefore, they should be granted ordination, and there is no need to give them a probationary period. 'Monks, I grant this special privilege to these kinsmen' means I give this specific, designated privilege to them. Why was this said? Even when they were ordained in other sectarian schools, they did not wish ill upon the Dispensation; rather, they were speakers of praise, saying, 'This is the Dispensation of our noble kinsman.' That is why it was said so.

## The Story of the Former Members of Other Sects is Finished.
277:
## The Story of the Five Diseases

In the region named Magadha, five diseases were prevalent among humans and non-human beings; they had increased, grown, and spread extensively. The story of Jīvaka Komārabhacca will become clear in the Cīvara-kkhandhaka. 'Monks, one afflicted by the five diseases should not be ordained' means those who are overcome and afflicted by these five diseases, such as leprosy, should not be granted ordination.

Among those diseases, leprosy (kuṭṭha) refers to red leprosy, black leprosy, or any variety such as skin-scab, ringworm, or eczema; all are called leprosy. If that leprosy is even the size of a little finger's nail but is in a state of spreading, one should not be ordained. However, if it is the size of a little finger's nail in a place normally covered by the inner and outer robes and is in a state of not spreading, it is allowable (to ordain). But if it is on the face, or on the backs of the hands or feet, even if it is in a state of not spreading and is smaller than a little finger's nail, it is still not allowable; so it is stated in the Kurundī Commentary. Even for one who is ordained after being treated, ordination should only be granted when the skin has returned to its normal color. One whose body is covered with powder resembling the back of an iguana is also not allowed to be ordained.

A boil (gaṇḍa) refers to a sebaceous cyst or any other kind of boil; if it is even the size of a jujube seed and is in a state of spreading, one should not be ordained. If it is in a covered place, is the size of a jujube seed, and is not spreading, it is allowable. If it is in an uncovered place like the face and is not spreading, it is still not allowable. Even for one who is ordained after being treated, ordination should only be granted after the skin has become clear. Growths called 'uṇṇigaṇḍa' (warts) hang from various parts of the body like a cow's teat or like fingers; these are also types of boils. If these are present, it is not allowable to ordain. In childhood, there are milk-spots (khīrapīḷakā), and in youth, there are acne (kharapīḷakā) on the face; these disappear in old age. These are not counted as boils; even if these are present, it is allowable to ordain. There are other rough pustules on the body called 'kharapīḷakā' (smallpox), others called 'padumakaṇṇikā' (lotus-seed-like), and others the size of mustard seeds called 'sāsapabījakā' (measles) which spread over the whole body; all these are varieties of leprosy. If these diseases are present, one should not be ordained.
278:
"Kilāsa" is a type of leprosy (vitiligo) that does not break or ooze, having the color of red or white lotus leaves, which makes the body mottled like a cow. Regarding this leprosy, the decision should be understood as previously stated. "Sosa" refers to consumption (tuberculosis). If that disease is present, one should not be ordained. "Apamāra" refers to epilepsy caused by bile or by spirit possession. Among those, one possessed by a non-human (spirit) with a past grudge is difficult to cure. Even if there is only a slight amount of epilepsy, one should not be ordained.

## The Discussion on the Five Diseases is finished.

## The Discussion on the Story of the Government Servant

In the story of the government servant—"Collect the border" means to develop the border regions. It means to drive away thieves, resettle villages that were abandoned due to the fear of thieves, provide protection, and resume agricultural work and so on. However, because the King was a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), he did not give orders to "kill or strike the thieves." "Great King, the head of the preceptor should be cut off," etc.—having considered that "In ordination, the preceptor is supreme, then the teacher, then the group," they said that this statement appears in the judicial decisions (vohāra aṭṭhavinicchaya).

"Monks, a government servant (rājabhaṭa) should not be ordained." In this context, whether he is a minister, a high official, a servant, or someone who has or has not attained a certain rank—anyone who receives food and wages from the king is counted as a "government servant" (rājabhaṭa); such a person should not be ordained. However, it is permissible to ordain the sons, grandsons, or brothers of that government servant who do not receive food and wages from the king.

One who returns to the king the regular endowments (nibaddha-bhoga) or the monthly or annual provisions received from the king; or one who has a son or brother take over that position and informs the king, "Great King, from today I am no longer your servant"; or one who has completed the task for which wages were taken; or one who has been permitted by the king, saying "Go and ordain"—it is also permissible to ordain such persons.

## The Discussion on the Story of the Government Servant is finished.

## The Discussion on the Story of the Robber

In the stories of the robbers—"People seeing" means those who had seen him during his time as a layman and those who heard from others, "This is he (Angulimala)." Upon seeing him, they tremble in body and are terrified in mind... [they flee, take other paths, turn away, or close doors]. However, in the houses of those who do not know him, he receives almsfood. "Monks, do not ordain"—this was said because the Blessed One, being the Lord of Dhamma himself, wished to prescribe a training rule so that monks would not do so in the future. In that context, regarding the word "dhaja" (banner), because a certain robber travels making a banner his sign, that robber is called "dhaja" (a notorious robber). It refers to a famous robber like Mūladeva in the world. Therefore, a robber who destroys villages...
279: They also close the doors. However, in the houses of those who do not know them, they receive alms. Because the Blessed One is himself the Lord of Dhamma, wishing to prescribe a training rule so that bhikkhus would not do this in the future, he said, "Bhikkhus, [such a person] should not be ordained." In that statement, one is called a dhajabandha (one with a banner) because they wander as if they have fixed a banner. It means a thief who is well-known in the world, like Mūladeva and others. Therefore, if a person wanders about committing acts such as destroying villages, highway robbery, or city burglary, and is well-known as "So-and-so does such-and-such," that person should not be ordained. However, a prince who destroys villages, etc., while aspiring for the kingship, may be ordained. This is because kings are usually pleased when such a prince ordains. If, however, the kings are not pleased, he should not be ordained. If a thief who was previously well-known among the public later gives up the life of a thief and undertakes the five precepts, and if the people know this, he may be ordained. Those who steal mangoes, jackfruits, etc., or even burglars who commit theft without being seen, and if it is not known later that "this person did this act," they also may be ordained. "Kāraṃ bhinditvā" means breaking out of foot-shackles and the like. In the term "abhayūvarā," they are called "bhayūvarā" because they avoid (uvaranti) danger (bhaya). These people are called "abhayūvarā" because, having received immunity (abhaya) from the king, they no longer need to avoid danger. It should be understood that here the letter 'p' has been changed to 'w'. "Bhikkhus, one who breaks out of prison should not be ordained"—here, "kāra" refers to a prison. In this Dispensation, whether it be wooden stocks, iron chains, ropes, or confinement to a village, a market town, a city, a guard, a district, or an island—if one flees by breaking, untying, opening, or releasing any of these bonds, whether seen or unseen by people, he is counted as a "prison-breaker" (kārabhedaka). Therefore, such a prison-breaker should not be ordained even if he flees from an island to another island. However, one who is not a thief but was bound by royal officials thinking, "If bound like this, he will work without fleeing," because he was not doing manual labor—if such a person flees after breaking out of confinement, he may be ordained. One who took a village, market town, or port on lease and was put in prison because he could not fulfill the payment—if he flees and comes, he should not be ordained. One who was living by farming, etc., and was bound by someone after being slandered with the claim "He has found a hidden treasure"—it is not allowable to ordain him in that same place, but if he flees to another place, it is allowable to ordain him there.
280:
Monks, regarding the rule 'one should not ordain a wanted man (likhitaka),' a wanted man does not merely mean one about whom it is written, 'Wherever he is seen, he should be killed there.' Rather, it refers to anyone who, having committed theft or another serious royal offense, has fled, and the king has caused it to be written on a palm leaf or in a book: 'Wherever this person of such-and-such a name is seen, he should be seized and killed there,' or 'His hands and feet should be cut off,' or 'He should be made to pay such-and-such a fine.' Such a person is called a wanted man. He should not be ordained.

Regarding the phrase 'one who has been flogged as a punishment (kasāhata katadaṇḍakamma),' it does not refer to someone who is beaten for failing to perform a task or errand. Rather, it refers to someone who, having taken something through taxes or other means and consumed it, is unable to pay it back, and is thus beaten with whips, with the order: 'Let this flogging itself be your punishment.' As long as such a person has fresh wounds from being beaten with a whip or any other instrument like a half-staff, he should not be ordained. He should only be ordained after the wounds have healed and returned to a normal state. If he is someone who was released after being struck with knees, elbows, coconuts, or stones, and lumps or swellings are visible on his body, he should not be ordained. He should be ordained only when those lumps have subsided and he has recovered.

Regarding the phrase 'one who has been branded as a punishment (lakkhaṇāhata katadaṇḍakamma),' the nature of the punishment should be understood in the same way as the previous method. This refers to someone whose forehead, thigh, or other parts have been branded with a hot iron. Even if such a person is a freeman, as long as the wound is fresh, he should not be ordained. If the wounds have healed and become level with the skin so that the mark is no longer distinct, or if the mark is in a place covered by the robe when worn covering the three circles (ti-maṇḍala), it is proper to ordain him. If the mark is in an uncovered place, it is not proper to ordain him.

## The Discussion on the Story of the Thief is concluded.

## The Discussion on the Story of the Debtor

Regarding the rule 'Monks, one should not ordain a debtor (iṇāyika),' a debtor refers to one who has inherited debt from parents or grandparents, or has taken the debt himself, or has been pawned to a creditor by parents who took some property. Such a person...
281:
## The Story of the Debtor. He is called a debtor because he carries the debt of others. A person who is pawned by relatives other than his parents is not a debtor. This is because those relatives have no authority to pawn him. Therefore, it is proper to ordain him; however, it is not proper to ordain the other (one pawned by parents). If his relatives say, 'We will pay the debt, please ordain him,' and take the debt as their own responsibility, or if someone else, seeing his accomplishment in conduct, says, 'Please ordain him, I will pay the debt,' then it is proper to ordain him. In the absence of such relatives, the monk should inform a supporter of such a person, saying, 'This being, who possesses the requisite conditions for ordination, cannot be ordained because of the burden of debt.' If the supporter agrees to take responsibility, he should be ordained. If the monk himself has allowable property (kappiya-bhaṇḍa) and thinks, 'I will give this property to settle it,' he should be ordained. However, if the relatives do not take responsibility and the monk has no property of his own, it is not proper to ordain him with the intention: 'After ordaining him, I will have him go on alms round and settle the debt to free him.' If one ordains him under such circumstances, one commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Even if he flees, he must be brought back and given to the creditor. If he is not given back, the entire debt falls upon the neck (becomes the responsibility) of the ordainer. There is no offense for one who ordains him without knowing he has a debt. However, if the monk sees the creditors, he must show the debtor to them. For a monk who does not see them, there is no responsibility on his neck.

If a debtor goes to another place and, when asked, says, 'I do not owe anything to anyone,' and is ordained, and the creditor comes there while searching for him, and the young novice flees upon seeing him, and that creditor approaches the elder monk and says, 'Venerable sir, who ordained this person? He has fled after taking such-and-such an amount of my property,' the elder should say, 'Lay follower, I ordained him because he said, "I am free of debt." What can I do now? Look only at my bowl and robes.' This is the proper conduct in that situation. If the novice has fled, there is no responsibility on the elder's neck.

If the creditor sees him in the presence of the elder and says, 'This is my debtor,' the elder should say, 'You alone know your debtor.' Even in this case, there is no responsibility on the neck. If the creditor says, 'Now that he is ordained, where will he go?' the elder should say, 'You alone know.' Even then, if the novice flees, there is no responsibility on the elder's neck. However, if the elder says, 'Where will he go now? Let him stay right here,' and the novice flees, then there is responsibility on the elder's neck. If that novice is a person with the requisite conditions and is accomplished in his duties, the elder should explain, 'This person is of such a character.' If the creditor says, 'Very well,' and releases him, that is good. If the creditor says, 'Give me half of the debt,' it should be given. If at a later time the novice becomes one who greatly pleases the creditor with his conduct, the creditor may say, 'The whole debt...'
282:
Even if it is said, "Give it," it must indeed be given. If that person is skilled in reciting and questioning, etc., and is of great help to the monks, the debt must be paid even by seeking it through the duty of going for alms.

## The Account of the Debtor is finished.

## The Account of the Slave

In the phrase "Monks, a slave (should not be ordained)," there are four types of slaves: one born in the house, one bought with wealth, one captured in war, and one who has entered slavery of his own accord. Among them, one born in the house (antojāta) means a slave by birth, being the son of a female slave in the house. One bought with wealth (dhanakkīta) means one who is bought by giving wealth to the parents for their son, or to the masters for their slave, and placing them in the conduct of a slave. Both these types of slaves should not be ordained. If one wishes to ordain them, they should be made non-slaves according to the local customs and then ordained.

One captured in war (karamarānīta) means those who are brought as free people from another country by plundering or by enticement. Or, within the country itself, the king orders, "Plunder!" a certain village that has committed an offense, and people are brought from there. Among those people, all men are slaves and all women are female slaves. Such a slave captured in war should not be ordained while living with those who brought him, or while imprisoned in a jail, or while being guarded by men. However, if he has fled and gone elsewhere, he may be ordained in the place where he has gone. If the king, being pleased, says, "Release the captured slaves," or if they are released from bondage by a general method applicable to all, they may indeed be ordained.

One who has entered slavery of his own accord (sāmaṃ dāsabyaṃ upagata) means one who has entered the status of a slave himself, saying, "I am your slave," for the sake of livelihood or for the sake of protection. Like the king's elephant keepers, horse keepers, cattle keepers, buffalo keepers, etc., such a slave should not be ordained. The sons born of the king's courtesans are like the sons of ministers; they also should not be ordained. If free women, without self-restraint, wander together with courtesans, it is proper to ordain the sons of those women. If they themselves...
283:
...voluntarily enter themselves into the register of slaves, it is not proper. The slaves of groups such as the followers of Bhaṭiputta and Mahāpinne should also not be ordained without being given by them. In monasteries, kings often donate people as monastery slaves (*ārāmika-dāsa*); it is not proper to ordain them either. It is proper to ordain them only after making them free (*bhujissa*). In the *Mahāpaccariya*, it is said: "If one brings slaves born in the house or bought with wealth and gives them, saying, 'We give them as monastery attendants to the Saṅgha of monks,' they become like those over whose heads buttermilk has been poured (i.e., they are purified/freed); it is proper to ordain them." However, in the *Kurundiya*, it is said: "If they give them using the allowable term, 'We give this monastery attendant,' regardless of what term is used for the gift, that person should not be ordained."

Poor people who become lay attendants (*kappiyakāraka*) in a monastery, thinking, "We will live depending on the Saṅgha," may be ordained. If both parents of a person are slaves, or if only the mother is a slave and the father is not, it is not proper to ordain that person. If, however, the mother is not a slave and only the father is a slave, it is proper to ordain that person. If relatives or supporters of a monk donate a slave, saying, "Please ordain this person; he will perform your services," even if he is the monk's own slave, he should be ordained only after being made free. If owners donate a slave, saying, "Please ordain this person; if he delights in the monkhood, let him be a non-slave, but if he disrobes, let him be our slave again," this is called a temporary (*tāvakālika*) slave; it is not proper to ordain him, as stated in the *Kurundiya*. If there is a slave without an owner, he too should be ordained only after being made free. If one ordains or grants full ordination without knowing and finds out later, it is proper only to make him free.

To clarify this meaning, they tell this story: It is said that a certain family slave woman fled from Anurādhapura with a man and, while living in the Rohaṇa region, gave birth to a son. When that son was ordained and reached full ordination, he became one who was conscientious and scrupulous regarding the Vinaya. Then one day, he asked his mother, "Lay devotee, do you have no elder or younger brothers or sisters? I see no relatives at all." She replied, "Dear son, I was a family slave in Anurādhapura; I fled with your father and live here." That virtuous monk, feeling a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), thinking, "My ordination is indeed not pure," asked his mother for the name and lineage of that master's family, went to Anurādhapura, and stood at the door of that family's house. Even when told, "Please pass on, Bhante," he did not move. They came and asked, "Why, Bhante?" He asked, "Did you have a slave woman of such-and-such a name who fled?" They replied, "We did, Bhante." He said, "I am her son. If you give me permission, I shall obtain the status of a monk. You are my..."
284:
The owners, being delighted and pleased, said, "Venerable sirs, your renunciation is pure," and having made him a free man (bhujissa), they let him reside in the Mahāvihāra and attended to him with the four requisites. While the Elder was residing in dependence on that family, he attained the fruit of Arahatship.

## The Story of the Slave (Dāsa-vatthu) is finished.

## The Discussion on the Story of Kammārabhaṇḍu, etc.

98-9. 'Kammārabhaṇḍu' refers to a young boy with five tufts of hair (pañcasikha), who is the son of a goldsmith (suvaṇṇakāra) and carries a gold scale. "To inform the Saṅgha for the purpose of bhaṇḍukamma" means that [the Buddha] allowed informing the Saṅgha for the purpose of the act of shaving the head. The procedure for this informing is as follows: Having assembled the monks within the boundary (sīmā) and bringing the candidate for ordination (pabbajjāpekkha) there, one should say three times, twice, or once, "Venerable sirs, I inform the Saṅgha of the shaving of this boy."

In this matter, it is also proper to say, "I inform [the Saṅgha] of the shaving of this boy," or "I inform [the Saṅgha] of the making of this boy a recluse (samaṇa)," or "I inform [the Saṅgha] of the going forth (pabbajjā) of this boy," or "This boy wishes to become a recluse," or "This boy wishes to go forth."

If it is a place where monks of the same communion (sabhāga) reside, and it is known that ten, twenty, or thirty monks live there, one should go to the place where they are standing or sitting and inform them in the same manner as mentioned before. Even without the candidate for ordination, it is proper to send junior monks or novices (sāmaṇera) to inform them, saying, "Venerable sirs, there is a candidate for ordination; we inform [the Saṅgha] of his shaving," and so forth.

If some monks have entered a dwelling or a thicket and are sleeping or practicing recluses' duties (samaṇadhamma), and the informers, though searching, do not see them and think, "We have informed all [monks]," since the act of going forth is a light matter, once he has gone forth, he is indeed well-ordained; there is no offense (anāpatti) for the one who ordains him.

However, if it is a large Mahāvihāra where many thousands of monks reside, it is difficult even to assemble all the monks, let alone to inform them one by one. In such a case, one should ordain him by standing in a small boundary (khaṇḍasīmā) or by going to a river, the ocean, etc. If a person has a newly shaved head, or is one who has disrobed (vibbantaka), or is one of another sect such as the Nigaṇṭhas...
285:
...or has hair two finger-breadths long or less than two finger-breadths, there is no need for the act of cutting the hair. Therefore, it is proper to ordain such a person even without informing [the Saṅgha] of the shaving (bhaṇḍukamma). But if one has hair longer than two finger-breadths, even if he has only a single tuft of hair, he must be ordained only after informing [the Saṅgha] of the shaving. The story of Upāli is just as mentioned in the Mahāvibhaṅga.

'By the ahiivātaka disease' means by a fatal pestilence. Wherever that disease arises, all two-legged and four-legged creatures perish. Only the one who escapes by breaking through a wall or a roof and goes to another village is saved. In this story, the father and son were saved in that way. Therefore, the Elder Upāli said, "Only the father and son remained."

'Kākuḍ္ဍepaka' (a crow-scaring boy) refers to one who, while sitting with a stone in his left hand, is able to scare away any crows that come and eat the food placed before him. It is proper to ordain such a boy.

'Ittara' means of a small measure; the meaning is that the stay will be for only a few days.

'By an ogaṇa' means by a diminished group, with a small group of monks. In the phrase "an incompetent one (avyatta) for as long as life," the judgment is this: if this incompetent monk does not find a teacher who is more senior than himself, even if he has sixty or seventy years of seniority (vassa) since his higher ordination (upasampadā), he must take dependence (nissaya) by sitting in a squatting position before a competent (vyatta) monk who is more junior than himself, raising his hands in salutation, and saying three times, "Friend, be my teacher; I will live in dependence on the venerable one." Even when asking for permission to enter a village, he should sit in a squatting position, raise his hands in salutation, and say, "Teacher, I ask permission to enter the village." This is the method in all types of asking for permission. Regarding the groups of five and six, the extent of learning (suta) required for one who is to be free from dependence (nissayamuttaka) has been stated in the Bhikkhunovādaka-vaṇṇanā. One should be known as 'one of little learning' (appassuta) due to the absence of that learning, and as 'one of much learning' (bahussuta) due to its presence. The rest is just as mentioned before.

## The Discussion on the Story of Kammārabhaṇḍu, etc., is finished.
286:
## The Account of the Story of Rāhula

"In whichever place Kapilavatthu is, to that place he set out on a journey." In this context, this is the sequential account. King Suddhodana, from the day the Great Being renounced the world, lived with an attentive ear, thinking, "My son has gone forth to become a Buddha; has he become a Buddha yet?" When the King heard of the Lord's practice of austerities, his realization of the Four Noble Truths, and the preaching of the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, etc., and heard that "Now my son is dwelling in dependence on the city of Rājagaha," he summoned a minister and sent him, saying, "Dear minister, I am old and aged; please show me my son while I am still alive." That minister consented, went to Rājagaha with a retinue of a thousand men, paid homage at the Lord's feet, and sat down. Then the Lord preached the Dhamma to him; he gained faith and requested both the going forth and higher ordination. Then the Lord ordained him with the Ehi Bhikkhu ordination. That minister, together with his retinue, attained Arahantship and dwelt there enjoying the bliss of fruition. In the same manner, the King sent eight other messengers. All of them, with their retinues, likewise attained Arahantship and remained there. There was no one even to report the news to the King, saying, "They do not return for such and such a reason."

Then the King, wishing to send the minister named Kāludāyī, who was born on the same day as the Bodhisatta, made the request as before. Kāludāyī said, "If I am allowed to go forth, I will show him to you." The King sent him, saying, "Even after going forth, show me my son." Kāludāyī also went with a retinue of a thousand men and, in the same way, attained Arahantship along with his retinue. One day, when all the crops had been harvested and the work of the country folk was finished, when the land and water flowers were in bloom and the road was suitable for travel, the Elder Kāludāyī paid homage to the Lord and praised the journey in sixty verses. The Lord asked, "What is this?" He replied, "Venerable Sir, your father, the Great King Suddhodana, is aged and sent me saying, 'Show me my son while I am still alive.' Venerable Sir, may the Lord show favor to his relatives; it is time to set out on a journey." The Lord said, "In that case, inform the Saṅgha; the monks will fulfill the duties of the journey." The Elder did so, saying, "Very well, Venerable Sir." The Lord set out from Rājagaha accompanied by ten thousand noble sons from Aṅga and Magadha and ten thousand from Kapilavatthu, making a total of twenty thousand Arahants. Thinking, "If I travel at the rate of one yojana per day to Kapilavatthu, which is sixty yojanas from Rājagaha, I will arrive in two months," he traveled with a leisurely pace. With reference to this journey, it is said: "In whichever place Kapilavatthu is, to that place he set out on a journey."

Furthermore, when the Lord traveled in this way, the Elder Udāyī, from the day of departure, performed the meal duties at King Suddhodana's palace. After serving the Elder, the King would rub the bowl with scented powder, fill it with excellent flavors of food, and place it in the Elder's hand, saying, "Venerable Sir, please offer this food to the Lord." The Elder did exactly that. Thus, the Lord partook only of the King's alms-food during the journey.
287:
The Lord, surrounded by twenty thousand Arahants, departed from Rājagaha and, considering that he would reach Kapilavatthu—sixty yojanas from Rājagaha—in two months by traveling one yojana each day, he set out on a leisurely journey. With reference to this, it is said: "Ye n a Kapilavatthu tena cārikaṃ pakkāmi." While the Lord was traveling in this manner, the Elder Udāyī, from the day of departure, performed the meal duties at King Suddhodana's palace. After serving the Elder, the King would rub the bowl with scented powder, fill it with excellent food, and place it in the Elder's hand, saying, "Please offer this to the Lord." The Elder did exactly that. Thus, the Lord partook only of the King's alms-food during the journey. After the meal, the Elder would daily inform the King, "Today the Lord has reached such a distance." Through talk connected with the virtues of the Buddha, he inspired faith in the Sakyans toward the Lord. Because of this, the Lord appointed the Elder to the position of foremost, saying, "Monks, among my monk disciples who inspire faith in families, Kāludāyī is the foremost."

The Sakyans, when the Lord arrived in due course, gathered, thinking, "We shall see our noblest relative." Searching for a place for the Lord to stay, they saw that the park of the Sakyan Nigrodha was delightful and had all preparations for maintenance made there. Holding scented flowers and such, they went out to welcome him. First, they sent young boys and girls of the city, adorned with all ornaments. Then they sent princes and princesses, and after them, they themselves went, worshipping with scented flowers and powder, and having received the Lord, they proceeded to the Nigrodhārāma. There, the Lord sat on the noble Buddha-seat prepared for him, surrounded by twenty thousand Arahants. The Sakyans, being proud by nature and stiff with pride, thought, "Prince Siddhattha is younger than us; he is our junior, our nephew, our son, our grandson." They said to the younger princes, "You pay homage; we will sit behind you."

The Lord, seeing their inclination as they sat thus, thought, "My relatives do not pay homage to me; well then, I shall make them pay homage." He entered the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for direct knowledge, and having emerged, he rose into the air by psychic power and performed a miracle similar to the Twin Miracle performed at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba mango tree, as if sprinkling dust from his feet upon their heads.
