When the King saw this wonder, he said, "Lord, on the day of your auspicious ceremony, I saw your feet turn and rest upon the head of the Brahmin when you were brought near to pay homage to him."
288:
The Buddha performed a miracle similar to the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya) near the white mango tree planted by the gardener named Kaṇḍa, as if scattering the dust clinging to his soles. King Suddhodana, seeing this wonder, said: "Lord, on the auspicious day of your naming ceremony, when you were brought to pay homage to the Brahmin (ascetic), I saw your feet turn and rest on the Brahmin's head, and I worshipped you; that was my first worship. On the day of the Ploughing Festival (Vappa-maṅgala), while you slept on the auspicious couch under the shade of the rose-apple (Jambu) tree, I saw the shade of the tree remain still without moving, and I worshipped your feet; that was my second worship. Now, seeing this miracle never seen before, I worship your feet; this is my third worship."

When King Suddhodana worshipped the Buddha, there was not a single Sakyan who remained without worshipping; everyone worshipped. Thus, having caused his relatives to pay homage, the Buddha descended from the sky and sat on the prepared seat. When the Buddha was seated, the gathering of relatives reached its peak, and all the relatives assembled with a concentrated mind. Then a great cloud caused the Pokkharavassa rain to fall; the red-colored water flowed down with a roaring sound. Not a single drop of rain fell on anyone's body [unless they wished it], and seeing this wonder, all the relatives were filled with great amazement. The Buddha said, "It is not only now that the Pokkharavassa rain falls at the gathering of my relatives; it fell in the past as well," and based on this event, he preached the Vessantara Jātaka. After hearing the Dhamma, all the relatives rose, worshipped, performed the right-side circumambulation (padakkhiṇa), and departed. Not even the King or a great minister invited him, saying, "Please accept our alms tomorrow."

On the second day, the Buddha, surrounded by twenty thousand monks, entered Kapilavatthu for alms; no one came out to welcome him, invite him, or take his bowl. Standing at the city gate-post (indakhīla), the Buddha reflected: "How did the former Buddhas wander for alms in their relatives' city? Did they go to the houses of the powerful by skipping others, or did they wander from house to house (sapadānacārika)?" Reflecting thus, he did not see a single Buddha who skipped houses. He thought, "I too must now uphold this lineage and tradition; in the future, my disciples will follow my example and fulfill the duty of wandering for alms." Starting from the house at the edge of the city, he wandered for alms from house to house. Hearing that "Prince Siddhattha is wandering for alms," the people opened the windows of their four-storied palaces and watched. Princess Yasodharā, Rāhula's mother, also thought: "My lord used to travel in this very city with great royal majesty in golden palanquins, but now, having shaved his hair and beard, wearing saffron-dyed robes, and holding a bowl in his hand, he wanders for alms. Is it fitting or not?" She opened the window and looked, seeing the Buddha illuminating the city streets with various radiant rays, beautiful with the glory of a Buddha, from the top of his head...
289:
Previously, he had traveled in golden palanquins and such by royal power, but now, having shaved his hair and beard, wearing dyed robes and holding an alms-bowl in his hand, he was wandering for alms. Thinking, "Will this conduct be graceful for us?" she opened the lattice window and looked out. She saw the Blessed One illuminating the city streets with the radiance of his body, shining with various colors, and resplendent with the glory of a Buddha. Then, praising him from the crown of his head to the soles of his feet with the eight verses known as the 'Narasīha' (Lion of Men) verses, she went to King Suddhodana and informed him, "Great King, your son is wandering for alms."

The King, with a trembling heart, adjusted his garment with his hand and hurriedly went out. Standing before the Blessed One, he said, "Venerable Sir, why do you put us to shame? Why do you wander for alms? Do you think that it is not possible to obtain food for this many monks?"

The Blessed One replied, "Great King, this wandering for alms is the custom of our lineage."

The King said, "Venerable Sir, is not our lineage the Mahāsammata royal lineage? In that royal lineage, not even a single king has ever wandered for alms."

The Blessed One said, "Great King, that royal lineage is your lineage. My lineage, however, is the Buddhavamsa (the lineage of the Buddhas). All the Buddhas have always wandered for alms." Standing in the middle of the street, he uttered this verse:

"One should arise and not be heedless; one should practice the Dhamma well. He who practices the Dhamma dwells happily in this world and the next."

At the end of the verse, the King realized the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Again, hearing this verse:

"One should practice the Dhamma well; one should not practice it poorly. He who practices the Dhamma dwells happily in this world and the next,"

he was established in the Fruit of Once-returning (Sakadāgāmi-phala). Later, after hearing the Dhammapāla Jātaka, he was established in the Fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-phala). At the time of his passing, while lying on the royal bed under the white parasol, he attained the Fruit of Arahantship (Arahatta-phala). For the King, there was no need for the task of practicing meditation while living in the forest.

Having realized the Fruit of Stream-entry, the King took the Blessed One's bowl and, together with the retinue, invited the Blessed One to the great palace and served him with choice food and delicacies. At the end of the meal, all the ladies of the court, except for the mother of Rāhula, came and paid homage to the Blessed One. Although the mother of Rāhula was urged by her attendants, "My lady, go and pay homage to your lord," she remained, saying, "If I have any virtue, my lord will come to me himself. Only when he comes will I pay homage." Then, the Blessed One, having the King carry his bowl, went to the princess's chamber together with the two Chief Disciples. He said, "Let the princess pay homage as she wishes; do not restrain her in any way," and sat on the prepared seat. The princess came quickly, took hold of the Blessed One's ankles, placed her head on his feet, and paid homage as she desired, rolling her head [on his feet]. The King recounted the princess's virtues, such as her love and reverence for the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "Great King, it is not surprising that now, when her wisdom is mature and she is protected by you, the princess protects herself. In the past, when her wisdom was not yet mature and she was wandering at the foot of a mountain without protection, she also protected herself," and he preached the Candakinnara Jātaka. On the second day after arriving in Kapilavatthu, Prince Nanda's ceremonies of hair-cutting and crowning...
290:
"My lord will surely come; when he has come, I will pay homage to him," she said and did not go. Then the Blessed One, having the King carry his bowl, went to the princess's auspicious chamber with the two Chief Disciples and said, "When the princess pays homage as she pleases, nothing should be said to her," and sat on the prepared seat. She came quickly, took hold of his ankles, and placing her head on the tops of his feet, she paid homage as she desired, rolling her head again and again.

The King spoke of the princess's excellence in virtues such as love and great respect for the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "Great King, it is not surprising that now, when her wisdom is mature and she is protected by you, the princess protects herself. Formerly, when her wisdom was not yet mature and she was wandering at the foot of a mountain without protection, she also protected herself," and he told the Candakinnara Jātaka.

On that very day, for Prince Nanda, there were five great auspicious ceremonies: the hair-cutting ceremony, the crowning ceremony, the house-warming ceremony, the wedding ceremony, and the parasol-raising ceremony. The Blessed One had Prince Nanda carry his bowl, spoke words of blessing, and rising from his seat, departed. Janapadakalyāṇī, seeing the prince leaving, stretched out her neck and looked, saying, "My lord, please return quickly." The prince, not daring to say to the Blessed One, "Please take the bowl," followed him all the way to the monastery. Even though he was unwilling, the Blessed One ordained him. Thus, the Blessed One, having arrived at Kapilavatthu, ordained Prince Nanda on the second day.

On the seventh day, the mother of Rāhula adorned the prince and sent him to the Blessed One, saying, "Dear son, look at that monk who is surrounded by twenty thousand monks, who has a golden complexion and a form like that of Brahmā. This monk is your father. He used to have great treasures. Since he left for the forest, we have not seen those treasures. Go and ask him for your inheritance. Say, 'Father, I am a prince. I shall become a Universal Monarch by raising the parasol. I have need of wealth. Give me wealth, for a son is the owner of his father's property.'" 

When Prince Rāhula went to the Blessed One, he immediately felt a father's love and, with a joyful heart, stood there saying, "O Monk, your shadow is indeed pleasant," and spoke many other appropriate words. The Blessed One, having finished his meal and given the blessing (anumodanā), rose from his seat and departed. The prince followed the Blessed One, saying, "O Monk, give me my inheritance; O Monk, give me my inheritance." Therefore, it is said, "Wandering on his journey in due course, he reached Kapilavatthu... (and so on) ...O Monk, give me my inheritance."
291:
"I am a prince; I shall be a king who sets the wheel of sovereignty in motion. I desire wealth; a son is the rightful owner of his father's property. Therefore, give me my inheritance." Thus, his mother sent him. Prince Rāhula went to the Blessed One, and feeling affection for his father, his heart was filled with joy. He said, "Venerable Sir, your shadow is very pleasant," and remained standing there, speaking other appropriate words. When the Blessed One had finished his meal and given thanks (anumodanā), he rose from his seat and departed. The prince followed the Blessed One, saying, "Venerable Sir, give me my inheritance; give me my inheritance." Thus it is said: "As he was wandering by stages, he arrived at Kapilavatthu... 'Venerable Sir, give me my inheritance.'"

Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Sāriputta. The Blessed One did not forbid Prince Rāhula from following him. Nor did the attendants dare to stop the prince as he went along with the Blessed One. Upon reaching the monastery, the Buddha thought: "This prince asks for his father's wealth. That wealth is bound to the cycle of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and is accompanied by suffering. Now, I shall give this prince the sevenfold noble wealth (ariya-dhana) that I attained at the foot of the Bodhi tree; I shall make him the owner of the supramundane inheritance." He then called Venerable Sāriputta and said, "Sāriputta, in that case, you should ordain Prince Rāhula." The meaning is: since this prince asks for an inheritance, ordain him so that he may obtain the supramundane inheritance.

At that time, the Blessed One had authorized both the initial ordination (pabbajjā) and the higher ordination (upasampadā) through the three refuges in Bārāṇasī. Later, he set aside the higher ordination by refuges, elevating it to a more serious status, and authorized higher ordination through the formal act with a motion and three proclamations (ñatticatuttha-kamma). However, the initial ordination (pabbajjā) was neither abolished nor re-authorized. Therefore, in the future, doubt might arise among monks: "This ordination was formerly the same as higher ordination. Should it now be performed with a formal act (kammavācā) like higher ordination, or through the three refuges?" Knowing this, the Blessed One wished to re-authorize the novice ordination (sāmaṇera-pabbajjā) through the three refuges. Therefore, the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, knowing the Blessed One's intention and wishing for the Buddha to re-authorize the ordination, asked: "Venerable Sir, how should I ordain Prince Rāhula?"

Then the Venerable Sāriputta ordained Prince Rāhula. The Elder Mahāmoggallāna shaved the prince's hair, gave him the saffron robes, and administered the refuges. The Elder Mahākassapa became the instructor (ovādācariya). However, since both ordination and higher ordination are rooted in the preceptor (upajjhāya), the preceptor alone is the authority in that matter, not the instructor. Therefore, it is said: "Then the Venerable Sāriputta ordained Prince Rāhula."

Hearing that "the prince has ordained," King Suddhodana, with a heart full of agitation (saṃvega), spoke all those words. In that context, when a monk who lives by wandering for alms is told without distinction, "I ask for a boon," it is inappropriate to say, "Ask for it," nor is it the custom of the Buddhas. Therefore, he said, "Gotama, the Tathāgatas have transcended boons." The meaning is: "Venerable Sir, I ask for a boon that is allowable for you to give, which is blameless, and which, because of my acceptance, will not be censured by the wise." Likewise, regarding Prince Nanda and Prince Rāhula, there was excessive...
292:
Regarding the phrase beginning with "Rāhule" (the commentator explains): Just as the soothsayers predicted on the auspicious day of the Bodhisatta's birth that he would become a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), they also predicted on the auspicious days of Prince Nanda and Prince Rāhula that they would become Universal Monarchs. At that time, the King, filled with the expectation that "I shall see the glory of my son as a Universal Monarch," suffered a great disappointment of his wishes due to the Buddha's act of ordaining him. Later, he generated the same expectation thinking, "I shall see the glory of Prince Nanda as a Universal Monarch," but the Buddha ordained Prince Nanda as well. Thus, having endured that suffering, he again generated the expectation thinking, "Now I shall see the glory of Rāhula as a Universal Monarch," but the Buddha ordained Rāhula as a novice too. Because of this, even greater suffering arose for the King, who thought, "Now the lineage has been cut off; where indeed shall I see the glory of a Universal Monarch?" Therefore, it was said, "Likewise, there was excessive suffering regarding Nanda and Rāhula." It should be known that after this excessive suffering, the King attained the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-phala).

Why did he say, "It is well, Bhante"? It is said that the King thought: "If even I, who am devoted to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, cannot endure the pain of separation from relatives when my own beloved sons are ordained, how will other people endure the pain of separation from relatives when their sons and grandsons are ordained? Therefore, let such suffering not happen to others besides me." Thus he made the request. The Buddha, knowing that "The King speaks for the sake of the Dispensation's (Sāsana) deliverance (from blame)," gave a Dhamma talk and laid down the training rule: "Monks, a son should not be ordained without the permission of his parents."

In that context, "parents" refers to the biological mother and father. If both are alive, both must be asked for permission. If either the father or the mother has died, the one who is alive must be asked. Even if the parents are ordained, they must still be asked. When asking, one may go and ask in person, or send someone else, or send the son himself, saying, "Go, ask your parents for permission and then return." If he says, "I have received permission," a monk who believes him may ordain him. If the father himself is ordained and wishes to ordain his son, he must ask the mother before ordaining him. If the mother herself is ordained and wishes to ordain her daughter, she must ask the father before ordaining her. If a father, having no desire for his wife and child, has run away, and the mother gives the son to the monks saying, "Please ordain this boy," and when asked "Where is his father?" she says, "He has run away to play as he pleases," then it is proper to ordain that boy. If the mother has run away with some man, and the father gives the son saying, "Please ordain him," the same principle applies. If the father is in a distant place and the mother gives permission to ordain the son,
293:
## 

and when asked, "Where is his father?" she says, "What use is the father to you? I will take responsibility," it is stated in the Kurundī Commentary that it is proper to ordain him.

If the parents have died and the boy has grown up under the care of a stepmother or others, relatives might quarrel or criticize if that boy is ordained. Therefore, to cut off disputes, he should be ordained only after asking them. However, there is no offense (āpatti) for a monk who ordains him without asking. Those who take and raise a child from a young age are also called parents; the same principle applies to them. A son might live depending on himself and not on his parents. Even if he is a King, he should be ordained only after asking permission. If one who was ordained with his parents' permission disrobes and then returns, even if he ordains and disrobes a hundred times, he must be ordained only after asking permission again and again each time he comes. However, if the parents say, "This person, having disrobes and returned home, does not do our work; while ordained, he does not fulfill your duties; there is no need to ask permission for this person, ordain him whenever he comes," if they have thus renounced him, it is proper to ordain him again even without asking.

If a child was given at a young age with the words, "This boy is given to you; ordain him whenever you wish," such a boy may also be ordained when he comes without asking again. However, if they gave permission at a young age saying, "Bhante, please ordain this boy," but do not give permission later when he has reached adulthood, he should not be ordained without asking. If a person, having quarreled with his parents, comes and says, "Please ordain me," and when told, "Come back after asking permission," he says, "I will not go; if you do not ordain me, I will burn down the monastery, or I will strike you with a weapon, or I will cause harm to your relatives and supporters by destroying their gardens, etc., or I will die by jumping from a tree, or I will join a gang of thieves, or I will go to another country," then it is proper to ordain him for the sake of protecting his life. If his parents come and ask, "Why did you ordain our son?" they should be informed of the matter and told, "We ordained him to protect his life; please understand regarding your son." If someone climbs a tree saying, "I will jump from the tree," and lets go of his hands and feet, it is certainly proper to ordain him.
294:
If a person goes to another place and requests to be ordained, if he comes after having asked permission from his parents, he should be ordained. If he comes without having asked permission, a junior monk should be sent to ask for permission, and only then should he be ordained. If the place is extremely far, it is also allowable to ordain him first and then send him back with other monks to show him to his parents. However, in the Kurundī Commentary, it is stated: "If the journey is long and involves a great forest with many dangers, it is allowable to ordain him with the intention, 'We will go and ask for permission later.'" If the parents have many sons and say, "Venerable sirs, please ordain whichever of these boys you desire," then after examining the boys, the one desired should be ordained. If an entire clan or an entire village has given permission, saying, "Venerable sirs, please ordain anyone you desire from this clan or this village," then the one desired should be ordained.

"Yāvatake vā pana ussahati" means as many novices (sāmaṇeras) as one is able to provide instruction and advice to.

## The Discussion on the Story of Rāhula is finished.

## Discussion on the Story of the Precepts and Punishment

Among the ten precepts, the transgression of the first five is the cause for expulsion (nāsana), and the transgression of the last five is the cause for performing an act of punishment (daṇḍakamma).

"Appatissa" refers to not placing monks in a position of seniority or authority (a lack of respect). "Asabhāgavuttika" means not having a similar livelihood, but having a dissimilar livelihood. "Alābhāya parissakkati" means striving so that they do not receive gains. "Anatthāya" means for the sake of causing harm or misfortune. "Avāsāya" means striving with the thought, "By what means can I make it so they cannot reside in this monastery?" "Akkosati paribhāsati" means reviling and threatening by showing danger. "Bhedeti" means causing a split by carrying tales (slander). "Āvaraṇaṃ kātuṃ" means to prohibit them, saying, "Do not enter here." "Yattha vā vasati yattha vā paṭikkamati" refers to the place where one resides or enters and exits; by both of these, it refers to both one's private precinct and the communal lodgings (saṅghika senāsana) received according to seniority.

"Mukhadvārikaṃ āhāraṃ āvaraṇaṃ karonti" means prohibiting them by saying, "Do not chew, do not eat today." Monks, prohibiting food that goes into the mouth...
295:
...is [not] to be done. In this context, for a monk who says, "Do not chew, do not eat," or for a monk who, intending to block food, hides the bowl and robes inside, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in all such efforts. However, for a novice who practices what should not be practiced and is difficult to admonish, it is allowable to perform an act of punishment and, while showing him gruel, rice, or bowl and robes, say, "When you have carried out this much punishment, you shall receive this." The Blessed One only spoke of the act of punishment that consists of blocking [food]. However, the Elders who recited the Dhamma at the Council stated that, according to the fault, making them carry water, wood, sand, etc., should also be done; therefore, that should also be done. And indeed, such carrying of water, wood, and sand should be done out of compassion, thinking, "He will desist, he will refrain." It is not allowable to do so with a wicked intention such as, "He will perish, he will disrobe," or with the thought, "I will perform an act of punishment," to make him lie on hot stones, or to make him place stones, bricks, etc., on his head, or to make him enter into water.

## The Discussion on the Story of the Precepts and Punishment is finished.

## Discussion on the Story of Not Prohibiting Without Asking

In the words, "Monks, one should not [punish] without asking the Preceptor (Upajjhāya)," if one has said three times, "Venerable sir, your novice has such-and-such a fault; please perform an act of punishment on him," and if the Preceptor does not perform the punishment, it is allowable to do it oneself. If the Preceptor has said from the very beginning, "If there is a fault in my novices, you yourselves perform the punishment," then it is certainly allowable to do so. Just as an act of punishment is to be performed on novices, so too is it allowable to perform an act of punishment on one's co-residents (saddhivihārika) and pupils (antevāsika).

"Apalāḷenti" means enticing them to serve oneself by saying, "We will give you a bowl, we will give you robes." In the words, "Monks, another's followers should not be enticed," whether they be novices or ordained monks, it is not allowable to break up and take away the followers of another, even down to an immoral monk. However, it is allowable to speak of the disadvantages, saying, "By living in dependence on an immoral person, you are like one who has come to bathe but becomes smeared with dung." If that person, realizing it for himself, requests a Preceptor or a Teacher (nissaya), it is allowable to give it.

In the words, "Monks, I allow the expulsion of a novice endowed with ten factors," among the three types of expulsion (nāsana) mentioned in the commentary on the Kaṇṭaka precept, only the destruction of the outward sign (liṅga-nāsana) is intended here. Therefore, if a novice performs even one of the acts such as killing living beings, he should be expelled by the destruction of the outward sign. Just as there are various offenses for monks in killing living beings and so forth, it is not so for novices. For a novice, even by killing a tiny insect or an ant, or by breaking a bug's egg...
296:
That novice reaches the state of having his outward appearance (as a monk) destroyed. At that very moment, for that novice, the refuges, the taking of a preceptor, and the acceptance of lodging cease. He no longer receives the gains of the Saṅgha, and only the outward appearance alone remains. If that novice is one whose faults are pervasive and does not abide by restraint in the future, he should be expelled. If, having suddenly failed, he thinks, "I have done wrong," and wishes to abide by restraint again, there is no need for the act of destroying his outward appearance. The refuges should be given to him while he is still wearing his robes as usual, and a preceptor should be given. The precepts, however, are fulfilled by the refuges alone. This is because the taking of the refuges by novices is similar to the ordination formal act (upasampadā-kammavācā) of monks. Therefore, just like the Fourfold Purification Virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) of monks, this novice has already undertaken the ten precepts. Even so, for the sake of firmness and to establish him in future restraint, they should be given again. If the refuges were taken again at the earlier time, he will receive the portion of the rains-residence later. If they were taken later, the gains should be given after informing the Saṅgha.

In the case of theft, even with an object as small as a blade of grass; in the case of unchaste conduct, by committing a transgression in any of the three paths; in the case of false speech, if one speaks a lie even with the intention of joking, he is no longer a recluse (samaṇa) and reaches the state of being destroyed. Regarding the drinking of intoxicants, for a monk, if he drinks an intoxicant starting from the seed even without knowing, he commits a pācittiya offense. A novice reaches the breach of virtue only if he drinks knowingly, not if he drinks unknowingly. If his other five precepts are broken, he should not be expelled, but a disciplinary penance (daṇḍakamma) should be performed. Whether the precepts are given again or not, it is acceptable. However, they are indeed given for the purpose of placing him in future restraint by punishing him with disciplinary penance. The drinking of intoxicants by novices is a matter of defeat (pārājika) involving intention; this is the distinction.

Regarding the speaking of dispraise, if a novice speaks dispraise of the Buddha by way of opposition to "Arahaṃ Sammāsambuddho," etc., or of the Dhamma by way of opposition to "Svākkhāto," etc., or of the Saṅgha by way of opposition to "Suppaṭipanno," etc., thereby insulting and blaming the Triple Gem, the teachers and preceptors should restrain him by showing the danger of speaking dispraise, saying, "Do not speak thus." If, even after being told up to three times, he does not stop, he should be destroyed like the destruction of the novice named Kaṇṭaka; thus it is stated in the Kurundī Commentary. In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, however, it is said: "If, while being told thus, he gives up that view, he should be made to perform disciplinary penance and confess his fault. If he does not give it up, then taking him as he is..."
297:
...and if he persists in upholding (that appearance), he should be expelled by way of destroying his outward appearance; this statement is appropriate. For in this context (of speaking dispraise), only this destruction of appearance is intended.

The same method applies to a novice with wrong views (micchādiṭṭhi). For if a novice who holds either the view of Eternalism (sassata) or Annihilationism (uccheda) is admonished by teachers and others and gives up (that view), he should be made to perform disciplinary penance and confess his fault. If he does not give it up, he should be expelled. Among these (ten factors of destruction), a novice who defiles a nun is certainly included by the term "one who is unchaste" (abrahmacārī); however, an unchaste novice who wishes to abide by restraint in the future is allowed to be ordained as a monk after being given the refuges. A novice who defiles a nun, even if he wishes to abide by restraint in the future, cannot even obtain the status of a novice, let alone ordination as a monk. To show this meaning, it should be understood that this tenth factor, "defiler of a nun" (bhikkhunidūsaka), is stated separately.

## The discussion beginning with the story of the prohibition of those who do not ask permission is finished.

## Discussion on the Story of the Eunuch (Paṇḍakavatthu)

"Dahare dahare" means those who are young. "Moḷigalle" means those with stout bodies. "Hatthibhaṇḍe assabhaṇḍe" means elephant-keepers and horse-keepers.

"Monks... a paṇḍaka"—in this statement, there are five types of paṇḍakas: the sprinkled eunuch (āsitta-paṇḍaka), the envious eunuch (usūya-paṇḍaka), the surgical eunuch (opakkamika-paṇḍaka), the fortnightly eunuch (pakkha-paṇḍaka), and the congenital eunuch (napumsaka-paṇḍaka). Among them, one whose fever of passion is calmed by taking the male organ of others in his mouth and being sprinkled with semen is called an āsitta-paṇḍaka. One whose fever is calmed when envy arises while watching others commit sexual misconduct is called an usūya-paṇḍaka. One whose testicles have been removed by effort (surgery) is called an opakkamika-paṇḍaka. A certain person, by the power of the result of unwholesome kamma, becomes a paṇḍaka during the dark fortnight, but during the bright fortnight, his fever is calmed; he is called a pakkha-paṇḍaka. One who is born without the male or female faculty from the very moment of conception is called a napumsaka-paṇḍaka.

Among those paṇḍakas, the novice-ordination of the āsitta-paṇḍaka and the usūya-paṇḍaka is not prohibited; the novice-ordination of the other three types is prohibited. Among them, for the pakkha-paṇḍaka, the novice-ordination is prohibited only during the fortnight in which he is a paṇḍaka; thus it is stated in the Kurundī. With reference to those among these paṇḍakas whose novice-ordination is prohibited, this was said: "One not yet ordained should not be ordained; if already ordained, he should be expelled."
298:
That paṇḍaka also should be expelled only by destroying the appearance of a monk. Hereafter, in places where it is said "should be expelled," this same method applies.

## The Explanation of the Story of the Paṇḍaka is finished.

## The Explanation of the Story of the One who Lives in Communion by Theft (Theyyasaṃvāsaka)

"A son of a former family" (purāṇakulaputta) means the son of a family that has gradually reached ruin. Because relatives from both the mother's and father's sides have been exhausted, destroyed, or died, he is called "one whose lineage is exhausted" (khīṇakolañña). "Unattained" (anadhigata) means the Dhamma that has not yet been reached. "To increase" (phātiṃkātu) means for the purpose of growth. "Ingha" is a particle in the sense of urging. "Being questioned" (anuyuñjiyamāno) means being taken to a certain place and questioned about the shaving of hair and beard, receiving the robes, taking the refuges, taking a preceptor, the kammavācā, and the nissaya (dependence). "He informed of this matter" (etamatthaṃ ārocesi) means telling from the beginning how he ordained himself.

Monks... regarding the one who lives in communion by theft (theyyasaṃvāsaka), there are three kinds: one who steals the appearance (liṅgatthenaka), one who steals the communion (saṃvāsatthenaka), and one who steals both (ubhayatthenaka). Among those three, if a person ordains himself, goes to a monastery, does not count the years of monkhood (vassa), does not accept the salutation according to seniority, does not obstruct with a seat, and does not appear in the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā etc., he is called "one who steals the appearance" (liṅgatthenaka) because he steals only the appearance.

If a person, being a novice (sāmaṇera) ordained by monks, goes to another place and speaks falsely, saying "I have ten years" or "I have twenty years," counts the years of monkhood, accepts salutation according to seniority, obstructs with a seat, and appears in the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā etc., he is called "one who steals the communion" (saṃvāsatthenaka) because he steals only the communion. Indeed, all actions such as counting the years of monkhood should be known as "communion" (saṃvāsa) in this context. The same method applies to one who, after giving up the training, thinks "No one can know me" and conducts himself in this way.

If a person ordains himself, goes to a monastery, counts the years of monkhood, accepts salutation according to seniority, obstructs with a seat, and appears in the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā etc., he is called "one who steals both" (ubhayatthenaka) because he steals both the appearance and the communion. These three kinds of persons who live in communion by theft should not be ordained; if they have been ordained, they should be expelled; even if they beg for ordination again, they should not be ordained.
299:
In order to avoid confusion regarding this matter of the theyyasaṃvāsaka, this miscellaneous note should be understood:

"Whoever takes the mark here [in this Dispensation] because of fear of kings, famine, wilderness, disease, or enemies, or for the purpose of bringing robes; as long as he, being pure-minded, does not yet accept communion, so long is he not called a theyyasaṃvāsaka."

The detailed explanation of that verse is as follows: In this world, a king might be angry with a certain person. That person thinks, "If I take the mark of a monk in this way, I will be safe," and he takes the mark of a monk by himself and flees. Seeing him, people inform the king. The king, thinking, "If he has become a monk, nothing can be done to him," lets go of his anger toward him. If that person, thinking, "The danger from the king has ceased for me," comes back and takes the lay mark without having entered the midst of the Saṅgha, he may be ordained. Alternatively, if he feels a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), thinking, "I have gained my life by depending on the Dispensation; now I shall truly ordain," and comes with that same mark but does not accept the duties of a guest monk, and whether questioned by monks or not, clearly reveals his true situation and requests ordination, he should be ordained after removing that mark. However, if he accepts the duties of a guest monk, shows the behavior of a monk, and practices all the procedures mentioned before, such as counting the years, he should not be ordained.

In this Dispensation, if a certain person, being unable to survive during a famine, takes the mark of a monk by himself and lives eating the food shared with those of other sects, and when the danger of famine has passed, comes back and takes the lay mark without having entered the midst of the Saṅgha, everything is the same as the previous case.

Another person wishes to cross a great wilderness. Caravan leaders take monks along with them. That person thinks, "If I take the mark of a monk in this way, the caravan leader will take me along," and he takes the mark of a monk by himself, crosses the wilderness with the caravan leader, and upon reaching safety, comes back and takes the lay mark without having entered the midst of the Saṅgha; this is also the same as the previous case.

Another person, being unable to survive when the danger of disease arises, takes the mark of a monk by himself and lives eating the food shared with those of other sects. When the danger of disease has subsided, the Saṅgha...
300:
The entire statement about coming back in lay form without entering the midst of the Saṅgha is just as previously stated.

Another person has an enemy who is angry and wanders about seeking to kill him. He thinks, 'In this way, I shall be safe,' and takes the monastic appearance on his own and flees. When the enemy searches, asking 'Where is he?' and hears 'He has ordained and fled,' he thinks, 'If he has ordained, it is not proper to do anything to him,' and dispels his anger toward him. He thinks, 'The danger from my enemy has subsided,' and returns in lay form without entering the midst of the Saṅgha—the entire statement is just as previously stated.

Another monk goes to his relatives' house, renounces the training, and becomes a layman. He thinks, 'These robes will perish here in this house. If I take these robes and go to the monastery, they will catch me on the way, calling me a "thief." It would be better if I go in the appearance that should be carried on the body.' For the purpose of carrying the robes, he dresses and wraps himself in them and goes to the monastery. Seeing him coming from afar, the novices and junior monks go out to meet him and show him the proper duties. He does not accept those duties and reveals himself as he truly is. If the monks, thinking 'Now we will not let you go,' wish to ordain him by force, his robes should be removed and he should be ordained again. However, if he thinks, 'These monks do not know that I have returned to the lower state,' and professes that very state of a monk, practicing the various Vinaya customs such as the counting of years (seniority) as previously mentioned, he should not be ordained.

Another senior novice (mahāsāmaṇera) goes to his relatives' house, disrobes, and being oppressed by work, thinks again, 'Now I will just be a recluse; the elder (thera) does not yet know that I have disrobed.' Taking his bowl and robes, he comes to the monastery. He does not inform the monks of the matter and professes the state of a novice; this person is a 'communion by theft' (theyyasaṃvāsaka) and can no longer receive ordination. Even if, at the time of taking the appearance, he thinks, 'I will not tell anyone,' but tells them upon reaching the monastery, he is a theyyasaṃvāsaka by the very act of taking the appearance. On the other hand, if the thought 'I will tell them at the time of taking the appearance' arose, but upon reaching the monastery and being asked, 'Friend, where did you go?', he thinks, 'Now these people do not know me,' and deceives them by not telling, then at the moment he gives up the responsibility (dhura) of telling, he is also a theyyasaṃvāsaka. But if the thought 'I will tell them' arose at the time of taking the appearance and he indeed tells them upon reaching the monastery, he can receive ordination again.
301:
In another case, whether it is a young novice or an elder but ignorant one, he disrobes in the same manner as before. Not wishing to do work such as tending cattle at home, his relatives dress him in those very robes, place a bowl or a dish in his hand, and send him out from the house, saying, 'Go, just be a recluse.' He goes to the monastery. The monks do not know, 'This person, having disrobed, has returned to ordain on his own,' nor does he himself know, 'One who ordains in this way is called a theyyasaṃvāsaka (one who lives in communion by theft).' If they grant him higher ordination (upasampadā) when he reaches twenty years of age, he is well-ordained. However, if before higher ordination, while still a novice, he hears the Vinaya decision and knows, 'One who ordains in this way is called a theyyasaṃvāsaka,' he should inform the monks, 'I have done this.' If he informs them, he can receive ordination again. If he thinks, 'Now no one can know me,' and remains without informing them, he becomes a theyyasaṃvāsaka at the moment he gives up the responsibility.

If a monk renounces the training and disrobes but does not discard the monastic appearance, whether he commits an act of immorality or not, and then practices the procedure such as the counting of years as previously mentioned, he is a theyyasaṃvāsaka. One who, without renouncing the training, remains in the monastic appearance, commits sexual misconduct, and then enters the procedure such as the counting of years, is not a theyyasaṃvāsaka; he receives only the initial ordination (pabbajjā-matta). In the Andhaka Commentary, however, it is said that such a person is a theyyasaṃvāsaka; that statement should not be accepted.

A monk, while still having regard for the robes, puts on white lay clothes and commits sexual misconduct, then puts on the robes again and enters all the procedures such as the counting of years; this person is also not a theyyasaṃvāsaka, he receives only the initial ordination. If he abandons the regard for the robes, puts on white lay clothes, commits sexual misconduct, then puts on the robes again and enters all the procedures such as the counting of years, he is a theyyasaṃvāsaka.

A novice, while remaining in his appearance, even if he commits acts that are not for a recluse, such as sexual misconduct, does not become a theyyasaṃvāsaka. Even if, while still having regard for the robes, he removes the robes and commits sexual misconduct, then puts on the robes again, he does not become a theyyasaṃvāsaka. If, however, he abandons the regard for the robes and, being naked or wearing white lay clothes, through sexual misconduct, etc...
302:
If one who is not a monk wears the dyed robe (kāsāya), he becomes one who lives in communion by theft (theyyasaṃvāsaka). If, desiring the state of a layman, for the purpose of testing whether "the lay appearance suits me or not," he wears the robe by tucking it in at the back or in any other lay manner, he still preserves [his status as a monk] for that much. However, if after accepting that "it suits me," he again delights in the [lay] appearance, he becomes one who lives in communion by theft. The same method applies to testing and accepting while wearing white clothes.

If, however, he tests or accepts while wearing white clothes over the dyed robe he is already wearing, he indeed preserves [his status]. The same method applies to a bhikkhunī. If that bhikkhunī, desiring the state of a laywoman, wears the robe in a lay manner for the purpose of testing whether "the lay appearance suits me or not," she still preserves [her status] for that much. If she accepts that "it suits me," she no longer preserves it. The same method applies to testing and accepting while wearing white clothes. If she tests or accepts while wearing white clothes over the dyed robe she is already wearing, she indeed preserves [her status].

If someone ordained late in life, without counting the years (vassa) and not standing in the sequence of the Pāḷi, comes from one side and, like a hawk seizing a piece of meat, takes a bowl and stretches it out to receive a portion of rice and food served with a ladle from a large chest etc., he does not become one who lives in communion by theft. But if he takes it while counting the years of a monk [in the sequence], he becomes one who lives in communion by theft.

If a novice (sāmaṇera) himself takes it while counting false years in the sequence of novices, he does not become one who lives in communion by theft. If a monk takes it while counting false years in the sequence of monks, he should be dealt with according to the value of the goods.

## The Story of the One who Lives in Communion by Theft is Finished.

## Discussion on One who has Gone Over to a Heretical Sect

"Monks, a titthiyapakkantaka" means one who has gone to or entered among the heretics (titthiya). Such a person should not only not be ordained as a monk (upasampadā), but should not even be given the initial going forth (pabbajjā). The decision here is: if an ordained monk, thinking "I will become a heretic," goes to their dwelling while still in his own [monastic] appearance, he incurs an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) at every step. By merely taking on their appearance, he becomes a titthiyapakkantaka. If a monk himself, thinking "I will become a heretic," wears garments made of kusa grass etc., that monk...
303:
...if he himself, thinking "I will become a heretic," wears garments made of kusa grass etc., he indeed becomes a titthiyapakkantaka. If a monk, while bathing naked, looks at himself and thinks, "The state of an Ājīvaka suits me; I will become an Ājīvaka," and goes to the dwelling of the Ājīvakas while naked without taking his dyed robes, he incurs an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) at every step. If, along the way, shame and fear (hirottappa) arise in that monk, he is released [from the status of titthiyapakkantaka] by confessing the offenses of wrongdoing. Even if he reaches their dwelling, if he turns back because he is admonished by them or because he himself reflects, "The ascetic life of these people is extremely painful," he is indeed released.

If he asks, "What is excellent in your ascetic life?" and is told, "Plucking out hair and beard etc. is excellent," and he has even a single hair plucked; or if he undertakes practices such as the squatting posture; or if he wears peacock feathers etc.; or if he takes on their appearance; or if he accepts their excellence, thinking "This ascetic life is superior," he is not released and becomes a titthiyapakkantaka. If, for the purpose of testing "Does the heretical ascetic life suit me or not?", he wears garments of kusa grass, ties his hair in a topknot, or takes up the heretical carrying pole, his [original] view protects him as long as he does not accept [their view]; the moment he accepts it, he becomes a titthiyapakkantaka. However, a monk who wears garments of kusa grass because his robes were stolen, or a monk who takes on a heretical appearance due to fear of kings etc., does not become a titthiyapakkantaka because of the absence of [heretical] views.

This term "titthiyapakkantaka" is spoken with reference to an ordained monk (upasampanna); therefore, it is stated in the Kuruṇdī commentary that even if a novice goes to a heretical place in his own appearance, he can still receive the going forth and the higher ordination again. The previously mentioned "theyyasaṃvāsaka" (one who lives in communion by theft) is spoken with reference to one not yet ordained (anupasampanna); therefore, a monk does not become a non-monk (assamaṇa) even if he counts his years deceitfully. It is said that one who is diligent in the monk's appearance does not become a theyyasaṃvāsaka even if he counts monk's years after having committed a pārājika offense.

## The Discussion on One who has Gone Over to a Heretical Sect is Finished.

## The Story of the Animal

In the phrase "he is weary of being born in the Naga species," although that Naga king, during his lifetime, enjoys sovereign prosperity similar to the prosperity of the devas due to the result of wholesome kamma...
304:
For that Naga who has a rebirth-linking resulting from unwholesome kamma, the physical form of a Naga—which moves in water and feeds on frogs—becomes manifest both when engaging in sexual intercourse with a female Naga of the same species and when falling into a deep, relaxed sleep. Therefore, that Naga is weary of that Naga birth. "Harāyati" means being ashamed. "Jigucchati" means being disgusted with one's own physical form. "Tassa bhikkhuno nikkhante" means when that other monk has gone out, or it means because of that monk's departure. "Vissaṭṭho niddaṃ okkamī" means that before the monk left, the Naga slept while nodding off like a monkey's sleep (kapimiddha), not letting go of mindfulness for fear of making a strange sound; but when the monk left, he let go of mindfulness and fell into a deep, relaxed sleep without suspicion. "Vissaramakāsi" means that due to fear, he abandoned the perception of being a monk and made a strange, loud sound.

"Tumhe khottha" is "Tumhe kho attha," where the letter "a" has been elided. The summary meaning here is: "You Nagas, being incapable of attaining Jhana, Vipassana, Magga, and Phala, are not of a nature to thrive in this Dispensation (Dhamma-Vinaya); you are not those who have the nature of growth." "Sajātiyā" refers only to a female Naga. However, when engaging with those of another species, such as a human woman, he becomes like a celestial deva. In this context, the phrase "two causes" is mentioned to show the frequent manifestation of one's true Naga nature during the course of existence. For Nagas, their true Naga nature becomes manifest on five occasions: at the time of rebirth-linking, at the time of sloughing the skin, at the time of sexual intercourse with a female Naga of the same species, at the time of falling into a deep, relaxed sleep, and at the time of death.

In the phrase "Monks, one who is an animal," whether it be a Naga, a young Garuda, or any other non-human species down to the lowest Sakka, the king of devas, all are to be understood as "animals" in this context. Such a being should not be given the Going-forth (pabbajjā) nor the Higher Ordination (upasampadā); if already ordained, he must be expelled.

## The Story of the Animal is Finished.

## The Story of Matricide and Others

In the stories of matricide and others, "Nikkhantiṃ kareyyuṃ" means they shall carry out the departure, removal, or expulsion. In the phrase "Monks, one who kills his mother," the person who...
305:
If one, being human oneself, intentionally deprives of life (kills) one's biological mother who is a human woman, this person is called a matricide (mātughātaka) because of the matricidal action which is an ānantarika-kamma (an action with immediate result). For such a person, the Going-forth and Higher Ordination are prohibited. However, if one kills a foster mother, a grandmother, or an aunt who is a human woman but not the biological mother, or if one kills a biological mother who is not a human woman, the Going-forth is not prohibited for that person, and it is not an ānantarika-kamma. If one who is himself an animal kills a mother who is a human woman, he also does not incur ānantarika-kamma; however, because he is an animal, his Going-forth is prohibited. The remaining words are clear. The same principle applies to a patricide (pitughātaka). Even if he is the son of a prostitute and does not know "This is my father," if he kills the man by whose semen he was conceived, he is still counted as a patricide and incurs ānantarika-kamma.

One who kills an Arahant (arahantaghātaka) should also be understood only in terms of a human Arahant. For if one intentionally deprives of life a male or female child who is a human being and has destroyed the taints (an Arahant), even if that child is not ordained, one becomes an arahantaghātaka and incurs ānantarika-kamma; the Going-forth is also prohibited for him. However, by killing a non-human Arahant or any other Noble Person (ariya) who is a human being but not an Arahant, one does not incur ānantarika-kamma, and the Going-forth is not prohibited; nevertheless, the kamma is powerful. If an animal kills a human Arahant, it does not incur ānantarika-kamma, but the kamma is heavy (bhāriya); this is the decision here. "Te vadhāya onīyanti" means they are led away for the purpose of execution; they are taken to be killed. The meaning of the phrase "Sacā ca mayaṃ" in the Pali is "If we (capture)." Where "Sace" should be said, the particle "Sacā ca" is used here. Or the reading is "Sace ca." There, "Sace" is a particle in the sense of supposition, and "ca" is a mere functional filler. There is also a reading "Sacajja mayaṃ," which means "If today we (capture)."

In the phrase "Monks, one who violates a nun (bhikkhunidūsaka)," if a person violates a virtuous nun in any of the three paths (orifices), he is called a bhikkhunidūsaka. For him, both the Going-forth and Higher Ordination are prohibited. However, if one causes the destruction of her virtue through physical contact (without penetration), the Going-forth and Higher Ordination are not prohibited. One who violates an unwilling nun even after forcibly making her wear white lay clothes is still a bhikkhunidūsaka. But one who violates a willing nun after forcibly making her wear white lay clothes...
306:
(That person) is not a defiler of a bhikkhunī (bhikkhunidūsaka). Why? Because as soon as she accepts the status of a laywoman, that bhikkhunī becomes a non-bhikkhunī (a layperson). One who later defiles a bhikkhunī whose virtue has already been ruined once, or one who behaves wrongly towards a female probationer (sikkhamānā) or a female novice (sāmaṇerī), is not called a defiler of a bhikkhunī; he may receive both the going forth (pabbajjā) and full ordination (upasampadā).

In the phrase "Monks, a schismatic (saṅghabhedaka)," a schismatic is one who, like Devadatta, misrepresents non-Dhamma as Dhamma and non-Vinaya as Vinaya, and splits the Saṅgha by means of any one of the four formal acts. For such a person, both the going forth and full ordination are prohibited.

In the phrase "Monks, one who sheds blood (lohituppādaka)," this also refers to one who, like Devadatta, with a corrupt and murderous mind, causes blood to flow from the living body of the Tathāgata, even as much as a small fly might drink. Such a person is called a shedder of blood. For him, both the going forth and full ordination are prohibited. However, one who, like Jīvaka, cuts with a knife to remove putrid flesh and blood for the purpose of curing a disease and brings about well-being, produces much merit.

## The Discussion on the Cases of Matricides and Others is Finished.

## The Discussion on the Case of the Hermaphrodite

"Monks, a hermaphrodite (ubhatovyañjanaka)" refers to one who has both signs (genitalia) due to kamma that produces the female sign and kamma that produces the male sign. "He performs" means he performs the act of sexual intercourse with women using the male sign. "He causes to be performed" means he instigates another and causes them to perform (sexual intercourse) in his own female sign. That hermaphrodite is of two types: the female-hermaphrodite and the male-hermaphrodite.

Among those two, for the female-hermaphrodite, the female sign is apparent and the male sign is concealed. For the male-hermaphrodite, the male sign is apparent and the female sign is concealed. When the female-hermaphrodite performs the role of a male with women, the female sign becomes concealed and the male sign becomes apparent. When the male-hermaphrodite assumes the state of a female with men, the male sign becomes concealed and the female sign becomes apparent. The female-hermaphrodite can both conceive a womb herself and cause another to conceive. The male-hermaphrodite, however, cannot conceive himself but can only cause another to conceive. This is the distinction between them. In the Kurundī Commentary, however, it is said: "If, while the male sex is present at the moment of rebirth-linking, the female sex arises; if, while the female sex is present at the moment of rebirth-linking, the male sex..."
307:
...arises." In that statement, the sequence of investigation should be understood in detail from the Atthasālinī, the commentary on the Dhammasaṅgaṇī. However, it should be understood here that for these two types of hermaphrodites, there is neither going forth nor full ordination.

## The Discussion on the Case of the Hermaphrodite is Finished.

## The Discussion on the Cases of Those Without a Preceptor and Others

"At that time" refers to the time when the Blessed One had not yet prescribed the training rule. "One without a preceptor (anupajjhāyaka)" refers to one who is entirely without a preceptor, not having been made to take one. Those who are thus ordained receive no support either in terms of Dhamma or in terms of material requisites; they only decline and do not prosper. "Monks, one without a preceptor should not be ordained" means that one should not be ordained without being made to take a preceptor. From the time this training rule was prescribed, if anyone should ordain such a person, there is an offence of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) for the ordainer, but the formal act (of ordination) is not invalidated. Some teachers say the act is invalidated, but that statement should not be accepted. The same principle applies to cases starting with making the Saṅgha a preceptor and ending with making a hermaphrodite a preceptor.

## The Discussion on the Cases of Those Without a Preceptor and Others is Finished.

## The Discussion on the Cases of Those Without a Bowl and Others

"They go about for alms with their hands" means they wander for the sake of alms received in their hands. "Like the sectarians" means just as the sectarians named Ajivikas go about for alms with their hands. Those sectarians eat only the alms placed in their hands, mixed with curries and sauces. "There is an offence of wrongdoing" means the offence is incurred only by the Saṅgha that ordains them in this manner, but the formal act is not invalidated. The same principle applies to the cases of those without robes and others.

"With a borrowed bowl" means a bowl obtained by asking, "Please give it until we perform the ordination," implying it is borrowed for a temporary period. For the Saṅgha that ordains someone with such a bowl, or with such a robe, or with both such a bowl and robe, there is an offence, but the formal act is not invalidated. Therefore, only one who has a complete bowl and robes should be ordained. If that person does not have them, and the teacher or preceptor wishes to give them, or other monks wish to give them, they should be given as a bowl and robes suitable for determination (adhiṭṭhāna), having been relinquished without any lingering attachment. However, it is allowable to give the going forth to a candidate for novicehood even with a borrowed bowl and robes, or by taking them through trust (vissāsa) from a suitable person.

If he comes bringing an unbaked bowl and cloth sufficient for robes, it is allowable to give that candidate, while he stays in the monastery until the bowl is baked and the robes are made, the first portion of alms-food that has not yet been partaken of; it is allowable to eat from an alms-bowl. Before eating, it is allowable to give a portion of material gifts equal to a novice's share. Accepting a monastery, or alms-food by lottery, designated alms, or invited alms, etc., is not allowable. After eating, a portion of medicine such as oil, honey, or molasses equal to a novice's share is allowable. If that candidate becomes ill, it is allowable to provide him with medicine and all the care that would be given to a novice. Thus should the conclusion be understood.

In the cases of those with severed hands and others, if a person has one hand or both hands severed at the palm, the wrist, the elbow, or any other place, he is called one with severed hands (hatthacchinna). If a person has one foot or both feet severed at the toes, the knee, the ankles, the 'horse-head' (astragalus), or any other place...
308:
It is allowable to give the first portion of almsfood that has not yet been handled to a candidate for novicehood residing in the monastery. It is allowable for him to eat from a dish. It is allowable to give a portion of material food equal to a novice's share before the meal. However, accepting a lodging, food by tickets, designated food, food by invitation, and so forth, is not allowable. After the meal, a portion of medicine such as oil, honey, and molasses equal to a novice's share is allowable. If he is ill, it is allowable to provide medical treatment; it is allowable to provide all forms of care just as one would for a novice.

## The Discussion on the Story of Those Without Bowls, etc., is Finished.

## The Discussion on the Story of Those with Severed Hands, etc.

Regarding the stories of those with severed hands and so forth—a person with a severed hand (hatthacchinna) is one whose hand is severed at the palm, the wrist, the elbow, or at any other place, involving either one hand or both hands. A person with a severed foot (pādacchinna) is one whose foot is severed at the forefoot, the ankles, the knee, or at any other place, involving either one foot or both feet. A person with severed hands and feet (hatthapādacchinna) is one who, in the manner already described, has two, three, or all four limbs severed. A person with a severed ear (kaṇṇacchinna) is one whose ear is severed at the base or the lobe, involving either one ear or both ears. However, if a person's ear is severed at the piercing but can be reattached, he should be ordained after the ear has been reattached. A person with a severed nose (nāsacchinna) is one whose nose is severed at the part shaped like a goat's hoof, at the tip, at one nostril, or at any other place. However, if a person's nose can be repaired, he should be ordained after it has been made well. A person with both severed ears and nose (kaṇṇanāsacchinna) should be understood by both criteria. A person with a severed finger (aṅgulicchinna) is one who has one or many fingers severed such that no trace of the nail is visible. If even a thread-width of the nail remains visible, it is allowable to ordain him. A person with a severed thumb or big toe (aḷacchinna) is one who, in the manner already described, has one or many of the four thumbs/big toes severed. A person with severed tendons (kaṇḍaracchinna) is one whose major tendons, called 'kaṇḍara', are severed either at the front or the back; because even one of these is severed, he walks on his toes, or on his heels, or is unable to step on his foot at all.

A person with webbed hands (phaṇahatthaka) is one whose fingers are joined together like a bat's wing. If one wishes to ordain such a person, one should split the spaces between the fingers, remove all the intervening skin, and ordain him after making it well. For a person who has six...
309:
...fingers or toes, if one wishes to ordain him, the extra digit should be severed, and after making it well, he should be ordained.

A hunchback (khujja) is one whose body is bent because of a protrusion from the chest, the back, or the side. However, if a person's limbs or extremities are only slightly crooked, it is allowable to ordain him. This is because only a Great Man (Mahāpurisa) has a body as straight as a Brahma; among other beings, there is no such thing as one who is not 'hunchbacked' to some degree.

A dwarf (vāmana) is one who is short in the shins, short in the waist, or short in both. For one short in the shins, the lower body from the waist down is short, while the upper body is full. For one short in the waist, the upper body from the waist up is short, while the lower body is full. For one short in both, both parts of the body are short; because of this shortness, their physical form is like a large-bellied jar, similar to a bhūta-spirit. It is not allowable to ordain any of these three types.

A person with a goiter (galagaṇḍī) is one who has a swelling in the throat like a pumpkin. This is merely a general teaching; in truth, if there is a tumor or swelling in any place, one should not be ordained. The decision regarding one with a goiter should be understood in the same manner as stated in the passage: 'Bhikkhus, one afflicted by the five diseases should not be ordained.' What should be said regarding those branded with marks, those scourged, and those inscribed with a penalty has already been stated in the passage: 'Bhikkhus, one branded with marks (should not be ordained),' and so forth.

A person with elephantiasis (sīpadī) is called one with a heavy foot. If a person's foot is thick, covered in pustules, and rough, he should not be ordained. However, if the foot has not yet become rough, and it is possible to make it thin by applying poultices, placing it in a water-pit, and filling it with wet sand until the veins become visible and the shin becomes like a tube of oil, then it is allowable to ordain him after making the foot so. If it grows large again, he should be ordained (given higher ordination/upasampadā) only after treating it in that same manner.

A person with a foul disease (pāparogī) is one who is constantly ill with any disease such as hemorrhoids, fistula, diseases of bile or phlegm, cough, or consumption; one whose disease is incurable, loathsome, and unpleasant. Such a person should not be ordained.

A spoiler of the assembly (parisadūsaka) is one who spoils the assembly by his own deformity. He may be extremely tall, such that the height of others' heads is only at the level of his navel...
310:
Or one who is extremely short like a dwarf-statue that is both hunchbacked and horse-headed; or one who is extremely black like a burnt stump in a field; or one who is extremely white like the color of polished copper rubbed with curds and buttermilk; or one who is extremely emaciated, having only bones, veins, and skin with little flesh and blood; or one who is extremely corpulent with much flesh; or one who has a large belly like a great earth-spirit; or one who has an extremely large head as if a basket were placed upon it; or one who has an extremely small head that is disproportionate to the body; or one who has a head like a cluster of palm fruits; or one who has a head that tapers toward the top; or one who has a tube-shaped head like a large bamboo joint; or one who has a head split into two like the frontal lobes of an elephant; or one who has a head that slants to one of the four sides; or one who has sores on the head; or one who has a putrid head; or one who has hair growing in patches like crops in a field eaten by insects; or one who has a hairless head; or one who has thick, coarse hair like palm fibers; or one who has naturally white hair from birth; or one who has naturally red hair as if it were aflame; or one who has hair whorls that turn upwards like the whorls on a cow's body; or one who has eyebrows that are continuous with the hair of the head as if a net were woven across the forehead.

One whose eyebrows meet; or one who has no eyebrows; or one who has eyebrows like a monkey's; or one who has extremely large eyes; or one who has extremely small eyes like holes punched in buffalo hide with the point of an awl; or one who has eyes of unequal size; or one who has uneven eye sockets, with one being higher and the other lower; or one who is cross-eyed; or one who has deep-set eyes where the pupils are visible like bubbles in a deep well; or one who has protruding eyes like a crab's; or one who has ears like an elephant's with large ear-flaps; or one who has small ear-flaps like a mouse's or a bat's; or one who has no ear-flaps but only ear-holes...
311:
One who has no ear-flaps but only ear-holes, or one whose ears are not pierced (is also unfit for ordination). However, one of Yona lineage who has no ear-holes is not a 'spoiler of the assembly' because that is their natural state. One who has an ear fistula and whose ears always smell putrid; or one who has an abscess in the ear with pus constantly draining; or one who has pointed or long ears like the tip of a tube used for feeding a cow; or one who has extremely red eyes (like a cat's eyes) (these are also unfit for ordination). However, it is proper to ordain one who has amber eyes like the color of honey. One who has no eyelashes; or one whose eyes constantly tear; or one who has a growth in the eye; or one who has chronic eye inflammation (these are also unfit for ordination).

One who has an extremely large nose; or one who has an extremely small nose; or one who has a flat nose; or one who has a crooked nose that does not sit in the middle but leans to one side; or one who has a nose so long, like a parrot's beak, that it can be licked with one's own tongue; or one whose nose is constantly running (these are also unfit for ordination).

One who has a large mouth where only the mouth-mark is wide like the frog named Pataṅga, but the actual mouth is extremely narrow like a gourd seed; or one who has a harelip; or one who has a crooked mouth; or one who has large lips like the rim of a pot; or one who has lips so thin and tight like the leather of a drum-head that they cannot cover the teeth; or one who has an extremely large lower lip; or one who has an extremely thin upper lip; or one who has an extremely thin lower lip; or one who has an extremely large upper lip; or one whose lip is severed; or one whose mouth constantly drivels; or one who has sores at the corners of the mouth; or one who has lips like a conch-shell beak, white on the outside and very red on the inside; or one whose mouth smells putrid like a corpse (these are also unfit for ordination).

One who has large teeth like the teeth of a harrow; or one who has protruding teeth that stick out above or below (these are also unfit for ordination). However, if the teeth can be covered by the lips and are only visible when speaking but not when silent, it is proper to ordain such a person. One who has decayed teeth; or one who has no teeth (these are also unfit for ordination). However, if there are fine teeth like squirrel teeth between the gaps, it is proper to ordain such a person.

One who has a large jaw like a cow's jaw; or one who has a long jaw; or one who has a jaw so short and flat that it seems to have receded inward; or one who has a cleft jaw; or one who has a crooked jaw; or one who has no beard or whiskers and has a face like a bhikkhunī; one who has a long neck like a crane's neck; or one who has a neck so short it seems to have receded inward; or one who has a tilted neck; or one who has drooping shoulders; or one who has no hands; or one who has only one hand (these are also unfit for ordination).
312:
Those with very short hands, very long hands, a sunken chest, a sunken or broken back, scabies on the body, an itching body, ringworm on the body, or a body like an iguana from which powder-like scales fall off. All these descriptions are spoken in detail regarding physical deformity. The decision regarding these (such as kacchugatta, etc.) should be understood according to the method stated in the passage: 'Monks, one with the five diseases [should not be ordained].'

One with a drooping waist, one with large buttocks protruding like the legs of a tripod, one with large thighs, one with a hydrocele, one with large knees, one with knock-knees that strike each other, one with long shanks like a staff, one with deformed feet, one with withered feet, or one with large calves protruding either downwards or upwards. Such a person is of two types: one with large calves protruding downwards and one with large calves protruding upwards. Also, one with large shanks, one with thick calves, one with large feet, one with large heels, one with shanks arising from the middle of the top of the foot, or one with crooked feet. Those with crooked feet are of two types: those with feet turning inward and those with feet turning outward. One with knotted fingers like pieces of ginger, or one with 'blind' nails that are black and rotten. All these are called 'spoilers of the assembly.' Such a spoiler of the assembly should not be ordained.

'One-eyed' (kāṇa) refers to one who is blind in one eye, whether from birth or due to diseases like cataracts. One who cannot see with either one or both eyes should not be ordained. In the Mahāpaccariya Commentary, however, one who is blind in one eye is called kāṇa, while one who is blind in both eyes is included under andha (blind). In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, one who is blind from birth is called andha. Therefore, both explanations are appropriate in their respective contexts. 'Crooked-limbed' (kuṇī) refers to those with crooked hands, crooked feet, or crooked fingers and toes. If any limb, such as a hand, is seen to be crooked, he is called kuṇī. 'Lame' (khañja) refers to those with bent knees, broken shanks, those who walk on the middle of the top of the foot because the sole is contracted, those who walk on the tip of the top of the foot because the tip is contracted, those who walk only on the toes, those who walk on the heels, those who walk on the outer edge of the foot, those who walk on the inner edge of the foot, or those who walk on the entire top of the foot because of a break above the ankles. All these are simply called khañja, and such a person should not be ordained.
313:
'Paralyzed' (pakkhahata) refers to one who cannot comfortably use one hand, one foot, or one side of the body. 'One whose posture is cut off' (chinniriyāpatho) refers to one who moves about on a stool (pīṭṭhasappī). 'Weak from old age' (jarādubbalo) refers to one who is so weak due to old age that he cannot even perform his own duties, such as dyeing robes. However, an elderly person who is strong and able to look after himself may be ordained. 'Blind' (andha) refers to one who is blind from birth. 'Dumb' (mūga) refers to one who cannot speak. Even if one can speak but cannot clearly recite the Refuges, such a stammerer (mammana) should not be ordained. However, one who can recite at least the Refuges clearly may be ordained.

'Deaf' (badhira) refers to one who cannot hear any sound at all. However, one who can hear a loud sound may be ordained. Terms like 'blind-dumb' are mentioned based on the combination of both defects. Just as Pabbajjā (initial ordination) is forbidden for these people, Upasampadā (higher ordination) is also forbidden. If, however, the Sangha ordains such a person as one with severed hands, they are all considered properly ordained (su-upasampanna), but the performing Sangha, the kammavāca chanter, and the preceptor (upajjhāya) are not exempt from an offense. As will be stated in the Cammayekkhandhaka: 'Monks, there is a person who is not fit for admission (osāraṇa); if the Sangha admits him, some (like those with severed hands) are well-admitted, while others (like women) are ill-admitted.' The meaning of this statement will become clear in its proper place.

## The account of those with severed hands, etc. (Hatthacchinnādivatthukathā) is finished.

## The account of living in dependence on a shameless person (Alajjīnissayavatthukathā)

In the phrase 'they live in dependence on the shameless' (alajjīnaṃ nissāya vasanti), the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative (the object). It means they live in dependence on shameless individuals. 'Until I know their commonality with the monks' means until one knows that the monk providing nissaya possesses the qualities of a scrupulous monk (lajjī), such as virtue, which is common among monks. Therefore, a monk who has arrived at a new place, even if told, 'Come, monk, take nissaya,' should only take nissaya after investigating and reflecting on the scrupulousness of the provider for four or five days.

If, having heard from other monks that 'the elder is scrupulous,' he wishes to take nissaya on the very day of arrival, and the elder says, 'Wait a while, you will know as you live here,' and gives nissaya after investigating the junior monk's conduct for a few days, this is also proper. Normally, a monk who has gone to a place to take nissaya should take it on that very day; he should not remain even for a single day without protection (parihāra) from an offense. If, during the first watch, the teacher is not free and the monk thinks, 'I will take it at dawn,' and falls asleep, there is no offense if he wakes at dawn. However, if he falls asleep without the intention to take it and dawn breaks, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). A person who arrives at a place he has never been before and intends to leave after staying for two, three, or up to six days, may stay without taking nissaya. If a monk intends to stay for seven days, he must take nissaya. The elder also, to one who will stay for about seven days...
314:
There is no exemption (parihāra) from the offense. If, in the first watch, the teacher is not free and the student, not getting the opportunity, sleeps thinking, "I will take [dependence] at dawn," and does not even realize when dawn has broken, there is no offense. However, if he sleeps without the intention of "I will take [it]," and dawn breaks, he incurs a dukkaṭa offense. A monk who arrives at a place he has not visited before and wishes to leave after staying for two or three days may stay without taking dependence (nissaya). But a monk who feels attachment, thinking, "I will stay for seven days," must take dependence. If the elder says, "What is the use of dependence for one staying only seven days?" and refuses, then from the time of that refusal, he receives an exemption from the offense.

## The Discussion on the Case of Dependence for Shameless Monks is finished.
## The Discussion on the Case of Dependence for Travelers and Others

"Nissayakaraṇīyo" means one who has dependence to be made; it means "I must take dependence." "Nissayaṃ alabhamānena" means not obtaining dependence because there is no one to give dependence among the monks traveling the long journey with him. Thus, not obtaining it, he may travel for many days without being dependent. If he enters a residence where he has previously lived after taking dependence, he must take dependence even if staying for only one night. If he rests mid-journey or stays for a few days while searching for a caravan, there is no offense. However, during the Rains Retreat (vassa), he must reside permanently and must take dependence. For a monk traveling by boat, if the time for the Rains Retreat arrives and he does not find anyone to give dependence, there is no offense.

"Yāciyamānena" means the monk who is requested by that sick monk should stay without dependence. If the sick monk is told, "Please request me," but does not request out of pride, the other may leave.

"Phāsu hotī" means being at ease by virtue of attaining tranquillity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). This exemption from offense is not obtained by Stream-enterers (sotāpanna), Once-returners (sakadāgāmī), Non-returners (anāgāmī), or Arahants; nor is it obtained by those who have attained strong concentration (samādhi) or insight. As for foolish worldlings (bāla-puthujjana) who have abandoned meditation (kammaṭṭhāna), there is no need to mention them. Indeed, whoever's tranquillity or insight is still tender (taruṇa) obtains this exemption. The favor of invitation (pavāraṇā) is also permitted only for such a person. Therefore, even if this person goes after inviting the teacher, he should form the intention, "When a suitable giver of dependence arrives, I will stay depending on him," and again...
315:
It is allowable to stay without taking dependence (nissaya) until after the full moon of Āsāḷha. If the teacher does not come during the month of Āsāḷha, one should go to a place where dependence can be obtained.

"To proclaim also by clan (gotta)" means He allowed proclaiming by mentioning the clan, such as "the candidate for ordination of Mahākassapa."

"By proclaiming two simultaneously" means proclaiming two together. It means He allowed ordaining by proclaiming the kammavācā at the same moment, either by two teachers—one for one person and another for the other—or by a single teacher.
