"To proclaim two or three simultaneously, and that proclamation with a single preceptor" means He allowed proclaiming two or three persons together as in the previous method. It means He allowed that act of proclamation only with a single preceptor. Therefore, one teacher should proclaim for two or three. Or, two or three teachers should perform two or three kammavācās simultaneously, each for one person separately. If there are separate teachers and separate preceptors, and if Venerable Tissa proclaims for Venerable Sumana's student, and Venerable Sumana proclaims for Venerable Tissa's student, and they complete the quorum for each other, it is allowable. If there are separate preceptors but only one teacher, it is not allowable because He prohibited it, saying, "Not with separate preceptors." This prohibition was made with reference to a single teacher proclaiming with separate preceptors.

## The Explanation of the Story of Dependence for Travelers etc. is finished.

## The Explanation of the Procedure for Ordination (Upasampadāvidhi)

In the phrase "First, he should be made to take a preceptor," he is called a preceptor (upajjhāya) because he closely observes what is a fault and what is not. That preceptor should be taken by having the candidate say, "Venerable sir, be my preceptor."

"Vitthāyanti" means having bodies that are distorted and stiff. "Yaṃ jātaṃ" means that when being questioned in the midst of the Saṅgha about obstructive qualities that have arisen and are present in your body, if they exist, one should say, "They exist, bhante," and so on. "Ullumpatu maṃ" means "May you lift me up (from saṃsāra)."

## The Explanation of the Procedure for Ordination is finished.
316:
## Discussion on the Four Requisites and So Forth

"Tāvadēva" means immediately after attaining the status of a monk (upasampadā). "The shadow should be measured" means the shadow should be compared and measured as one person's length or two persons' length. "The measurement of the season should be told" means the measurement of the season should be told as "the rainy season, the winter season, the summer season." In this context, the season itself is called the measurement of the season. If the rainy season and so forth are not yet complete, one should carefully note the number of days by which the season is incomplete for that person and state that part of the day. Or else, the measurement of the season should be told as "This is the name of the season, and it is either complete or incomplete." The part of the day should be told as "morning or evening."

"Saṅgīti" means putting all these together and asking: "What season do you get? How much is the shadow for you? What is the measurement of the season? What is the part of the day?" If asked, one should answer: "I get the rainy season, winter, or summer of this name; this is my shadow; this is the measurement of the season; this is the part of the day." This is how it should be told.

"Ohāya" means having abandoned. "Dutiyaṃ dātuṃ" means he allows giving a companion to a monk going from the ordination hall (māḷaka) to the precinct (pariveṇa), and also telling the four things not to be done (akaraṇīya). "Paṇḍupalāsa" means a yellowed, withered leaf. "Bandhanā pavutto" means fallen from the stalk. "Abhabbo haritatthāya" means no longer capable of becoming green again. "Puthusilā" means a large stone slab.

"Alabbhamānāya sāmaggiyā anāpatti sambhoge saṃvāse" means as long as the harmony (sāmaggī) of the Saṅgha cannot be obtained to perform the act of suspension (ukkhepaniya-kamma) for that monk, there is no offense in sharing material things (sambhoga) or in communal living (saṃvāsa) such as performing Uposatha or Pavāraṇā with him. All the remaining words are clear because they are easy to understand as stated in the Mahāvibhaṅga.

## The Discussion on the Four Requisites and So Forth is finished.

## In the Vinaya Commentary named Samantapāsādikā,

## the explanation of the meaning of the Mahākhandhaka,

## adorned with one hundred and seventy-two stories, is finished.

## The Mahākhandhaka Commentary is finished.
317:
## 2. Uposathakkhandhaka

## Discussion on the Permission to Assemble and Others

In the Uposathakkhandhaka—in the word 'aññatitthiyā', 'tittha' means a doctrine or view. Another doctrine is called 'aññatittha'. Those who hold such other doctrines are 'aññatitthiya'. It means those who hold views other than this Dispensation (Sāsana). 'Dhammaṃ bhāsanti' means they preach what should and should not be done by them. 'Te labhanti' means those people obtain or gain. 'Mūgasūkarā' means pigs with fat bodies.

In the phrase 'anajjhāpanno vā hoti āpajjitvā vā vuṭṭhito', the meaning should be understood thus: if a monk has not committed an offense, or having committed it, has emerged from it, this offense is called 'asanti' (non-existent in oneself). 'Sampajānamusāvāde kiṃ hoti' means if there is a deliberate lie by that monk, what does it become in terms of offense; what kind of offense does it become? 'Dukkaṭaṃ hotī' means it is a dukkaṭa offense. It should be understood that this dukkaṭa offense is not due to the characteristic of lying, but according to the word of the Blessed One, it is an offense arising from non-performance (akiriya-samuṭṭhāna) at the door of speech. For it will be said in the Parivāra:

'Without speaking to any human,
Without uttering a word to others,
One may fall into a verbal offense, not a physical one;
This problem has been considered by the wise who are skilled in Vinaya.'

'Antarāyiko' means one who causes an obstacle. 'Kissa phāsu hoti' means for what purpose is there comfort? 'Paṭhamassa jhānassa adhigamāya' means for the sake of attaining the first jhāna, there is comfort and happiness for that monk. This method applies in all places. Thus, the Blessed One showed the first Pātimokkha recitation (Pātimokkhuddesa) through summary (uddesa) and exposition (niddesa).

'Devasikaṃ' means daily. 'Cātuddase vā pannarase vā' means in the third and seventh fortnights of a single season, it occurs twice on the 14th day, and in the remaining six times, it occurs on the 15th day. This is one meaning. This meaning, however...
318:
It is spoken by way of natural custom (pakati-cāritta). According to the words, "Once a fortnight, on the fourteenth or the fifteenth day," if such a cause exists, it is proper to recite the Pātimokkha on that fourteenth or fifteenth day. If it is the fourteenth day for the resident monks and the fifteenth day for the visiting monks, if the resident monks are more numerous, the visiting monks should follow the wish of the resident monks; this point should be understood according to that statement.

## The Discussion on the Authorization of the Sīmā

First, the landmarks (nimittas) must be announced. The Vinaya expert should ask, "What is the landmark in the eastern direction?" The answer should be, "Venerable sir, it is a mountain." Again, the Vinaya expert should announce the landmark thus: "This mountain is the landmark." However, it is not proper to announce it as, "Let us make this mountain the landmark," "I will make it," "The landmark has been made," "Let it be the landmark," "It is," or "It will be." The same method applies to stones and so forth. In the southeastern direction, southern direction, southwestern direction, western direction, northwestern direction, northern direction, and northeastern direction, when asked, "What is the landmark?" the answer should be, "Venerable sir, it is water." After announcing, "This water is the landmark," one should not stop there, but ask again, "What is the landmark in the eastern direction?" and answer, "Venerable sir, it is a mountain," and announce, "This mountain is the landmark." Thus, the landmark that was first announced must be announced again before stopping. Only in this way are the landmarks connected to each other. After announcing the landmarks in this manner, the Sīmā should be authorized immediately after with the prescribed Kammavācā. At the conclusion of the Kammavācā, the area inside the landmarks becomes the Sīmā, and the landmarks themselves are outside the Sīmā. In that authorization, even if the landmarks are announced only once, they are considered announced. However, in the Andhaka Commentary, it is said that the landmarks should be announced while connecting the boundary circle three times. Whether it be a monk or a non-ordained person (layperson or novice), it is proper for them to say, "Venerable sir, it is a mountain... Venerable sir, it is water."

Now, the decision regarding mountain landmarks and so forth should be understood—there are three types of mountains: pure earth mountains, pure stone mountains, and mixed mountains. All three types are valid. A sand heap, however, is not valid. Other mountains that are smaller than the size of an elephant are not valid. From the size of an elephant up to the size of Mount Sineru, they are valid. If there are four mountains in the four directions, or three mountains in three directions, it is proper to authorize the Sīmā with only those four or three mountain landmarks. With two landmarks...
319:
It is not proper to authorize with only one landmark. The same method applies to other landmarks such as stone landmarks. Therefore, one who designates a mountain landmark should ask, "Is this mountain continuous or not?" If it is continuous, it should not be made (as multiple landmarks). This is because even if one announces it in four or eight directions, only one landmark is announced. Therefore, for a mountain that stands surrounding a monastery in a circular shape, after announcing it as a landmark in one direction, for other directions, that mountain should be kept outside and other landmarks should be announced inside.

If one wishes to include one-third or one-half of a mountain within the Sīmā, one should not announce the mountain as the landmark, but rather announce one of the landmarks such as a tree or an anthill growing on that mountain beyond the area one wishes to include inside. If one wishes to include an entire mountain of one or two yojanas in size within the Sīmā, one should announce landmarks such as trees or anthills growing on the ground beyond the mountain.

Regarding stone landmarks—an iron ball also falls under the category of stone. Therefore, any stone is valid. In terms of size, a stone the size of an eight-cubit elephant falls under the category of a mountain, and therefore that stone is not valid. However, a stone the size of a large ox or a large buffalo is valid. As a lower limit, a stone the size of a lump of molasses (guḷapiṇḍa) weighing thirty-two palas is valid. A stone smaller than that, or a brick even if it is large, is not valid. A heap of stones insufficient to be a landmark is also not valid, let alone heaps of earth or sand. If there is a rock slab level with the ground like a threshing floor, or a stone rising from the ground like a tree stump, it is valid if it meets the size requirements. Even if a rock slab is very large, it still falls under the category of stone. Therefore, if one wishes to include a portion of a large rock slab within the Sīmā, one should not announce that rock slab as the landmark, but should announce another stone on top of it as the landmark. If a monastery is built on a rock slab, or if a rock slab pierces through the middle of a monastery, such a rock slab is not valid. This is because if one announces it as a landmark, the monastery would be on top of the landmark; since a landmark is naturally outside the Sīmā, the monastery would also fall outside the Sīmā. A rock slab that surrounds a monastery should be announced as a landmark in one place and should not be announced in other places.

Regarding forest landmarks—a grass forest or a forest of trees with heartwood in the bark such as palms, coconuts, and so forth, is not valid. However, a forest of trees with heartwood inside such as teak (sāka) or sal (sāla), or a forest mixed with trees having internal heartwood, is valid. Indeed, such a forest must consist of at least four or five trees...
320:
A forest of trees is allowable as a boundary marker (nimitta). Such a forest must consist of at least four or five trees; if there are fewer than that, it is not allowable. At the maximum, even one that is a hundred yojanas in extent is allowable. However, if a monastery is built in the middle of a forest, the forest should not be designated as the nimitta. Those who wish to establish a portion [of the forest] within the boundary should not designate the forest itself, but should designate the trees, stones, etc., within that forest. A forest that surrounds a monastery should be designated in one place and not in another.

Regarding the tree nimitta (rukkha-nimitta): Trees whose strength is in the bark, such as the palmyra or coconut, are not allowable. A living tree with heartwood (antosāra) is allowable, even if it is at least eight finger-breadths in height and has a girth the size of a stylus; if it is smaller than that, it is not allowable. At the maximum, even a well-established banyan tree (nigrodha) twelve yojanas in size is allowable. A tree of the required size that has been grown from a seed in a bamboo tube, a reed tube, or a small pot is not allowable. However, if it is removed from such a tube, planted in the ground at that moment, a mound is made, and it is watered, then it is allowable to designate it. The emergence of new roots or branches is not a requirement [for it to be valid]. However, in the case of a tree planted by cutting the trunk, the emergence of new roots and branches is appropriate. When designating, one may say "tree" (rukkha), or "teak tree" (sāka-rukkha), or "sal tree" (sāla-rukkha). A single connected tree, like a large well-established banyan, should be designated in one place and not in another.

Regarding the road nimitta (magga-nimitta): Forest paths, field paths, river paths, and tank paths are not allowable. A footpath or a cart road is allowable, provided it is a road that passes through two or three villages. If a footpath diverges from a cart road and then returns to the same cart road, or if there are footpaths and cart roads that are not in use, they are not allowable. Only roads that are constantly used by groups of people or caravans of carts are allowable. If two roads emerge and then merge into one like the pole of a cart, they should be designated once at the point of divergence or at the point of convergence, and not designated again, because they constitute a single connected nimitta.

If four roads surrounding a monastery go in the four directions, if one is designated in the middle, another should not be designated, because they constitute a single connected nimitta. However, a road that passes through the corner of the monastery may be designated on the other side. A road that passes through the middle of the monastery should not be designated, because the monastery would then be situated above the designated nimitta. If the inner wheel-track of a cart road is made the nimitta, the road is outside the boundary (sīmā). If the outer wheel-track is made the nimitta, only the outer wheel-track is outside the boundary, and the rest belongs within the boundary.
321:
## Road Nimitta
A monk designating a road as a nimitta may do so using any of the ten names, such as "magga", "pantha", "patha", or "pajja". A road that surrounds a monastery in the manner of a moat should be designated in one place and not designated again in another.

## Anthill Nimitta
Regarding the anthill nimitta (vammika-nimitta), the decision is: at the minimum, an anthill that has grown on the day of designation, being eight finger-breadths in height and the size of a cow's horn, is allowable. If it is smaller than that, it is not allowable. At the maximum, even one as large as the Himalaya mountains is allowable. An anthill that surrounds a monastery and is a single connected entity should be designated in one place and not designated again in another.

## River Nimitta
Regarding the river nimitta (nadī-nimitta), the decision is: during the time of righteous kings, if the rain falls every half-month, every ten days, or every five days without fail, a river whose current is interrupted merely because the clouds have cleared does not count as a "river". A river counts as a "river" if, during such a time of good rainfall, the current is not interrupted throughout the four months of the rainy season, and if a bhikkhunī crossing at any point would have her inner robe (antaravāsaka) soaked, covering the three circles (the knees and the waist). For monks establishing a boundary, this can be a nimitta. This same definition of a river applies to a bhikkhunī crossing to the other side, to the performance of Sangha-kamma such as the Uposatha, and to the consecration of a boundary on the other side of the river.

A river that flows around a monastery in the shape of a cart-pole or a moat, like a road, should be designated in one place and not designated again in another. The same principle applies to a group of four rivers that flow through the four directions of a monastery and intersect. However, four rivers that do not mix may each be designated. If the river's current is blocked with vines, straw, etc., by planting tree trunks as if making a fence, but the water still overflows the obstruction and continues to flow, it is allowable to make it a nimitta. If a bridge is made such that the water cannot flow, a river that does not flow is not allowable as a nimitta. In a place where the water flows, it is a river nimitta; in a place where the water stands without flowing, it is allowable to make it a water nimitta (udaka-nimitta).

A river that does not flow because of a lack of water during a drought or in the summer is also allowable. When a canal is drawn from a great river, even if that canal is like a small river and flows constantly, providing for three crops, it is not allowable to make it a nimitta. A canal that emerges from a great river at its source, but over time, by that water...
322:
If a river is diverted through an outlet and flows naturally, and later becomes a river filled with crocodiles and the like, and is navigable by boats and such, it is valid to use that channel as a sign.

Regarding the water-sign (udakanimitta): in a waterless place, it is not valid to fill water into a boat or a jar and the like and proclaim it as a water-sign; only water situated on the ground is valid. Furthermore, that water on the ground must be still water existing in a pit, a square pond, a reservoir, a lake, a salt-well, the ocean, and so on. However, unstable water existing in a fast-flowing river, a flood, or an irrigation channel is not valid. In the Andhaka Commentary, it is said: 'Water drawn from deep pits and the like should not be made a sign.' This statement is poorly said and is merely his own opinion. In fact, even water existing in a hole dug by a pig or in a play-pond of village children, or water filled into a small pit dug in the ground at that moment using jars, is valid—whether it be little or much—provided it remains until the end of the kammavācā. In that place, for the purpose of marking the sign, a heap of stones, sand, or earth, or a stone pillar or a wooden post should be made. It is valid for a monk to make it himself or have another make it. However, it is not valid in a lābhasīmā (boundary for gains). The samānasaṃvāsakasīmā (boundary of common communion) does not oppress anyone; it only facilitates the Vinaya acts of the monks. Therefore, it is valid to [establish signs] in this boundary.

It is valid to designate a boundary with these eight types of signs, whether unmixed or mixed with one another. A boundary thus designated and bound might not be bound by one or two signs, but it can be bound by various signs of the types mentioned, starting from three up to hundreds. If that boundary is bound by three signs, it is triangular (siṅghāṭaka) in shape. If bound by four, it is square, or it may be triangular, crescent-shaped, drum-shaped (mudiṅga), and so on. If bound by more signs than that, it will have various shapes. Monks wishing to bind that boundary should inquire about the boundary limits of the respective monasteries from the monks of nearby monasteries. They must leave a boundary-interval (sīmantarika) from the boundaries of monasteries with established boundaries, and a precinct (upacāra) from the boundaries of monasteries without established boundaries. At a time when there is no movement of monks from other places, if they wish to bind a boundary within a single village territory, they must send a message to the monks in the monasteries with established boundaries in that village, saying, 'We will bind a boundary today; do not go outside your own boundary limits.' As for the monks in monasteries without established boundaries, they must be gathered together in one place, and the consent (chanda) of those monks entitled to give consent must be brought. If other village territories...
323:
...are also intended to be included within [the boundary], the monks residing in those villages must also come. Mahāsumma Thera said that the consent of those who do not come must be brought. Mahāpaduma Thera, however, said: 'Various village territories are like separately bound boundaries; consent and purity (pārisuddhi) do not come (apply) from them. Only the monks who have entered within the signs must come.' He further said: 'At the time of designating a samānasaṃvāsakasīmā, both coming and not coming are valid. But at the time of designating an avippavāsasīmā, the monks who have entered within the signs must come, and the consent of those who do not come must be brought.'

When the monks have thus assembled and the consent of those entitled to give consent has been brought, for the purpose of quickly bringing visiting monks into the hatthapāsa (hand-reach) or keeping them outside the boundary at various paths, river landings, village gates, and so on, monastery attendants and novices should be stationed. After giving a signal with a drum or a conch and proclaiming the signs, the boundary should be bound with the kammavācā beginning with 'Listen to me, venerable sirs, the Saṅgha.' Only at the conclusion of the kammavācā, having excluded the signs to the outside and taking the water that supports the earth below as the limit, is the boundary established.

Monks designating this samānasaṃvāsakasīmā should first bind a khaṇḍasīmā (small boundary) to easily perform Saṅgha acts such as pabbajjā (going forth) and upasampadā (ordination). When binding that khaṇḍasīmā, the proper practice (vatta) should be known. If it is bound in a monastery where all structures such as the Bodhi tree, the cetiya, and the refectory have already been established, it should not be bound in the middle of the monastery where many people gather, but in a secluded spot at the edge of the monastery. If it is bound before the monastery is built, the locations for the Bodhi tree, cetiya, and so on should be carefully noted so that when those structures are established, the boundary will be in a secluded spot at the edge of the monastery. It is valid if that boundary, at its minimum limit, can accommodate 21 monks. If it accommodates fewer than that, it is not valid. It is valid even if it accommodates more than a thousand monks. When binding that boundary, stones suitable as signs should be placed around the boundary courtyard (sīmāmāḷaka). Monks standing in a khaṇḍasīmā must not bind a mahāsīmā (great boundary), and monks standing in a mahāsīmā must not bind a khaṇḍasīmā. Only by standing in a khaṇḍasīmā should a khaṇḍasīmā be bound; only by standing in a mahāsīmā should a mahāsīmā be bound.

In this regard, the procedure for binding is as follows: Having proclaimed the signs all around, such as 'This stone is a sign,' the boundary should be designated with the kammavācā. Then, for the sake of making that very boundary firm, the avippavāsa-kammavācā should be performed. In this way (when the avippavāsa-kammavācā is performed), [thinking] 'We shall abolish the boundary'...
324:
Those who come will not be able to uproot the boundary (sīmā). After the boundary has been established, stones should be placed in the boundary interval (sīmantarika) outside the boundary. The boundary interval is valid if it is at least one cubit in measure. In the Kurundī, it is stated that even a span in measure is valid; in the Mahāpaccariya, it is stated that even four finger-breadths in measure is valid. If the monastery is large, two, three, or even more small boundaries (khaṇḍasīmā) should be established.

After establishing the khaṇḍasīmā in this manner, when the time comes to establish the great boundary (mahāsīmā), the bhikkhus should leave the khaṇḍasīmā and, standing within the mahāsīmā, circumambulate the khaṇḍasīmā in order, reciting the marks (nimittas) of the stones in the boundary interval. Thereafter, having recited the remaining marks of the mahāsīmā, and without leaving the forearm's length (hatthapāsa), they should establish the boundary of common affiliation (samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā) with the formal act (kammavācā). To make that boundary firm and stable, the formal act for the boundary of non-separation from the three robes (avippavāsa-kammavācā) should also be performed. If this is done, those bhikkhus who come with the intention of uprooting the boundary will not be able to do so. If they recite the marks of the khaṇḍasīmā, then the marks of the boundary interval, and then the marks of the mahāsīmā—having thus recited the marks in these three places—it is proper to first establish whichever boundary they desire. Even so, it should be established starting from the khaṇḍasīmā according to the method already mentioned. When the boundaries have been established in this way, bhikkhus standing in a khaṇḍasīmā do not invalidate the formal act of bhikkhus performing a formal act in the mahāsīmā; nor do those standing in the mahāsīmā invalidate the act of those in a khaṇḍasīmā. However, those standing in the boundary interval do not invalidate the acts of those performing acts on either side. But those standing in the boundary interval do invalidate the acts of those performing acts while standing in the village territory (gāmakhetta). This is because the boundary interval belongs to the village territory.

This so-called boundary is not considered established only when it is established on the ground. Indeed, if it is established on a rock surface, in a hut-dwelling, in a cave, in a palace (pāsāda), or on a mountain top, it is truly established. When establishing a boundary on a rock surface, one should not make a mark by carving a line or digging a mortar-like hole on the rock surface; rather, stones suitable for marks should be placed and the marks recited. At the conclusion of the formal act, the boundary descends as far as the water that supports the earth. Since the marking stones do not remain in their original positions, a line should be carved around them, or stones should be engraved at the four corners, or letters should be inscribed saying, "This is the limit of the boundary." Some envious people, saying "We will burn the boundary," set fire to it; only the stones burn, not the boundary.
325:
When establishing a boundary in a hut-dwelling (kuṭigeha) on the ground, the bhikkhus should not recite the wall as a mark, but should include the space for twenty-one bhikkhus inside, place stone marks, and establish the boundary; the boundary exists only within the walls. If there is no space for twenty-one bhikkhus within the walls, the stone marks should be placed nearby and the boundary established. If even this is not sufficient, the marks should be placed at the place where the eaves-drop water falls outside and the boundary established. In a boundary established in this way, the entire hut-dwelling is situated within the boundary.

In a cave (leṇa) with four walls, those establishing the boundary should not recite the walls but only the stones. If there is no space inside, the marks should be placed nearby. If that is not sufficient, the stone marks should be placed at the place where the eaves-drop water falls outside, the marks recited, and the boundary established. Thus, the boundary exists both inside and outside the cave.

On the upper floor of a palace (pāsāda), the boundary should be established by placing stones inside without reciting the walls. If it is not sufficient, stones should also be placed nearby and the boundary established. A boundary established in this way exists only on the upper floor of the palace and does not descend below. However, if the wall on the lower floor of a palace built upon many pillars and above beams and rafters is within the marks, and thus rises and remains connected as one with the beams and wooden structures, it also descends below. A boundary established on the upper floor of a single-pillar palace descends below if there is space for twenty-one bhikkhus at the top of the pillar. If the boundary is established by placing stones on the projecting ends of beams (niyyūhaka) and such, which extend from the palace walls, the palace walls are within the boundary. Whether that boundary descends below or not should be understood according to the method already stated. Those reciting marks on the lower floor of a palace should not recite the walls or the wooden pillars. However, it is proper to recite stone pillars that are attached to the walls. A boundary recited in this way exists only within the pillars at the edge of the lower palace. If the wall of the lower palace is connected to the upper floor, it also ascends to the upper palace. If the marks are made at the place where the eaves-drop water falls outside the palace, the entire palace is situated within the boundary.
326:
If there is a surface on a mountain top sufficient for twenty-one monks, they may establish a boundary (sīmā) there as if on a flat rock. Below the mountain, the boundary extends down according to that same limit. On a mountain shaped like the base of a palm tree, a boundary established above also extends below. If a mountain is shaped like a canopy, having space for twenty-one monks above but no space below, the boundary established above does not extend below. Similarly, whether it is shaped like a mudiṅga drum or a paṇava drum, if there is no sufficient measure for a boundary below or in the middle, the boundary established above does not extend below. If between two nearby peaks, neither peak alone is sufficient for the measure of a boundary, one should fill the gap between the peaks with bricks or stones, or fill it with earth or sand to make it continuous, and then establish the boundary above.

If there is a mountain shaped like a cobra's hood, and a boundary is established because there is sufficient measure above, if there is an open space (cavern) below, the boundary does not extend down. If, however, there is a hollow rock in the middle with sufficient measure for a boundary, it extends down. That rock is considered to be within the boundary. If the wall of a cave below stands touching the edge of the peak, the boundary extends down; it exists both below and above. If below, there is a cave inside that exceeds the limit of the upper boundary, the boundary does not extend to the outside. If there is a cave outside within the limit of the upper boundary, the boundary does not extend inside. If the boundary limit above is narrow and the cave below is wide, exceeding the boundary limit, the boundary exists only above and does not extend below. If the cave has the minimum measure for a boundary and the upper boundary is large and covers it, the boundary extends down. If the cave is very narrow and does not have the measure of a boundary, the boundary exists only above and does not extend below. If half of that boundary breaks and falls, even if it has the measure of a boundary, the part that fell outside is not the boundary. If the remaining part that has not fallen has the measure of a boundary, it remains a boundary.

If a khandasīmā (small boundary) has a low foundation and is filled with earth to make it high, it remains a boundary. If a house is built on a boundary, it is still the site of a boundary. If a pond is dug in a boundary, it remains a boundary. If a flood flows over the boundary circle, it is permissible to perform a saṅghakamma (legal act of the Sangha) by building a scaffold on the boundary platform (sīmāmāḷaka). If there is an underground river below the boundary, a monk with psychic powers might sit in that river. If that river existed first and the boundary was established later...
327:
...it does not invalidate the act (kamma). If the boundary was established first and the river came later, it invalidates the act. However, a monk standing on the ground below the boundary [by psychic power] certainly invalidates the act.

If there is a vaṭa tree (Banyan) in a sīmāmāḷaka, and its branch or an aerial root extending from it touches the ground of a mahāsīmā (great boundary) or trees growing in that mahāsīmā, the act should be performed only after clearing the mahāsīmā, or those branches and aerial roots should be cut to keep them outside. Monks who have climbed onto branches that do not touch [the other boundary] must be brought within the hatthapāsa (forearm's length). Similarly, if a branch or an aerial root of a tree growing in a mahāsīmā stands in a sīmāmāḷaka in the manner described, the act should be performed only after clearing the boundary in the same manner, or those branches and aerial roots should be cut to keep them outside.

If an act is being performed in a sīmāmāḷaka and a monk enters the sīmāmāḷaka and sits on a branch suspended in the air (coming from a mahāsīmā), if his feet reach the ground or his robes touch the ground, it is not proper to perform the act. But it is proper to perform it if he is made to lift his feet and robes. This characteristic should also be understood in the previously mentioned method. This is the distinction: in the previous method, it is not proper to perform it by lifting [feet/robes]; he must simply be brought within the hatthapāsa. If a mountain rises into the sky from within the boundary, a monk standing on that mountain must be brought within the hatthapāsa. The same applies to a monk who enters the inside of a mountain by psychic power. Why? Indeed, a boundary established by kammavācā does not extend to a place without measure. Anything like a mountain growing in an established boundary, if it is connected to the established boundary at any place, it is counted as the boundary itself.

140. Regarding the term 'tiyojanaparamaṃ': The maximum measure for that boundary is three yojanas; therefore, it is called 'tiyojanaparama'. A monk establishing it should stand in the middle and establish it so that it is one and a half yojanas in each of the four directions. If, standing in the middle, they make it three yojanas in each direction, it is not proper because it becomes six yojanas. A monk establishing a square or triangular boundary should establish it so that it is three yojanas from corner to corner. If it exceeds three yojanas by even a hair's breadth at any edge, an offense is committed, and the boundary is not a valid boundary.

Regarding the term 'nadīpāraṃ': It is called 'nadīpāra' because it spans the river; it means a boundary that covers the river. In this 'nadīpāra' boundary, the characteristics of a river should be understood according to the method already stated in the section on river-marks (nadīnimitta).
328:
## The characteristic of a river is exactly as described in the section on river-marks (nadī-nimitta).

Regarding the phrase "Yatthassa dhuvanāvā vā" (where there is a permanent boat), it means there should be a boat that constantly plies the ferries at the place where the boundary (sīmā) is being established. At the very least, that boat must be capable of carrying three people, including the oarsman. Even if that boat is taken away for some purpose, either upstream or downstream, with the intention of returning, or if it is stolen by thieves, it is still considered a "permanent boat" (dhuvanāvā) if it will certainly be recovered. If the boat's moorings are broken by the wind and it is carried into the middle of the river by waves, it is still a permanent boat if it must certainly be brought back. Even if it is placed on dry land because the water has receded, or if it is kept for maintenance such as plastering or coating with resin, it remains a permanent boat. However, if it is broken or if its planks have come apart and it is ruined, it is not suitable (for establishing a boundary). Elder Mahāpaduma, however, said: "Even if a boat is borrowed temporarily and placed at the site of the boundary establishment, and the marks (nimitta) are proclaimed, it is still a permanent boat."

On this point, Elder Mahāsumma said: "The mark and the boundary are completed only by the formal act (kammavācā), not by the boat. However, since the Blessed One authorized a permanent boat, establishing a boundary is valid only with a boat that is regularly present."

Regarding the phrase "Dhuvasetu vā" (or a permanent bridge), it means there should be a bridge made of a raft of logs, or one joined with planks, or a footbridge, or a large bridge suitable for the passage of elephants, horses, and so on. At the very least, even a small single-log bridge made by cutting down a tree at that moment for people to cross is counted as a "permanent bridge" (dhuvasetu). However, if one cannot cross by that bridge even by holding onto ropes or vines tied above with one's hands, it is not suitable.

Regarding the phrase "Evarūpaṃ nadīpārasīmaṃ sammannituṃ" (to authorize such a boundary across a river), it means that if such a permanent boat or permanent bridge exists at the ferry crossing directly facing the boundary, the Buddha authorizes the establishment of a boundary that spans the river. If a permanent boat or permanent bridge is not at the ferry crossing directly facing the boundary, but exists slightly upstream or downstream, it is also valid. Elder Karavīkatissa, however, said: "It is valid if it is within the distance of a gāvuta."

A monk establishing this boundary across a river should stand on one bank and proclaim the mark on the riverbank upstream. From there, enclosing the area as much as he desires, he must proclaim the mark on the riverbank downstream at the end of that desired extent. Then, he must proclaim the mark on the riverbank at the spot directly opposite on the other bank. From there, according to the extent he desires, he should proclaim marks along the riverbank until he reaches the spot directly opposite the first mark proclaimed upstream, and then bringing it back...
329:
...it must be connected with the first proclaimed mark. Then, having made all the monks standing within the marks come within the forearm's length (hatthapāsa), the boundary should be established with the formal act (kammavācā). Monks who are in the river but do not come (to the assembly) do not invalidate the formal act. At the conclusion of the establishment, excluding the river, the far bank and this bank within the marks become a single boundary. The river, however, is not counted as an established boundary (baddha-sīmā), for it is separately a river-boundary (nadī-sīmā) only.

If there is a small island (dīpaka) in the river, a monk who wishes to include that island within the boundary should proclaim the marks on the bank where he stands, just as in the previous method, and then proclaim marks at the near edge and the far edge of the island. Then, having proclaimed a mark at the spot directly opposite the mark on this bank of the river, as well as on the far bank, and starting from that mark, he should proclaim marks as far as the spot directly opposite the first mark proclaimed upstream, just as in the previous method. Then, having proclaimed marks at the far edge and the near edge of the island, and bringing it back, it must be connected with the first proclaimed mark. Then, having made all the monks on both banks and on the island come within the forearm's length (hatthapāsa), the boundary should be established with the formal act (kammavācā). Monks who are in the river and do not come do not invalidate the formal act. At the conclusion of the establishment, excluding the river, the two banks and the island within the marks become a single boundary; the river, however, remains only a river-boundary (nadī-sīmā).

If the island is longer than the extent of the monastery boundary (vihara-sīmā) either upstream or downstream, one should proclaim a mark at the near edge of the island directly opposite the mark that defines the monastery boundary. Starting from that mark and enclosing the tip of the island, one should proclaim a mark at the far edge opposite the mark at the near edge of the island. After that, starting with the opposite mark on the far bank as in the previous method, one should proclaim the marks on the far bank and the marks at the far and near edges of the island, and then make the connection with the first proclaimed mark. A boundary established by proclaiming in this way has the shape of a mountain (pabbata-saṇṭhāna).

If the island is longer than the extent of the monastery boundary both upstream and downstream, one should make the connection of marks by proclaiming marks while enclosing both tips of the island, just as in the previous method. A boundary established by proclaiming in this way has the shape of a mudiṅga drum (mudiṅga-saṇṭhāna).
330:
If the small island is small within the limits of the monastery boundary (vihāra-sīmā), the marks (nimittas) should be proclaimed on the small island according to the first method among all methods for small islands. A boundary thus proclaimed and authorized has the shape of a drum (paṇava).

## The Discussion on the Authorization of Boundaries is Finished.

## Discussion on the Uposatha House, etc.

'Anupariveṇiyaṃ' means in each enclosure in a large monastery with a single boundary. 'Asaṅketena' means without making an appointment. 'Ekaṃ samūhanitvā' means removing one [Uposatha house] by a formal act (kammavācā).

'Yato pātimokkhaṃ suṇāti' means that wherever a monk sits within arm's length (hatthapāsa) of other monks and listens to the Pātimokkha, the Uposatha is considered performed for him. This is stated according to the incident; in fact, for a monk sitting within arm's length, even if he does not hear it, the Uposatha is still considered performed.

'Nimittā kittetabbā' means that at the front of the Uposatha house, marks such as small or large stones, bricks, pieces of wood, or sticks should be proclaimed, having made a sign in an open space or on a terrace (māḷaka) or anywhere else. Alternatively, 'nimittā kittetabbā' means that marks such as mountains (suitable as marks) or mats (unsuitable as marks) should be proclaimed to know the limits.

In the phrase 'the assembly of senior monks (theras) first,' if the Great Elder (Mahāthera) does not arrive first, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). In the phrase 'all should assemble in one place and perform the Uposatha,' if the old monastery is in the center of the monastery complex and has enough space for the monks to sit, they should assemble there and perform the Uposatha. If the old monastery is weak and cramped, and another later-built monastery is not cramped, the Uposatha should be performed in that monastery.

In the passage 'wherever the Elder monk dwells,' if the Elder's dwelling is sufficient for all and is comfortable, the Uposatha should be performed there. If that dwelling is in a remote or uneven place, the Elder should be told: 'Venerable sir, your dwelling is in an uncomfortable place; there is no room for all the monks here...'
331:
"...'There is room in such-and-such a monastery; it is proper to go there.' If the Elder does not come, his consent (chanda) and purity (pārisuddhi) should be brought, and the Uposatha performed in a comfortable place sufficient for all.

## The Discussion on the Authorization of the Boundary for Not Being Separated [from the Three Robes]

'Andhakavinda' is a village named Andhakavinda, three gāvutas from the city of Rājagaha. The Elder (Mahākassapa) lived depending on that village. While coming from there to Rājagaha to perform the Uposatha, [this incident occurred]. All eighteen great monasteries (mahāvihāras) surrounding Rājagaha were of a single boundary; the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) had established their boundary. Therefore, it means he was coming to provide the harmony of the Saṅgha at the Veḷuvana monastery. 'Crossing the river' means while crossing the river named Sippinikā. 'He was almost swept away' means he reached a state of nearly being carried off. That river flows from Mount Gijjhakūṭa with a violent current. The Elder, not paying attention to the water flowing with force, was almost swept away; however, he was not actually swept away, but his robes became wet from the splashing waves.

From the time this formal act (kammavācā) arose—'The Saṅgha authorizes that boundary as a boundary for not being separated from the three robes (ticīvara-avippavāsa), excluding the village and the village precinct'— the previous formal act is no longer valid for monks. This is because this formal act alone is firm and lasting. For nuns (bhikkhunīs), however, this is not valid; only the previous one is valid. Why? Because the community of nuns lives within the village. If it were so, they would not be able to have the privilege of the three robes (ticīvara-parihāra) by this formal act, yet they also have such a privilege; therefore, only the previous one is valid. For the community of nuns, both types of boundaries are obtainable. Among them, it is proper to authorize a boundary for nuns even by overlapping the monks' boundary or within the monks' boundary. For monks, the same method applies to the nuns' boundary. This is because they do not complete the quorum for each other's acts, nor do they make the formal act divided. Here, market towns (nigama) and cities (nagara) are also included under the name 'village' (gāma).

'Village precinct' (gāmūpacāra) means the enclosure for a fenced village, and the space suitable for an enclosure for an unfenced village. A monk who has determined his three robes (adhiṭṭhita-ticīvarika) does not receive protection (the privilege of not being separated from robes) in those villages and village precincts.
332: In this way, the avippavāsa-sīmā of the monks does not overlap the village or the village precincts; only the samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā overlaps them. Between these two types of boundaries, the samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā exists by its own nature. The avippavāsa-sīmā, however, exists only where the samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā exists. This is because there is no separate proclamation of marks (nimitta) for that avippavāsa-sīmā. Among these, if a village exists at the time of establishing the avippavāsa-sīmā, that boundary does not overlap the village. If a village is established later after the boundary has been designated, that village also comes under the designation of the avippavāsa-sīmā. Just like a village established later, an area that expands later from a village established earlier also comes under the designation of the avippavāsa-sīmā. If houses were built at the time of establishing the boundary and there was the intention to reside, saying "we will enter and live here," but people have not yet entered, or if they have abandoned an old village along with the houses and gone elsewhere, that place is considered a non-village, and the avippavāsa-sīmā overlaps it. However, if even a single family has entered or arrived to reside, it remains a village, and the avippavāsa-sīmā cannot overlap it. "Monks, in this way, the avippavāsa-sīmā which is not separate from the three robes should be abolished"—in this statement, the monk who wishes to abolish the boundary must know the duty (vatta). Herein, this is the duty: standing in a khaṇḍa-sīmā, one should not abolish an avippavāsa-sīmā; likewise, standing in an avippavāsa-sīmā, one should not abolish a khaṇḍa-sīmā. One standing in a khaṇḍa-sīmā should abolish only a khaṇḍa-sīmā; likewise, one standing in another avippavāsa-sīmā should abolish another avippavāsa-sīmā. Boundaries are abolished for two reasons: to make a naturally small boundary large for the expansion of the monastery, or to make a naturally large boundary small to provide space for other monasteries. In such abolishing, if they know both the khaṇḍa-sīmā and the avippavāsa-sīmā, they will be able to both abolish and establish them. Even if they know the khaṇḍa-sīmā but do not know the avippavāsa-sīmā, they will still be able to abolish and establish them. Those who do not know the khaṇḍa-sīmā but know only the avippavāsa-sīmā, standing in places free from doubt such as the courtyard of a shrine (cetiya), the courtyard of a Bodhi tree, or an uposatha hall, might be able to abolish it; however, they will certainly not be able to re-establish it. If they were to establish it, they might cause an overlap of boundaries (sīmā-sambheda), turning a monastery with a boundary into one without a boundary; therefore, it should not be abolished. Those who know neither of the two boundaries will be able to neither abolish nor establish them. A boundary becomes a non-boundary either through a formal act (kammavācā) or through the disappearance of the Dispensation (sāsana). Those who do not know the boundary cannot perform the formal act; therefore, it should not be abolished. Indeed, only after knowing it well should it be abolished and established.
333: ## Discussion on Village Boundaries and Others. Having thus shown the state of common communion (samānasaṃvāsa) and the performance of a single uposatha (ekūposatha) by means of established boundaries (baddha-sīmā), he now says, "Monks, in a boundary that is not established, not defined," etc., in order to show that state even in places with unestablished boundaries (abaddha-sīmā). In that passage, "aṭṭhapitāya" means "not defined." By the mention of "village" (gāma), "city" (nagara) is also included here. In those villages, cities, or market towns, whatever area the administrators of that village receive taxes from, whether that area is small or large, it is designated only as a village boundary (gāma-sīmā). The same method applies to city boundaries and market town boundaries. Even within a single village territory, if the king demarcates a certain area saying, "Let this be a separate village," and gives it to someone, that area also becomes a visuṃgāma-sīmā (separate village boundary). Therefore, that visuṃgāma-sīmā and other natural village, city, and market town boundaries are just like established boundaries; however, they do not receive the privilege of being separate from the three robes (ti-cīvara-vippavāsa-parihāra). Having thus shown the definition of boundaries for those living in villages, he now says, "And in a place where there is no village," etc., in order to show the definition of boundaries for those living in the forest. In that passage, "agāmake ce" (in a place where there is no village) refers to a forest area not defined by village, market town, or city boundaries. Or, if a monk lives in a forest like the Vijjha forest, the extent of seven abbhantara (satta-abbhantara) all around from the place where he stands is called the samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā. This boundary also receives the privilege of being separate from the three robes. Therein, one abbhantara is twenty-eight cubits in length. For a monk standing in the middle, the seven abbhantara all around, when measured through (as a diameter), amount to fourteen abbhantara. If two groups of the Sangha perform separate legal acts of the Vinaya, another single abbhantara should be placed between those two sets of seven abbhantara for the sake of the precinct (upacāra). The remaining discussion concerning the satta-abbhantara boundary should be understood according to the method stated in the commentary on the Udositasikkhāpada in the Mahāvibhaṅga. "Monks, all rivers are not established boundaries"—in this statement, even if one proclaims the marks for a river that possesses the characteristics of a river, saying, "We shall make this an established boundary," it remains a non-established boundary. However, that river is naturally like an established boundary; it is proper to perform all Sangha acts in that river. The same method applies to the ocean and natural lakes (jātassara). Herein, a natural lake (jātassara) refers to a lake that was not dug by anyone but is a naturally formed depression filled with water coming from all around.
334:
In this way, having rejected the status of a bound boundary (baddha-sīmā) for rivers, oceans, and natural lakes, and wishing to show the definition of an unbound boundary (abaddha-sīmā) in those rivers and so forth, the Buddha said: "Monks, in a river..." and so on. In that Pali text, "a water-splash by a man of average strength" refers to the area defined by the splashing of water upwards and around by a man of average strength.

How should the water be splashed? Just as dice-players throw a wooden ball, so too should a man of average strength take either water or sand in his hand and throw it with all his might. The place where the water or sand thus thrown falls is called one water-splash distance (udakukkhepa). A monk who stands within that water-splash distance but outside the forearm's length (hattha-pāsa) invalidates the legal act. As the assembly increases, the water-splash boundary also increases. The measurement is exactly one water-splash distance from the edge of the assembly. The same method applies to natural lakes and oceans.

Among these rivers, if a river is not too long and the Saṅgha sits from the source to the mouth without breaking the forearm's length, there is no need for a specific water-splash boundary act; the entire river is sufficient for those monks. The statement made by the Elder Mahāsumma, "In a river flowing for one yojana, one should leave the upper half-yojana and perform the act in the lower half-yojana," was rejected by the Elder Mahāpaduma. Indeed, the Blessed One only stated the measurement of a river as: "The inner robe of a bhikkhunī who crosses [a river] is wetted at whatever place while covering the three circles (the two knees and the navel)"; He did not mention a yojana or a half-yojana. Therefore, by the power of this Pali text, it is permissible to perform a Saṅgha act from the source of a river that has the characteristics previously mentioned.

If many monks perform separate acts in this river, all of them must leave another water-splash distance between their own water-splash limit and that of others for the purpose of a boundary interval (sīmantarika). It is stated that more than that distance is permissible, but less than that is not. The same method applies to natural lakes and oceans.

When monks go to perform an act in a river, if the river water is full to the brim, they should perform the act within the river itself, even if they have to wear a water-bathing robe. If they are unable to do so, they should perform it while standing on a boat. However, it is not permissible to perform the act on a moving boat. Why? Because the boundary is only the extent of a water-splash, and the boat passes that water-splash distance very quickly. If this happens, the motion (ñatti) would occur in one boundary and the proclamation (anusāvana) in another. Therefore, the boat must be stopped either by an oar or by [tying it to] a rock...
335:
...by tying it to a tree growing within the river, or by hanging onto it, the act should be performed. It is permissible to perform the act while standing on a scaffold built within the river or on a tree growing within the river.

However, if a branch of a tree growing in the river, or an aerial root extending from it, rests upon a monastery boundary (vihāra-sīmā) or a village boundary (gāma-sīmā) on the riverbank, the act should be performed only after clearing the boundary or cutting the branch. It is not permissible to perform the act by tying a boat to a branch or an aerial root of a tree growing on the riverbank that has entered the river. Monks wishing to perform the act must clear the boundary, or else destroy the connection to the land by cutting that branch. Tying a boat to a stake driven into the riverbank and standing in it to perform the act is also not permissible.

When a bridge is built across a river, if the bridge itself and the bridge pillars are located only within the river, it is permissible to perform the act while standing on the bridge. However, if the bridge or the bridge pillars rest upon the bank outside the river, it is not permissible to perform the act; it must be done only after clearing the boundary. If the bridge pillars are within the river but the bridge itself is in the air above both banks, it is permissible. If there is a rock or a small island in the river, any part of it that is submerged by water throughout the four months of the normal rainy season, as previously mentioned, is counted as part of the river. However, a place submerged by a flood only during a time of excessive rain should not be taken as the river; that place is counted only as part of the village boundary.

Those who draw a canal from a river may build a weir in the river; if the water flows either over or through that weir, it is permissible to perform the act in all places where the water flows. However, if the current is cut off by a weir or a blockage and the water does not flow, it is not permissible to perform the act in the place where the water does not flow. It is also not permissible to perform the act on top of the weir. If some part of the weir is submerged by water like the aforementioned rocks and islands, it is permissible there, because that part is counted as part of the river. When a lake is made by destroying a river and an embankment is built below, if the water comes and fills the lake and remains stagnant, it is not permissible to perform the act in this lake. It is permissible in the upper part where the water flows, and from the place where the diverted water overflows and flows back into the river below. It is also permissible in a dry river during the winter and summer seasons when it is not raining. It is not permissible in a canal drawn from a river.
336:
If that dug canal breaks over time and becomes a river, it is valid (for performing Saṅghakamma). If a certain river shifts its course over time, encroaching upon a village or town and flows (continuously throughout the four months of the rainy season) over the village or town boundary, it is considered a river; it is valid for performing Saṅghakamma. However, if it encroaches upon a consecrated boundary (baddha-sīmā) connected to a monastery, it is reckoned only as a monastery boundary (vihara-sīmā).

In the ocean as well, for monks performing a Saṅghakamma, it is not valid to do so in a place where swelling water or natural waves surge and overflow with force. The place where natural waves overflow and settle is called the 'inner ocean' starting from the edge of the water; a Saṅghakamma should be performed while standing there. If the force of the waves is troublesome, it should be performed while standing on a boat or a platform. The decision regarding those boats and platforms should be understood in the same way as mentioned for the river. In the ocean, there may be a rocky plateau; sometimes waves come and overflow it, and sometimes they do not. It is not valid to perform a Saṅghakamma there, because that rocky plateau is reckoned only as a village boundary (gāma-sīmā). However, if it is always overflowed by natural water, whether waves come or not, it is valid. If there is a small island or a mountain, and if that island or mountain is in a remote place where fishermen cannot go and return within a day, it is reckoned only as a forest boundary (arañña-sīmā). If it is on this side of the limit where they can go and return within a day, it is reckoned as a village boundary. In that place, it is not valid to perform a Saṅghakamma without clearing the village boundary. If the ocean overflows and stays over a village boundary or a town boundary, it is considered the ocean; it is valid to perform a Saṅghakamma there. If it overflows a monastery boundary, it is reckoned only as a monastery boundary.

For monks performing a Saṅghakamma in a natural lake (jātassara), if there is no water for drinking or washing hands and feet as soon as the rain stops during the rainy season as mentioned before, and it dries up, this is not a jātassara; it is reckoned only as village land. A Saṅghakamma should not be performed there. If the water remains continuously during the rainy season as mentioned before, this alone is called a jātassara. In whatever part of that jātassara the water remains throughout the four months of the rainy season, it is valid to perform a Saṅghakamma there. If the water is deep, it is valid to perform it while standing on a platform that is tied, or on a platform tied to a tree growing inside the jātassara. The decision regarding rocky plateaus and small islands in this jātassara is the same as mentioned for the river. A jātassara that is sufficient for performing Saṅghakamma during a time of normal rainfall is valid for performing Saṅghakamma there even if it dries up and becomes waterless during a time of drought or during the summer or winter. The statement in the Andhaka Commentary, 'Every natural lake (jātassara), when dry...' (should not be accepted).
337:
"...when it is waterless, it resorts only to the village land"—that statement should not be accepted. If, in this lake, they dig a hole or a pond etc. for the sake of water, that place becomes a non-natural lake (ajātassara) and falls within the category of a village boundary (gāma-sīmā). The same principle applies when gourds, cucumbers, etc., are planted.

If they fill that lake and make it dry land, or if they build an embankment on one side and turn the whole thing into a large reservoir, it all becomes a non-natural lake and falls only within the category of a village boundary. A salt lake also falls within the category of a natural lake (jātassara). It is valid to perform a Saṅghakamma in a place where water remains throughout the four months of the rainy season.

"They mix boundary with boundary" means they mix another's consecrated boundary (baddha-sīmā) with their own boundary. If, to the east of an old monastery, there are two trees, a mango tree and a jambu tree, with branches intertwined, and of those trees, the jambu tree is to the west of the mango tree. If the monastery boundary was consecrated by including the jambu tree inside and designating the mango tree as the mark (nimitta). Later, if monks building a new monastery to the east of that monastery and consecrating a boundary include that mango tree inside and designate the jambu tree as the mark, the boundary is mixed with the boundary. The group of six monks (chabbaggiya) did this; therefore, it is said, "They mix boundary with boundary."

## They overlap boundary with boundary means they overlap another's consecrated boundary with their own boundary.

They consecrate their own boundary by including the whole of another's consecrated boundary or a part of that boundary within it. Regarding the phrase "to consecrate a boundary leaving a boundary-interstice (sīmantarika)," if the boundary of the monastery built first has not yet been consecrated, the precinct (upacāra) of the boundary should be left. If it has been consecrated, a boundary-interstice of about one cubit (hattha) from the furthest edge should be left. In the Kurundī, it is said that even about one span (vidatthi) is valid, and in the Mahāpaccari, even about four finger-breadths (caturaṅgula) is valid. A single tree can also be a mark for two boundaries, but as it grows, it causes the mixing of boundaries (sīmā-saṅkara); therefore, it should not be made a mark.

## Uposathabhedādikathā

In the phrase "the Uposatha of the 14th day and the 15th day," in the preliminary duties (pubbakicca) of the 14th day Uposatha, it should be said, "Today is the Uposatha of the 14th day."
338: Regarding the phrases beginning with "Adhammena vagga," the Vinaya should be understood as follows: If four monks reside in a monastery and three of them perform the Pārisuddhi-uposatha after bringing the purity of consent (chanda-pārisuddhi) from one monk; or if three monks reside and two of them recite the Pātimokkha after bringing the purity of consent from one monk, it is an unlawful and incomplete (adhammena vagga) Uposatha act. If all four monks assemble and perform the Pārisuddhi-uposatha, or if three or two monks recite the Pātimokkha, it is called an unlawful and complete (adhammena samagga) Uposatha act. If among four persons, three recite the Pātimokkha after bringing the purity of one; or if among three persons, two perform the Pārisuddhi-uposatha after bringing the purity of one, it is called a lawful and incomplete (dhammena vagga) Uposatha act. If all four residing in one place assemble and recite the Pātimokkha, or if three assemble and perform the Pārisuddhi-uposatha, or if two perform the Pārisuddhi-uposatha with each other, it is called a lawful and complete (dhammena samagga) Uposatha act. ## Pātimokkhuddesakathā Having recited the Nidāna (Introduction), the rest should be made known by the word 'heard' (suta). This means: having recited this Pātimokkha Nidāna, "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs... [as in the text]... for one who has revealed it, there is comfort," one should say, "Venerable sirs, the Nidāna has been recited. Therein, I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this? A second time I ask... [as in the text]... thus I bear this in mind. Venerable sirs, the four Pārājika rules have been heard... [as in the text]... they should be practiced without dispute." In this manner, the Pārājika-uddesa and the rest following the Nidāna are made known by the word 'heard'. By this method, the remaining four types of Pātimokkha recitations should also be understood. "Savarabhaya" refers to the danger from forest-dwelling people (forest thieves). Regarding the terms beginning with "Rājan-tarāya," the distinctions should be understood as follows: While monks are sitting with the intention, "We shall perform the Uposatha," if a king arrives, this is the danger from a king (rājan-tarāya). If thieves arrive, this is the danger from thieves (cora-ntarāya). If a forest fire approaches, or if a fire breaks out in the residence, this is the danger from fire (aggi-ntarāya). If rain clouds arise, or if a flood comes, this is the danger from water (udaka-ntarāya). If many people arrive, this is the danger from humans (manussa-ntarāya). If a non-human (yakkha) seizes a monk, this is the danger from non-humans (amanussa-ntarāya). If fierce wild beasts such as tigers arrive, this is the danger from wild beasts (vāḷa-ntarāya). If creatures such as snakes bite a monk, this is the danger from reptiles (sarīsapa-ntarāya). If a monk becomes ill, or passes away, or if enemies seize him wishing to kill him...
339:
...this is the danger to life (jīvitantarāya). If people seize one or many monks wishing to make them fall away from the holy life (brahmacariya), this is the danger to the holy life (brahmacariyantarāya). When such dangers exist, the Pātimokkha should be recited in brief, or the first section (uddesa) should be recited, or the first two, three, or four sections. Furthermore, if a danger arises while the second or subsequent sections are being recited but not yet finished, that section should also be made known only by the word 'heard' (suta).

"Anajjhiṭṭha" means not commanded, not urged, or not requested. Here, the invitation (ajjhesanā) pertains to the monk appointed by the Sangha to preach or to the Elder of the Sangha (saṅghatthera). In the absence of such an appointed preacher, one may preach if one asks the Elder or is requested by him. Even for the Elder, if there are many Dhamma-preachers (dhammakathika) in the monastery, they should be told in turn: "You preach the Dhamma," "Explain the Dhamma," or "Give the gift of Dhamma." If one is told "Osārehi" (Recite the text), one only has the right to recite the Pali. If told "Kathehi" (Explain), one only has the right to explain the meaning. If told "Sarabhaññaṃ bhaṇāhi" (Chant in a melodic style), one should only chant. The Elder, while sitting on a high seat, does not have the right to request [another to preach]. If both a preceptor (upajjhāya) and a student (saddhivihārika) are present, and the preceptor, sitting on a high seat, says "Preach," the student should resolve to recite (sajjhāya) and then preach. If there are junior monks present, one should preach with the thought "I shall preach to them."

If the Elder in the monastery only allows his own dependents to preach and does not invite others who are sweet-voiced, the other monks should say, "Venerable sir, let us have the monk named so-and-so preach." If he says "Let him preach" or remains silent, it is proper to have him preach. If he forbids it, he should not be made to preach. If the listening to Dhamma has already begun before the Elder arrives, there is no need to stop and ask for permission when he arrives. A monk who is explaining the meaning after reciting the Pali should explain it whether he has asked permission or not; the same rule applies even if the Elder arrives while he is explaining.

In the "upanisinnakathā" (talk given to those sitting nearby), the Elder is also the authority. Therefore, he should preach himself or tell another monk, "Preach." However, he should not do so while sitting on a high seat. It is proper, however, to tell laypeople, "Preach." If laypeople ask a monk they know, that monk should ask the Elder before preaching. If the Elder is asked, "Venerable sir, these people are asking a question"...
340:
If he says "Preach" or remains silent, it is proper to preach. This same method applies when entering a house for Anumodanā and so forth. If the Saṅghatthera, whether in the monastery or in a house, gives permission saying, "You may preach even without asking me," it is considered a valid allowance; it is proper to preach in all places.

A monk performing Sajjhāya (recitation) must also ask the Thera. If another Thera arrives while one is reciting after having asked one Thera, there is no need to ask again. If one stops to rest and another Thera arrives, one must ask again when restarting. This same method applies to a monk who has already started reciting before the Saṅghatthera arrives. If a Saṅghatthera gives permission saying, "Recite as you wish even without asking me," it is proper to recite as one pleases. However, if another Thera arrives, one should recite only after asking that Thera.

"One should authorize oneself" means one authorizes oneself. A monk who wishes to ask [a question] should look at the assembly, and if there is no danger to himself, the Vinaya should be asked.

153. "Even when permission is given, after weighing the person" means investigating thus: "Is there danger to me from this person or not?" "Puramhākaṃ" means "first to us." "Paṭikacceva" means "especially beforehand." "To grant permission after weighing the person" means it is allowed to grant permission after investigating thus: "Will he speak of a true offense or an untrue offense?"

## Discussion on Protesting Unlawful Acts and so forth

An unlawful act (adhammakamma) is as previously explained. "Paṭikkosituṃ" means to protest or prevent. "To also make one's view known" means to declare one's view in the presence of another thus: "This act is an unlawful act; I do not approve of it." Mentioning "four or five" etc., is for the purpose of those monks being free from danger. "Knowingly not making them hear" means they recite softly while intending, "We will recite so that others do not hear."

155. "Therādhikaṃ" means related to the Thera, or having to follow the Thera's will. There is also a variant reading "Therādheyyaṃ." Therefore, the Thera himself should recite, or he should urge another. The procedure for urging here is the same as that mentioned in the Dhamma-jjhesana (invitation to preach).

In the phrases such as "He grants permission for the Uposatha," He grants permission for the two types of Uposatha: the 14th-day Uposatha and the 15th-day Uposatha; and the nine types of Uposatha (namely: Saṅgha-uposatha, Gaṇa-uposatha, Puggala-uposatha, Suttuddesa-uposatha, Pārisuddhi-uposatha, Adhiṭṭhāna-uposatha, Cātuddasika-uposatha, Pannarasika-uposatha, and Sāmaggī-uposatha). The four types of Adhammavagga-uposatha-kamma, Adhammasamagga-uposatha...
341:
In the phrases such as "Na jānāti uposathaṃ vā" (He does not know the Uposatha), he does not know the two types of Uposatha: Cātuddasī and Pannarasī; he does not know the nine types of Uposatha such as Saṅgha-uposatha; he does not know the four types of Uposatha-kamma; he does not know the two types of Pātimokkha: Bhikkhu-pātimokkha and Bhikkhunī-pātimokkha; he does not know the nine types of Pātimokkhuddesa (recitation of the Pātimokkha).

In the passage "Yo tattha bhikkhu vyatto paṭibalo" (Whichever monk there is competent and capable), although a junior monk who is competent is allowed to recite the Pātimokkha, this is the intention here: If the Thera does not know five, four, or three Pātimokkhuddesas by heart, but two uddesas are unbroken, very clear, and memorized, then the Pātimokkha recitation belongs to the Thera. However, if he cannot even make these two uddesas clear, it belongs to the competent monk.

"Sāmantā āဝāsā" refers to nearby monasteries. "Sajjukaṃ" means for the purpose of returning on that very Uposatha day. In the passage "Naṃ bhikkhuṃ āṇāpetuṃ" (To command a new monk), only a junior monk who is capable of learning should be sent; an incompetent one should not be sent.

## Discussion on Learning the Calculation of the Fortnight and so forth

In the passage "Katimī bhante" (Which day is it, venerable sir?), it is called "katimī" because it completes a certain number of days. "Kālavato" means early in the morning or beforehand.

In the passage "Yaṃ kālaṃ sarati" (Whatever time he remembers), it is proper to inform even in the evening, "Today is the Uposatha day; bear it in mind."

In the passage "Thereṇa bhikkhunā navaṃ bhikkhuṃ āṇāpetuṃ" (The senior monk commanding a new monk), a monk who is always performing some work, or a single monk who bears the burden [of duties], or any one among the Sarabhāṇaka (intoners), Dhammakathika (preachers), etc., should not be commanded to sweep the Uposatha hall. The remaining monks should be commanded in turn. If the commanded monk does not get even a temporary broom, he should sweep after making a suitable branch; if he does not get even that, it is valid with whatever he obtains.

In commanding the preparation of seats, it should be done according to the method already mentioned. If the commanded monk finds no seats in the Uposatha hall, he should bring them from the Saṅghika dwelling, arrange them, and then return them. If there are no seats, it is proper to spread mats or reed mats. If there are no reed mats...
342:
Broken branches should be made allowable and spread out. For a monk who does not obtain an attendant (kappiyakāraka) to make them allowable, what has been obtained is itself allowable.

In lighting a lamp, one should also command in the same manner as mentioned. The commanding monk should say: "In such and such a place, there is oil, or a wick, or a lamp-bowl; take it and do it." If oil and so forth are not available, they should be sought. For a monk who does not obtain them after seeking, what has been obtained is itself allowable. Indeed, fire should also be lit in the bowl.

## Disaṅgamikādivatthukathā

"He should be welcomed" (saṅgahetabbō) means he should be favored with pleasant words such as: "Venerable sirs, it is good that you have come. Alms-food is easy to get here, and there is curry and side dishes. Please stay without being dissatisfied." He should be supported by doing so repeatedly. He should be persuaded by making him give a reply such as "Yes, I will stay." Or else, he should be welcomed and supported with the four requisites. He should be persuaded with pleasant words; it means he should be spoken to with words pleasant to the ear. He should be served with bathing powder and so on.

"An offense of wrong-doing" (āpatti dukkaṭassa) means if the entire Saṅgha does not do it, there is a dukkaṭa offense for all. In performing this service, neither the great elders nor the juniors are exempt; everyone should serve in turn. There is an offense for a monk who does not serve during his turn. However, that learned monk should not consent to the sweeping of the precinct or the giving of tooth-sticks by the great elders. Even so, the great elders should come to the morning and evening service (upaṭṭhāna). Knowing their arrival, that monk should go to serve the great elders first. If he has fellow-monks as attendants, he should say: "I have attendants; may the venerable sirs remain unconcerned." If he has no fellow-monks, but one or two monks endowed with duties in that monastery say: "We will perform the duties for the elder; let the remaining monks live at ease," then there is no offense for anyone.

"That residence should be visited" (sō āvāsō gantabbō) means one should go to that monastery every fortnight for the purpose of performing the Uposatha. And that going is only during the rainy season among the three seasons. To show what should be done during the rainy season, it is said: "Fools and the incompetent spend the vassa..." etc. Therein, "Monks, those monks should not spend the vassa in that residence" means one should not enter the vassa without a reciter of the Pātimokkha in the first vassa (purimikā vassa). If for those who have entered the vassa...

## Pārisuddhidānakathā

"Conveys by the body" (kāyēna viññāpēti) means making the giving of purity (pārisuddhi) known by some part of the body. If he is able to reply by speech, he should convey it by speech. If he is able to do both, he should convey it by both body and speech. "The Saṅgha, having gone there, should perform the Uposatha" means if there are many such sick monks, the Saṅgha, standing in order, should include all the sick monks within the hatthapāsa of the Saṅgha and perform the Uposatha. If the sick monks are many and far apart...
343:
...if he departs, disrobes, or dies, if there is another monk who can recite the Pātimokkha, it is proper to stay in the second vassa (pacchimikā vassa). If there is none, one should go elsewhere. For those who do not go, there is a dukkaṭa offense. But if he departs, disrobes, or dies during the second vassa, one should stay for the full two months (from the full moon of Sāvaṇa to the full moon of Assayuja).

## Pārisuddhidānakathā

"Conveys by the body" means making the giving of purity known or understood by some part of the body. If he is able to speak, he conveys it by speech. If he is able to do both, he conveys it by both body and speech. "The Saṅgha, having gone there, should perform the Uposatha" means if there are many such sick monks, the Saṅgha, standing in order, should have everyone within the hatthapāsa.
