If they are very far apart and the Saṅgha is insufficient, the Uposatha should not be performed on that day; the Uposatha should never be performed by a divided Saṅgha.

"Departs from that very place" means going somewhere from the place where the purity was given without coming to the midst of the Saṅgha. "Acknowledges as a novice" means acknowledging "I am a novice," or reporting the actual state of being a novice, or later remaining in the stage of a novice. This method is the same everywhere.

"Having reached the Saṅgha, he departs" means he departs after reaching the hatthapāsa of the four monks assembled for the Uposatha, which is the minimum requirement. This method is the same everywhere. In this matter of conveying purity, even if one monk conveys the purity of many monks, it is indeed conveyed. However, if that monk, on the way, meets another monk and gives the purity of the monks he is carrying as well as his own, only his own purity arrives. The other purity is called "cat-chain purity" (biḷālasaṅkhalika-pārisuddhi). That purity does not arrive.

"Falling asleep, he does not report" means having arrived, he falls asleep and thus does not report, "Purity was given by so-and-so." In the phrase "There is no offense for the conveyor of purity," if he intentionally does not report, he incurs a dukkaṭa offense, but the purity is indeed conveyed. There is no offense only because of reporting unintentionally (due to forgetfulness). The Uposatha of both monks is indeed valid.
344:
## Discussion on Giving Consent (Chanda-dāna)

Regarding the giving of consent (chanda), the decision is the same as what has already been stated regarding the giving of purity (pārisuddhi). In the statement, "One who gives purity also gives consent," if one gives only purity and not consent, the performance of the Uposatha is accomplished. However, if the Saṅgha performs any other act (kamma) besides the Uposatha act, that act is not accomplished. If one gives only consent and not purity, both the Uposatha act and other acts are accomplished for the Saṅgha of monks; however, for the monk who gave consent, the performance of the Uposatha is not accomplished. Even if a certain monk comes after having determined the Uposatha at a river or within a boundary (sīmā), he is not allowed to remain silent thinking, "I have already performed the Uposatha"; he must give either harmony (sāmaggī) or consent (chanda).

The phrase "sometimes remembers the Uposatha and sometimes does not" means that at one time he remembers and at another time he does not. There is also the case of one who does not remember at all; if a monk does not remember at all, there is no need for the task of granting authorization (sammuti) to him. Even if he does not come, he cannot cause the Saṅgha act to fail.

## Discussion on the Saṅgha Uposatha and Others

In the phrase "having swept that place" (so deso sammajjitvā), the first case (nominative) "so deso" stands in the sense of the second case (accusative). As for the terms such as "drinking water and water for use," their meanings are quite clear. Why is this said? It is said to show the preliminary duties (pubbakaraṇa) and so forth of the Uposatha. Therefore, the teachers of the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) said:

"Sweeping and lighting the lamp,
Setting out water and spreading the seats—
These four are called the preliminary duties (pubbakaraṇa)
of the Uposatha."
Thus, these four are declared as "pubbakaraṇa."

"Hearing the consent and purity, announcing the season,
Counting the monks, and hearing the exhortation (ovāda)—
These five, which are to be done after the preliminary duties,
are called the preliminary tasks (pubbakicca)."
Thus, these five, which are to be performed after the pubbakaraṇa, are declared as "pubbakicca."

"The occurrence of the Uposatha day, the assembly of all monks eligible for the act,
The absence of shared offenses (sabhāgāpatti),
And the absence of excluded persons in that place—
These four are called the proper conditions (pattakalla)."
Thus, these four are declared as "pattakalla."
345:
One should perform the Uposatha together with those arriving monks after performing these preliminary duties and so forth. In the phrase "Today is my Uposatha," if it is the fifteenth-day Uposatha, it is also proper to determine, "Today is my fifteenth-day (pannarasa) Uposatha." The same method applies to the fourteenth-day (cātuddasika) Uposatha.

## Discussion on the Procedure for Remedying Offenses (Āpattipaṭikamma-vidhi)

It should be understood that the rule prescribed by the Blessed One, "The Uposatha should not be performed by one who has an offense," is established by the words beginning with "Whoever may have an offense," as well as by the prescription of giving purity and the prescription of the Purity Uposatha (Pārisuddhi-uposatha). Regarding "an offense of such a name," one should take the name of one of the offenses such as Thullaccaya and say, "a Thullaccaya offense" or "a Pācittiya offense." The phrase "I confess that offense" is well-spoken even if one says, "I confess it in the presence of the venerable ones" or "I confess it in your presence." The question "Do you see it?" should be said as, "Friend, do you see that offense?" or "Venerable sirs, do you see that offense?" The response "Yes, I see it" is well-spoken even if said as, "Yes, venerable sir, I see it" or "Yes, friend, I see it." In the phrase "Restrain yourself in the future," if one is speaking to an elder, one should say, "Please restrain yourselves in the future." The monk who is thus addressed must say, "Very well, I will restrain myself very well."

In the phrase "when he is without doubt," if this monk is not without doubt (i.e., he has doubt), it is stated in the Andhaka Commentary that it is proper to confess only after announcing the matter (vatthu). Herein, this is the procedure for confession: If, while the sun is covered by clouds, a monk eats while doubting, "Is it the right time for us or not?", that monk should announce the matter thus: "Venerable sir, I ate while having doubt. If it was the right time, I have fallen into many Dukkaṭa offenses; if it was not the right time, I have fallen into many Pācittiya offenses." Then he should say, "Venerable sir, whatever many Dukkaṭa or Pācittiya offenses I have fallen into due to that matter of eating, I confess them in your presence." This method applies to all offenses.

In the phrase "Monks, a shared offense (sabhāgā) [should not be confessed]," it refers to an offense which two persons fall into due to the same object, such as eating at the wrong time. Such an offense of the same object...
346:
An offense of a similar nature is called "sabhāgā." A monk who has incurred an offense due to eating at the wrong time (vikālabhojana) is permitted to confess in the presence of a monk who has incurred an offense due to eating food that was not left over (anatirittabhojana). This offense of similar grounds (vatthusabhāgā), when confessed, is indeed well-confessed. However, they both incur an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa); the one who confesses incurs it due to the act of confession, and the one who receives it incurs it due to the act of receiving. Since that dukkaṭa has different grounds (confessing and receiving), they are permitted to confess to each other.

In the phrase "a nearby monk should be addressed thus," it refers only to addressing a monk who is sabhāga (having a similar offense) to oneself. If a visabhāga (one with a dissimilar offense) monk is addressed, it may lead to quarrels, disputes, schism in the Saṅgha, and so on. Therefore, the Andhakaṭṭhakathā states that without speaking to that monk, one should form the intention, "I will rise from this assembly and remedy the offense," and then perform the Uposatha.

## Anāpattipannarasakādikathā
In the Anāpattipannarasaka (the fifteen cases of non-offense), the phrase "they do not know" means they do not know whether others have already entered the boundary (sīmā) or are currently entering it. The phrase "then other resident monks come" means that those monks, having gone to a village or a forest for some business, return to the place where those monks are seated. "Being a group but perceiving unity" means that although they are a group (vaggā) because they have entered the boundary, they perceive it as unity (samaggasaññino) because they are unaware of the entry into the boundary.

In the Vaggāvagga-saññī-pannarasaka, "they know" means that while standing on a mountain or high ground, they see the monks who have already entered or are entering the boundary. The Vematika-pannarasaka is self-evident.

In the Kukkuccapakata-pannarasaka, just as one overcome by desire is called "icchāpakata," so too, monks who are overcome by remorse (kukkucca)—characterized by perceiving the unallowable as unallowable at the moment of the act, even if a decision was made beforehand—should be known as "kukkuccapakata."

In the Bhedapurekkhāra-pannarasaka, a grave offense (thullaccaya) is taught because of the strength of the unwholesome intention.

## Sīmokkantikapeyyālakathā
In the repetition series (peyyāla) concerning resident and incoming monks: just as it was stated in the previous repetition series for resident and resident monks, "they do not know, other resident monks..." and so on, it should be understood in the same way as "they do not know, other incoming monks..." and so forth.
347:
Everything should be understood in this manner. In the repetition series for incoming and resident monks: just as the previous repetition series mentioned "resident monks assemble," here it should be brought in as "incoming monks assemble." In the repetition series for incoming and incoming monks: in both instances, it should be applied by way of incoming monks.

In the statement, "For the resident monks it is the fourteenth-day Uposatha, and for the incoming monks it is the fifteenth-day," it should be understood that those for whom it is the fifteenth-day have either come from another country or have performed the previous Uposatha on the fourteenth day. "They should follow the lead of the resident monks" means that while the resident monks are performing the preliminary duties (pubbakicca), stating "today is the fourteenth-day Uposatha," the incoming monks should follow their lead and not object. "It should not be given without consent" means it must not be given if there is no desire to do so.

## Liṅgādidassanakathā
"Āwāsikākāra" refers to the aspect (ākāra) of the resident monks. This method applies everywhere. "Ākāra" (aspect) refers to the manner of conduct by which it is perceived whether those monks are accomplished in their duties or not, such as through well-arranged couches, stools, etc. "Liṅga" (sign) refers to that which makes known the monks who are hidden in various places; it means it makes them known even if they are not yet seen. "Nimitta" (indication) refers to that which, upon being seen, allows one to know that those monks are present. "Uddesa" (description) refers to that by which those monks are pointed out as having such requisites; it means they receive a designation. All these terms are names for well-arranged couches, stools, etc., as well as for the sound of footsteps and so on. However, they should be applied as appropriate. This same method applies to the aspect (ākāra) of incoming monks and so forth. Therein, "aññātaka" means the property of others. "Pādānaṃ dhotāṃ udakanissekaṃ" refers to the pouring of water from washed feet (foot-washing water). The plural should be understood as singular. Alternatively, there is a reading "pādānaṃ dhotudakanissekaṃ," which means the pouring of water that is the washing of the feet.

In the cases of monks of different communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka) and so forth: "samānasaṃvāsakadiṭṭhi" refers to the view that "these monks are of the same communion (samānasaṃvāsaka) as I am." "They do not ask" means they do not ask about their views (laddhi); without asking, they perform the major and minor duties and conduct the Uposatha together. "They are unable to overcome" means they are unable to suppress or overcome the state of being of different communion; it means they cannot make them give up that view.

## Nagantabbagantabbavārakathā
"Monasteries with monks" refers to those monasteries where there are monks who will perform the Uposatha. From that monastery to whichever monastery one is unable to reach on that very day...
348:
One should not go from a monastery where monks reside to another monastery from which one cannot return on that same Uposatha day, without having performed the Uposatha. One should not go except when apart from monks sufficient to form a Saṅgha, or except for the ten kinds of dangers mentioned previously. However, at the minimum limit, if there are four monks including oneself, or if there is danger, it is allowable to go. An *anāvāsa* refers to any place such as a rest house under construction. Just as one should not go to monasteries and so on, if the Uposatha is performed in a *vihāra-sīmā*, one should not go to a *khaṇḍa-sīmā* or a river for the purpose of the Uposatha determination. If there is a certain monk in that place, it is allowable to go to him. It is also allowable to go to monasteries where the Uposatha has been released; a monk who goes thus also gets the opportunity to make the determination. A forest monk, having wandered for alms in a village on the Uposatha day, should return only to his own monastery. If he enters another monastery, he should return only after performing the Uposatha there; it is not allowable to return without performing it.

If one knows, "I can go to that monastery this very day," one should go to such a monastery. For even if he performs the Uposatha with the monks there, he will not be causing an obstacle to his own Uposatha.

## Vajjaniyapuggala-sandassana-kathā

In the phrases beginning with "*bhikkhuniyā nisinnaparisāya*," the measure is simply reaching the distance of a forearm's length (*hatthapāsa*). "Except for an assembly that has not yet risen" means that the giving of the *pārivāsika-pārisuddhi* is not allowable from the time the assembly has risen, but it is allowable in an assembly that has not yet risen. Therefore, it is said: "*aññatra avuṭṭhitāya parisāya*." Its characteristics should be taken from the description of the *pārivāsika-chanda-dāna* in the *Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga*. "*Anuposathe*" means on a day other than the two Uposatha days, the 14th and the 15th. "*Aññatra saṅghasāmaggiyā*" means except for the concord of the Saṅgha when a divided Saṅgha, like the Kosambī monks, becomes united again. At that time, it should be performed after saying: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me; today is the Uposatha of the concordant Saṅgha." Monks who have postponed the Uposatha for some minor reason and then become concordant again should perform the Uposatha only on the Uposatha day.

## Uposathakkhandhaka-vaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.
349:
## 3. Vassūpanāyika-kkhandhaka

## Vassūpanāyikā-nujānana-kathā

In the *Vassūpanāyika-kkhandhaka*—*apaññatta* means not yet allowed or not yet prescribed. In "*te idha bhikkhū*," it means those monks; the word "*idha*" is a mere particle. *Saṅghātaṃ āpādentā* means bringing about destruction. *Saṅkasāyissanti* means they will live in a fixed residence without concern. *Sakuntakā* means birds. *Vassāne vassaṃ upagantuṃ* means one should enter the Rains for the three months of the season called *Vassāna*. "*Kati nu kho vassūpanāyikā*" is a question: "How many ways are there of entering the Rains?" In the word *aparajjugatāya*, because it has reached the day other than the full moon of *Āsāḷhī* (the 1st day of the waning moon), that day is called *aparajjugatā*; it means on another day after that day has passed. In the second method also, because it has reached one month, it is called *māsagatā*; it means when that one month is completed and passed. Therefore, on the day of the 1st waning moon immediately following the full moon of *Āsāḷhī*, or on the day of the 1st waning moon immediately following the full moon after the *Āsāḷhī* full moon, one should clean the monastery, set out drinking and usable water, complete all respectful duties such as worshipping the shrine, and then enter the Rains by reciting once, twice, or thrice: "I enter the Rains in this monastery for these three months."

## Vassāne-cārikā-paṭikkhepādi-kathā

185-6. In the word "*yo pakkameyya*," an offense should be understood as occurring by going without regard or by letting the dawn rise in another place. In the word "*yo atikkameyya*," offenses should be understood according to the number of monasteries. If on that day one enters and oversteps the precincts of a hundred monasteries, a hundred offenses are incurred. If one oversteps the precinct of one's own monastery but returns without entering the precinct of another monastery, only one offense is incurred. A monk who cannot enter the *purimikā-vassa* (the first retreat) due to some danger should enter the *pacchimikā-vassa* (the later retreat).

*Vassaṃ ukkaḍḍhitukāmo* means wishing to push forward the first month called *Vassa* (the month of *Āsāḷhī*); it means wishing to make the month of *Āsāḷhī* again without making it the month of *Sāvaṇa*. *Āgame juṇhe* means in the coming month. In "Monks, I allow you to comply with kings," because there is no such thing as a decline in virtue etc. for monks in pushing forward the Rains...
350:
(The Buddha) allows (one to follow the wishes of kings); therefore, one should follow (their wishes) in other matters that are consistent with the Dhamma. However, in matters not consistent with the Dhamma, one should not follow anyone's wishes.

## Discussion on the Allowance for Seven-Day Business

187-8. Regarding seven-day business—"to go for seven-day business" means that an activity to be performed within seven days is called 'seven-day business' (sattāhakaraṇīya); the meaning is that (the Buddha) allows going for the sake of that seven-day business. "To go when sent for" means that (the Buddha) allows going only when a messenger is sent by these seven types of persons, such as monks. "Return should be made within seven days" means that one must return within seven days only; the meaning is that the dawn of the eighth day should not be allowed to rise while one is still there.

From the passage "referring to the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha," these three—the latrine (vaccakuṭi), the sweat-house (jantāghara), and the sweat-house hall (jantāgharasālā)—are omitted (from the previously mentioned list).

Terms such as 'udosita' (shed) are the same as those mentioned in the Udositasikkhāpada and others. "Rasavatī" refers to a house for cooking rice (a kitchen). "Vāreyya" (marriage) has already been explained in the Sañcarittasikkhāpada. "Before this Sutta is destroyed" means as long as this Sutta one has learned is not destroyed, as long as this Sutta does not disappear. By the phrase "or if there is some other business or duty for him," all types of prepared duties are included. In all cases, one should go when sent for with the proper words: "I wish to give a gift, to hear the Dhamma, and to see the monks," or with synonymous expressions of those words. The sequence of the ellipsis (peyyāla) should be understood as follows: "A lay follower (upāsaka) has built monasteries and so on for the Saṅgha, for many monks, for one monk, for the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha, for many nuns, for one nun, for many female trainees (sikkhamānā), for one female trainee, for many male novices (sāmaṇera), for one male novice, for many female novices (sāmaṇerī), or for one female novice, or has built a house for his own benefit." Likewise, all should be stated as: "A female lay follower (upāsikā), a monk, a nun, a female trainee, a male novice, or a female novice (has built) for the Saṅgha." In these seven types of duties, one should go when sent for.

## Discussion on the Allowance to Go for Five Types of Persons Even Without Being Sent For

"By the seven-day business of the five types of persons" refers to the business of those fellow practitioners (sahadhammika) such as monks, (thinking:) "I will search for food for the sick, or food for the attendant of the sick, or medicine..."
351:
"...or I will inquire, or I will attend to them." For such reasons explained in detail later, one should go even if a messenger is not sent, let alone when one is sent. One should go to a monk for these ten reasons: the monk is sick, dissatisfaction (anabhirati) has arisen, remorse (kukkucca) has arisen, wrong view (diṭṭhigata) has arisen, he has committed a grave offense (garudhamma) and is worthy of probation (parivāsa), he is worthy of being sent back to the beginning (mūlāyapaṭikassanā), he is worthy of penance (mānatta), he is worthy of rehabilitation (abbhāna), the Saṅgha wishes to perform a legal act (kamma) against him, or the Saṅgha has already performed a legal act. One should go to a nun for nine reasons. One should go to a female trainee (sikkhamānā) for six reasons: the first four reasons plus "her training is disturbed" and "she wishes to be ordained." To a male novice (sāmaṇera) also for six reasons: the first four reasons plus "he wishes to ask about the rainy season (vassa)" and "he wishes to be ordained." To a female novice (sāmaṇerī), excluding ordination, one should go for five reasons including "wishing to give the training rules."

In the case where permission is granted for parents later on, the same method applies. However, in the Andhaka Commentary (Andhaka-aṭṭhakathā), it is said: "There are those who attend to parents, whether they are relatives or non-relatives; it is proper to go to them even if a messenger is not sent." This statement is not mentioned in the (Maha) Aṭṭhakathā nor in the Pali; therefore, it should not be accepted.

## Discussion on the Allowance Only When Sent For

"Bhikkhugatika" refers to a man who lives together with monks in a monastery. "Undriyati" means it is destroyed. "Goods have been ordered to be cut" (bhaṇḍaṃ chedāpitaṃ) means building materials such as timber have been ordered to be cut. "They should have them brought" (āvahāpeyyuṃ) means they should cause them to be carried. "I shall give" (dazzāhaṃ) means "I will donate." In the phrase "by the business of the Saṅgha" (saṅghakaraṇီyena), any work to be done for the Uposatha halls and so on, for the lodgings, or for the umbrellas and railings of a stupa, and even down to the personal lodging of a monk—all is considered the business of the Saṅgha. Therefore, to complete that business of the Saṅgha, one should go to bring building materials or to give food and wages to carpenters and others.

Here is the decision regarding the interruption of the night (ratticcheda) that is outside the Pali: It is not proper to go for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma without being invited. If, in a large monastery, an agreement was made beforehand saying, "We shall assemble on such and such a day," then it is considered as being invited and it is proper to go. It is not proper to go of one's own accord thinking, "I will wash my belongings." If teachers, preceptors, and others send one for the sake of robe-work and so on, it is proper to go. If the monastery is in a place that is not too far, to that monastery...
352:
If teachers or preceptors send [a monk] (for matters such as robe-work, etc.), it is permissible to go. If there is a monastery in a place that is not too far, and even if he is unable to reach it with the thought "I will return this very day," it is permissible to go. However, it is not permissible to go for the purpose of learning the Pali text or the Commentaries, etc. But he is allowed to go with a *sattāhakaraṇီya* (seven-day business) with the thought "I will see my teacher." If the teacher says to that monk, "Do not go yet today," it is permissible [to stay]. He is not allowed to go to visit his supporting families or relatives.

## Discussion on Breaking the Rains Retreat Without Offense Due to Danger

Regarding the phrase "going to where the village is," etc., if the village has moved to a place not far away, one must go for alms in that village and return to stay in the monastery itself. If it has moved to a distant place, one must let the dawn rise at the monastery once every seven days. If one is unable to return to the monastery, one must stay in a suitable (*sabhāga*) place in that village. If people offer food such as *salākabhatta* (food by tickets) as they usually do, one must say, "We no longer stay in that monastery." If, despite saying so, they say, "We do not offer to the monastery or the palace; we offer to the venerable ones; please stay and eat wherever you like," then it is permissible to eat as one pleases; that food belongs only to those monks. If they say, "Please have the food brought to where the venerable ones stay and eat," then it should be brought to the place of residence and eaten according to the seniority of the rains (*vassagga*).

If they offer *vassāvāsika* (rains-residence) robes at the time of *Pavāraṇā*, they should be accepted if the monk has let the dawn rise [at the monastery] once every seven days. Monks who have broken the rains retreat, however, must say, "We did not stay there; we are those who have broken the rains retreat." If they say, "Let only the venerable ones who have reached our monastery take them," then they should be accepted. If distributable goods (*vebhaṅgiya-bhaṇḍa*) such as robes deposited at the monastery are brought to this new location to prevent them from being lost, one must go back to that very monastery and inform [the Sangha] before distributing them. The same rule applies to the requisites arising from lands, etc., donated to lay attendants (*kappiyakārakas*) with the instruction, "Provide the four requisites to the venerable ones from these lands, etc." Whether the distributable goods belonging to the Sangha are inside the monastery or outside the boundary (*sīmā*), it is not permissible to distribute them by informing monks who are outside the boundary. However, even if the goods are in both places, it is permissible to distribute them by informing the monks who are inside the boundary.
353:
## Discussion on Breaking the Rains Retreat Without Offense Due to Sangha Schism
Regarding the phrase "The Sangha is split," if the Sangha has already split, there is no duty to go. Indeed, the word "split" is said in reference to the suspicion that "the Sangha will split." In the phrase "The Sangha is split because of many bhikkhunīs," it should not be understood that the bhikkhunīs themselves split the Sangha. Is it not so? For the Blessed One said, "Upāli, a bhikkhunī does not split the Sangha." Indeed, this is said in reference to the suspicion that "monks might split [the Sangha]" by relying on and being encouraged by those bhikkhunīs.

## Discussion on Entering the Rains Retreat in Cattle Pens and Other Places
*Vaja* means the dwelling place of cowherds. Regarding the phrase "to whichever cattle pen," there is no offense for a monk who goes along with that cattle pen even if the rains retreat is broken.

*Upakaṭṭhāya* means when it is near (near the full moon of Āsāḷha). Regarding the phrase "to enter the rains retreat in a caravan (*sattha*)," on the day of entering the retreat, that monk should say to the lay devotees (*upāsakas*), "It would be good if I could get a small hut (*kuṭi*)." If they build and offer one, he should enter it and say three times, "I enter the rains retreat here." If they do not offer one, he should enter the retreat under a cart located within a rest house. A monk who does not get even such a cart should make an *ālaya* (mental resolve). It is not permissible to enter the rains retreat in a caravan [without any arrangement]. *Ālaya* means the mere arising of the thought, "I will stay here for the three months of the rains." If the day of *Pavāraṇā* arrives while the caravan is still on the journey, the *Pavāraṇā* should be performed in that very place. If the caravan reaches the monk's desired destination during the rains and then passes it, he should stay at the desired destination and perform *Pavāraṇā* with the monks there. If the caravan stops at a village along the way during the rains or if the group disperses, he should stay in that village with the monks and perform *Pavāraṇā*; it is not permissible to go to another place from that village without performing *Pavāraṇā*.

A monk entering the rains retreat in a boat must also enter the retreat only in a hut (*kuṭi*). A monk who cannot find one after searching should make an *ālaya*. If the boat remains at sea for the entire three months of the rains, the *Pavāraṇā* should be performed on that boat. If the boat reaches the shore and this monk wishes to go elsewhere, it is not permissible to go. He must stay in the village where the boat landed and perform *Pavāraṇā* with the monks. Even if the boat goes elsewhere along the coast, if the monk wishes to stay only in the village first reached, let the boat go; the monk must stay in that village and perform *Pavāraṇā* with the monks.
354:
Thus, in these three places—a cattle pen, a caravan, or a boat—there is no offense due to the interruption of the rains-retreat (vassaccheda), and one is allowed to perform Pavāraṇā. However, in the cases mentioned previously, starting from "being oppressed by wild beasts" up to the "schism in the Saṅgha," there is only non-offense (anāpatti), but one does not get the chance to perform Pavāraṇā.

"Monks, one should not enter the rains-retreat in a hollow tree." In this statement, it is not allowable to enter the rains-retreat in just a bare tree hollow. However, it is allowable to enter the rains-retreat by making a small hut with a plank roof inside a large tree hollow and fitting an entrance door. It is also allowable to cut a tree and make a small hut with a plank roof on top of the stump. "One should not enter the rains-retreat in the fork of a tree." In this statement also, it is not allowable to enter the rains-retreat in just a bare tree fork. However, one should enter the rains-retreat by building a platform in a large tree fork and making a small hut with a plank roof there. "One who has no lodging should not enter the rains-retreat." This means a monk who does not have a lodging (senāsana) roofed with any of the five types of roofing—grass, leaves, bricks, stone, or plaster—and fitted with a door-fastening, should not enter the rains-retreat. "Monks, one should not enter the rains-retreat in a corpse-hut (chavakuṭī)." A corpse-hut refers to a hut such as a bedstead with carved legs, etc. It is not allowable to enter the rains-retreat there. However, it is allowable to enter the rains-retreat by making another small hut in a cemetery. "Monks, one should not enter the rains-retreat under a sunshade (chatta)." In this statement also, it is allowable to enter the rains-retreat by placing a sunshade on four posts, making an enclosure, and fitting a door; this is called a "sunshade-hut" (chattakuṭikā). "One should not enter the rains-retreat in a jar." In this statement also, it is allowable to enter the rains-retreat by making a hut with a large pot-sherd in the manner described for the sunshade.

## Discussion on Unrighteous Agreements and So Forth

"An agreement of such a nature." In this statement, it means that an unrighteous agreement of such a nature, other than the agreement to ordain a novice during the rains-retreat, should not be made. The characteristics of such an agreement have been stated in the Mahāvibhaṅga.

207-8. "There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in the promise." In this statement, an offense is not incurred merely by promising to enter the rains-retreat by saying, "Stay for the rains-retreat in this monastery for these three months." An offense of wrong-doing is also incurred in various promises such as, "Accept alms-food for these three months; we both will stay for the rains-retreat here; we will have the Pali texts recited together." Indeed, that offense of wrong-doing occurs because, although the mind was pure at the time of the initial promise, one later breaks the word. However, for a monk whose mind was not pure even at the time of the initial promise, there is a pācittiya offense for the promise and a dukkaṭa offense for breaking the word; thus, the dukkaṭa offense is combined with the pācittiya.
355: In the phrases "He is not to be done on that very day" (so tadahēva akaraṇīyo) and so on, the decision should be understood as follows: If one departs without entering the rains retreat, or if after entering one spends seven days outside, and the earlier rains retreat (purimikā vassa) is not evident, there is an offense of wrong-doing due to the promise. For a monk who departs on the very day of entering the rains retreat before dawn with a seven-day commitment (sattāha-karaṇīya) promising to return within seven days, there is no offense if he returns within seven days. Needless to say for one who stays for two or three days and returns within seven days. In the words "having stayed for two or three days," it should be understood that the rains retreat is broken if one crosses the monastery precincts (upacāra) without any concern (for returning). If there is concern and attachment, thinking "I will stay here," but one fails to enter the rains retreat due to lack of mindfulness, the accepted dwelling (senāsana) is considered well-accepted; he is not one who has broken the rains retreat and he certainly gets the opportunity to perform Pavāraṇā. In the words "seven days before the Pavāraṇā," it is appropriate to go starting from the 9th day of the waxing moon of Assayuja. Whether he returns or not, there is no offense. The remaining words are clear. ## Conclusion of the Commentary on the Vassūpanāyika-kkhandhaka.
356:
## 4. Pavāraṇākkhandhaka
## Discussion on Living Uncomfortably

In the Pavāraṇākkhandhaka—regarding the phrase "we shall neither greet nor converse with one another," *ālapa* means the first speech, and *sallapa* means the subsequent speech. "By *hatthavilaṅghaka*" means by raising the hand (gesturing with hands and feet). "Living like animals (*pasusaṃvāsa*)" refers to living in the manner of animals. Indeed, animals do not inform one another of the happiness or suffering that arises for them, nor do they perform mutual greetings (*paṭisanthāra*); likewise, these monks did not do so. Therefore, their living together is called "living like animals." This method is the same in all places. "Monks, the vow of silence (*mūgabbata*), which is an undertaking of the sectarians, should not be practiced" means that such an undertaking of a vow as "I shall not speak for these three months of the rains-residence" should not be made, because this is an unlawful covenant (*adhammakatikā*). "Mutual compliance (*aññamaññānulomatā*)" means the state of being compliant for the purpose of speaking to one another. Indeed, it is possible to say something only to a monk who says, "Venerable sirs, let the venerable ones speak to me," but not to the other. "Rising from offenses and putting the Vinaya first" means the state of rising from offenses and the state of conducting oneself by putting the Vinaya at the forefront. Indeed, it is said that a monk who speaks thus, "Venerable sirs, let the venerable ones speak to me," will rise from offenses and will dwell putting the Vinaya first.

"Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. Today is the Pavāraṇā day. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform Pavāraṇā." This motion (*ñatti*) is called "all-inclusive" (*sabbasaṅgāhikā*). When this is said, it is proper to perform Pavāraṇā with a three-fold, two-fold, or one-fold statement. It is not proper for those of equal seniority (*samānavassika*). However, when it is said, "Let them perform Pavāraṇā with a three-fold statement," only the three-fold statement is proper, not any other. When it is said, "Let them perform Pavāraṇā with a two-fold statement," both the two-fold and three-fold statements are proper, but the one-fold statement and Pavāraṇā by those of equal seniority are not proper. When it is said, "Let them perform Pavāraṇā with a one-fold statement," the one-fold, two-fold, and three-fold statements are all proper, but only Pavāraṇā by those of equal seniority is not proper. When it is said, "by those of equal seniority," all forms of Pavāraṇā are proper.

"They stay (*acchanti*)" means they remain seated and do not rise. "During that interval (*tadamantarā*)" means in that interval, meaning for that much time.
357:
## Discussion on the Different Types of Pavāraṇā
Between the Pavāraṇā on the fourteenth day and the Pavāraṇā on the fifteenth day, for the fourteenth-day Pavāraṇā, the preliminary duties should be performed thus: "Today is the fourteenth-day Pavāraṇā." For the fifteenth-day Pavāraṇā, (the preliminary duties should be performed thus:) "Today is the fifteenth-day Pavāraṇā."

In the acts of Pavāraṇā, if five bhikkhus reside in a monastery and, having brought the Pavāraṇā of one bhikkhu, the four bhikkhus perform Pavāraṇā after setting forth a group motion (gaṇa-ñatti); or if four or three bhikkhus reside and, having brought the Pavāraṇā of one bhikkhu, the three or two bhikkhus perform Pavāraṇā after setting forth a Sangha motion (saṅgha-ñatti); all such Pavāraṇā acts are unlawful and incomplete (adhamma-vagga).

If all five bhikkhus assemble together and perform Pavāraṇā after setting forth a group motion; or if four, three, or two bhikkhus assemble together and perform Pavāraṇā after setting forth a Sangha motion; all such Pavāraṇā acts are unlawful and complete (adhamma-samagga).

If among five bhikkhus, having brought the Pavāraṇā of one bhikkhu, the four bhikkhus perform Pavāraṇā after setting forth a Sangha motion; or if among four or three bhikkhus, having brought the Pavāraṇā of one bhikkhu, the three or two bhikkhus perform Pavāraṇā after setting forth a group motion; all such Pavāraṇā acts are lawful and incomplete (dhamma-vagga).

If all five bhikkhus assemble together and perform Pavāraṇā after setting forth a Sangha motion; or if four or three bhikkhus assemble together and perform Pavāraṇā after setting forth a group motion; or if two bhikkhus perform Pavāraṇā toward each other; or if a bhikkhu residing alone performs Pavāraṇā by determination (adhiṭṭhāna-pavāraṇā); all such Pavāraṇā acts are called lawful and complete (dhamma-samagga).

## Discussion on the Authorization of Giving Pavāraṇā
In the phrase "if Pavāraṇā is given," when Pavāraṇā is thus given, the bhikkhu who conveys the Pavāraṇā should approach the Sangha and perform Pavāraṇā as follows: "Venerable sirs, the bhikkhu Tissa invites the Sangha by what is seen, heard, or suspected. Venerable sirs, may the Sangha speak to him out of compassion; seeing the fault, he will make amends. For the second time... for the third time, venerable sirs, the bhikkhu Tissa invites the Sangha... he will make amends." If that bhikkhu is a senior elder (venerable), one should say, "Venerable sir, the Venerable Tissa..." In this way, the conveyor of Pavāraṇā is said to perform Pavāraṇā for the benefit of that bhikkhu Tissa.
358:
Regarding the phrase "The monk giving Pavāraṇā also gives consent (chanda)": the giving of consent should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Uposathakkhandhaka. In this Pavāraṇakkhandhaka as well, the giving of consent is for the sake of the remaining acts (kamma) other than Pavāraṇā. Therefore, if a monk giving Pavāraṇā gives consent, and the Pavāraṇā is brought in the manner stated, then both that monk and the Sangha have indeed performed Pavāraṇā. 

If he gives only Pavāraṇā but not consent, and when that monk's Pavāraṇā is announced and the Sangha has performed Pavāraṇā, the Pavāraṇā is well-performed for everyone; however, any act other than the Pavāraṇā act is invalidated (kuppati). If he gives only consent but not Pavāraṇā, the Sangha's Pavāraṇā and the remaining acts are not invalidated, but that monk has not performed Pavāraṇā. On the day of Pavāraṇā, a monk who arrives after having determined Pavāraṇā outside the boundary (sīmā) should also give consent; by doing so, the Sangha's Pavāraṇā act is not invalidated.

Regarding the phrase "Today is my Pavāraṇā": if it is a Pavāraṇā to be performed on the fourteenth day, it should be determined thus: "Today my Pavāraṇā is the fourteenth-day Pavāraṇā." If it is to be performed on the fifteenth day: "Today my Pavāraṇā is the fifteenth-day Pavāraṇā."

The passage beginning with "An offense is incurred by performing Pavāraṇā on that day" is just as previously stated.

## Discussion on Non-offense on the Fifteenth Day, etc.

"Should perform Pavāraṇā again" means that after performing the preliminary duties again and setting the motion (ñatti), Pavāraṇā should be performed starting from the Sangha Elder (saṅghatthera). The rest should be understood in the same manner as stated in the commentary on the Uposathakkhandhaka.

"Visiting monks should follow the resident monks" means they should perform only this preliminary duty: "Today is the fourteenth-day Pavāraṇā." The same method applies during the turn of the fifteenth-day Pavāraṇā. "Resident monks should go outside the boundary and perform Pavāraṇā"—at the end of this statement is this extracanonical decision (pāḷimuttaka-vinicchaya): If five monks have entered the first retreat (purimikā), and five monks have also entered the second retreat (pacchimikā), when the monks of the first retreat have performed Pavāraṇā after setting the motion, the monks of the second retreat should perform the Uposatha of purity (pārisuddhi-uposatha) in their presence; two motions should not be set in a single Uposatha hall. If the monks who entered the second retreat are four, three, two, or one, the same method applies. If there are four in the first retreat and four, three, two, or one in the second retreat, the same method applies. If there are three in the first retreat and three or two in the second retreat, the same method applies. Herein, this is the defining characteristic: if the monks who entered the second retreat [are...] than the monks who entered the first retreat...
359:
...are fewer or equal, and they complete the group for the Sangha Pavāraṇā, the motion (ñatti) should be set forth by the power of the Sangha Pavāraṇā. If there are three earlier residents and one later resident, together they are four. It is not proper to perform Pavāraṇā for the four by setting forth a Sangha motion. However, for a group motion (gaṇa-ñatti), that person is one who completes the group. Therefore, the motion should be set forth by the power of the group, and Pavāraṇā should be performed together with the earlier residents. The other (the later resident) should perform the Pārisuddhi-uposatha in their presence. If there are two earlier residents and two or one later resident, the method is the same. If there is one earlier resident and one later resident, one should perform Pavāraṇā in the presence of the other, and the other should perform the Pārisuddhi-uposatha. If the later residents are more than the earlier residents by even one, the Pātimokkha should be recited first, and afterwards, the fewer (earlier residents) should perform Pavāraṇā in their presence.

Regarding the Pavāraṇā on the Kattika full moon, if the later residents are more than or equal to the earlier residents who have already performed the Mahāpavāraṇā, the Pavāraṇā should be performed after setting forth the Pavāraṇā motion. After they have performed Pavāraṇā, the others should afterwards perform the Pārisuddhi-uposatha. If the bhikkhus who performed the Mahāpavāraṇā are many, and the later residents are few or only one, after the Pātimokkha has been recited, that person (the later resident) should perform Pavāraṇā in their presence.

Bhikkhus, Pavāraṇā should not be performed without cause, except for the unity of the Sangha. In this context, unity similar to the unity of the Kosambī bhikkhus should be understood. The preliminary duties should be performed thus: "Today is the Pavāraṇā of unity." Those bhikkhus who postpone the Pavāraṇā for some minor reason and then become united should perform Pavāraṇā only on the Pavāraṇā day. Those performing the Pavāraṇā of unity should do so in the interval starting from the first day of the waning moon after the first Pavāraṇā until the Kattika full moon. It is not proper to do so after or before that period.

## Discussion on Pavāraṇā with Two Recitations, etc.
In the context of performing Pavāraṇā with two recitations (dve-vācika), the one setting forth the motion should also say: "If it is suitable for the Sangha, let the Sangha perform Pavāraṇā with two recitations." In the case of one recitation...
360:
...one should say: "Let [the Sangha] perform Pavāraṇā with single recitation." Also for those of equal vassa, one should say: "Let [the Sangha] perform Pavāraṇā for those of equal vassa." In this case, even if there are many of equal vassa, they are allowed to perform Pavāraṇā together.

## Discussion on the Suspension of Pavāraṇā
In the phrase "spoken, uttered, not finished," there are two types of suspension of Pavāraṇā: universal and individual. Among these, in the universal suspension, in the words "Let the Sangha hear me, venerable sirs... let the Sangha perform Pavāraṇā with three-fold recitation," from the syllable 'Su' to the syllable 're', the Pavāraṇā is spoken and uttered but not finished. If one prohibits it even with a single word in this interval, the Pavāraṇā is said to be suspended. It is finished only when reaching the syllable 'yya'; therefore, even if one prohibits it after that, it is as if it were not prohibited.

In the individual suspension, in the words "Venerable sirs, I invite the Sangha... for the third time, venerable sirs, I invite the Sangha by what is seen... seeing, I shall redress (paṭikarissāmi)," from the syllable 'Saṃ' to the final syllable 'ṭi' [in 'paṭi'], the Pavāraṇā is spoken and uttered but not finished. If one prohibits it even with a single word in this interval, the Pavāraṇā is said to be suspended. It is finished only when saying "karissāmi"; therefore, even if one prohibits it when reaching the word "karissāmi", it is as if it were not prohibited. This same method should be understood for two-fold, single, and equal-vassa Pavāraṇās. In these Pavāraṇās as well, the end of the syllable 'ṭi' is the only occasion for suspension.

"Being questioned" (anuyuñjiyamāno) means being asked according to the method to be mentioned later: "Why do you suspend it?" "Having subdued" (omadditvā) means subduing by saying words such as "Enough, monk, do not quarrel." Here, subduing by words is intended by "omaddanā". "Confesses to a groundless accusation" (anuddhaṃsitaṃ paṭijānāti) means confessing thus: "I have groundlessly accused this monk of a Pārājika offense." "According to the rule" (yathādhammaṃ) means dealing with it according to the law: a Pācittiya if the accusation was of a Saṅghādisesa, and a Dukkaṭa if it was of other offenses. "Having destroyed" (nāsetvā) means expelling by destroying the monastic status (liṅga-nāsana).

One should tell that monk, "That offense has been redressed according to the rule," and let him perform Pavāraṇā. One should not say, "Such and such an offense," because saying so is a cause for quarrel.

## Discussion on the Suspension Based on the Matter, etc.
In the phrase "The matter is known, but not the person," it is heard that: Thieves caught fish from a pond in a forest monastery, cooked them, ate them, and left.
361:
That monk, having seen that altered state, or having seen an alteration caused by a rogue within the monastery, reflects: "This act must be the deed of a certain monk," and says: "Let the Saṅgha perform Pavāraṇā, setting aside the incident (vatthu)." This means: "When we come to know that person, then we shall reproach him. For now, let the Saṅgha perform Pavāraṇā." "Speak of him right now" means: "If you have suspicion about any person regarding this incident, point him out right now." If he can point him out, the Pavāraṇā should be performed after investigating that person. If he cannot point him out, Pavāraṇā should be performed saying, "We shall know after investigating and reflecting."

In the statement, "This person is known, but the incident (vatthu) is not," a certain monk has honored a cetiya with flowers, scents, and ointments, or he has drunk ariṭṭha medicine (fermented liquor); that monk has a body odor corresponding to that. That monk (who objects to the Pavāraṇā), referring to that odor, says: "This monk has such a body odor," and wishing to make the incident known, says: "This person is known, but the incident is not." "Let the Saṅgha perform Pavāraṇā, setting aside the person" means let the Saṅgha perform Pavāraṇā excluding that person. "Speak of him right now" means you have set aside a certain person; speak of that person's fault right now. If he says, "This is his fault," the Pavāraṇā should be performed after that person has been cleared. If he says, "I do not know," Pavāraṇā should be performed saying, "We shall know after investigating and reflecting."

"Both this incident and the person are known" means, as in the previous method, having seen the place where thieves caught, cooked, and ate fish, or the place where they bathed with scents and so on, and thinking, "This is the deed of a monk," that monk says so. "Speak of him right now" means speak right now of the person suspected regarding that incident. If both this incident and the person are seen, Pavāraṇā should be performed only after deciding the matter from the time they were seen. "It is proper to speak" means it is proper to reproach; it is suitable to reproach. Why? Because it was not yet decided before the Pavāraṇā, and because the reproach is made after seeing it later. "An offense of pācittiya for reopening (ukkōṭanaka)" means that if monks see both this incident and the person before the Pavāraṇā and perform Pavāraṇā only after deciding the matter, then an offense is committed by the monk who reopens that case.

## Bhaṇḍanakārakavatthukathā

In the phrase, "To perform two or three fourteenth-day (cātuddasī) Uposathas," the fourth and fifth are two, while the third is naturally a fourteenth-day Uposatha anyway.
362:
Therefore, two or three fourteenth-day Uposathas should be performed, such as the third and fourth, or the third, fourth, and fifth. Then, if they hear [that the quarrelsome monks are coming] after the fourth Uposatha has been performed, the fifth Uposatha should be performed as a fourteenth-day Uposatha. Even so, there are two fourteenth-day Uposathas. These monks, acting in this way, will perform the fifteenth-day (pannarasī) Pavāraṇā on either the 13th or 14th day [of the waxing moon of Kattika] for the quarrelsome monks. Those monks performing Pavāraṇā in this way should place novices outside the boundary (sīmā), and upon hearing "Those monks are coming," they should assemble quickly and perform Pavāraṇā. To show this point, it was said: "If, monks, those monks... let them do likewise."

"Asaṃvihitā" means those who are without arrangement, whose arrangements have not yet been made for the purpose of knowing the arrival of the quarrelsome monks, meaning they remain unaware. "Tesaṃ vikkhitvā" means having caused great confusion by such means as saying, "Venerable sirs, you are tired; please rest for a moment."

"No ce labhetha" means if they do not get the opportunity to go outside the boundary, the quarrelsome monks would be constantly followed by novices and junior monks. "Āgame juṇhe" refers to the upcoming full moon of Kattika, where they have made a formal motion (ñatti) saying, "We shall perform Pavāraṇā on the upcoming full moon." On that upcoming full moon day, which is the full moon of Kattika when the kumuda lotuses bloom at the end of the four months of rain, Pavāraṇā must be performed even if they do not wish to; it must certainly be performed, because it is not permissible to perform Pavāraṇā after passing that day. "If, monks, those monks are invited (pavāriyamāne)" means when they are thus invited on the full moon of Kattika at the end of the four months of rain.

## Pavāraṇāsaṅgahakathā

"Aññataro phāsuvihāro" means either tender tranquility (samatha) or tender insight (vipassanā). "Paribāhirā bhavissāma" means we shall be outside of living comfortably, being unable to fulfill the practice of meditation due to unstable night-quarters and day-quarters, etc. By the words "All should assemble together," the giving of consent (chanda) is prohibited. At the time of reconciling a divided Saṅgha, in the settlement by covering over with grass (tiṇavatthāraka-samatha), and in this postponement of Pavāraṇā (pavāraṇā-saṅgaha)—in these three instances, it is not proper to give consent. This so-called postponement of Pavāraṇā should not be given to monks who have neglected their meditation subjects, nor to those with strong tranquility and insight, nor to those who are stream-enters (sotāpanna) and so on. However, for those who have attained tender tranquility and insight, whether they are all, or half, or just one person, it should be given by the power of that one person. When it is given...
363:
In the postponement of Pavāraṇā (pavāraṇā-saṅgaha), there is protection during the rainy season; visiting monks are not allowed to take their lodgings. Those monks also must not be ones who have broken their rains-retreat. To show that they are allowed to set out on a journey even during the interval after performing Pavāraṇā at the end of the four months of rain on the full moon of Kattika, it was said: "If, monks, those..." and so on. The rest of the words are clear throughout the Pavāraṇā-kkhandhaka.

## The Commentary on the Pavāraṇā-kkhandhaka is finished.
364:
## 5. Cammakkhandhaka
## The Story of Soṇa Koḷivisa

In the Cammakkhandhaka—'issariyādhipaccaṃ' means being endowed with both sovereignty as a ruler and lordship as a leader. 'Rajjaṃ' means either the state of being a king or the duties to be performed by a king. In the phrase 'Soṇo nāma Koḷiviso', 'Soṇa' is the name of that merchant's son, and 'Koḷivisa' is his clan. 'Pādatalesu lomāni' means that on the red soles of his feet, there were fine, collyrium-colored hairs that grew beautifully due to past kamma. In a past life, that merchant's son was the leader of eighty thousand men, and together with them, he built and offered a leaf-roofed hall at the dwelling place of a Paccekabuddha. He placed his own splendid woolen rug as a foot-wipe at the spot where the Paccekabuddha would step. For three months, all of them attended to and served the Paccekabuddha. This is the past meritorious deed of that Soṇa and the eighty thousand villagers.

'Asītigāmikasahassāni' refers to the eighty thousand sons of good families living in those villages. 'Kenacideva karaṇīyena' means as if summoned for some business; however, the King had no other purpose than the desire to see Soṇa. When the King gathered those eighty thousand sons of good families, he did so with the thought, 'Soṇa will come without hesitation.' 'Diṭṭhadhammike atthe' means after instructing them in the benefits pertaining to this present world, such as 'Farming, trade, etc., should be done righteously; parents should be supported righteously,' he meant, 'That Blessed One of ours will instruct you in the benefits pertaining to the future life.'

'Bhagavantaṃ paṭivedemi' means 'I shall inform the Blessed One.' 'Pāṭikāya nimujjitvā' means diving into the moonstone [semicircular stone] at the foot of the stairs. 'Yassa dāni bhante bhagavā kālaṃ maṇyati' means 'Venerable Sir, the Blessed One knows the proper time to act for the benefit of those eighty thousand villagers.' 'Vihārapacchāyāyaṃ' means in the shadow at the edge of the monastery. 'Samannāharanti' means they repeatedly reflect on him with the power of devotion. 'Bhiyyosomattāya' means 'Please show a more distinguished miracle once again.' 'Antaradhāyati' means vanishing from sight.

'Lohitenupphuhohoti' means becoming blistered with blood or being smeared with blood. 'Gavāghātanaṃ' means it is like a place where cattle are slaughtered. 'Vīṇāya tantissare' refers to the state of one who is skilled in playing the lute. 'Accāyatā' refers to lute strings that are tuned too tightly and played harshly. 'Saravatī' means being melodious. 'Kammaññā' means being fit for the act of playing. 'Atisithilā' refers to lute strings that are too loose and played poorly. 'Same guṇe patiṭṭhitā' refers to lute strings that are tuned and played at a middle pitch. 'Vīriyasamataṃ adhiṭṭhahā' means 'Establish the equilibrium of energy,' or 'Join energy with tranquility.' 'Yasañca samataṃ paṭivijjhati' means penetrating the equilibrium of the faculties, namely faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. By joining faith with wisdom, wisdom with faith, energy with concentration, and concentration with energy, one can know the equilibrium of the faculties. 'Tattha ca nimittaṃ gaṇှāhi' means 'At that time, while being mindful, one should take the sign (nimitta) of tranquility (samatha), insight (vipassanā), the path (magga), and fruition (phala).'
365:
## Account of the Ordination of Elder Soṇa

'Lohitena phuṭo hoti' means being smeared with blood. 'Gavāghātanaṃ' means a place similar to where cows are killed. 'Kusalo' means one who is skilled in playing the lute. 'Vīṇāya tantissare' means one who is skilled in the sound of the lute strings. 'Accāyatā' refers to the sound that comes out harshly because the strings are played while tuned too tightly. 'Saravatī' means being melodious. 'Kammaññā' means being fit for the act of playing. 'Atisithilā' refers to the sound produced when played poorly. 'Same guṇe patiṭṭhitā' refers to the sound produced when tuned and played at a middle pitch.

'Vīriyasamataṃ adhiṭṭhahā' means 'Establish the equilibrium of tranquility joined with energy,' or 'Join energy with tranquility.' 'Indriyānaṃ ca samataṃ paṭivijjha' means 'Penetrate the state of equilibrium of the faculties such as faith.' In knowing this, join faith with wisdom, wisdom with faith, energy with concentration, and concentration with energy, and thus penetrate the equilibrium of the faculties. 'Tattha ca nimittaṃ gaṇှāhi' means 'While that tranquility exists, take and produce the sign of tranquility, the sign of insight, the sign of the path, and the sign of fruition, which should arise just like a reflection of a face in a mirror.'

'Aññaṃ vyākareyyaṃ' means 'I should make it known that I am an Arahant.' 'Cha ṭhānāni' refers to the six grounds. 'Adhimutto hoti' means standing having penetrated and realized them. The entire passage starting with 'Nekkhamma-adhimutto' is spoken by way of the fruition of Arahantship. This is because Arahantship is called 'Nekkhamma' (renunciation) because it has departed from all defilements; 'Paviveka' (seclusion) because it is secluded from those very defilements; 'Abyāpajja' (non-ill-will) because there is no destructive anger; 'Upādānakkhaya' (destruction of clinging) because it occurs at the end of the path leading to the destruction of clinging; 'Taṇhakkhaya' (destruction of craving) because it occurs at the end of the destruction of craving; and 'Asammoha' (non-delusion) because there is no confusion.

'Kevalaṃ saddhāmattakaṃ' means mere faith that is not mixed with penetrative wisdom of the path, being devoid of the wisdom of the path. 'Paṭicayaṃ' means growth through repeated practice. 'Vītarāgattā' means that because lust has been removed through the penetration of the path, one stands having penetrated Arahantship, which is called 'Nekkhamma'. It means one dwells only in the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) and has a mind inclined only toward that Arahantship. In the remaining terms, the method should be understood in this same way.
366:
Lābhasakkārasiloka refers to the acquisition of the four requisites, the excellence of those requisites, and the speaking of words of praise. Nikāmayamāno means one who desires or longs for. Pavivekādhimutto means declaring Arahantship by saying, "I am intent on the fruition of Arahantship, which is secluded from defilements."

Sīlabbataparāmāsa is merely the misapprehension and clinging to practices such as those of cattle. Sārato paccāgacchanto means knowing by way of essence or excellence. Abyāpajjādhimutto means declaring Arahantship as being free from suffering. In this same manner, the meaning should be understood in all sections.

Bhusā refers to powerful sense objects. Nevassa cittaṃ pariyādiyanti means they are unable to overwhelm and take possession of the mind of that monk who is an Arahant. Amissīkata means the state where defilements do not mix the mind with sense objects. This is because defilements tend to mix the mind with objects; due to the absence of those defilements, the state of being unmixed is called amissīkata. Ṭhitaṃ means the state of being established. Āneñjappattaṃ means having reached the state of imperturbability. Vayañcassānupassatī means seeing both the arising and the passing away of that mind.

Nekkhammaṃ adhimuttassa means the state of one who stands having penetrated the fruition of Arahantship. By the remaining terms, only the fruition of Arahantship is spoken of. The word upādānakkhayassa is in the genitive case (sāmivacana) used in the sense of the accusative (upayoga). Asammohañca cetaso means the state of one who is intent on the fruition of Arahantship, which is the non-delusion of the mind. "Having seen the arising and passing away of the sense bases" refers to disvā āyatanuppādaṃ. Sammā cittaṃ vimuccati means that by the right cause and method, through this practice of insight (vipassanā) and the power of this attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), the mind is liberated from defilements and is intent on the object of Nibbāna. Santacittassa means the state of one with a peaceful mind. Tādino means the state of that Such One (Tādī), who is unshakeable by attraction or repulsion toward desirable or undesirable objects.

## Discussion on the Rejection of Double-layered Sandals, etc.

245. Aññaṃ byākarontī means they declare the fruition of Arahantship or the state of being an Arahant. Attho ca vutto means the meaning by which one is known as an Arahant has been stated. The meaning of the Sutta, however, should be taken only from the Sutta commentary (Suttavaṇṇanā). Attā ca anupanīto means one should not present oneself by saying, "I am an Arahant," through such words and letters. Atha ca panidhekacce moghapurisā means that other vain men, as if joking, declare the non-existent fruition of Arahantship as if it exists merely by words. Ekapālāsi-kaṃ means having a single layer or a single fold...
367:
Single-layered (sandals). In the term asītisakaṭavāha, the load of two carts should be known as one vāha. In the term sattahatthika anīka, a group of seven elephants consisting of six females and one male is called one anīka. Seven such anīkas are called a sattahatthika anīka. Diguṇa means double-layered sandals. Tiguṇa means triple-layered sandals. Gaṇanguṇūpāhana refers to sandals with four or more layers (many-layered).

## Discussion on the Rejection of All-blue Sandals, etc.

Sabbanīlikā means sandals that are entirely blue in color. The same method applies to sandals that are entirely yellow, and so on. Among them, the blue sandals have the color of the flax flower (butterfly pea). The yellow sandals have the color of the Kaṇikāra flower. The red sandals have the color of the Jayasumana flower (hibiscus). The madder-colored sandals have the color of madder dye. The black sandals have the color of a wet soap-nut (or a wet crow's wing). Sandals dyed with mahārangaratta have the color of a centipede's back. Sandals dyed with mahānāmaratta have a mixed color, like the color of a withered leaf. In the Kurundī Commentary, however, they are said to have the color of a red lotus (or a cockscomb flower). If any of these sandals are obtained, one should rub the dye with an old cloth to spoil the color before wearing them. Even if the color is only slightly spoiled, they may be worn.

Nīlakavaddhika refers to sandals where only the straps are blue. The same method applies to straps of other colors. These sandals should also be worn only after spoiling the color. Khallakabaddha refers to sandals made with a heel-cover attached to the heel of the sandal to cover it. Puṭabaddha refers to the boots worn by the Yonaka (Greek/foreigner) people, which cover the entire foot up to the calf. Pāliguṇṭhima refers to wrapped sandals that cover only the top of the foot and not the calf. Tūlapuṇṇika refers to sandals made by stuffing them with cotton. Tittirapattika refers to sandals with ornate straps resembling the wings of a partridge. Meṇḍavisāṇavaddhika refers to sandals made by attaching straps in the shape of a ram's horn (or goat's horn) at the junction of the straps. The same method applies to sandals with goat-horn shaped straps, etc. Vicchikāḷika also refers to sandals made by attaching straps in the shape of a scorpion's tail at that same junction. Morapiñchaparisibbita refers to sandals sewn around the soles or the straps with peacock feathers that resemble threads. Citra means ornate sandals. Among these, if any are obtained, and if it is possible to use them after removing the heel-covers and so on, they should be used after removal. If one uses them while those heel-covers etc. are still present, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Sīhacammaparikkhaṭa refers to sandals made by attaching lion skin to the edges, like the border of a robe. Lūvakacammaparikkhaṭa means...
368:
There are also sandals covered with the skin of a flying fox. If one obtains any of these sandals, one must remove that skin before wearing them.

'Omukka' refers to sandals that have been removed after being worn. 'Nava' refers to new sandals that have not yet been used.

## Discussion on the Prohibition of Wearing Sandals within the Monastery Grounds

'Abhijīvanika' means by means of which craft one makes a living; it means because of that craft. In the phrase "Idha kho taṃ bhikkhave," the word "taṃ" is merely a particle. The meaning is, "Monks, in this Dispensation, you should be graceful." "Yaṃ tumhe" means "those of you." Or it means "if you (should live)." This particle is used in the sense of the word "yadi" (if). In the words beginning with "ācariyesu," the four types of teachers—the teacher for novice ordination (pabbajjācariya), the teacher for full ordination (upasampadācariya), the teacher who gives dependence (nissayācariya), and the teacher who gives instruction in the Pali (uddesācariya)—are all considered teachers here. For a monk with no rains (vassa), a monk with six rains is like a teacher. This is because when that monk reaches four rains, he must live in dependence on the monk with six rains. Similarly, for a monk with one rain, a monk with seven rains; for a monk with two rains, a monk with eight rains; for a monk with three rains, a monk with nine rains; and for a monk with four rains, a monk with ten rains are like teachers. These monks are also just like teachers. The familiar companions of a preceptor (upajjhāya), or any monks who are senior by ten rains, are all called those who are like preceptors. While this many monks are walking on the walking path (caṅkama) without sandals, an offense is committed by a monk who walks on the walking path wearing sandals.

'Pādakhīlābādha' (the foot-stake ailment) refers to the protrusion of flesh from the sole of the foot resembling a stake.

'Tiṇapādukā' refers to sandals made of any kind of grass. 'Hintālapādukā' refers to sandals made of date palm leaves or fan palm leaves. Sandals made of nipa palm leaves are also unallowable. 'Kamalapādukā' refers to sandals made of mountain lotus grass; some also call them sandals made of vetiver grass (usīrapādukā). 'Kambalapādukā' refers to sandals made of wool. 'Asaṅkamanīyā' refers to sandals that are firmly fixed to the ground and cannot be moved.

"Aṅgajātaṃ chupanti" means touching the genitals with the genitals. "Ogāhetvā mārenti" means killing by entering the water and holding firmly.
369:
## Discussion on the Prohibition of Vehicles and So Forth

'Itthiyutta' refers to a vehicle yoked with a cow. 'Purisantara' refers to having a male charioteer. 'Purisayutta' refers to a vehicle yoked with an ox. 'Itthantara' refers to having a female charioteer. 'Gaṅgāmahiyāya' refers to playing at festivals in the Ganges and Mahi rivers. Between a vehicle yoked with an ox (purisayutta) and a hand-drawn vehicle (hatthavaṭṭaka), in the case of the ox-yoked vehicle, it is allowable whether a woman or a man drives it. As for the hand-drawn vehicle, it is allowable whether women or men pull it. 'Yānugghāta' refers to the vibration of the entire body of the person riding the vehicle due to such riding. 'Sivika' refers to a litter made with a bench. 'Pāṭaṅki' refers to a cloth sedan chair made by hanging it from a bamboo pole.

In the words beginning with 'uccāsayana mahāsayana,' 'uccāsayana' refers to a couch that exceeds the prescribed measurements. 'Mahāsayana' refers to unallowable floor coverings. In the words beginning with 'āsandī,' 'āsandī' refers to a seat that exceeds the prescribed measurements. 'Pallanka' refers to a couch made with the figures of wild beasts such as lions and tigers on its legs. 'Gonaka' is a large wool rug with hair longer than four finger-breadths; it is said that the hair of that gonaka exceeds four finger-breadths. 'Cittaka' is a wool rug with patterns made beautiful through weaving. 'Paṭika' is a white rug made of wool. 'Paṭalika' is a red rug made of wool with dense flower patterns; that rug is also called a cloth decorated with emblic myrobalan flowers. 'Tūlika' is simply a mattress made by filling it with natural cotton or floss. 'Vikatika' is a wool rug made beautiful with figures of lions, tigers, and so forth. 'Uddalomī' is a wool rug with hair protruding from one side; there is also a variant reading 'uddhdlomī.' 'Ekantalomī' is a wool rug with hair protruding from both sides. 'Kaṭṭissa' is a bedspread made of gold and silver threads, sewn and surrounded with gems. 'Koseyya' is a bedspread made of silk threads, sewn and surrounded with gems; however, a pure silk covering without gems is allowable.

'Kuttaka' is a wool rug suitable for sixteen dancing girls to stand and dance upon. 'Hatthatthara' and 'assatthara' are simply rugs spread on the backs of elephants and horses. The same method applies to rugs for chariots. 'Ajinappaveṇī' is a rug made by sewing together black antelope skins to the size of a couch. 'Kadalimigapavarapaccattharaṇa' means an excellent bedspread made from the skin of the animal called the kadali-deer (antelope). It is said that they make that rug by spreading and sewing the kadali-deer skin over a white cloth. 'Sauttaracchada' means a bed with an upper covering, together with a red canopy fastened above.
370:
The meaning is: A white canopy is also not allowable if there is an unallowable bedspread underneath; however, if there is none, it is allowable. "Ubhatolohitakūpadhānaṃ" means having red pillows at both the head and foot of the couch; this is not allowable. If there is only one bolster, whether it is red, lotus-colored, or variegated on both sides, it is allowable if it is of the proper size. The Great Pillow (Mahā-upadhāna), however, is forbidden by the Blessed One.

## Sabbacamma-paṭikkhepādi-kathā

"Dīpicchāpa" means a young leopard (leopard cub). "Ogumphiyanti" refers to wrapping and binding around wall posts and the like.

"Abhinisīditum" means to sit leaning against, or to sit making a support. In the phrase "gilānena bhikkhunā saupāhanena," a sick monk refers to one who is unable to enter a village without sandals.

"Kuraraghare" means in the city of that name; by this, his alms-resort village is mentioned. "Papatake pabbate" means on the mountain named Papataka; by this, his place of residence is mentioned. "Soṇa" is his name. Because he wore an ear-ornament worth a crore (ten million), he is called "Koṭikaṇṇa." Koṭikaṇṇa means one who has an ear-ornament worth a crore. "Pāsādikaṃ" means inspiring confidence. "Pasādanīyaṃ" is a synonym for the same meaning. "Uttama-damatha-samathaṃ" means supreme self-control, tranquility, wisdom, concentration, and the calming of body and mind. "Dantaṃ" (tamed) means one who is tamed because all fluctuations of views have ceased; it means one whose defilements are exhausted. "Guttaṃ" (guarded) means one who is protected by the guard of restraint. "Santindriyaṃ" means one with peaceful faculties (one who restrains the faculties). "Nāgaṃ" means one who is free from evil. "Tiṇṇam me vassānam accayena" means after three years have passed from the day of my going forth. "Upasampadaṃ alatthaṃ" means "I have received the higher ordination (upasampadā-kamma)." "Kaṇhuṭṭarā" refers to ground where black fine soil has increased (covered) on top. "Gokaṇṭaka-hatā" refers to ground struck (afflicted) by thorns resembling cow-hooves that have arisen from ground trodden by cow-hooves. Single-layered sandals cannot protect against those thorns; the ground is that rough. "Eragū, moragū, majjārū, jantū" are these four types of grasses. They make mats and coarse mats from these grasses. In this context...
371:
"Eragū" is eraka grass (sedge); it is coarse. "Moragū" grass (peacock grass) has red tips, is soft, and pleasant to the touch. A mat made of that grass, as soon as one gets up from lying down, swells up again and remains so. They also make garments from "majjārū" grass. The color of "jantū" grass is like a ruby.

"Prepared the lodging" means he prepared either a rug or a mat. After preparing it, he informed Soṇa: "Friend, the Teacher wishes to stay in the same dwelling with you; your lodging has been prepared right in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī)."

"This is his time" means this would be the time. "Showed" means he pointed out specifically. "Speak this and that": The meaning here is, "Now is the time to report the instruction that my preceptor made me know; I shall now report that message."

"With a Vinaya-expert as the fifth" means with a reciter of the Kammavācā as the fifth member of the Saṅgha. "Monks, I allow multi-layered sandals in all border regions": In this context, sandals made of any skin except human skin are allowable. The same method applies to sandal-cases, knife-cases, and key-cases. "Leather spreads": In this context, it is allowable to lie or sit after spreading any sheepskin or goatskin. Among skins, only the skins of these animals are allowable: the Eṇī deer, the wind-deer (vātāmiga), the barking deer (pasada), the kuraṅga deer, the migamātuka (hog-deer), and the rohita deer. Regarding other skins:

The skins of monkeys, brown pigs, sarabha deer, kadali deer, and any fierce beasts of prey are not allowable.

In that context, "beasts of prey" (vāḷamiga) refers to lions, tigers, bears, and hyenas. Not only these, but except for those animals whose skins are said to be allowable, all remaining animals such as cows, buffaloes, rabbits, cats, etc., should be understood as "beasts of prey" in this sense. The skins of all these are not allowable.

"As long as it does not come into the hand, it does not enter into the count" means as long as it has not been brought and offered, or as long as one has not been informed by a messenger saying, "Venerable sir, a robe has arisen for you," it does not enter into the count. The meaning is: if it has not been determined (anadhiṭṭhita), it is allowable, and it does not yet enter into the count of determined robes. But when it has been brought and offered, or when one hears that a robe has arisen, from that time onwards, one receives a period of only ten days for keeping it.

## The Commentary on the Chapter on Skins is finished.

## 6. Bhesajjakkhandhaka
## Pañcabhesajjādikathā
In the Bhesajjakkhandhaka, the phrase 'sāradikena ābādhena' refers to an illness caused by bile that arises during the autumn season (the month of Tazaungmon). This is because during that autumn season, people get wet from rainwater, tread in mud, and the intermittent sunlight is also intense. Due to such dampness and other factors, the bile of those monks enters into the intestines. The phrase 'āhāratthañca phareyya' means it should be able to fulfill the purpose of nourishment.

'Nacchādenti' means they do not digest, or they are unable to alleviate illnesses caused by wind. 'Senehasitāni' means those that are smooth (soft or oily). 'Bhattācchādakena' means due to a lack of appetite (arocaka) for food.

Regarding the terms 'acchavasa' and so forth, the decision should be understood in the same manner as stated in the commentary on the Nissaggiya. In the phrases 'kāle paṭiggahitaṃ' and so forth, the meaning is to consume after having received, cooked, and strained it before the noon hour has passed. 'Telaparibhogena paribhuñjituṃ' means to consume by using oil which is a seven-day medicine (sattāhakālika).

The decision regarding 'mūlabhesajja' (root medicines) and so forth is also just as stated in the Khuddaka commentary. Therefore, in this Bhesajjakkhandhaka, I shall only explain those terms that have not been mentioned before. 'Vacattha' refers to sweet flag (Acorus calamus) or *saik-phu*. 'Nisadaṃ nisadapottakaṃ' refers to the grinding stone and the pestle (the stone used for grinding). 'Phaggava' is a type of creeper. 'Nattamāla' is the Indian Beech tree (Karanju). 'Hiṅgu', 'hiṅgujatu', and 'hiṅgusipāṭikā' are all varieties of asafoetida. 'Taka', 'takapatti', and 'takapanni' are varieties of lac (resin).

'Sāmudda' refers to salt that exists like sand on the seashore. 'Kāḷaloṇa' is natural salt (black salt). 'Sindhava' is white-colored salt that originates in mountains (rock salt). 'Ubbhida' is salt that arises from the earth like a sprout. 'Bila' is salt cooked together with other substances, and it is red in color.

264-6. 'Kāyo vā duggandho' means that some monks may have a body odor like that of a horse or similar animals; for such a monk, powders made from Sirīsa flowers and the like, or any kind of scented powders, are allowable. 'Chakaṇa' is cow dung. 'Rajananippakka' is the residue or dregs of dye. Even ordinary powder, when crushed and moistened with water, is allowable for bathing; this also falls under the category of dye-residue.
373:
In the passage "He eats raw meat and drinks raw blood," it is not that the bhikkhu eats the raw meat or drinks the raw blood. It is only a non-human (amanussa) who, having eaten and drunk, departs. Therefore, it is said: "That non-human affliction of that bhikkhu was cured."

'Añjana' is a collective term for all types of eye-salve (collyrium). 'Kāḷañjana' is one variety of eye-salve. 'Rasañjana' is made from various medicinal ingredients. 'Sotañjana' is eye-salve that originates in river currents and the like. 'Geruka' is red chalk (ochre) that has a golden hue. 'Kapalla' is the soot collected from a lamp flame. 'Añjanūpapiṃsanehi' means with materials that are ground together with the eye-salve. In fact, any material ground with eye-salve is allowable. 'Candana' refers to red sandalwood or any kind of sandalwood. Tagara and so forth are well-known. Other items such as the blue lotus (nīluppala) are also allowable.

'Aṭṭhimaya' refers to items made of bone, excluding human bone. 'Dantamaya' refers to items made of any kind of tusk, such as elephant ivory.
