Even for an eye-salve tube made of horn (visāṇa), there is nothing unallowable. Those made of reeds (naḷa) and so forth are definitely allowable. 'Salākaṭṭhāniya' means a hollow tube or a bag where the eye-salve rod is kept; the meaning is that the Blessed One allowed such items. 'Aṃsabaddhaka' is a shoulder strap for carrying the eye-salve bag. 'Yamakanatthukaraṇi' refers to a single nose-medicine applicator with two tubes of equal flow.

In the statement "Bhikkhus, I allow the cooking of oil," all oil that is cooked by adding any kind of medicine is already permitted. 'Atipakkhittamajjāni' refers to preparations where liquor is excessively added; that is, medicines formulated by adding a large amount of liquor.

'Aṅgavāta' is a wind-ailment in the limbs (hands and feet). 'Sambhāraseda' is sudation (sweating) by means of various types of leaves. 'Mahāseda' is a great sweat-treatment. The meaning is that the Blessed One allowed the following: one fills a pit the size of a man with embers, covers it with earth, sand, etc., and then spreads various wind-dispelling leaves over it; then, having smeared the body with oil, one lies down on those leaves and rolls around to induce sweating. 'Bhaṅgodaka' is water boiled with various broken leaves. One should induce sweating by repeatedly pouring those leaves and that water over the body. 'Udakakoṭṭhaka' means that in a water-room, one fills a large jar or a trough with hot water and enters it to perform the sweat-treatment; this is the meaning of the Blessed One's permission.
374:
"Pabbavāto hoti" means wind-colic or wind blowing in every joint. "Lohitaṃ mocetuṃ" means to let blood with a small knife. "Pajjaṃ abhisaṅkharituṃ" means to prepare medicine for the feet; it refers to the preparation of various medicines by putting them into a coconut, etc., to heal cracked feet, or to cook medicine suitable for the feet. "Tilakakkena attho" means a need for ground sesame paste. "Kabaḷikaṃ" means to place a medicinal bolus on the opening of a wound. "Sāsapakuḍḍena" means with fine mustard powder. "Vaḍḍhamaṃsaṃ" means excess flesh rising like a wart (proud flesh). "Loṇasakkharikāya chindituṃ" means to cut with a razor. "Vikāsikaṃ" means a coarse cloth used to block oil. "Sabbaṃ vaṇapaṭikammaṃ" means whatever treatment is done for a wound; it means that all such wound treatments are allowed.

"Sāmaṃ gahetvā" (taking by oneself) applies not only to one bitten by a snake but also when bitten by other venomous creatures; one may take and consume it by oneself. In other circumstances, however, it is only proper to consume after it has been formally offered. "Why is it not to be offered again?" If it has touched the ground, it must be offered; if it has not yet touched the ground, it is allowable to take it.

"Gharadinnakābādha" is an illness arising from drinking a potion given to gain control over someone. "Sītāloḷiṃ" means that the Buddha allowed drinking fine mud that sticks to the plowshare of a person plowing, after stirring it in water.

"Duṭṭhagahaṇiko" refers to one with impaired digestion; it means that excrement is passed with difficulty. "Āmisakhāraṃ" is alkaline water strained from the ashes of burnt dried rice. "Muttaharītakaṃ" is myrobalan (Harītaka) infused with cow's urine. "Abhisannakāyo" refers to one whose body has an excess of humors. "Acchakañjiyaṃ" is clear rice-scouring water. "Akaṭayusaṃ" is water cooked with green gram without oil. "Kaṭākaṭaṃ" is that same green gram broth prepared with a little oil. "Paṭicchādanīyena" means with meat broth.

## Guḷādianujānanakathā

"Monks, if cooked green grams should sprout" means that even if cooked green grams sprout, they should be consumed as one pleases. This is because, being cooked, they are indeed allowable (kappiya).
375:
"Antovuttha" means stored inside an unallowable hut (akappiyakuṭi). "Sāmaṃ pakka" means cooked by oneself; in this context, it is not proper for a monk to cook any kind of food (āmisa) himself. Even if people put shushu leaves, basil leaves, fresh ginger, or salt into a monk's hot gruel, it is not proper to stir that gruel; however, it is proper to stir it with the thought, "I will cool the gruel." Even if one receives rice cooked with undercooked grains, it is not proper to cover it. However, if people cover it and then offer it, it is allowable. It is also allowable to cover it with the thought, "Let the rice not get cold." If milk, buttermilk, etc., have boiled once, it is proper to apply fire and cook them again, because re-cooking is permitted. "Ukkapiṇḍakāpi khādantī" refers to cats, mice, monitor lizards, and mongooses nibbling. "Damaka" refers to those who eat leftovers.

"Tato nīhaṭa" refers to what is taken away from the place where those invited are eating.

"Vanaṭṭhaṃ pokkharaṭṭhaṃ" means what grows in the forest or in a lotus thicket. "Abīja" refers to young fruit with seeds that cannot produce a sprout. "Nibbaṭṭabīja" refers to things like mangoes and jackfruits that are to be eaten after removing the seeds.

"Duropayo vaṇo" refers to a wound where new flesh grows with difficulty and which returns to its normal state with difficulty. "Dupparihāraṃ satthaṃ" means handling a surgical instrument (sattha) with difficulty in a sensitive area (sambādha). Regarding surgical operations (satthakamma) or the use of a clyster/enema (vatthikamma), one should not perform cutting, splitting, piercing, or scratching with a knife, needle, thorn, spear, gravel, or fingernail in the designated areas. All of this constitutes a surgical operation (satthakamma). One should also not perform pressure with a clyster (vatthipīဠန - vatthipīḷana) using any leather or cloth; all of this is vatthikamma. Here, the phrase "two inches around the sensitive area" is said with reference only to surgical operations. Vatthikamma is prohibited even in the sensitive area (genitals) itself. However, it is proper to apply alkaline water (khāra) there or to tie it with any small string. If it is severed by doing so, it is well-severed. In the case of a hydrocele (muttakya), surgical operation is not proper; therefore, one should not split the scrotum and remove the testicles with the thought, "I will make him free from disease." There is no prohibition against heating with fire or applying medicine. In the rectum (vaccamagga), it is proper to insert a medicated cloth plug or to use a small bamboo tube to perform alkaline treatment or to introduce oil.
376:
"Pavattamaṃsa" refers to the meat of a creature that is already dead. "Māghāta" refers to a day on which it is not permissible for anyone to deprive any living being of life (to slaughter). "Potthanika" refers to a small knife used for cutting meat. "Kimpimāya" means "What else is there for this Suppiyā (to offer other than her own flesh)?" "The Blessed One is not able" means the Blessed One is not capable. "Yatra hi nāma" is because that (Suppiyā) even gave up her own flesh. "Paṭivekkhi" means investigated or inquired. "Appaṭivekkhitvā" means without inquiring. If one knows what kind of meat it is, there is no need to inquire; if one does not know, one should eat only after inquiring.

## Discussion on the Prohibition of Elephant Meat and Others

Regarding dog meat: in this context, wild dogs (jackals/wolves) are similar to dogs; the meat of those wild dogs is allowable. However, the meat of a dog born from the mating of a village bitch and a wild dog, or a wild bitch and a village dog, is not allowable, as it pertains to both kinds. Regarding snake meat: the meat of any kind of snake, which is footless and long-bodied, is not allowable. Lion meat and others are well-known.

In this context, human meat is prohibited because of being the same species; elephant and horse meat are prohibited because they are royal attributes (limbs of the king); dog and snake meat are prohibited because they are loathsome; and the five kinds including lion meat are prohibited for the sake of one's own safety (to avoid harm from those animals). All parts—meat, bone, blood, skin, and hair—of these ten kinds of beings, including humans, are unallowable. Whether a monk eats it knowing or not knowing, an offense is incurred. When he realizes it, he must confess. For a monk who receives it with the intention "I will eat without inquiring," an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa) is incurred for the act of receiving. If he receives it with the intention "I will eat after inquiring," there is no offense. Regarding meat specifically killed for oneself (udissakata), an offense is incurred only if one eats it while knowing; if one finds out later, he should not be made to undergo the penalty for the offense (he need not confess).

## Discussion on Gruel, Honey Balls, etc.

"Ekattaka" means alone, meaning "I have no companion." "Having prepared much gruel and honey balls" means that the Brahmin had them prepared by spending a hundred thousand (units of currency). At the end of the appreciation verses (anumodanā gāthā), the words "patthayataṃ icchataṃ" should be connected with "alameva dātuṃ." If there is a variant reading "patthayatā icchatā," that version should be taken.

"Bhojjayāgu" means gruel that causes satisfaction (completing the meal). "Yadaggena" means starting from which time. "Heaven has been attained for you" means that the merit leading to rebirth in heaven has been accumulated.
377:
"It should be done according to the Dhamma" means the decision should be made based on the rule of successive meals (paramparabhojana). This is because by consuming the gruel, an invitation (pavāraṇā) has been made.

"Kaccāna, I do not eat that molasses" means that deities placed a subtle essence (ojā) into that remaining molasses. That subtle essence cannot be digested by anyone other than the Buddha and his disciples. Therefore, this was said. "Gilānassa guḷaṃ" means that for a monk who is ill with such a disease, molasses is allowed after the meal (or at night).

## Pāṭaligāmavatthukathā
"Sabbasanthariṃ" means as if the entire guest house has been spread and prepared.

"Sunidhavassakārā" refers to the two chief ministers of the King of Magadha named Sunidha and Vassakāra. "Vajjīnaṃ paṭibāhāya" means for the purpose of cutting off the entry and exit routes and the revenue of the Vajjī princes. "Vatthūni" refers to house sites or plots of land. "Cittāni namanti nivesanāni māpetuṃ" means those deities possess the bodies of those who know the science of sites (vatthuvijjā) and incline their minds to build houses. Why? With the intention that "they will make offerings to us accordingly."

"Tāvatimsehi" means that in the world, because of Sakka, the king of devas, and Vissakamma, the fame of the Tāvatiṃsa devas being wise has spread. Therefore, it means they build as if they were consulting with the Tāvatiṃsa devas. "Yāvatā ariyam āyatanaṃ" refers to all the abodes of noble people. "Yāvatā vaṇippatho" refers to all the places for buying and selling where merchants pile up the goods they have brought. "Idaṃ agganagaraṃ" means that among those abodes of nobles and trading places, this city will be the chief city. "Puṭabhedanaṃ" means a place where bundles are opened (a center of commerce).

In the phrases "aggito vā" and so forth, the word "vā" expresses the sense of combination. In that city of Pāṭaliputta, one part will face danger from fire, one part from water, and one part from internal dissension. "Uḷumpaṃ" is a raft made by hammering in pegs to cross to the other side. "Kullaṃ" is a raft made by binding with creepers and the like.

The word "aṇṇavaṃ" is a name for a body of water that is about one league (yojana) long at its boundary, and is both deep and wide. Here, "saraṃ" refers to a river. This is the meaning:

Those virtuous ones who follow the words of the Buddha cross the river of craving (taṇhā), which is bottomless and deep, and wide as it permeates all three worlds. They cross by constructing the bridge of the Noble Path, without touching the swampy depths. However, while these ordinary people wish to cross even this small water of the Ganges, they must construct rafts. But the wise Buddha and the disciples of the Buddha have already crossed over without needing a raft.
378:
Those virtuous ones cross the deep and wide river of craving; having made the bridge of the Noble Path, they cross over the water-filled depressions without touching them. While these people, even wishing to cross this small amount of water, bind a raft, the wise Buddhas and their disciples have crossed over without a raft.

'Ananubodhā' means due to not understanding. 'Sandhāvitaṃ' means running by way of moving from one existence to another. 'Saṃsaritaṃ' means wandering by way of repeated going. 'Mamañceva tumhākañca' means 'both I and you.' Alternatively, 'sandhāvitaṃ saṃsaritaṃ' should be understood as 'the running and wandering of both myself and you has occurred.' 'Saṃsitaṃ' means wandered. 'Bhavanetti samūhatā' means the cord of craving, which is the cause of running from existence to existence, is well destroyed, cut off, and made not to arise.

'Nīlā' is a general term. 'Nīlavaṇṇā' etc. are said to show the varieties of that blue color. Their natural complexion is not blue; this is said because of the variety of blue ointments. 'Paṭivaṭṭesi' means struck. 'Sāhāraṃ dajjayātha' means 'give together with the countryside.' 'Aṅguliṃ phoṭesuṃ' means they snapped their fingers (moved their fingers). 'Ambakāyā' means a woman. 'Oloketha' means 'look.' 'Apaloketha' means 'look again and again.' 'Upasaṃharatha' means 'bring near.' It means: 'Bring this assembly of Licchavīs to the assembly of Tāvatiṃsa gods with your mind; look at them by making them equal to the Tāvatiṃsa gods.'

## The Story of General Sīha and Others

'Dhammassa ca anudhammaṃ byākaronti' means they speak reasons consistent with the reason taught by the Blessed One. 'Sahadhammiko vādānuvādo' means: 'Does even a slight reason for criticism by the wise come to your speech, being based on reasons spoken by others?' This means: 'Is there no reason for blame in your speech in every way?' 'Anabbhakkhātukāmā' means not wishing to speak by way of misrepresenting.

'Anuviccakāraṃ' means: 'Do what should be done after investigating, reflecting, and weighing.' 'Ñātamanussānaṃ' means 'to people well-known in the world (it is good).'
379:
'Hoti' means it is good. 'Paṭākaṃ parihareyyuṃ' means they should wander about proclaiming in the city, raising a banner. Why? Because they think, 'In this way, our greatness will be known.' 'Opānabhūtaṃ' means existing like a prepared well. 'Kulaṃ' means a house. 'Dātabbaṃ maññeyyāsi' is an advice: 'Do not cut off the gifts to be given to these Nigaṇṭhas; it is only right to give to those who have arrived.' 'Okāra' means 'avakāra', a state of meanness or lowliness. 'Sāmukkaṃsikā' means taken up by oneself alone, not shared with others. 'Uddissa kataṃ' means meat prepared specifically for oneself.

'Paṭiccakamma' means an action done depending on oneself. Alternatively, 'paṭiccakamma' is a synonym for 'nimittakamma' (the kamma of killing due to the reason of eating meat); because there is kamma caused by that meat, the meat is also called 'paṭiccakamma'. Indeed, one who consumes such meat also becomes an heir to that kamma; it means that just as the killer has the kamma of taking life, so does the consumer. 'Jiridanti' means they grow old; it means those who slander do not come to an end, they do not reach the end of their slandering. The discussion on 'purity in three ways' (tikoṭiparisuddha) was mentioned in the explanation of the training rule on schism in the Saṅgha.

## Discussion on the Allowance of the Kappiya-ground

'Sakaṭaparivaṭṭa' means staying as if surrounded by carts. 'Paccantima': this word is merely a statement; however, because it is said in the Great Commentary, 'whatever the Saṅgha desires,' even the main monastery is suitable to be authorized; it is also suitable by way of notification (apalokana) without reciting the formal act (kammavācā). 'The sound of crows' refers to the cawing of crows that have gathered early to eat food after entering various places. The one named Yasoja was the foremost person among the five hundred sons of fishermen who went forth at the end of the Kapila Sutta.

In the words beginning with 'ussāvanantikā', first, the ussāvanantikā-kuṭi should be made thus: For a monastery built either on top of pillars or by burying the foot of the walls, the stones supporting the pillars below are just like the ground. When many monks surround and utter the words, 'We make a kappiyakuṭi, we make a kappiyakuṭi,' while laypeople are lifting and establishing the first pillar or the first wall-foot, one should establish the pillar or wall-foot either by touching it or by lifting it oneself. In the Kurundī and Mahāpaccarī commentaries, it is said that it should be established after saying, 'Kappiyakuṭi, kappiyakuṭi.' In the Andhaka commentary, it is said, 'I resolve upon the kappiyakuṭi of the Saṅgha.' Even without saying that, by the method mentioned in the commentaries...
380:
Even if it is said so, there is no fault. In this matter, the general characteristic is that the planting of the post and the conclusion of the words must occur simultaneously. If the post is planted before the words are finished, or if the words are finished before the post is planted, it does not constitute a kappiya-kuṭī (allowable storehouse). For this reason, it is stated in the Mahāpaccari: "It should be recited while being surrounded by many monks; in this way, surely the conclusion of the words of at least one monk and the planting of the post will occur at the same time."

In the case of dwellings with walls made of bricks, stones, or mud, they may be constructed with or without laying a brick foundation at the bottom. From whichever point they wish the wall to rise, the kappiya-kuṭī should be established according to the aforementioned method, starting by taking the very first brick, stone, or lump of mud. Bricks and such that are below the first layer of the wall's bricks are not suitable (as they are considered part of the ground), but posts are suitable because they rise upwards. In the Andhaka Commentary, it is stated: "When constructing with posts, four posts should be established at the four corners; in a dwelling with brick walls and such, two or three bricks should be established at the four corners." However, even if it is not done in that manner, there is no fault, for only what is stated in the Commentaries is the standard.

There are two types of gonisādikā: ārāma-gonisādikā and vihāra-gonisādikā. Among them, a place where neither the park nor the lodgings are fenced is called "ārāma-gonisādikā." A place where all or some of the lodgings are fenced, but the park is not fenced, is called "vihāra-gonisādikā." Thus, in both cases, the fact that the park is unfenced is the standard. It is stated in the Kurundī, Mahāpaccari, and other commentaries that even if the park is half-fenced or mostly fenced, it is still called "fenced." In such a place, it is proper to obtain a kappiya-kuṭī.

"Gahapati" refers to when laypeople, having built a dwelling, say, "We offer this as a kappiya-kuṭī; please make use of it." Such a dwelling is called a gahapati. Even if they say, "We offer this for the purpose of making a kappiya-kuṭī," it is also suitable. In the Andhaka Commentary, however, it is stated: "Because the property of others—excluding monks but including all other fellow practitioners, devas, and humans—which is received from their hands, stored, or kept within (antovuttha), is allowable for a monk, therefore their houses or the kappiya-kuṭī offered by them are called gahapati." Furthermore, it is stated: "Excluding the vihāra of the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, the dwelling of bhikkhunī, the house of monastery attendants, the dwelling of non-Buddhists, the mansions of deities, the mansions of nāgas, and even the mansions of Brahmās can become a kappiya-kuṭī." That statement is well-said.
381:
A house belonging to the Saṅgha or to an individual monk is not called a gahapati-kuṭī. A sammuti-kuṭī is one that is made by reciting the kammavācā.

All food (āmisa) stored in these four types of kappiya-grounds does not fall under the category of "stored within" (antovuttha). This is because kappiya-kuṭī were allowed for the purpose of freeing monks and nuns from the offenses of storing within (antovuttha) and cooking within (antopakka). However, if property belonging to the Saṅgha or the personal property of a monk or nun is kept even for one night in a house suitable for sleeping together in a non-allowable ground (akappiyabhāmi), it is called "stored within." Anything cooked in that place is called "cooked within." This is not allowable. However, seven-day-limit (sattāhakālika) and life-long (yāvajīvika) items are allowable.

In this matter, there is this decision: If a novice (sāmaṇera) brings food such as rice for a monk, places it in a kappiya-kuṭī, and cooks and offers it the next day, it does not become "stored within." If any item such as ghee stored in a non-allowable storehouse (akappiya-kuṭī) is added to that food and offered, it is called "storing in the mouth" (mukhasannidhi). In the Mahāpaccari, however, it is stated as being "stored within." In both cases, the difference is merely in the name. If a monk cooks and consumes ghee kept in a non-allowable storehouse together with a life-long leaf, it is allowable for seven days without the presence of food (āmisa). If he consumes it mixed with food, both the offense of "stored within" and the offense of "cooking by oneself" (sāmampāka) occur. By this method, all types of mixing should be understood.

When do these kappiya-kuṭī lose their status (zahitavatthuka)? An ussāvanantika-kuṭī is made by planting it above posts or at the base of walls. That dwelling is said to have lost its status when all the posts and wall bases are removed. However, if the posts or wall bases are replaced, and the existing post or wall base remains in its respective place, it does not lose its status even if all are replaced. In the case of a structure made of bricks and such, it is said to have lost its status when the bricks, stones, or lumps of mud placed for the purpose of the wall above the foundation are destroyed. However, even if the bricks that were established are removed, if other bricks remain, it does not lose its status.

A gonisādikā-kuṭī is said to have lost its status when it is enclosed by a wall or such. At that time, it is proper to re-establish a kappiya-kuṭī in that park. However, if the walls and such are broken in various places and cattle enter through those places, it becomes a kappiya-kuṭī again. As for the other two types (gahapati-kuṭī and sammuti-kuṭī), even a single rafter (gopānasī)...
382:
If the entire roof is destroyed, leaving only the rafters, they become abandoned sites. If even a single duck-wing-shaped ridge-cover remains above the rafters, it still preserves the status of the allowable ground (kappiyabhūmi).

If none of the four kinds of allowable grounds mentioned above exist in that place, what should be done? It should be given to an unordained person (anupasampanna), and after making it his property, it may be used. In this matter, there is this story: The Elder Kurunditissa, a leader among the experts of the Vinaya, went to the presence of the Elder Mahāsīva. Seeing a pot of ghee by the light of a lamp, he asked, "Venerable Sir, what is this?" The Elder replied, "Friend, this is a pot of ghee brought from the village to be eaten with meals on days when the food is coarse." Then the Elder Tissa said, "Venerable Sir, it is not allowable." The Elder had it placed in the front hall the next day. The Elder Tissa came again on another day, and seeing the pot, he asked as before and said, "Venerable Sir, it is not allowable to keep it in a place sufficient for sleeping together (sahaseyya)." The Elder had it taken outside and kept there the next day, and thieves stole it. On another day when the Elder Tissa came, the Elder said to him, "Friend, that pot which you said was 'not allowable' was placed outside and has been stolen by thieves." Then the Elder Tissa said, "Venerable Sir, should it not have been given to an unordained person? For after giving it to an unordained person and making it his property, it is allowable to use it."

296-9. The Meṇḍaka story is quite clear. However, in this story, the phrase "Monks, I allow the five products of the cow (pañca gorasa)" means that I allow these five products of the cow to be consumed individually. In the phrase "to seek provisions for a journey (pātheyya)," if some people know by themselves and offer them, that is good. If they do not offer, they should be sought from relatives or those who have given an invitation (pavārita), or by the practice of alms-gathering. If they are not obtained in that way, they should be taken even by requesting from those who are not relatives or have not given an invitation. For a journey that can be traveled in one day, provisions for one meal should be sought. If it is a long journey, as much provisions as needed to cross the wilderness should be sought.

## The Story of Keṇiya the Ascetic
"Having them carried by carrying-poles" means having one thousand pots of well-prepared jujube juice carried by five hundred carrying-poles. "Having given a Dhamma talk on this occasion, in this matter" means "Monks, it is good that the disciples of the Ascetic Gautama, while not drinking the juice..."
383:
"...the disciples of the Ascetic Gotama do not give rise to the view that they live for the sake of an abundance of requisites; they show respect to me, and I have generated respect for you; for this reason, I am very pleased with you," and after giving a Dhamma talk in this manner, he said, "Monks, I allow eight kinds of drinks (aṭṭha pānāni)," and so forth.

Among those drinks, mango juice (ambapāna) is a drink made from either raw or ripe mangoes. Among those, if one wishes to make it with raw mangoes, one should cut young mangoes, put them in water, cook them by the heat of the sun (ādiccapāka), strain them, and mix them with honey, sugar, camphor, etc., that are received on that same day. A drink made in this way is allowable only before noon. However, if one obtains a drink made by unordained persons and it is received before noon, it is allowable to consume it even with food (sāmisa) before noon; in the afternoon, it is allowable to consume it without food (nirāmisa) until dawn. This is the method for all drinks.

Among them, jambu juice (jambupāna) is a drink made from rose-apples. Coca juice (cocapāna) is a drink made from seeded bananas. Moca juice (mocapāna) is a drink made from seedless bananas. Madhuka juice (madhukapāna) is a drink made from the natural juice of Madhuka fruits; that drink is allowable only when mixed with water, but not when pure. Grape juice (muddikapāna) is a drink made by pressing grapes in water, like mango juice. Sālūka juice (sālūkapāna) is a drink made by pressing the edible roots of red or blue water-lilies. Phārusaka juice (phārusakapāna) is a drink made from Phārusaka fruits like mango juice. These eight kinds of drinks are allowable whether they are cold or cooked by the sun; they are not allowable if cooked by fire.

Grain juice (dhanyaphalarasa) is the juice of the fruits of the seven kinds of grain. Vegetable juice (ḍākarasa) is the juice of cooked vegetables. The juice of cooked leaves that are temporary (yāvakālika) is allowable only before noon. The juice of leaves cooked together with life-long (yāvajīvika) requisites like ghee that have been received and kept is allowable for seven days. If they are cooked with pure water, they are allowable for life. However, it is not allowable to cook them with milk and such. Other cooked items are also counted only as cooked vegetable juice. In the Kurundī Commentary, it is said, "Even for leaves that are temporary (yāvakālika), the juice made by pressing them with cold water or cooked by the sun is allowable."

In the phrase "except for the juice of Madhuka flowers," the juice of Madhuka flowers, whether cooked by fire or by the sun, is not allowable in the afternoon. Even in the morning, any drink that people take to make into liquor is not allowable from the very beginning. However, Madhuka flowers, whether fresh, dry, or roasted, or the molasses made from them, are all allowable in the morning as long as they do not make liquor from them. Sugarcane juice is allowable in the afternoon if it is free of dregs.
384:
It is allowable. By allowing these drinks, the Blessed One means that these four types of juices (from fruits, leaves, flowers, and bark) are also allowed. In the phrase "Agghihuttamukhā yaññā" etc., it means that among sacrifices, the fire sacrifice is foremost; the fire sacrifice is the best; the fire sacrifice is the leader.

## The Story of Roja the Mallian and Others

301-2. The story of Roja the Mallian is clear in meaning. In that story, "saṅkaraṃ akaṃsu" means they made an agreement (covenant). "This welcoming of yours is indeed excellent" is the meaning. "Venerable Ānanda, I did not come here out of great faith or reverence for the Buddha and so forth"—this is what he intended to show. "Sabbañca ḍākaṃ" refers to all kinds of vegetables, whether cooked with ghee etc., or uncooked. "Piṭṭhakhādanīyaṃ" is food made from flour. It is said that Roja had both these vegetables and flour-based foods prepared at a cost of one hundred thousand [kahāpaṇas].

Manjukā means those with sweet speech. Paṭibhāneyyakā means those endowed with sharp intelligence in their respective skills. Dakkhā means those who are clever or not lazy. Pariyodātasippā means those with flawless skills. "Nāḷiyāvāpakena" refers to [a kit] with a needle-case and a bag. "Āvāpaka" refers to a bag where whatever is obtained is placed. In the passage "Monks, one who was not previously a barber should carry a razor-bag," it means it is not allowable to carry it [for use as a barber], but it is allowable to cut hair with another's razor. If one cuts hair for a fee, it is not allowable. If a monk was not previously a barber, it is allowable for him to carry a razor-bag, and it is allowable to cut hair using that razor or another.

"Bhāgaṃ datvā" means having given a tenth part. Giving a tenth part is said to be an ancient custom in Jambudīpa. Therefore, having made ten parts, one part should be given to the landowners.

## The Four Great Standards

The Blessed One spoke these Four Great Standards, beginning with "Whatever, monks, has not been prohibited by me as unallowable...", so that the monks could understand the method. Regarding those Great Standards, the Elders who conducted the Recitation (Saṅgāyana), while repeatedly reviewing the Sutta texts, saw this matter. By the phrase "excluding the juice of grain fruits," the juices of the seven kinds of grain are rejected as unallowable after noon. The nine large fruits—palmyra, coconut, jackfruit, breadfruit, bottle gourd, pumpkin, white gourd, striped cucumber, and spinach—and all pulses are of the same nature as grain. Although those large fruits and pulses are not directly prohibited, they fall under the category of the unallowable. Therefore, they are not allowable after noon.
385:
Eight kinds of drinks are allowed. Other drinks made from small fruits such as cane, tamarind, citron, wood-apple, and kapiṭṭha are of the same nature as those eight drinks. Although those drinks are not specifically allowed, they are allowable because they conform to what is allowable. Indeed, the Kurundī states that, excluding the juice of the seven kinds of grain which are conformable [to grain], there is no other fruit juice that is unallowable; all are only 'temporary' (yāmakālika).

The Blessed One allowed six types of robes. The Elders of the Council allowed another six types that are conformable to those: fine linen (dukūla), silk (pattuṇṇa), Chinese silk (cīnapaṭṭa), Somāra silk, robes created by psychic power, and robes given by devas. Therein, "pattuṇṇa" is cloth produced from insects in the Pattuṇṇa region. Two types of cloth are mentioned by the name of the region. Those three are conformable to silk robes. Fine linen is conformable to hempen robes. The other two are conformable to cotton robes or to all robes.

The Blessed One rejected eleven types of bowls and allowed two types: the iron bowl and the clay bowl. Iron bowls, clay bowls, and copper bowls are conformable to those. The Blessed One allowed three types of containers (tumba): iron, wood, and fruit-shell. Pitchers, lacquer-ware, and water-gourds are conformable to those. In the Kurundī, it is said: "Drinking conchs and small drinking cups are conformable to these containers." Two types of waistbands were allowed: the plain strip and the "pig-tail" [braided] waistband. Waistbands made of cloth strips or small cords are conformable to those. Three types of umbrellas were allowed: the white umbrella, the bamboo-mat umbrella, and the leaf umbrella. An umbrella made of a single leaf is conformable to those. In this manner, by considering the Pali and the Commentaries, the conformability of other allowable and unallowable things should be understood.

"What is received on that day is allowable at the [proper] time" etc., was said with reference to mixed flavors. For if a coconut is received as a drink without even removing the husk, then after removing the coconut [meat/shell], that drink is allowable even at the wrong time (vikāla). When offering a cold milk-rice with a lump of ghee placed on top, the ghee that is not mixed with the milk-rice may be removed and consumed for up to seven days. The same method applies to solidified honey, molasses, and so forth. When offering alms-food decorated with nutmeg, mace, and so forth, those fruits may be removed, washed, and consumed for life (yāvajīvika). The same method applies to ginger etc., placed in gruel, or licorice etc., placed in oil. Thus, whatever has not mixed its flavor, even if received together...
386:
In whatever way a kālika (time-limited offering) remains unmixed in flavor, even if it is received together with others, if it is purified by washing or scraping, it is allowable to be used according to its respective time limit. If it is purified in such a way, it is allowable to be used according to the time limit of that particular kālika.

However, if the flavors are mixed and blended, it is not allowable. This is because a yāvakālika (allowable until noon) brings the other three types of kālika, such as yāmakālika, which are mixed with it, into its own nature of being allowable only until noon. A yāmakālika brings the two types of kālika, such as sattāhakālika, mixed with it, into its own nature of being allowable only until the end of the watches of the night. A sattāhakālika also brings a yāvajīvika mixed with it into its own nature of being allowable for only seven days.

Therefore, a yāvajīvika received on that same day or previously, when mixed with a sattāhakālika received on that day, is allowable for seven days. If mixed with a sattāhakālika received two days ago, it is allowable for six days; if mixed with one received three days ago, for five days... and if mixed with a sattāhakālika received seven days ago, it should be understood that it is allowable only for that day. Because it is allowable for seven, six days, etc., in this manner, the Buddha did not specifically say, "Monks, a yāvajīvika received on that day together with a sattāhakālika," but rather said, "The received (sattāhakālika) is allowable for seven days."

In this mixing of kālikas, offenses should be understood respectively according to the training rules on untimely eating (vikālabhojana), storing up (sannidhi), and medicines (bhesajja), due to exceeding the morning, the watch of the night, or the seven days. Among these four kālikas, only yāvakālika and yāmakālika cause the offenses of "storing indoors" (antovuttha) and "storing up" (sannidhikāra). As for sattāhakālika and yāvajīvika, it is allowable to keep them even in an unallowable hut (akappiyakuṭi), and they do not cause the offense of storing up. All the remaining words are clear throughout the Bhesajjakkhandhaka.

## The Commentary on the Bhesajjakkhandhaka is finished.
387:
## 7. Kathinakkhandhaka
## Discussion on the Allowance of the Kathina
In the Kathinakkhandhaka, "Pāveyyakā" refers to those who reside in the Pāveyya country. Pāveyya refers to a country located in the western part of the Kosala region; it means those who dwell there. This is a designation for the Bhaddavaggiya elders, who were brothers of the same father as King Kosala. Among those elders, the eldest was a Non-returner (Anāgāmī) and the youngest was a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). There was not a single person who was either an Arahant or a worldling (puthujjana).

"Āraññika" (forest-dwellers) refers to those who dwell in the forest by virtue of undertaking ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), not merely by the fact of living in a forest. The same principle should be understood for other practices such as "Piṇḍapātika" (alms-food eater). Although this term "Āraññika" is spoken foremost, those monks practiced by undertaking all thirteen ascetic practices. "Udakasangaha" (collection of water) means being joined, connected, or mixed with water, signifying that the high ground and the low ground have become a single sheet of water.

"Udakacikkhalla" (watery mud) refers to the kind of mud that rises up wherever one steps and strikes as high as the buttocks. "Okapuṇṇa" means being filled with water. It is said that because the robes of those monks were very thick, the water that fell on them did not drain away but remained like a bundle of rice; therefore, it is said "with robes filled with water." In some versions, there is also the reading "Oghapuṇṇehi."

In the phrase "we spent the Vassa without disputes," those monks did not live comfortably because they were visitors and lacked comfortable lodgings, and because they were distressed by not being able to see the Blessed One. Therefore, they did not say, "We spent the Vassa comfortably without disputes." "Having spoken a Dhamma talk" means that the Blessed One preached the Anamataggiya Sutta to those monks. At the conclusion of the talk, all those monks attained Arahantship and flew into the sky from the very place where they were sitting. It is in reference to that Anamataggiya Dhamma that it is said, "Having spoken a Dhamma talk."

After preaching thus, the Blessed One thought, "If the spreading of the Kathina had been prescribed, these monks would not have been so exhausted, as they would have come with only their upper and inner robes, having left one robe behind. Furthermore, the spreading of the Kathina is something allowed by all Buddhas." Desiring to allow the spreading of the Kathina, he addressed the monks and said, "I allow, monks, the spreading of the Kathina," and so forth.
388:
In that Pali text, in the phrase "atthatakathinānaṃ vo", the word "vo" is merely a particle, and it means "atthatakathinānaṃ" (for those monks who have spread the kathina). Only if it is a particle does the subsequent phrase "that robe will belong to them" become appropriate. Otherwise, the word "vo" is simply a genitive case (indicating possession). In the phrase "so nesaṃ", it means that the arising robe belonging to the Saṅgha will belong to those monks who have spread the kathina.

Among those five benefits, "anāmantacāra" means that as long as the kathina is not withdrawn, it will be allowable to go to a house without informing an existing monk; there will be no offense against the Caritta training rule. "Asamādānacāra" means wandering without taking the triple robe; being away from the robe will be allowable. "Gaṇabhojana" means that eating a group meal will also be allowable. "Yāvadatthacīvara" means that keeping as many robes as desired without formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) or assignment (vikappanā) will be allowable. "Yo ca tattha cīvaruppādo" means that whether it is the robe of a deceased monk within the boundary (sīmā) where the kathina was spread, or a robe offered to the Saṅgha, or a robe obtained through Saṅgha property—in whatever way a Saṅgha robe arises, that robe will belong to those monks.

In the passage "Monks, in this way the kathina should be spread," as to who receives the spreading of the kathina and who does not—by way of number, at least five monks receive it, and up to one hundred thousand may receive it; if there are fewer than five, they cannot receive it. By way of the rainy season (vassa) residence, those who entered the first rainy season (purimikā vassa) and performed the invitation (pavāraṇā) on the first pavāraṇā day receive it; those who broke the vassa or those who entered the later rainy season (pacchimikā vassa) cannot receive it. It is stated in the Mahāpaccariya that monks who spent the vassa in another monastery also cannot receive it (in this monastery). All those who entered the first vassa serve as quorum-fillers (gaṇapūraka), but they do not all receive the benefits (āniśaṃsa); the benefits accrue only to the other (participating) monks. If there are only four, three, two, or one monk who entered the first vassa, other monks should be made quorum-fillers to spread the kathina. If there are four monks and one novice (sāmaṇera) who has completed the vassa, and if that novice is ordained as a monk during the later vassa period, he becomes a quorum-filler and also receives the benefits. The same logic applies to three monks and two novices, two monks and three novices, or one monk and four novices. If the monks who entered the first vassa are not skilled in spreading the kathina, they should seek and bring Khandhakabhāṇaka elders (reciters of the Khandhakas) who are skilled in spreading the kathina. Those elders will recite the kammavācā, have the kathina spread, consume the offerings, and then depart. The benefits, however, accrue only to the remaining monks who entered the first vassa.
389:
By whom is it suitable for the Kathina to be offered? It is suitable if offered by anyone—whether a deva, a human, or any one of the five classes of fellow Dhamma practitioners (sahadhammika). There are duties for the Kathina donor; if the donor does not know those duties and asks, "Venerable sir, how should the Kathina be offered?" he should be told: "It is suitable to offer a cloth sufficient for one of the three robes at sunrise, saying, 'We offer this Kathina robe.' For the preparatory work (parikamma) of that Kathina robe, it is suitable to offer this many needles, this much thread, this much dye, and to offer rice gruel and a meal to the monks who perform the preparatory work."

The monk who spreads the Kathina must also know the duties when spreading a Kathina robe obtained rightfully and lawfully. A cloth that is starched, brought directly from a weaver's house, is not suitable; a dirty cloth is also not suitable. Therefore, upon receiving the cloth for spreading the Kathina, it should be washed well, and after preparing the robe-making equipment such as needles, it should be sewn together with many monks on that very day. When the needlework is finished, it should be dyed, marked with the ritual mark (kappabindu), and then the Kathina should be spread. If another Kathina cloth is brought before that cloth is spread, and many other accessory cloths for the Kathina benefit are given, the Kathina should be spread using the cloth of the person who gives many accessory cloths. The other person should be advised and made to understand as appropriate.

By whom should the Kathina be spread? The monk to whom the Saṅgha gives the Kathina robe spreads it. To whom should the Saṅgha give it? It should be given to the monk who has an old robe (jiṇṇacīvara). If there are many who have old robes, it should be given to the senior monk. Among the seniors, it should be given to the one who has a large following and is able to make the robe and spread it on that very day. If the senior is unable but a junior is able, it should be given to him. However, it is proper for the Saṅgha to show favor to the Mahāthera; therefore, it should be said, "Venerable sir, please accept it; we will make it and offer it to you." Among the three robes, it should be given for the sake of whichever one is worn out. For a monk who normally has a double-layered robe (dupaṭṭacīvara), it should be given for the sake of a double-layered one. Even if his single-layered robe is thick and the Kathina cloth is thin, it should be given as a double-layered one to be suitable. It is proper to give a double-layered one even to a monk who says, "If I do not get it, I will wear just a single-layered one." It should not be given to a monk who is greedy by nature. Such a monk should not accept it with the thought, "I will spread the Kathina and later sew it to make two robes." To whichever monk it is given, it should be given according to the prescribed procedure.
390:
To demonstrate that procedure, the formal act (kammavācā) for the donation was first taught, beginning with "Monks, in this way the Kathina is to be spread," and "Venerable Sir, may the Saṅgha listen to me," etc.

When the Kathina is thus given, if that Kathina cloth has its preparatory work (parikamma) completed, it is excellent. If the preparatory work is not completed, it should not be done by a single monk, even if he says, "I am a Great Elder (Mahāthera)" or "I am one of great learning (Bahussuta)". All monks must assemble and complete the washing, sewing, and dyeing. This Kathina duty is praised by the Buddhas. In the past, the Blessed One Padumuttara also performed the Kathina duty. It is said that his chief disciple, the Elder Sujāta, received the Kathina, and the Teacher, together with six million eight hundred thousand monks, performed that Kathina duty.

Having taken the Kathina robe that has been completed, the monk who spreads it should do so according to the procedure stated in the Parivāra, such as: "If he wishes to spread the Kathina with the outer robe (saṅghāṭi), the old outer robe must be withdrawn (paccuddharitabba), and the new outer robe must be determined (adhiṭṭhātabba). He must utter the words, 'I spread the Kathina with this outer robe.'" After spreading it, that monk who spread the Kathina should approach the Saṅgha, arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, raise his joined palms, and say: "Venerable Sirs, the Kathina of the Saṅgha has been spread; the spreading of the Kathina is in accordance with the Dhamma; please approve." Those monks who are to approve should arrange their upper robes over one shoulder, raise their joined palms, and say: "Friend, the Kathina of the Saṅgha has been spread; the spreading of the Kathina is in accordance with the Dhamma; we approve." In this way, according to the procedure stated in the Parivāra, he should have them approve, and the other monks should also approve. Thus, the Kathina is spread for all. For it is said in the Parivāra: "The Kathina is spread for two persons: the one who spreads it and the one who approves." Furthermore, it is said: "The Saṅgha does not spread the Kathina, the group (gaṇa) does not spread the Kathina; only an individual spreads the Kathina. Through the approval of the Saṅgha, through the approval of the group, and through the spreading by the individual, the Kathina is spread for the Saṅgha, the Kathina is spread for the group, and the Kathina is spread for the individual."

When the Kathina has been thus spread, if the donors bring accompanying gifts along with the Kathina robe and say, "We give these only to the monk who received our Kathina..."
391:
...if they give it in that way, the Saṅgha of monks has no authority over it. However, if they give it without specifying and then depart, the Saṅgha of monks has authority. Therefore, if the other robes of the monk who spread the Kathina are also worn out (insufficient), the Saṅgha, after obtaining permission (apaloketvā), should give those cloths for his benefit as well. However, the formal act (kammavācā) is valid only once. Regarding the remaining Kathina benefits, strong (good) cloths should be given according to the order of the rainy season residence (vassāvāsika-ṭhitikā). If there is no such order, they should be given starting from the Elder's seat. Communal property (garubhaṇḍa), however, should not be distributed. If there are many monasteries within a single boundary (sīmā), all monks must be assembled and the Kathina must be spread in only one place; it is not proper to spread it separately.

Now, to show in detail the method by which the Kathina is considered spread and how it is not spread, the Buddha said, "Monks, in this way the Kathina is spread, and in this way it is not spread." First, wishing to show the characteristics of not being spread, which are improper and involve a wide range of grounds, he showed twenty-four modes beginning with "not by mere marking" (na ullikhitamattena). Thereafter, wishing to show the characteristics of being spread, he showed seventeen modes beginning with "spread with a new cloth" (ahatena atthataṃ). In the Parivāra also, these same characteristics are stated: "By twenty-four modes the Kathina is not spread; by seventeen modes the Kathina is spread."

Among those (modes of not being spread), "by mere marking" (ullikhitamattena) means by merely taking the measurements by length and by breadth. For a monk, when taking measurements, marks the cloth with his fingernails or rubs it against his forehead, etc., to recognize various parts; therefore, that taking of measurements is called "mere marking" (ullikhitamatta). "By mere washing" (dhovanamattena) means by merely washing the Kathina cloth. "By mere consideration of the robe" (cīvaravicāraṇamattena) means by merely deciding, "Let it be five-fold, seven-fold, nine-fold, or eleven-fold." "By mere cutting" (chedanamattena) means by merely cutting the cloth as decided. "By mere binding" (bandhanamattena) means by merely applying temporary threads (moghasutta). "By mere basting" (ovaṭṭiyakaraṇamattena) means by merely sewing long stitches following the temporary threads. "By mere knotting" (kaṇḍusakaraṇamattena) means by merely tying the knots (muddhiya). "By mere doubling" (daḷhīkammakaraṇamattena) means by merely sewing two layers together. Alternatively, it also means when the first layer is already joined and set, merely sewing the Kathina cloth as an inner lining (kucchicimilika) for that layer.
392:
In the Mahāpaccariya Commentary, it is stated: "By giving support to one's own natural robe." In the Kurundī Commentary, however, it is stated: "By merely attaching it to the inner lining in order to make the robe, which is bound with a natural layer, double-layered." Anuvātakaraṇamatta (merely making a border) means merely placing the border from the layer on the outside of the robe. Paribhaṇḍakaraṇamatta (merely making a binding) means merely placing the border from the width on the inside of the robe. Ovaddheyyakaraṇamatta (merely adding a layer) means merely adding an upper layer. Or, it means merely taking a layer from a Kathina robe and placing it on another non-Kathina robe.

Kambalamaddanamatta (merely dipping in dye) means a robe that has been dipped only once in dye, having the color of ivory or the color of a pale leaf. However, if it is dyed once or twice and the color is suitable for monks, it is allowable. Nimittakata (cloth obtained by a sign) means cloth obtained by making a sign such as, "I will spread the Kathina with this cloth." Only this much is stated in the Parivāra. In the Commentaries, however, it is stated: "This cloth is excellent; it is possible to spread the Kathina with this," and thus it refers to cloth obtained by making such a sign.

Parikathākata (cloth obtained by roundabout talk) means cloth obtained by speaking in a roundabout way, such as, "It is proper to give Kathina; the donor of Kathina generates much merit." The Kathina is something extremely noble; it is not proper even to inform (request) one's mother; only cloth obtained spontaneously, as if it had descended from the sky, is proper.

Kukkukata (cloth allowed temporarily) means cloth that is allowed for a moment. Regarding sannidhikata (stored cloth), there are two types of storage: karaṇasannidhi (storage by action) and nicayasannidhi (storage by accumulation). Among these, karaṇasannidhi is when the Kathina act is not performed on the day of donation but is kept and performed later. Nicayasannidhi is when the Saṅgha receives the Kathina cloth today but gives it only on the next day.

Nissaggiya (forfeited cloth) means cloth forfeited because the night has passed. It is also stated in the Parivāra: "Nissaggiya means the dawn rises while the robe is being made." Akappakata (a robe not made with a kappabindu) means a robe that has not yet been marked with the kappabindu mark.

"Aññatra saṅghāṭiyā" (except for the outer robe) and so forth means that if it is spread with other items such as bedspreads, excluding the outer robe (saṅghāṭī), the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), and the inner robe (antaravāsaka), the Kathina is not considered spread. "Aññatra pañcakena vā atirekapañcakena vā" (except with five panels or more than five panels) means it is allowable only with a robe made by creating five or more panels, showing the large and small circles (maṇḍala). Only when done this way is it called "made with circles"; apart from that, it is not allowable to spread the Kathina with an un-cut cloth or a cloth with only two, three, or four panels.

"Aññatra puggalassa atthārā" (except for the spreading by an individual) means that excluding the spreading by an individual, it is not considered spread by the spreading of the Saṅgha or a group. "Nissīmaṭṭho anumodati" (rejoicing while standing outside the boundary) means the rejoicing by a monk who is standing outside the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā).
393:
Ahata means a robe that has not yet been used (brand new). Ahatakappa means a robe that is like new, having been washed once or twice. Pilocatikā means cloth that has been discarded (old cloth). Paṃsukūla means a refuse-rag robe obtained from various places. It is also stated in the Kurundī and Mahāpaccariya Commentaries that a robe made from rags obtained by a refuse-rag-wearing monk wandering for rag-alms (is suitable for spreading Kathina). Pāpaṇika means that if one picks up a worn-out cloth fallen at a shop entrance and offers it for the sake of Kathina, it is suitable to spread the Kathina with that robe. The remaining words should be understood by the reverse of what was said for nimittakata, etc. In this context, the statement "How many factors arise simultaneously with the spreading of Kathina?" etc., has been mentioned in many commentaries. Since all those words are already included in the Parivāra Pali, they should be understood according to the method presented in that Pali. Even if those words are not mentioned here, there is no deficiency for the monk who spreads the Kathina.

After explaining the spreading of Kathina in this way, the Buddha now spoke the words beginning with "And how, monks, is the Kathina removed?" to explain the removal (ubbhāra). In that Pali, mātikā means "mothers" or "originating causes." This is because these eight things cause the removal of Kathina. Among those mātikās, it is called pakkamannantika because it ends with the departure from the precinct boundary. The remaining mātikās should be understood in this same way.

## Discourse on the Seven Sets of Taking Away

Na paccessaṃ means "I will not return again." In this pakkamannantika removal of Kathina, first the robe impediment (cīvarapalibodha) is broken, and later the residence impediment (āvāsapalibodha) is broken. For a monk who departs in this way, the robe impediment is broken within the precinct boundary itself, and the residence impediment is broken only when he crosses the boundary. This is also stated in the Parivāra: "The removal of Kathina called pakkamannantika was spoken by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun. I shall answer that removal for you: first the robe impediment is broken, and later the residence impediment is broken."

Cīvaraṃ ādāya means taking an unmade robe. Bahisīmagatassa means when one has reached another nearby monastery other than one's own. Evaṃ hoti means the arising of such a thought upon seeing the comfort of lodgings or the excellence of companions in that monastery. In this niṭṭhānantika removal of Kathina, however, the residence impediment is broken first. That impediment is broken as soon as the thought "I will not return again" arises in the mind. This statement is also (mentioned in the Parivāra Pali).
394:
“The removal of the Kathina ending in the completion of the robe was taught by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun. I shall explain that removal of the Kathina to you: first, the impediment of residence (āvāsapalibodha) is severed; when the robe is finished, the impediment of robes (cīvarapalibodha) is severed,” so He said.

In this manner, the meaning should also be understood in the analysis of the remaining matrix terms (mātikā). This, however, is the distinction—in the removal of the Kathina ending in decision, at the very moment the thought arises, “I will not have this robe made, nor will I return,” both impediments are severed simultaneously. Thus it was also taught—

“The removal of the Kathina ending in decision was taught by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun. I shall explain that removal of the Kathina to you: the two impediments are severed simultaneously, neither before nor after,” so He said.

In this way, the severing of impediments in all removals of the Kathina should be understood. Since that severing of impediments can be known by this aforementioned method and because it appears in the Parivāra, it is not explained in detail here. The summary here is: in the removal of the Kathina ending in loss (nāsanantika), the impediment of residence is severed first; when the robe is lost, the impediment of robes is severed. Because the impediment of robes is severed when the robe is lost, it is called “nāsanantika.”

In the removal of the Kathina ending in hearing (savanantika), the impediment of robes is severed first; therefore, for that monk, the impediment of residence is severed along with the hearing.

In the removal of the Kathina ending in the cutting off of expectation (āsāvacchedika), the impediment of residence is severed first. When the expectation of the robe is cut off, the impediment of robes is severed. Because this āsāvacchedika has various divisions and its teaching is mixed with other removals of the Kathina—such as in the manner of “obtaining without expectation, not obtaining despite expectation, and the thought arising in that monk, ‘I will make this robe right here, I will not return’” and so on—it will be taught separately in detail later, and is not taught here. Here, however, immediately after the savanantika, the removal of the Kathina ending in crossing the boundary (sīmātikkantika) is taught. In that sīmātikkantika, the impediment of robes is severed first; when he reaches outside the boundary, the impediment of residence is severed. In the joint removal with other monks (sahubbhāra), the two impediments are severed simultaneously, neither before nor after.
395:
316-325. Having thus shown the seven removals of the Kathina in the section on taking away (Ādāya-vāra), he again shows those same seven as they may occur in the section on taking with (Samādāya-vāra), and in the sections on taking away and taking with for a monk whose robe is unfinished. After that, without considering the procedure of "I will return" or "I will not return" within the boundary (sīmā), but considering only the procedure of "I will not return," he shows the removals of the Kathina that are applicable by the method of "Anadhiṭṭhitena" and so forth.

After that, by the method of "He departs with the hope for a robe" (Cīvarāsāya pakkamati) and so forth, he shows the removal of the Kathina due to the cutting off of hope (Āsāvacchedika) through a method mixed with the other removals many times. Then, he shows the removals of the Kathina applicable to the completion (Niṭṭhānantika) and so forth, by virtue of going to another direction and by virtue of living comfortably. 

Having thus shown the removal of the Kathina by its divisions, he now wishes to show the opposites of those things which were said to be the impediments (palibodha) that are severed by each respective removal of the Kathina, and thus he said, "Monks, there are these two impediments of the Kathina," and so forth. In that context, "Cattena" (by relinquishing) means the mind by which that monastery is relinquished; that is called "catta," meaning by that relinquishing mind. The same principle applies to "Vantamutta." The remaining words are clear in all respects.

## The Commentary on the Kathinakkhandhaka is finished.
396:
## 8. Cīvarakkhandhaka
## The Story of Jīvaka
In the Cīvarakkhandhaka—‘padakkhiṇā’ means those who are skilled and proficient. ‘Abhisaṭā’ means those who have approached. If it is asked, “Who has approached?”—people who are in need have approached. Having used the possessive case (genitive) in the sense of the instrumental, it is said, “atthikānaṃ atthikānaṃ manussānaṃ” (of the people in need). ‘Paññāsāya ca rattiṃ gacchati’ means he goes at night taking fifty kahāpaṇas. ‘Negamo’ is a group of householders (merchants).

‘Sālavatiṃ kumāriṃ gaṇikaṃ vuṭṭhāpesuṃ’ means the townspeople gave two hundred thousand and the king gave one hundred thousand, thus giving three hundred thousand, as well as other defined portions such as parks, gardens, and vehicles, and established her in the position of a courtesan. ‘Paṭisatena ca rattiṃ gacchati’ means she goes at night for a fee of one hundred. ‘Gilānaṃ paṭivedeyyuṃ’ means they should make known the state of being ill. ‘Kattarasuppe’ means in an old and worn-out winnowing basket.

Why did he ask, ‘Kā me deva mātā, ko pitā’ (Your Majesty, who is my mother, who is my father)? It is said that while playing with other young princes, when a quarrel arose, they would say to Jīvaka, “One without a mother, one without a father.” And just as the stepmothers or maternal aunts of other children would send some gifts during festivals and such, no one sent anything to Jīvaka. Thus, having thought about all that, and wishing to know, “Am I truly one without a mother?” he asked, “Your Majesty, who is my mother, who is my father?”

‘Yannūnāhaṃ sippaṃ sikkheyyaṃ’ means he thought, “It would be good if I were to learn the medical art.” This thought occurred to him: “These arts of elephantry, horsemanship, and so on, are connected with the harming of others; the medical art, however, is preceded by loving-kindness and is connected with the welfare of beings.” Therefore, intending only the medical art, he thought, “It would be good if I were to learn an art.”

Furthermore, one hundred thousand aeons ago, this Jīvaka saw a physician who was an attendant to the Blessed One Padumuttara, and whose virtues were spread among the four assemblies as “this man is an attendant to the Buddha.” Thinking, “O, may I too attain such a position,” he gave gifts for seven days to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, and having paid homage to the Blessed One, he made an aspiration, “Blessed One, may I too...” Being urged by that past aspiration, Jīvaka thought, intending only the medical art, “It would be good if I were to learn an art.”
397:
"May I be the attendant of the Buddha in the future, just as this physician is your attendant," he made an aspiration. Driven by that previous aspiration, Jīvaka, intending to learn the medical craft, thought, "It would be good if I could learn the medical craft."

Disāpāmokkha means one who is known in all directions, famous, or pre-eminent. At that time, merchants from Takkasilā came to see Prince Abhaya. Jīvaka asked, "Where have you come from?" They replied, "From Takkasilā." He asked, "Is there a master physician there?" They said, "Yes, Prince, a world-renowned (Disāpāmokkha) physician lives in Takkasilā." Hearing this, he said, "When you return, please inform me." The merchants did so. Jīvaka went to Takkasilā with those merchants without asking his father's permission. Thus it is said, "Without asking Prince Abhaya," and so forth.

"Teacher, I wish to learn the craft." Seeing Jīvaka approaching, the physician asked, "My dear, who are you?" Jīvaka replied, "I am the grandson of King Bimbisāra and the son of Prince Abhaya." "My dear, why have you come here?" He replied, "To learn the craft from you, teacher," and said, "Teacher, I wish to learn the craft."

"He learns much" means that while other princes and such learn by giving wealth to the teacher without performing service, Jīvaka did not do so. Without giving wealth, he became a dhammantevāsika (resident pupil), sometimes performing duties for the teacher and sometimes studying. Nevertheless, this noble son, endowed with past merit, was able to learn much and learn quickly due to his wisdom; he reflected well and did not forget what he had learned.

"Though I have studied for seven years, I do not see the end of this craft." In this context, it is said that Jīvaka learned in seven years everything the teacher knew and what others would take sixteen years to learn. Sakka, the king of gods, thought, "This man will be the attendant and the most trusted confidant of the Buddhas; let me teach him the preparation of medicines." Entering the teacher's body, he taught Jīvaka the preparation of medicines such that he could cure any disease, except those resulting from the ripening of kamma, with a single application. Jīvaka thought, "I am learning from the teacher." Therefore, "Now Jīvaka is capable of curing..."
398:
When Sakka departed after teaching through the teacher's body, Jīvaka thought he was capable of curing and questioned the teacher. The teacher, realizing, "This was not learned through my power, but through the power of a deity," said, "Then, my dear Jīvaka, go," and so forth.

Regarding his wandering for a league (yojana) around: he went out through one gate each day, wandering for four days. The teacher gave him only a small amount of provisions. Why? It is said the teacher thought: "This youth is from a great family; as soon as he arrives, he will receive great honor from his parents and grandparents. Because of that, he will not recognize my merit or the merit of the craft. But if his provisions run out on the way and he has to employ the craft, he will surely recognize my merit and the merit of the craft." Thus, he had only a small amount of provisions given.

## The Story of the Treasurer's Wife and Others
"Pasatena" means with one handful. "Picunā" means with a wad of cotton. "Yatrahi nāma" means "that housewife [made him take it]." "Kimpimāyaṃ" means "What is this [housewife] doing to me?" "Upajānāmetassa saṃyamassa" means "I know the benefit of the service rendered, the benefit of the ghee, and the benefit of the cure of the disease."

"Let all these ornaments be yours," the King said, thinking: "If he accepts these, I will place him in a suitable position. If he does not accept, I will make him a trusted inner confidant." Prince Abhaya and the dancers also thought, "Oh, may he not accept them." Jīvaka, as if knowing their minds, said, "Great King, these ornaments belong to my grandmothers (the queens); it is not proper for me to take them," and said, "Enough, Great King," and so forth. "May the King remember my service" means "May the King remember the help I have rendered." The King, being pleased, gave him a house complete with all features, a mango grove, a village yielding a hundred thousand in annual revenue, and great honors, and said, "Then, my dear Jīvaka, go," and so forth.

## The Story of the Treasurer of Rājagaha
Why did he ask, "Householder, will you be able?" It is said that the brain does not remain stable if one changes posture. Only if he lies still without moving for three weeks (twenty-one days) would the treasurer's brain be able to stabilize.
399:
Knowing that the brain would remain stable for one who lies without moving, he made him agree to periods of seven months each, thinking that he might be able to lie still for periods of seven days each. He then asked him, "Can you endure without changing your posture?" It is for this reason that the patient later said, "I knew it from the very beginning." "Having peeled back the skin of the head" means removing the skin that covers the head. "Having opened the suture" means opening the surgical seam. The statement "Teacher, I cannot endure it" was made because a great burning sensation arose in his body. "By three weeks" means three periods of seven days, one for each side.

"Having cleared the people away" means having the crowd removed to the outside.

## The Story of King Pajjota
"I detest ghee"—it is said that this king was born of a scorpion (or was the son of a scorpion). Although ghee is the medicine to counteract scorpion venom, it is repulsive to scorpions. Therefore, he spoke thus. "He will belch" means he will vomit or experience eructation. "Capable of traveling fifty leagues" means having the ability to travel a distance of fifty yojanas. It was not only the king's she-elephant named Bhaddavatikā that could travel fifty yojanas; the elephant named Nāḷāgiri could travel a hundred yojanas. The two horses named Celakaṇṇa and Muñcakesa could travel two hundred yojanas. The slave named Kāka could travel sixty yojanas.

In the time before the Buddha appeared, a certain young man of good family was sitting down to eat one day when a Paccekabuddha stood at his door. A man informed him, "A Paccekabuddha came and has now departed." Upon hearing this, the young man said, "Go, quickly bring back the bowl," and having it brought, he offered all the food prepared for himself and sent it back. That man, having brought the bowl and placed it in the hands of the Paccekabuddha, made a wish: "Venerable Sir, by this service performed with my body for you, wherever I may be reborn, may I be endowed with excellent vehicles." That man has now become the king named Pajjota. It is because of that wish that he is thus endowed with vehicles.

"Having made him drink ghee" means having administered the ghee and then instructing the attendants on the procedure for managing his diet. "Having placed the medicine with his fingernail" means taking the medicine with his fingernail and inserting it. "He caused him to purge" means he caused a bowel movement.
400:
## The Story of the Pair of Siveyyaka Cloths
Siveyyaka refers to the inauspicious cloth found in the charnel grounds of Uttarakuru. It is said that the people there wrap the dead in this cloth and discard them. Birds with beaks like elephant trunks, perceiving the bodies as "lumps of meat," carry them to the Himalayan peaks, remove the cloth, and eat the flesh. Then, forest dwellers find the cloth and bring it to the King. This is how King Pajjota obtained it. Others say it is cloth woven by women in the Sivi kingdom who are skilled in spinning, using three strands of thread.

## The Story of the Thirty-fold Purge
When Jīvaka requested, "Please drink the oil," if one asks whether the Blessed One's body was rough, the answer is no. Indeed, deities always infuse divine essence (dibbōja) into the Blessed One's food. However, drinking oil softens the impurities such as phlegm and bile throughout the body and also softens the veins; therefore, Jīvaka made this request. "Three handfuls of lotuses" means one to remove coarse impurities, one to remove medium impurities, and one to remove subtle impurities. Before long, the Blessed One's body returned to its normal healthy state. When the Blessed One had thus recovered, the townspeople prepared offerings. Jīvaka came and said to the Blessed One, "Exalted One, today the townspeople wish to make offerings to you; please do not enter the village for alms."

The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera thought, "From whom should the first alms-food for the Blessed One be obtained today?" Then he thought, "The merchant's son Soṇa, from the time he prepared his field, has eaten fragrant Sāli rice grown by being watered with milk without mixing it with other grains. I will bring alms-food for the Blessed One from that merchant's son." He went there by psychic power and manifested himself upon the upper floor of the merchant's son's palace. The merchant's son took the Thera's bowl and offered excellent alms-food. Seeing the Thera's manner of departing, he said, "Venerable Sir, please eat first." The Thera explained the reason, and the merchant's son said, "Venerable Sir, please eat; I will offer other alms-food for the Blessed One." After the Thera had eaten, the merchant's son rubbed the bowl with perfumes, filled it with alms-food, and offered it. The Thera brought that food and offered it to the Blessed One.

King Bimbisāra also thought, "What will the Blessed One eat today?" and came to the monastery. As he was entering, he smelled the fragrance of the alms-food and felt a desire to eat.
401:
When the Buddha's two types of alms-food—the one offered by Sujātā and the one offered by Cunda the smith's son at the time of the Parinibbāna—reached the bowl, the devas infused them with essence (ojā). In other alms-food, they infused essence into every single morsel. Therefore, the Buddha, knowing the King's wish, gave the King only a small amount of alms-food into which the devas had not yet infused essence. After eating, the King asked, "Venerable Sir, is this food brought from Uttarakuru?" The Buddha replied, "Great King, it is not from Uttarakuru; indeed, this is the food of a householder's son living in your own kingdom," and he described the prosperity of Soṇa. Hearing this, the King wished to see Soṇa and, as described in the Cammakkhandhaka, arranged for Soṇa's arrival along with eighty thousand clansmen. Having heard the Buddha's Dhamma teaching, they became Stream-enterers (sotāpanna). Soṇa, however, went forth and was established in Arahantship. The Buddha had the alms-food given to the King for this very purpose.

## Varayācanakathā

When the Buddha had finished his meal in this manner, Jīvaka Komārabhacca took that pair of Siveyyaka cloths... and said this. The decision regarding the word "Atikkantavarā" should be understood according to the method stated in the Mahākhandhaka. In the statement, "Venerable Sir, the Buddha and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus are wearers of rag-robes (paṃsukūlika)," it means that for twenty years from the time the Buddha attained Enlightenment until this cloth appeared, no monk accepted robes offered by householders; all were wearers of rag-robes. Therefore, Jīvaka made this request. "Gahapati-cīvara" refers to robes offered by householders. "Dhammiyā kathāyā" refers to a talk related to the benefits of offering cloth. "Itarītarepapi" means with any kind of robe, whether of low value or high value. "Pāvāro" is a type of cloth made of cotton or similar materials with fur. In the phrase "I allow, O monks, a rug (kojava)," only an ordinary rug is permissible; a Mahāpiṭṭhiya rug is not permissible. A "Mahāpiṭṭhiya rug" is a large rug similar to a pāvāra made of wool, intended to be spread on the back of an elephant.

## Kambalānujānanādikathā

"Kāsirājā" refers to the King of Kāsi, who was a brother of King Pasenadi by the same father. In the word "Aḍḍhakāsika," a blanket worth a thousand is called "Kāsī," and because this blanket is worth only five hundred, it is called "Aḍḍhakāsika." Therefore, it was said, "Aḍḍhakāsīnaṃ kambalānaṃ" (blankets worth half a Kāsi). "Uccāvacāni" refers to good clothes and bad clothes. It is also said that the cloth named "Bhaṅga" is a robe made of hemp (bark-fiber) woven by mixing five types of thread such as linen (khoma).
402:
A blanket called Kāsī is worth a thousand. This blanket, however, is worth five hundred; therefore, it is called "Aḍḍhakāsika" (half-Kāsi). For this reason, it was said, "Accepting blankets called Aḍḍhakāsī." "Uccāvacāni" refers to good clothes and bad clothes. "Bhaṅga" is a cloth woven by mixing five types of thread such as linen (khoma). It is also said to be a cloth made of hemp (bark-fiber). The Buddha allowed only one type of robe, not two; those monks understood the meaning of "with any one of the robes" as "either a householder's robe or a rag-robe." "Nāgamesuṃ" (they did not wait) means those monks did not wait until they returned from the cemetery but departed. "Akāmā bhāgaṃ dātuṃ" (not to give a share against one's will) means it is not for giving without desire; however, if they wish to give, it should be given. "Āgamesuṃ" (they waited) means they waited in the vicinity of the cemetery. Therefore, the Buddha said, "O monks, I allow giving a share to those who are waiting, even if it is not desired." If people offer saying, "Only those who come here should take," or if they leave a mark and go away saying, "Let those who arrive take," then all monks who arrive are entitled to a share. If they leave it and go away, the monk who takes it first is the owner. "They descended to the cemetery equally" means they all descended together or descended at the same time. "They made an agreement" means they made a pact even outside the cemetery that they would divide and take all the rag-robes obtained.

"Robe-receiver" (cīvarapaṭiggāhaka) refers to the monk who accepts robes being offered to the Saṅgha by householders. In the words "one who does not go to the wrong path of desire" (chandāgati), etc., among robe-receivers, accepting first for one's own relatives even if they arrive later, or accepting by showing affection to certain people, or diverting it to oneself due to a greedy nature, is called going to the wrong path of desire. Accepting later out of anger even for one who arrived first, or accepting while showing contempt for poor people, or obstructing the Saṅgha's gain by saying, "Is there no place to keep it in your house? Take your property and go back," is called going to the wrong path of hatred (dosāgati). One who acts without mindfulness and clear comprehension is called going to the wrong path of delusion (mohāgati). Accepting first out of fear of powerful rulers even if they arrive later, or being terrified thinking, "The task of receiving robes is very burdensome," is called going to the wrong path of fear (bhayāgati). Knowing "I have received this robe, but I have not yet received this robe" is called knowing what has been received and what has not. Therefore, without going by way of desire, etc., and without making a distinction between relatives and non-relatives, the wealthy and the poor...
403:
He should be one who accepts [robes] in the order they arrive without making distinctions (such as whether they are relatives or not, wealthy or poor, etc.). He must be endowed with virtue and practice, mindful, wise, and learned. He must be able to inspire faith in the donors by performing the appreciation (anumodanā) with clear speech and perfect articulation of words and syllables. A monk of such nature should be appointed [as a robe-receiver].

In the words "Monks, he should be appointed thus," it is appropriate to appoint him either by the aforementioned formal act (kammavācā) or by announcement (apalokana), in the midst of the entire Saṅgha within the monastery or within a small boundary (khaṇḍasīmā). A monk thus appointed should not reside at the edge of the monastery or in a meditation house.
