He should sit in a place at the front of the monastery where people who come and go can easily see him, with a fan placed at his side, properly dressed and robed.

Regarding the phrase "discarding right there," it means they go away after discarding the robes at the very place of receipt, saying, "Our only responsibility is the acceptance [of the robes]." The term 'cīvaranidahaka' refers to the monk who stores and preserves the robes. In the phrases such as "one who does not follow favoritism (chandāgati)," and in all subsequent instances, the decision should be understood according to the method already stated. The decision regarding the appointment (sammuti) should also be understood according to the sequence already described.

## Discussion on the Appointment of a Storekeeper and Others

Regarding the words "or a monastery," etc., a monastery (vihāra) or a curved house (aḍḍhayoga) that is in the middle of the park, not secluded from the park-attendants and novices, and is a gathering place for everyone, should be appointed [as a storehouse]. A dwelling at the edge [of the monastery] should not be appointed. This storehouse (bhaṇḍāgāra) should not be appointed by those sitting in a small boundary (khaṇḍasīmā) after going there; it must be appointed only in the middle of the monastery.

In the phrase "he should know whether it is secured or unsecured," if there is no defect in the roof, etc., of a storehouse, it is 'secured'. If the thatch or tiles of the roof have fallen anywhere, and because of that it leaks, or if rats and such enter, or if there is a hole anywhere in the walls, etc., or if termites are infesting it, all such a storehouse is called 'unsecured'. Having noted this, it must be repaired. In the cold season, doors and windows must be kept well-closed, because robes can become moldy due to the cold. In the hot season, they should be opened occasionally to let the air in. A monk who acts in this way is said to know whether it is secured or unsecured.
404:
These three monks, starting with the robe-receiver, should also know their own duties. Among them, first, the robe-receiver should not take all the robes—whatever people give saying, "This is a timely robe (kālacívara)," or "an untimely robe (akālacívara)," or "an urgent robe (acceka-cīvara)," or "a rain-cloth (vassikasāṭika)," or "a sitting cloth (nisīdana)," or "a bedspread (paccattharaṇa)," or "a face-towel (mukhapuñchanacoḷa)"—by mixing them into a single pile. He should accept them only by separating them individually and then hand them over to the robe-storer after informing him accordingly. The robe-storer, when giving them to the storekeeper (bhaṇḍāgārika), should also give them only after informing him, "This is a timely robe... this is a face-towel." The storekeeper should also keep them by making individual marks in the same manner. Thereafter, when the Saṅgha says, "Bring a timely robe," he should give only a timely robe... when they say, "Bring a face-towel," he should give only that.

Thus, the Blessed One authorized the robe-receiver, the robe-storer, the storehouse, and the storekeeper. This was authorized not for the sake of accumulation or discontentment, but indeed for the benefit of the Saṅgha. For if the monks were to divide the robes by taking them as they were brought, they would not know what has been brought and what has not, what has been given and what has not, or what has been received and what has not. They might give whatever is brought to the seats of the elders, or they might cut them into pieces and take them. If this happens, it becomes an improper use, and it means the benefit of all monks has not been served. However, by keeping the robes in the storehouse, when they are abundant, they will give three robes, or two, or one to each monk. They will know what has been received and what has not. Knowing what has not been received, they will intend to provide the benefit.

In the words "Monks, a storekeeper should not be evicted from his place," other monks who should not be evicted should also be known. There are four types of monks who should not be evicted: a senior monk (vuddhatara), a storekeeper (bhaṇḍāgārika), a sick monk (gilāna), and a monk who has received a lodging from the Saṅgha. Among them, a senior monk should not be evicted by a junior monk because of his seniority. A storekeeper should not be evicted because the storehouse has been entrusted to him by the Saṅgha's appointment. A sick monk should not be evicted because of his illness. As for the monk who is very helpful to the Saṅgha through teaching, questioning, etc., and who bears the burden of the Saṅgha, the Saṅgha gives him a comfortable dwelling by making it a non-evictable lodging. Therefore, he should not be evicted because of his helpfulness and because it was received from the Saṅgha.
405:
"Ussannaṃ hoti" means there is a large accumulation, such that the storehouse cannot contain it. "Sammukhībhūtena" means one who is present within the precinct (upacārasīmā). "Bhājetuṃ" means to distribute in order after announcing the time. "Kolāhalaṃ akāsi" means making a great noise, saying, "Give to our teacher, give to our preceptor." Among the monks who distribute robes, one who gives an expensive robe to a monk of similar views even before his turn is said to follow the path of favoritism (chandāgati). One who gives a cheap robe instead of an expensive one to other senior monks when it is their turn is said to follow the path of ill-will (dosāgati). One who, being confused by delusion, does not know the duty of robe distribution is said to follow the path of delusion (mohāgati). One who gives an expensive robe to rude junior monks out of fear before their turn is said to follow the path of fear (bhayāgati). One who does not follow these four biased paths and is like a pair of scales, a standard, and impartial toward all monks should be appointed as a robe-distributor. "Bhājitābhājitaṃ" means knowing "this many clothes have been distributed, this many clothes have not yet been distributed"; this is what is meant by "he should know what is distributed and what is not."

"Uccinitvā" means selecting the clothes in this way: "This cloth is coarse, this is fine, this is thick, this is thin, this is used, this is unused, this is so much in length, this is so much in width." "Tulayitvā" means determining the value, such as "This cloth is worth this much." "Vaṇṇāvaṇṇaṃ katvā" means if every monk receives a cloth worth ten kahāpaṇas, that is good. If not, one should bundle a cloth worth nine or eight kahāpaṇas with another worth one or two kahāpaṇas, and in this way, make equal portions. "Bhikkhū gaṇetvā vaggaṃ bandhitvā" means if there is not enough time to distribute robes to each monk individually, it is permitted to count ten monks at a time, make a bundle of ten robe-portions, and set them aside as a group. In these robe-portions thus set aside, lots (kusa) should be cast. Those monks should then cast lots again within their own group to distribute them.

Regarding the phrase "upaḍḍhapṭivīsaṃ sāmaṇerānaṃ" (a half-share for novices): those novices who are independent and do not perform the communal duties for the Saṅgha, but are devoted only to their studies and perform duties only for their own teachers and preceptors, should be given only a half-share of what the monks receive. However, those novices who perform the duties of the Saṅgha both before and after meals should be given an equal share. This statement refers to out-of-season robes (akālacīvara). As for in-season robes (kālacīvara), they are given equally to both monks and novices. Regarding the rainy-season robes (vassāvāsika), they should be taken only after performing communal duties such as sweeping. Indeed, taking the rainy-season robe is the duty of all monks and novices. Regarding the out-of-season robes in the storehouse, if the novices come and cry out, "Venerable sirs, we cook gruel, we cook rice, we cook hard food, we clear the grass and trees, we bring tooth-sticks, we prepare the bark for dye; what task is there that we have not done?"...
406:
This statement (that novices are given a half-share) was spoken concerning out-of-season robes (akālacīvara) that arise at an improper time and are stored in the storehouse. In-season robes (kālacīvara), however, should be distributed equally. The rainy-season robes (vassāvāsika) that arise in that monastery should be taken only after performing communal duties for the Saṅgha, such as sweeping. This is the duty of everyone there. Regarding the robes in the storehouse, if the novices come and cry out, "Venerable sirs, we cook gruel, we cook rice, we cook hard food, we clear the grass and trees, we bring tooth-sticks, we prepare the bark for dye; what task is there that we have not done?" then an equal share should be given. This giving of an equal share is intended for when the novices protest in such a manner, or when the extent of their work is not known. In the Kurundī Commentary, it is said: "If the novices request, 'Venerable sirs, why should we not perform the duties of the Saṅgha? We will do them,' then an equal share should be given."

"Uttaritukāmo" means wishing to cross a river or a wilderness, or wishing to depart for another region after finding a caravan. The phrase "to give his own share" refers to a monk who wishes to go with a caravan and says, "Let me not miss the caravan," after the robes have been brought out from the storehouse and piled up, and the bell has been struck and the Bhikkhu Saṅgha has assembled. Therefore, it is not proper to give the share if the robes have not been brought out, or the bell has not been struck, or the Saṅgha has not assembled. When the robes have been brought out, the bell struck, and the Bhikkhu Saṅgha assembled, the robe-distributor should estimate, "This monk's share should be this much," and give the robe by way of estimation. This is because it is impossible to give exactly equal shares as if weighing them on a scale. Therefore, whether the robe given by way of estimation is slightly less or more, it is considered well-given. If it is less, no more should be given; if it is more, it should not be taken back.

"Atirekabhāgena" (with an excess share): Suppose there are ten monks and ten cloths, one of which is worth twelve kahāpaṇas while the remaining nine are worth ten each. When lots are cast based on the value of ten kahāpaṇas for all, the monk who receives the lot for the twelve-kahāpaṇa cloth wishes to depart with that excess share, thinking, "This robe is enough for me." The monks then say, "Friend, the excess belongs to the Saṅgha." Hearing this, the Blessed One, in order to show that "In the property of the Saṅgha or a group, there is no such thing as 'small'; one should be restrained in everything, and even the one receiving it should have remorse (kukkucca)," said: "Monks, I allow it when an anukkhepa (substitute) has been given." In this context, anukkhepa means any allowable article that should be given as a substitute.
407:
The meaning is that if an allowable item of equal value is given for the amount that is in excess in that monk's share, [it serves as compensation for that excess part].

In the phrase "vikalake tosetvā" (satisfying those who lack), there are two types: shortage of robes (cīvaravikalaka) and shortage of persons (puggalavikalaka). Shortage of robes (cīvaravikalaka) means that although five robes have been distributed to all monks, and there are still remaining cloths, if they are not enough for one robe per person, they should be cut and given. When cutting, they should be made into pieces sufficient for small patches (aḍḍhamaṇḍala) and so on, or for shoe bags and so on, and then given. At the minimum, it is allowable to give a piece that is four finger-breadths wide and long enough for a border (anuvāta); however, it should be known that it must not be made so small as to be unusable. Such a shortage of robes is called cīvaravikalaka. When it is cut and given, that person is satisfied; only then should the drawing of lots (kusapāta) be performed. If one or two robes are lacking in a monk's share, another suitable requisite (parikkhāra) for monks should be placed there, and that share should be given to the one who is satisfied with it, and then the drawing of lots should be performed. This is also called cīvaravikalaka in the Andhaka Commentary.

Shortage of persons (puggalavikalaka) means that when monks are counted in groups of ten to form a group, one group is not complete, having only eight or nine monks. To them, eight or nine shares should be given, saying, "You take these shares and divide them among yourselves." Such a shortage of persons is called puggalavikalaka. When given separately, that person is satisfied; having thus satisfied them, the drawing of lots should be performed. Alternatively, "vikalake tosetvā" means making the deficient share of robes equal with other requisites and then performing the drawing of lots.

## Cīvararajana-kathā

"Chakaṇena" means with cow dung. "Paṇḍumattikāya" means with red clay. Among root dyes and so on, with the exception of turmeric (haliddi), all root dyes are allowable. With the exception of madder (mañjiṭṭhi) and jackfruit wood (tuṅgahāra), all trunk dyes are allowable. "Tuṅgahāra" is a type of thorny tree, and its trunk dye is the color of yellow orpiment. With the exception of lodh bark (lodda) and kaṇḍula bark, all bark dyes are allowable. With the exception of henna leaves (allipatta) and indigo leaves (nīlipatta), all leaf dyes are allowable. However, it is allowable to dye a garment already used by laypeople once with henna leaves. With the exception of kimsuka flowers and safflower (kusumbha), all flower dyes are allowable. As for fruit dyes, there is nothing that is not allowable; all are allowable.
408:
Unboiled dye is called "sītudaka". "Uttarāḷumpa" refers to a circular support (rim); the meaning is that [the Buddha] allows placing that circular support in the middle of the dye pot and surrounding it before putting in the dye-barks. If done this way, the dye will not boil over. "Udake vā nakhapiṭṭhikāya vā" means that if the dye is well-cooked (or ready), a drop placed in a bowl of water does not spread quickly; likewise, it remains without spreading on the surface of a fingernail. "Rajanuluṅka" is a ladle (scoop) for the dye. "Daṇḍakathālaka" is that same bowl with a handle attached. "Rajanakolamba" is a dye jar (a pot like a vat). "Omaddanti" means they knead it well. "Na ca acchinne theve pakkamitun" means that as long as the dye drops are still flowing, one must not go elsewhere. "Patthinna" means being stiff and hard or very heavy due to excessive dyeing. "Udake osāretun" means to place it in water. When the excess dye has come out, that water should be discarded and the robe should be kneaded. "Dantakāsāvāni" refers to robes that are dyed only once or twice and worn with an ivory-like color.

## Chinnakacīvarānujānana-kathā

"Acchibaddha" means formed like square paddy fields. "Pāḷibaddha" means formed with long boundaries (dykes) in length and width. "Mariyādabaddha" means formed with short boundaries in between. "Siṅghāṭakabaddha" means formed in the shape of a four-way junction (crossroads) where one boundary pierces through another. "Saṃvidahitun" means to make or arrange. When asked, "Are you able, Ānanda, [to sew a robe like this]?", it means "Are you capable, Ānanda?". The reply "I am able, Blessed One" shows "I am capable according to the method given by You." "Yatra hi nāma" means "whoever". "Kusi" is the name for the long borders (anuvāta) in length and width. "Aḍḍhakusi" is the name for the short borders in between. "Maṇḍala" refers to the large circular panels (compartments) in each section of a five-fold robe. "Aḍḍhamaṇḍala" refers to the small circular panels. "Vivaṭṭa" is the middle section sewn by combining a large panel and a small panel.

"Anuvivaṭṭa" refers to the two sections on both sides of that middle section. "Gīveyyaka" is an additional border sewn on to strengthen the area where it wraps around the neck. "Jaṅgheyyaka" is a border sewn in the same way at the place reaching the shins. It is also said that both these names are simply the names of the borders at the neck and shin areas. "Bāhanta" refers to each section outside the side panels (anuvivaṭṭa). Thus, the five-fold robe is analyzed. Alternatively, "anuvivaṭṭa" means...
409:
The two sections on each side of the central section (vivaṭṭa), totaling four sections, are called 'anuvivaṭṭa'. 'Bāhanta' is the name for the two ends that face outward when a robe of standard measurement is draped and rolled up over the arm. This same method is stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā.

## Tīcīvarānujānanakathā
'Cīvarehi ubbhaṇḍike' means making the robes into a bundle and carrying them. It means making them like bundled goods. In the term 'cīvarabhisi', 'bhisi' refers to robes that are folded together like a bundle, combining two or three robes. Those monks, thinking 'The Blessed One will return quickly from Dakkhiṇāgiri,' left behind the robes they received in the story of Jīvaka and went. But now, thinking 'He will return after a long time,' they took them and departed. 'Antaraṭṭhakāsu' refers to the eight days between the months of Māgha and Phagguṇa (the coldest period). Although the Blessed One did not feel cold, he stayed in the open air to make it known to the people. Noble sons of a cold nature naturally suffer due to the cold. 'Diguṇaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ' refers to a double-layered outer robe (dukuṭ). 'Ekacciyaṃ' refers to a single-layered robe. Thus, to prevent the opportunity for saying, 'The Blessed One himself subsists with four robes, but allows us only three,' he allowed the double-layered saṅghāṭi and the other two single-layered robes (ekacciya), making four in total.

## Atirekacīvarādikathā
'Aggaḷaṃ acchupeyyaṃ' means patching a hole with a piece of cloth. 'Ahatakappānaṃ' refers to robes that have been washed once. 'Utuddhaṭānaṃ' refers to old clothes that have been stored for a long time. 'Pāpaṇike' refers to robes sewn from rags fallen in the market. Effort should be made in seeking such robes. In this rag-robe (paṃsukūla), there is no limit to the number of layers; even a hundred layers is allowable. This is said regarding a monk who is content. In 'aggaḷaṃ tunnaṃ', removing the worn-out part and patching it with a new piece of cloth is called 'aggaḷa', and sewing it with thread is called 'tunna'. Making it by rolling is called 'ovaṭṭika'. Cross-stitching is called 'kaṇḍusaka'. 'Daḷhīkamma' is patching by adding a piece of cloth over the worn-out part without removing it. The story of Visākhā is well-known. The words following that are just as decided previously. 'Saggikaṃ' (or sovaggika) is so called because it is a cause for reaching heaven. It dispels grief. 'Anāmayā' means freedom from disease. 'Saggamhi kāyamhi' means attaining heaven. Worldlings free from lust for sensual pleasures refers to those who have attained jhāna. 'Sandiṭṭha' is a friend who is merely an acquaintance. 'Sambhatto' is a firm friend with whom one has shared meals. 'Ālapito' is one who has made an invitation, saying, 'If you want any of my property, please take it.' Taking by way of intimacy with these types of people is allowable. 'Paṃsukūlakato' means making a rag-robe. It becomes a heavy robe due to adding patches on the worn-out parts.
410:
'Ovaṭṭika' is making it by rolling the cloth. Cross-stitching is called 'kaṇḍusaka'. 'Daḷhīkamma' is a piece of cloth (a patch) applied for support without removing the weak or worn-out part.

349-351. The story of Visākhā is clear in meaning. The words following the story of Visākhā are just as decided previously. 'Sovaggika' is so called because it is a cause for reaching heaven. Because it is a cause for reaching heaven, it is preached as 'sovaggika'. Because it dispels grief, it is called 'sokanuda'. 'Anāmaya' means the absence of disease. 'Saggamhi kāyamhi' refers to one who has reached heaven.

Worldlings who are free from lust for sensual pleasures refers to those who have attained jhāna.

'Sandiṭṭha' is a friend who is merely an acquaintance. 'Sambhatta' is a firm friend with whom one has shared meals. 'Ālapito' is one who has spoken thus: 'If you want any property that belongs to me, take it.' Because of these factors—being one who lives with any of these three types of friends and being one who is delighted when the item is taken—taking out of intimacy is established.

## Pacchimavikappanupagacīvarādikathā

'Paṃsukūlakata' means made of rags. 'Garuko hoti' means it becomes heavy due to placing patches on the worn-out parts. 'Suttalūkhaṃ kātuṃ' means to make a patch using only thread. 'Vikaṇṇo hoti' means that for monks who sew by repeatedly cutting the thread, one corner of the outer robe (saṅghāṭi) becomes long. 'Vikaṇṇāṃ uddharituṃ' means to cut off the long corner. 'Okiriyanti' means they fall off from the cut corner. 'Anuvātaṃ paribhaṇḍaṃ' refers to the longitudinal border and the latitudinal border. 'Pattā lujjanti' means the threads placed in the large openings of the borders fall out; because of that falling out, the borders are destroyed. 'Aṭṭhapadakaṃ kātuṃ' means to sew the opening of the border in the shape of an eight-square board (checkerboard pattern).

360. 'Anvādhiṃ pi āropetuṃ' means to add an extra piece or an extension. This extra piece should be added only to a robe that is insufficient. If it is sufficient, adding an extra piece is not allowable; it must be cut off.

361. In the words, 'Monks, a gift of faith (saddhādeyya) [should not be wasted],' a monk who gives to relatives other than his parents indeed wastes the gift of faith. However, if the parents, even if they are in the position of royalty, desire it, it should be given.
411:
*Gilāno* means one who is unable to go taking [the robes] due to illness. *Vassika-saṅketa* refers to the four months of the rainy season. *Nadīpāra* means having to eat a meal on the other side of a river. *Aggaḷagutti-vihāra* means that in all these circumstances—being ill, staying for the four months of the rainy season, going to the other side of a river, and the state of having the Kathina spread—the security of the door-bolt is the standard. Only in a secure dwelling is it allowable to leave [the robes] for these reasons and go outside; it is not allowable in an insecure one. The dwelling of a forest-dwelling monk is usually not well-secured; therefore, that monk should place [the robes] in a storage vessel, deposit them well-covered in a rock cavity, a tree hollow, or similar places, and then go.

## Discussion on the Arising of Saṅgha Robes

'Monk, those robes belong only to you' means that even if they are brought from another place, they belong only to you; no one else has authority over those robes. The Buddha said this, starting with '*Idha pana*', to show that in the future, monks will take them without remorse (*kukkucca*). 'Until the removal of the Kathina, those robes belong to that monk' means that if the Kathina has been spread after obtaining a quorum of monks, it is for five months; if it has not been spread, it is for the one month of the robe-season only. Whether they give saying, 'We give to the Saṅgha,' or 'We give dedicated to the Saṅgha,' or 'We give to the Saṅgha that has completed the Vassa,' or 'We give as rainy-season cloth (*vassāvāsika*)'; or if they enter that monastery without dividing the robes of a deceased monk—all those robes belong to that monk alone. If that monk takes rainy-season cloth from a deposit (*upanikkhepa*) set aside with interest for the sake of the Vassa residence, or from what arises (*uppāda*) in that monastery, it is all well-taken. The defining characteristic here is: robes that arise for the Saṅgha in whatever manner reach the monk for five months if the Kathina is spread, and for the one month of the robe-season if the Kathina is not spread. Robes given saying, 'We give this to the Saṅgha that has completed the Vassa here,' or 'We give as rainy-season cloth,' reach even a monk who has not spread the Kathina for five months. Regarding rainy-season cloth that arises after that, one should ask: 'Is this rainy-season cloth for the past Vassa or for the future Vassa?' Why? Because it arose in the later period (*piṭṭhisamaya*).

*Utukāla* refers to a time other than the rainy season. In the phrase 'taking those robes and going to Sāvatthī,' those robes remain Saṅgha property (*saṅghika*) wherever they go; the mere sight by monks is the standard here. Therefore, if some monks meet on the way and ask, 'Friend, where are you going?' and hear the account of those Saṅgha robes, and say, 'Friend, are we not the Saṅgha?' and divide and take them right there, they are well-taken. If that monk turns off the path and enters a certain monastery or a rest-house, or enters a house while wandering for alms, and other monks see him and ask for the full account and then divide and take them, they are well-taken. A monk who wishes to determine them as his own robes should know the cloth; I shall explain in detail. That monk, having struck the stone drum, the robes...
412:
"Friend, where are you going?"—having asked this and heard the matter, if they say, "Friend, are we not the Saṅgha?" and divide and take them right there, it is called "well-taken." If that monk turns off the path and enters a monastery, a sitting hall, or even a single house while wandering for alms, and monks see him there, ask about the matter, and divide and take them, they are indeed well-taken.

Regarding the word "adhiṭṭhātuṃ" (to determine), the monk wishing to determine [the robes as his own] should know the protocol. That monk should strike the gong, announce the time, and wait for a while. If monks arrive due to the signal of the gong or the announcement of the time, the robes should be divided with them. If they do not come, he should determine, "These robes reach me." When determined in this way, all robes belong only to him, but the "standing" (ṭhitikā) does not remain.

If he takes them one by one, saying, "This first portion reaches me, this second portion reaches me," the robes taken are well-taken, and the "standing" (ṭhitikā) remains. A monk who takes them by making them reach him in this way is also considered to have determined them. However, whether he strikes the gong or not, whether he announces the time or not, if he takes them thinking, "Only I am here; these robes are for me alone," they are ill-taken. If he takes them thinking, "There is no one else here besides me; these robes reach me," they are well-taken.

"Pātite kuse" means that once the lot (voting ticket) has been cast for a portion, even if a thousand monks are present, the robe is considered taken. A share need not be given against one's will. However, if they wish to give of their own accord, let them give. The same rule applies to a subsequent share (anubhāga).

"Sacīvarāni" means they thought, "We will give the robes offered during the robe-season to the Saṅgha along with these meals; if we prepare them separately, it will take too long," and so they quickly prepared the meals along with the robes. "There āgamma uppannāni" means they arose quickly due to devotion toward you.

When robes are offered saying, "We give to the Saṅgha," they are given gradually throughout the entire robe-season. In the two previous cases, it was said they did not give because the gift was terminated. "Sambahūlā Therā" refers to the leading elders who were masters of the Vinaya. This story, along with the previous story of the two brothers, occurred after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbana. These elders had seen the Tathāgata in the past; therefore, they spoke according to the method prescribed by the Tathāgata in the previous cases.
413:
## Story of Upananda Sakyaputta

"He went to a village residence" means he went there having noted the time of robe distribution, thinking, "When they distribute the robes, they might favor me as well." "Will you accept?" means "Will you take them?" In this story, although a portion did not reach Upananda, the monks living in that village monastery, thinking, "This Upananda lives in the city, is harsh-spoken, and is a preacher of Dhamma," said, "Will you accept?"

In this context of "Whoever should accept, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaᥩa)," although the offense is light, the robes that have been taken must be returned to the place where they were taken. If they are lost or worn out, the monk who took them is responsible for replacing them. If a monk is told "Give them back" and does not give them, he should be made to settle based on the value of the goods upon his relinquishing of responsibility.

"A single portion" means "Give only one portion, the portion of one person." Now, wishing to set out the procedure to show how that portion should be given, the Buddha said "But here..." and so on. Therein, "If half there, half there" means if one stays for one day or seven days in each monastery, half of the portion of robes received by a person who stays permanently in each monastery should be given. By giving in this way, it is called giving a single portion of robes for one person.

"Or where there is more" means if a monk living in one monastery causes the dawn to rise in another monastery once every seven days, he is said to stay mostly in the first monastery. Therefore, a portion should be given to that monk from the monastery where he stayed more. By giving in this way too, it is called giving a single portion. This statement is made regarding monasteries within a single precinct (sĩmā) that have different gains and different surroundings. However, in monasteries located in different precincts, the acceptance of lodgings is suspended. Therefore, a portion of robes does not reach those monasteries. But everything else, such as alms-food and medicine, reaches a monk who has entered within the precinct of any monastery.

## Story of the Sick Monk

"They laid him on a couch" means after washing him in this way and dressing him in another dyed cloth, they made him lie on a couch. After making him lie down, the Venerable Ānanda washed the robe soiled with urine and excrement and spread it on the ground.

"Monks, he who would attend on me should attend on the sick" means "Monks, whoever would attend on me by following my advice and instruction, that person should attend on the sick." The core meaning here is that the sick should be attended by one who follows my advice. It should not be understood here that attending on the Blessed One and attending on a sick monk are exactly the same.

"He should be attended by the Sa᥅gha" means if the sick monk has no preceptor or others in that monastery, and is a visiting monk traveling alone, he is the responsibility of the Sa᥅gha. Therefore, the Sa᥅gha must attend to the sick monk. If they do not attend, the entire Sa᥅gha incurs an offense. If they attend by taking turns, only the monk who does not attend during his turn incurs an offense. Even a senior Elder of the Sa᥅gha is not exempt if it is his turn. If the entire Sa᥅gha assigns the responsibility to one monk, or if a monk endowed with duties says, "I alone will attend," the Sa᥅gha is free from the offense.

366. In the passages beginning with "He approaches one who is approaching," one should understand the illness of the one who eats as: "When I eat such and such food, my illness increases; when I eat such and such food, my illness decreases; when I eat such and such food, my illness remains stable."
414:
The Sa᥅gha must attend to the sick monk. If they do not attend, the entire Sa᥅gha incurs an offense. When attending by taking turns, only the monk who does not attend during his turn incurs an offense. Even a senior Elder of the Sa᥅gha is not exempt if it is his turn. If the entire Sa᥅gha assigns the responsibility to one monk, or if a monk endowed with duties (vatta) says, "I alone will attend," the Sa᥅gha is free from the offense.

In the passages beginning with "He approaches or he approaches," the meaning should be understood as not revealing the illness as it truly is, such as: "When I consume this, my illness increases; when I consume this, it decreases; when I consume this, it remains as it is." "Not fit" (nāla᥃) means it is not proper or suitable to attend. "To manage medicine" means being unable to prepare medicine. "One with material gain as an internal motive" (āmisantaro) means material gain is the internal reason for that monk. "Internal" refers to the cause. It means he attends desiring congee, food, bowls, and robes because of the motive of material gain.

## Discussion on the Belongings of the Deceased

"When he has passed away" (kāla᥅kate) means due to death. In the phrase "To give to the attendants of the sick," whether it is given by the formal act (kammavācā) mentioned immediately after or given after asking permission, it is considered given and is allowable.

In the phrase "Whatever light articles are there, whatever heavy articles are there," the distinction between light articles (lahubha᥃ᥩa) and heavy articles (garubha᥃ᥩa) will be explained later. Regarding the gains received by those who attend to the sick monk, the decision from the beginning is as follows:

If he passes away while the entire Sa᥅gha of monks is attending, all are owners. If he passes away after some have completed their turns and others have not yet served, some teachers say: "Since all would have attended when their turns arrived, all are owners." Others say: "Only those who actually attended receive them; the others do not."

When a novice (sāma᥃era) passes away, if there are robes, they should be given to the attendants. If there are no robes, whatever is available should be given. If there are other requisites, they should be given after being valued as a portion of robes.
415: If a monk and a novice serve equally, they should be given equal shares. If the novice alone serves and the monk only manages, the novice should be given the larger share. If the novice only cooks gruel with water brought by the monk and makes the monk accept it, while the monk does the actual serving, the monk should be given the larger share. If many monks serve in harmony, all should be given equal shares. Among them, whoever serves exceptionally should be given a special share. One who cooks gruel or a meal, or prepares a bath as a caregiver (gilānupaṭṭhāka) even for a single day, is also considered a caregiver. One who merely sends medicine, rice, etc., without coming near is not a caregiver. Only one who searches for, brings, and comes near is a caregiver. One serves out of duty; another serves out of expectation (of inheritance). If both expect it at the time of death, it should be given to both. If one goes somewhere for the sick person's business or his own business after serving, with the thought 'I will return and serve again,' it should be given to him as well. If one serves for a long time but then gives up the burden saying 'I can no longer do it' and leaves, even if the sick person dies that very day, the caregiver's share should not be given to him. A caregiver may be a layperson, a monk, or even a woman; all receive a share. If that monk has only a bowl and robes and nothing else, everything should be given to the caregivers only. Even if (the bowl and robes) are worth a thousand, they do not get other many requisites; those belong only to the Saṅgha. If the remaining goods are many and valuable, but the triple robes (ticīvara) are of little value, the triple robes and requisites should be taken from those goods and given. All this is obtained only from what belongs to the Saṅgha (saṅghika). If that monk, while still alive, renounced all his requisites and gave them to someone, or if someone took them through intimacy (vissāsa), they belong to the person to whom they were given or by whom they were taken. The caregivers receive only according to that person's wish. Requisites kept in a distant place without being given to others also belong to the Saṅgha in those respective places. If one of two owners of undivided property dies, the other...
416:
...is the owner. The same rule applies to property owned by many, starting from three. When all have died, it becomes Saṅghika (property of the Saṅgha). If they give it to co-residents (saddhivihārika) etc. without dividing it, it is considered not given. If given after dividing, it is well-given. That property belongs to the co-residents etc. even when those monks die, not to the Saṅgha.

## Discussion on the Rejection of Kusa-grass Robes, etc.

Among kusa-grass robes etc., 'akkanāḷa' means cloth made from calotropis fiber. 'Potthaka' means cloth made from hemp (makaci) fiber. The remaining kusa-grass robes etc. were mentioned in the First Pārājika Vaṇṇanā. Among those items, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is incurred only for potthaka (hemp cloth). For the remaining kusa-grass robes etc., grave offenses (thullaccaya) are incurred. Cloth made from calotropis thread, banana fiber thread, and eraka-grass are of the same class as potthaka.

Robes that are entirely blue/dark in color etc. should be washed to remove the dye, re-dyed, and then worn. If they cannot be washed, they should be made into bedspreads. Or they should be placed in the middle of a double-layered robe. The differences in their colors should be understood according to the method mentioned in the commentary on sandals (upāhanā). Robes with uncut fringes or long fringes should be worn after cutting the fringes. If a jacket (kañcuka) is obtained, it is allowable to use it after tearing and dyeing it. The same rule applies to a turban (veṭhana). Tirīṭaka cloth is made from the bark of a tree; it is allowable to make that tirīṭaka into a foot-wiper.

A 'suitable recipient' means if any monk takes it thinking 'I will take his property,' it is meant that it should be given. Thus, among these twenty-three persons, it should be noted that sixteen persons do not receive, and seven persons do receive.

## Discussion on the Arising of Robes when the Saṅgha is Divided

The Saṅgha is divided means they become two factions like the monks of Kosambī. 'In one faction' means they give the water of donation, incense, etc., to one faction, and robes to the other faction. 'It belongs to the Saṅgha only' means it belongs to the entire Saṅgha, to both factions; the bell should be struck and it should be shared by both factions together at once. 'It belongs to the faction only' means when given in this way, the water belongs only to the faction to whom the water of donation was given. The robes belong only to the faction to whom the robes were given. Where the water of donation is the standard (measure), there one faction...
417:
Because robes are received on one side due to the receipt of the donation water, and on the other side robes are received simply because robes were obtained, it is said that robes are received; therefore, both sides should be combined and distributed according to seniority. It is stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā that this is the practice to be followed on the other side of the ocean (in the island of Sīhaḷa). Regarding the phrase "only in that group," however, the other group has no authority. The cases concerning the sending of robes are well-known.

## Aṭṭhacīvaramātikākathā

Now, in order to show the source of the robes mentioned from the beginning, he said: "Monks, there are these eight matrices (mātikā)," and so forth. The statement "He gives to the boundary (sīmā)" and so forth is spoken by way of the method based on the individual. Among these matrices, giving to the boundary is the first matrix, giving by agreement is the second matrix ... [pe] ... giving to an individual is the eighth matrix. Among those eight, one who gives by referring to the boundary in this way, "I give to the boundary," is said to give to the boundary. This method applies in all cases.

In the detailed explanation of the matrix beginning with "He gives to the boundary; the monks who have entered within the boundary should distribute it," regarding the phrase "He gives to the boundary," it should be understood that there are fifteen types of boundaries: khaṇḍa-sīmā (partial boundary), upacāra-sīmā (precinct boundary), samānasaṃvāsa-sīmā (boundary of common communion), avippavāsa-sīmā (boundary of non-separation), lābha-sīmā (boundary of gains), gāma-sīmā (village boundary), nigama-sīmā (town boundary), nagara-sīmā (city boundary), abbhantara-sīmā (inner boundary), udakukkhepa-sīmā (water-splash boundary), janapada-sīmā (district boundary), raṭṭha-sīmā (country boundary), rajja-sīmā (kingdom boundary), dīpa-sīmā (island boundary), and cakkavāḷa-sīmā (world-system boundary).

Among these boundaries, the khaṇḍa-sīmā has already been discussed in the Sīmākathā. The upacāra-sīmā is defined by the enclosure in a monastery that has an enclosure, and by the area suitable for an enclosure in a monastery that does not have one. Alternatively, the upacāra-sīmā should be understood as the area within two stone-throws of a man of average strength from the place where monks constantly assemble, or from the dining hall located at the edge, or from the dwelling where they regularly reside. This upacāra-sīmā expands as the dwellings increase and contracts as they decrease. However, in the Mahāpaccari Aṭṭhakathā, it is said, "It also expands as the monks increase." Therefore, if monks sit filling up to a hundred leagues (yojana) in a continuous line with the monks assembled in the monastery, even that hundred-league area becomes the upacāra-sīmā, and the gain reaches all of them. Both the samānasaṃvāsa-sīmā and avippavāsa-sīmā have also been discussed.
418:
What is called lābha-sīmā (boundary of gains) was not personally authorized by the Fully Enlightened Buddha, nor was it established by the Elders who conducted the Dhamma Councils. However, kings and their great ministers, after building a monastery, would demarcate an area of a gāvuta, half a yojana, or a full yojana all around, and after planting pillars inscribed with the name "This is the lābha-sīmā of our monastery," they would establish the boundary, saying, "Whatever gains arise within this area, we give them all to our monastery." This is called lābha-sīmā. The abbhantara-sīmā and udakukkhepa-sīmā within a village, town, or city should also be understood as previously stated. Janapada-sīmā means: within countries such as Kāsi and Kosala, there are many districts (janapada); the boundary of each individual district is the janapada-sīmā. Raṭṭha-sīmā is the boundary of countries such as Kāsi and Kosala. Rajja-sīmā is the area where the authority of each individual king extends, such as "the domain of the Coḷa king" or "the domain of the Keraḷa king." Dīpa-sīmā refers to the great islands and minor islands bounded by the ocean. Cakkavāḷa-sīmā is the boundary demarcated by the Cakkavāḷa mountains themselves.

Among these boundaries, if one sees the Saṅgha assembled for some legal act in a khaṇḍa-sīmā and says, "I give to the Saṅgha in this very boundary," only those monks who have entered within the khaṇḍa-sīmā should distribute it. Indeed, that gain reaches only them. It does not reach other monks standing in the sīmantarika (inter-boundary space) or in the upacāra-sīmā. However, it does reach a monk standing on a tree or a mountain within the khaṇḍa-sīmā, or one who is below in the middle of the earth. But a gift given with the words "I give to the Saṅgha in this upacāra-sīmā" also reaches those standing in the khaṇḍa-sīmā and the sīmantarika. A gift given with the words "I give in the samānasaṃvāsa-sīmā" does not reach those standing in the khaṇḍa-sīmā and the sīmantarika. A gift given in the avippavāsa-sīmā and lābha-sīmā reaches those who have entered within those boundaries. A gift given in the gāma-sīmā and so forth also reaches those standing in the baddha-sīmā (fixed boundary) within those boundaries. A gift given in the abbhantara-sīmā and udakukkhepa-sīmā reaches only those who have entered within them. In the janapada-sīmā, raṭṭha-sīmā, rajja-sīmā, dīpa-sīmā, and cakkavāḷa-sīmā, the decision should be understood just as stated for the gāma-sīmā and so forth.

If a person staying in Jambudīpa gives, saying, "I give to the Saṅgha in the island of Tambapaṇṇi," even a single monk coming from the island of Tambapaṇṇi is entitled to receive it for all. Even if a single fellow-monk (sabhāga-bhikkhu) there takes the share of other fellow-monks, he should not be prevented. Thus, first, the decision regarding the gift of one who gives by referring to a boundary should be understood.
419:
If a person does not know how to say, "I donate to the Saṅgha residing in such-and-such a boundary (sīmā)," but only knows the word "sīmā," and goes to the monastery saying, "I donate to the sīmā," or "I donate to the Saṅgha residing in the sīmā," that person should be asked: "There are many types of sīmā; which sīmā do you intend?" If he says, "I do not know the name of the sīmā; let the Saṅgha residing in the sīmā distribute and take it," in which sīmā should it be distributed? The Elder Mahāsīva said, "It should be distributed in the avippavāsasīmā (boundary of non-separation)." Then, other teachers said to him: "An avippavāsasīmā can be as large as three yojanas. If that is the case, monks staying three yojanas away would also receive the gains. One would have to fulfill the duties of a guest (āgantukavatta) after staying three yojanas away before entering the monastery. A traveling monk would have to ask permission for a lodging after traveling three yojanas. For a monk living in dependence (nissaya), his dependence would lapse upon crossing three yojanas. A monk undergoing probation (parivāsa) would have to cross three yojanas to see the dawn. A bhikkhunī would have to ask permission to enter the monastery while staying three yojanas away. All these matters should be handled only according to the extent of the upacārasīmā (precinct boundary). Therefore, it should be distributed only within the upacārasīmā."

'Katikāya' refers to an agreement of equal gains (samānalābha). For this reason, it is said, "Many monasteries have equal gains." In making such an agreement, it should be done as follows: When monks are assembled in one monastery, if they wish to support another monastery and make it have equal gains, they should mention the name of that monastery and state a reason, such as "This monastery is an ancient one," or "The Buddha once resided there," or "It receives few gains." Then, they should announce three times: "Does the Saṅgha approve of making this monastery have equal gains along with this monastery?" By this much announcement, even if one is staying in that monastery, it is as if one is staying here. In that monastery too, the Saṅgha should act in the same way. By this much, even if one is staying here, it is as if one is staying in that monastery. When gains are distributed in one monastery, it is proper to take a share for the Saṅgha staying in the other monastery. In this way, many monasteries can be made to have equal gains along with one monastery.

'Bhikkhāpaññattiyā' refers to the place where one's own charity is designated (where regular alms are offered). For this reason, it is said, "In the place where regular meritorious deeds (dhuvakāra) are performed for the Saṅgha." Its meaning is: in the monastery where the regular provision of food belonging to this donor of robes is maintained for the Saṅgha, or in the monastery where he takes responsibility for the monks and always feeds them at his house, or where...
420:
...or where this donor has had a monastery built, or where ticket-food (salākabhatta) and so on are regularly offered. If a person has established an entire monastery, there is no need to say more; such a place is called a 'dhuvakāra' (place of regular merit). Therefore, if that donor says, "I donate to the place where my regular meritorious deeds are performed," or "Give it there," and if there are regular meritorious deeds in many places, it is considered donated in all those places.

However, if there are many monks in one monastery, they should say, "Among the places of your regular merit, there are many monks in one place and few in another." If he says, "Please take according to the number of monks," then it is proper to distribute and take accordingly. Among these distributable items, things like cloth and medicine, even if few, are easily distributed. But if there is only one couch or chair, the donor should be asked, and it should be given to whichever monastery or, within a single monastery, whichever lodging the donor directs. If he says, "Let such-and-such a monk take it," that is also proper. If he says, "Give it to my place of regular merit," and leaves without specifying, it is proper for the Saṅgha to decide. It should be decided thus: "Give it to the place where the Elder of the Saṅgha resides." If that Elder's lodging is already well-equipped, it should be given where there is a shortage. If a monk says, "There are no lodgings or utensils in my place of residence," it should be given there.

"Giving to the Saṅgha" means entering the monastery and giving, saying, "I donate these robes to the Saṅgha." "To the Saṅgha present" means the Saṅgha within the upacārasīmā (precinct boundary) should strike the bell, announce the time, and distribute. One who takes a share for a monk who is within the boundary but has not yet reached the distribution site should not be prevented. The monastery may be large; while robes are being distributed starting from the Elder's seat, if some elderly monks who are slow arrive late, one should not say, "Venerable sirs, we are now giving to those with twenty years of standing; your turn has passed." The sequence should be paused, and after giving to those Elders, the distribution should continue according to the sequence.

Hearing that "Many robes have arisen in such-and-such a monastery," monks may come even from a monastery a yojana away. Robes should be given to the monks who arrive, starting from where they are standing. Even if they have not reached the distribution site, if they have entered the upacārasīmā and their pupils or others take a share for them, it must be given. If it is said, "Give to those standing outside the upacārasīmā," it should not be given. However, if those who have entered the upacārasīmā are continuous with those at the monastery gate or inside the monastery, the boundary is said to be extended by the power of the assembly (parisā).
421:
The precinct boundary (upacāra-sīmā) is said to expand (by the power of the assembly); therefore, [the gift] must be given [to those who arrive within that boundary]. Even if it has been distributed to the junior members of the Saṅgha, it must still be given to those who arrive later. However, when distributing the second portion, those who arrive while [the distributor] has reached the seat of the Elder do not deserve the first portion; they deserve [a share] starting from the second portion according to seniority (vassagga).

If there are ten monks in a monastery and someone offers ten robes saying, "I give these ten robes to the Saṅgha," they must be distributed individually. If they take them away thinking, "All these robes belong to us," they are improperly assigned and improperly taken; they remain communal property (saṅghika) wherever they are taken. However, it is proper if they set aside one robe and give it to the Elder of the Saṅgha (Saṅghatthera) saying, "This robe belongs to you, Venerable Sir," and then take the rest saying, "The remaining robes belong to us."

When only a single robe is brought with the words, "I give this to the Saṅgha," if they take it without distributing it, thinking, "It belongs to us," it is improperly assigned and improperly taken. It is proper to make a mark with a small knife or with turmeric, etc., and assign it to the Elder of the Saṅgha saying, "This portion belongs to you, Venerable Sir," and then take the rest saying, "The remaining portion belongs to us." It is not proper to make a division using a flower pattern or a crease already on the cloth. If they pull out a single thread and give it to the Elder of the Saṅgha saying, "This part belongs to you, Venerable Sir," and then take the rest saying, "The remaining part belongs to us," it is proper. If it is cut into pieces and distributed, it is certainly proper.

In a monastery where there is only one monk, when communal robes (saṅghika-cīvara) arise, if that monk takes them thinking, "All belong to me," as mentioned before, they are improperly taken, and the sequence of distribution (ṭhitikā) does not stand. If he sets aside each robe one by one and takes it thinking, "This robe belongs to me," the sequence of distribution stands. In a situation where the sequence of distribution does not stand, if another monk arrives while another robe arises, it must be cut in the middle and taken by both. If a junior monk arrives while a robe arises when the sequence of distribution is standing, the sequence of distribution descends. If a senior monk arrives, the sequence of distribution ascends. If there is no one else, he should assign it to himself and take it again.

A robe offered by any means referring to the Saṅgha, such as saying, "We give to the Saṅgha" or "We give to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha," is not suitable for those who wear dust-heap robes (paṃsukūlika). This is because it is said, "I reject householder robes (gahapati-cīvara) and undertake the dust-heap robe practice (paṃsukūlikaṅga)." The reason it is unsuitable is...
422:
...because it is unsuitable. Even if the Saṅgha requests and offers it, it should not be accepted. If a monk gives a robe that is his own property, it is called 'bhikkhudattiya' (given by a monk) and is suitable. However, it is not a dust-heap robe (paṃsukūla). Even so, the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) is not broken. If it is offered with the words, "We give to the monks," or "We give to the Elders," it is suitable even for those who wear dust-heap robes. If it is offered saying, "We give this cloth to the Saṅgha; let them make sandal bags, bowl bags, support straps (āyoga-paṭṭa), shoulder straps, etc., with this," it is also suitable. 

If the cloths given for bowl bags and such are many and are sufficient for a robe as well, it is suitable to make a robe from them and wear it. However, if the Saṅgha cuts the cloths remaining after distribution and distributes them for sandal bags, bowl bags, etc., it is not suitable to take them. Only what is designated by the owners (donors) is suitable; the other is not. 

If it is said, "We give to the Saṅgha of dust-heap robe wearers for the purpose of water-strainer cloth (dhammakaraṇa-paṭa), etc.," it is suitable to take. What is called a requisite (parikkhāra) is also to be desired by dust-heap robe wearers. It is also suitable to convert any excess cloth from those requisites into a robe. If thread is given to the Saṅgha, it should also be taken by the dust-heap robe wearers. This is the decision regarding robes given by entering a monastery and saying, "I give these robes to the Saṅgha."

However, if one sees monks traveling in the precinct area (upacāra) outside the monastery and informs the Elder of the Saṅgha or a junior member of the Saṅgha, "I give to the Saṅgha," even if the assembly is spread out for a league (yojana), if they are continuous, it reaches all of them. But it does not reach those monks who have not come within twelve cubits of the assembly.

Regarding the phrase "giving to the twofold Saṅgha (ubhatosaṅgha)," whether one says, "I give to the twofold Saṅgha," or "I give to the Saṅgha by dividing into two portions," or "I give to the two Saṅghas," or "I give to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha and the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha," it is considered as given to the twofold Saṅgha. In such a gift, two equal portions should be made and one portion given [to each]. In the case where it is said, "I give to the twofold Saṅgha and to you," if there are ten monks and ten nuns, twenty-one shares should be made; one share should be given to the individual, ten shares to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha, and ten shares to the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha. That monk who received the individual share is also entitled to take from the Saṅgha's share according to his seniority. Why? Because he was included in the mention of the twofold Saṅgha.
423:
Even if it is said, "I give to both Saṅghas and to the shrine (cetiya)," the same method applies. Specifically, in this offering, there is no portion for the shrine that comes from the Saṅgha's share; it is only a portion equal to that which goes to a single individual.

If it is said, "I give to both Saṅghas, to you, and to the shrine," then twenty-two portions are made: ten are given to the bhikkhus, ten to the bhikkhunīs, one to the individual, and one to the shrine. In that offering, the individual is also entitled to receive again from the Saṅgha's share according to their seniority (vassa); for the shrine, however, there is only one portion.

If it is said, "I give to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha and the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha," the gift should not be divided in the middle; it should be given by counting the bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs individually. If it is said, "I give to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha, the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha, and to you," the individual does not receive a separate portion; they receive only one portion from the place they belong. Why? Because they are included under the term "Bhikkhu-saṅgha." Even if it is said, "I give to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha, the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha, to you, and to the shrine," a portion equal to one individual is obtained for the shrine, but for the individual, a separate portion is not obtained. Therefore, after giving one portion to the shrine, the remainder should be distributed by counting the bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs.

Even if it is said, "I give to the bhikkhus and the bhikkhunīs," it should not be divided in the middle; it should be distributed only by the number of individuals. Even if it is said, "I give to the bhikkhus, the bhikkhunīs, to you, and to the shrine," a portion equal to one individual is obtained for the shrine, but for the individual, there is no separate portion; it should be distributed only by counting the bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs. Just as the method was led starting with the Bhikkhu-saṅgha, so too should the method be led starting with the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha. If it is said, "I give to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha and to you," a separate portion for the individual is not obtained; it should be taken only according to seniority. If it is said, "I give to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha and to the shrine," a separate portion for the shrine is obtained. Even if it is said, "I give to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha, to you, and to the shrine," it is obtained only for the shrine, not for the individual.

Even if it is said, "I give to the bhikkhus and to you," a separate portion is not obtained. If it is said, "I give to the bhikkhus and to the shrine," it is obtained for the shrine. Even if it is said, "I give to the bhikkhus, to you, and to the shrine," a separate portion is obtained only for the shrine, not for the individual. The same should be applied starting with the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha.

In the past, people gave offerings to both Saṅghas headed by the Buddha. The Blessed One sat in the middle. The bhikkhus sat on the right side, and the bhikkhunīs sat on the left side. The Blessed One was the Saṅgha-Elder (Saṅghatthera) of both Saṅghas. At that time, the Blessed One himself used the requisites he received.
424:
He also had them given to the monks. Nowadays, however, wise people set up an image containing relics or a shrine (cetiya) and give offerings to both Saṅghas—the Bhikkhu-saṅgha and the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha—headed by the Buddha. Placing an alms-bowl on a bowl-stand in front of the image or the shrine, and pouring the water of dedication, they give it saying, "We give to the Buddhas." In such an offering, they give the foremost choice food and snacks. Or, having brought them to the monastery, they give the alms-food, flowers, scents, etc., saying, "We give these to the shrine." In such a case of offering, how should one proceed?

First, flowers, scents, and so on should be offered to the shrine. Banners should be made from cloths. Lamps should be offered with oil. As for alms-food, honey, molasses, and so on, they should be given only to the person—whether a monk or a layperson—who constantly looks after and cleans the shrine. If there is no one who constantly looks after it, the brought alms-food should be set aside for a while, and after performing the duties of cleaning, it is allowable to consume it. If the time of noon is approaching, it is also allowable to perform the duties after consuming it.

Among flowers, scents, and so on, if it is said of any object, "Take this item and perform an offering to the shrine," it should be taken even to a distant place and offered. Even if it is said, "Take the alms-food to the Saṅgha," it should be taken. If it is said, "I am wandering for alms; there are monks in the sitting hall, they will take it," but the donor says, "Venerable sir, I give it only to you," then it is allowable to consume it. Or, if while a monk is carrying it intending to give it to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha, the time of noon approaches on the way, it is allowable for him to take it for himself and consume it.

"I give to the Saṅgha who have completed the vassa (rains retreat)" means entering a monastery and giving, saying, "I give these robes to the Saṅgha who have completed the vassa." In that monastery, however many monks have observed the first vassa (purima-vassa) without breaking it, only those monks should distribute it; it does not reach other monks. Even for a monk who has departed for another direction, if there is someone to receive it, it should be given until the Kathina is withdrawn. If the Kathina has not been spread, teachers who know the characteristics say that a robe given during the winter season saying, "I give to the Saṅgha who have completed the vassa," also reaches those monks who observed the later vassa (pacchima-vassa). However, this is not discussed in the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā).

If, standing outside the precinct boundary (upacāra-sīmā), one says, "I give to the Saṅgha who have completed the vassa," it reaches all the monks who have arrived. Or if one says, "I give to the Saṅgha who have completed the vassa in such-and-such a monastery," it reaches only the monks who completed the vassa in that monastery until the Kathina is withdrawn. If one says this starting from the first day of the summer season, it reaches all the monks present at that time. Why? Because it occurs outside the time of robe-giving. If it is said during the vassa, "I give to the monks who are observing the vassa," those who have broken their vassa do not receive it; only those who are observing the vassa receive it.
425:
During the robe-offering month (cīvaramāsa), if it is said, "I give to those spending the Vassa," it reaches only those who entered the later Vassa (pacchimikā); it does not reach those who entered the earlier Vassa (purimikā) or those who broke the Vassa.

From the robe-offering month until the last day of winter (the full moon day of Phagguna), if it is said, "I give to the monks who have spent the Vassa," it reaches only those who have emerged from the past Vassa (vassavuṭṭhāna), whether the kathina has been spread or not. If it is said from the first day of summer (the 1st waning day of Phagguna), a schedule (mātikā) should be set up to ask: "Five months have passed since the completion of the past Vassa, and the upcoming Vassa will begin in four months; for which Vassa residence do you give?" If the donor says, "I give to the monks who emerged from the past Vassa," it reaches only those who completed that Vassa. Even for those who have departed to other directions, the remaining compatible (sabhāga) monks have the right to receive their share.

If the donor says, "I give to the monks who will spend the upcoming Vassa," that robe should be kept and taken only when the day for entering the Vassa arrives. However, if the donor says, "The monastery is not secure, there is danger from thieves, it is not possible to keep it or to carry it around," and then says, "I give to those who have arrived," it should be distributed and taken. If the donor says, "Venerable sir, counting back from this year, I have not yet given to the monks who spent the Vassa in the third year; I give this robe for that year," it reaches the monks who completed the Vassa in that year. If those monks have departed to other directions, a trusted monk should take it for them. If only one monk remains and the others have passed away, that single monk receives everything. If not even one remains, it becomes the property of the Saṅgha (saṅghika) and should be distributed by the monks present.

"Giving by designation" (ādissa deti) means giving by specifying and defining. The same method applies to gruel (yāgu), medicine, and so on. For example, if monks are invited for gruel for today or tomorrow, and when they arrive at the house, gruel is offered; after they have drunk the gruel, if the donor says, "I give these robes to the monks who drank my gruel," it reaches only those invited monks who drank the gruel. It does not reach those monks who received gruel while on alms round at the door, those who entered the house and received it, those for whom people took their bowls from the rest house (sālā) to bring them gruel, or those sent by the elders. However, if many other monks arrive along with the invited monks, filling the inside and outside of the house, and the donor says, "Whether invited or not, let these robes be for all those to whom I have given gruel," then all of them receive it. It does not reach those monks who received gruel from the hands of the elders.
426:
If the donor says, "I give these robes to the monks who drank my gruel," it reaches only those invited monks who drank the gruel. It does not reach those monks who received gruel at the house door while on alms round, those who entered the house and received it, those for whom people took their bowls from the rest house to provide gruel, or those to whom gruel was sent by the elders. However, if many other monks arrive along with the invited monks, filling the inside and outside of the house, and the donor says, "Whether invited or not, let these robes be for all those monks to whom I have given gruel," then all of them receive it. It does not reach those monks who received gruel from the hands of the elders. If the donor says, "Let it be for all who drank my gruel," then it reaches everyone. The same method should be understood for meals (bhatta) and snacks (khādanīya).

In the case of robes (cīvara), if a donor who has previously invited monks to stay for the Vassa and given them robes, after offering a meal to the monks, says, "I have previously given robes to certain monks; let this robe, or this thread, or clarified butter, honey, molasses, etc., be for those same monks," then everything reaches only those monks. In the case of lodgings (senāsana), if it is said, "Let this be for the monk who resides in the monastery or the dwelling (pariveṇa) built by me," it belongs only to that monk. In the case of medicine (bhesajja), if it is said, "We occasionally give medicines such as clarified butter to the elders; let this robe be for those same monks who received them," it belongs only to those monks.

In giving to an individual (puggala), one gives either in their absence, saying, "I give this robe to the monk named so-and-so," or in their presence, placing it at their feet and saying, "Venerable sir, I give this to you." If the donor says, "I give this to you and to your pupils (antevāsika)," it reaches both the elder and the pupils. If there is a monk who has come to learn the Pali (uddesa) and one who is leaving after learning, it reaches them as well. If it is said, "I give to the monks who are constant companions (nibaddacārika) with you," it reaches all those who perform duties for the resident pupils, learn the Pali and its commentaries, and live there. This is the decision regarding the term "giving to an individual." The remaining words are clear in meaning throughout the entire Khandhaka.

## The Commentary on the Robe Chapter (Cīvarakkhandhaka-vaṇṇanā) is finished.
427:
## 9. Campeyyakkhandhaka
## The Story of the Bhikkhu Kassapagotta

In the Campeyyakkhandhaka, 'Gaggarāya pokkharaṇiyā tīre' means on the bank of the pond constructed by the woman named Gaggarā. 'Tantibaddho' means bound by the sequence of duties to be performed in that monastery. In the words beginning with 'Ussukkampi akāsi yāguyā,' it is proper to exert effort only in such places where people have requested, 'Venerable sirs, if visiting monks arrive, please inform them (that there is rice gruel)'; one should not exert effort in places where no such request has been made. The Buddha's command 'Gaccha tvaṃ bhikkhu' (Go, monk) was spoken because He saw that the lodging in that very place was suitable for the bhikkhu Kassapagotta.

The specific details of the phrases beginning with 'Adhammena vaggakammaṃ karonti' will appear later in the Pali text itself.

'Aññatrāpi dhammā kammaṃ karonti' means they perform the formal act by setting aside the nature of Dhamma. Alternatively, this reading itself might be the original. A formal act performed with a true basis is called 'performed according to Dhamma'; the meaning is that they do not perform it in that manner. In the phrases 'Aññatrāpi vinayā kammaṃ' and 'Aññatrāpi satthusāsanā kammaṃ,' the same method should be understood. Here, 'Vinaya' refers to accusation (codanā) and reminding of an offense (sāraṇā). 'Satthusāsana' refers to the completeness of the motion (ñattisampadā) and the completeness of the proclamation (anussāvanasampadā). The meaning is that they perform the act without such accusation, reminding, or completeness of motion and proclamation. 'Paṭikuṭṭhakataṃ' means it is both protested and performed. A formal act performed while other monks are protesting is both protested and performed. The meaning is that they perform such acts.

In the words beginning with 'Chayimāni bhikkhave kammāni adhammakammaṃ,' 'Dhamma' is a name for the Vinaya Pali. Therefore, a formal act not performed in accordance with the Vinaya Pali as taught is to be known as 'adhammakamma' (an act not in accordance with Dhamma). This is just a summary here; the details are already given in the Pali text itself. Those details are provided by way of the motion-and-second act (ñattidutiyakamma) and the motion-and-fourth act (ñatticatutthakamma). Since in a motion-only act (ñattikamma) there is no reduction or alteration as in motion-and-second or motion-and-fourth acts, and since an announcement act (apalokanakamma) is performed only after informing the Saṅgha, these (ñattikamma and apalokanakamma) were not shown in the Pali. The decision on all these acts will be explained later.
428:
## Discussion on the Act Performed by a Group of Four, etc.

Now, to show the divisions of the Saṅgha by whom the sixth act, called 'a legal act in accordance with Dhamma by a complete assembly' (dhammena samaggakamma), should be performed, the words beginning with 'Pañca saṅghā' (Five [types of] Saṅgha) were spoken. 'Kammapatto' means one who has reached the act, one who is suitable for the act, or one who is worthy of the act. It means it is not the case that he is unworthy to perform any act.

The words beginning with 'Catuvaggakaraṇañce bhikkhave kammaṃ bhikkhunicatuttho' were spoken to show the failure of the act due to the assembly. There, by taking 'ukkhittaka' (a suspended person), a bhikkhu who is 'different in communion due to a legal act' (kammanānāsaṃvāsaka) is included. By taking 'nānāsaṃvāsaka,' a bhikkhu who is 'different in communion due to views' (laddhinānāsaṃvāsaka) is included. 'Nānāsīmāya ṭhitacatuttho' means becoming a group of four together with one standing within the forearm's length (hatthapāsa), whether in the boundary interval (sīmantarika) or outside the boundary (bahisīmā).

The words beginning with 'Pārivāsikacatuttho' were spoken to show the failure due to the assembly only in acts such as probation (parivāsa); the decision on those acts will be explained later (in the Cullavagga).

The words beginning with 'Ekaccassa bhikkhave saṅghamajjhe paṭikkosanā ruhati' were spoken to show whether a protested act is valid or invalid. 'Pakatattassa' refers to one whose virtue is unimpaired, who has not committed a Pārājika offense. 'Ānantarikassa' refers to one sitting immediately adjacent to oneself.

## Discussion on the Two Expulsions, etc.

'Dvemā bhikkhave nissāraṇā' etc. was spoken to show the validity or invalidity of acts due to the basis (vatthu). There, the phrase 'If the Saṅgha should expel one who has not yet reached expulsion, it is well-expelled' was spoken with reference to the act of banishment (pabbājanīyakamma). Indeed, they expel from the monastery by the act of banishment; therefore, that act is called 'nissāraṇa' (expulsion). Because that monk is not a corrupter of families (kuladūsaka), he has not reached expulsion by that specific characteristic. However, because it was said 'The Saṅgha, if it so desires, may perform the act of banishment,' he is 'well-expelled.' 'If the Saṅgha should expel him' means if the Saṅgha expels by way of the act of censure (tajjanīyakamma) etc. In that expulsion: 'Monks, the Saṅgha, if it so desires, may perform the act of censure against three types of monks—one is a maker of strife, a maker of quarrels, a maker of disputes, a talkative person, a maker of legal cases in the Saṅgha; one is...'
429:
“If one is endowed with even one of these factors: being foolish, being inexperienced, being full of offenses, being unrestrained (having no limit to offenses), and living in improper association with laypeople,” expulsion (nissāraṇa) is permitted. Therefore, such a person is well-expelled.

‘Osāraṇā’ means admittance (re-admitting into the Dispensation or ordaining). In that context, ‘the Saṅgha admits him’ means admitting by way of the act of ordination (upasampadakamma). ‘Dosārito’ means badly admitted (admitted wrongly). Even if ordained a thousand times, that person (who is unfit) remains unordained. The teachers and preceptors, as well as the entire performing Saṅgha, also incur an offense; no one is free from the offense. Thus, the admittance of these eleven types of incapable persons (abhabba-puggala) is a bad admittance (dosārita). However, the thirty-two types of persons, such as those with severed hands, are well-admitted (su-osārita). If they are ordained, they are truly ordained. Nothing should be said against them (as not being monks). Nevertheless, the teachers, preceptors, and the performing Saṅgha incur an offense (for ordaining those who are forbidden); no one is free from the offense.

The passage beginning with “Monks, in this Dispensation, there is no offense to be seen in a monk” is spoken to show an illegal act (adhamma-kamma) by way of a false basis and a legal act (dhamma-kamma) by way of a true basis. In that passage, ‘paṭinissajjitā’ means ‘should be relinquished.’

## Discussion on Upāli’s Questions
In the questions of Upāli as well, legal and illegal acts are analyzed solely by way of the basis. There are two methods: the single-root method (ekamūlaka) and the double-root method (dvimūlaka). The single-root method is quite clear. In the double-root method, just as ‘disciplinary procedure for the mindful’ (sativinaya) is paired with ‘disciplinary procedure for the no-longer-insane’ (amūḷhavinaya) to form one question, so too amūḷhavinaya and others are paired with ‘disciplinary procedure for the further-punishment’ (tassapāpiyyasikā) and so on. At the end, there is only the single phrase: “he ordains one who is fit for ordination.” In the subsequent section for monks, starting with sativinaya, each should be combined with the remaining phrases.

## Discussion on the Act of Censure
In the passage beginning with “Monks, in this Dispensation, a monk is a maker of strife,” a cycle is formed by way of these phrases: “an incomplete act by what is not Dhamma, a complete act by what is not Dhamma, an incomplete act by Dhamma, an incomplete act by what resembles Dhamma, a complete act by what resembles Dhamma,” regarding the seven acts such as the act of censure (tajjanīyakamma) and their revocations...
430:
This statement is made for the purpose of showing the failure (vipatti) of the seven types of formal acts, such as the act of censure (tajjaniya-kamma), as well as in the settling of those acts. In the Pali passage beginning with "Idha pana bhikkhave bhikkhu bhaṇḍanakārako," the term "anapadāno" means being devoid of a limit (apadāna). A limit is called "apadāna"; the meaning is being devoid of the limit of the offense. After that, in order to show the various types of prohibited acts that have been performed, that same Pali passage is stated in comparison with phrases such as "akataṃ kammaṃ." In that Pali, it is not that any interpretation cannot be understood by following the Pali text; therefore, we have not provided a detailed explanation.

## The Explanation of the Campeyyakkhandhaka is finished.
431:
## 10. Kosambaka Chapter
## Discussion on the Dispute at Kosambī
In the Kosambaka Chapter, regarding the statement “They suspended that monk for not seeing an offense,” this is the sequential account. It is said that two monks lived in a certain monastery: a Vinaya expert (vinayadhara) and a Sutta expert (suttantika). Among them, the Sutta expert monk one day entered the toilet and left after leaving the remaining rinsing water in the vessel. The Vinaya expert entered later, saw that water, and upon coming out, asked that monk: “Friend, did you leave this water?” “Yes, friend,” he replied. “Do you not know that there is an offense in this?” he asked again. “Yes, I do not know,” he replied. “Friend, there is an offense in this,” he said. “If there is an offense, I shall confess it,” he replied. “Friend, if you did it unintentionally or through lack of mindfulness, there is no offense,” he said. That monk then held the view that there was no offense in that matter.

The Vinaya expert then told his own pupils, “This Sutta expert does not know even when he commits an offense.” When those pupils saw the pupils of that monk, they said, “Your teacher does not know he has committed an offense even after committing one.” They went and told their teacher. That teacher said, “This Vinaya expert previously said there was no offense, and now he says there is an offense; he is a liar.” Those pupils went and said, “Your teacher is a liar,” and thus they increased the mutual quarrel. Because of that increase, the Vinaya expert, finding an opportunity, performed an act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma) against that monk for not seeing his offense. Therefore, it is said, “They suspended that monk for not seeing an offense.”

“The Saṅgha of monks is split, the Saṅgha of monks is split”—in this statement, (in truth) it was not yet split. However, just as when it rains, it is said, “Now the crops are finished” (because the crops will certainly be finished), even so, because of this cause, it will certainly split in the future.
