Furthermore, that splitting is by way of a quarrel, not by way of a formal schism (saṅghabheda); therefore, it is said “is split.” Here, the repetition (of ‘The Saṅgha of monks is split’) should be understood by way of the meaning of urgency or alarm.
432:
Regarding the statement, "Having spoken this matter, he rose from his seat and departed," why did he depart after speaking thus? If the Blessed One had said to the monks who performed the excommunication (ukkhepaka), "You have excommunicated that monk without cause," or if he had said to the monks who followed the excommunicated one (ukkittānuvattaka), "You have committed an offense," they would have harbored a grudge, saying, "The Blessed One is a partisan of these people; the Blessed One is a partisan of those people." Therefore, leaving only the scriptural authority (tanti), he rose from his seat and departed after speaking this matter.

In the phrase, "He himself makes himself (one of different communion)," it refers to a monk who, while sitting in the faction of the unrighteous (adhammavādī) who have been excommunicated by the Saṅgha, asks, "What do you say?" and after hearing their views and the views of others, gives rise to the thought, "These are unrighteous, the others are righteous." Such a monk, even while sitting in their midst, becomes one of different communion (nānāsaṃvāsaka) with them; he invalidates the legal act (kamma), and because he has not come within the reach (hatthapāsa) of the others, he also invalidates their act. In this way, he himself makes himself one of different communion.

In the phrase, "one of the same communion (samānasaṃvāsaka)," it should be understood that a monk who, while sitting in the faction of the unrighteous, enters their midst (knowing), "These are unrighteous, the others are righteous," or who, sitting in whichever faction, takes the view, "These are righteous," such a monk makes himself one of the same communion.

In the phrase, "bodily action, verbal action," it should be understood that those who strike with the body perform bodily action, and those who speak harsh words perform verbal action. "They perform touching with hands" means they touch one another with their hands under the influence of anger. "While performing unrighteous acts" means while carrying out unrighteous matters. "While living without mutual joy" means while living without speech that causes mutual joy. This itself is the original text. The meaning is: while living without speech of mutual rejoicing. In the phrase, "By this much, not each other (harming)," one should sit in two rows, leaving the immediate proximity (upacāra). However, when acting according to the Dhamma and while living with mutual joy, one should sit with one seat's distance between them, making each seat an interval.

457-458. In the words beginning with "Do not quarrel," taking the remaining text "do not perform (akattha)," the meaning should be understood as "Do not perform quarreling." "Unrighteous speaker" (adhammavādī) refers to one of the monks who follow the excommunicated one. This monk, however, desires the welfare of the Blessed One; this, it is said, was his intention.
433:
The intention is: "These monks are overcome by anger and do not accept the words of the Teacher; let the Blessed One not be weary by admonishing them." That is why he spoke thus. The Blessed One, however, thinking, "Later they will gain sense and desist," spoke by bringing a story of the past out of compassion for them. In that past story, "anatthatto" means "anattho ato," meaning "There is no benefit to me from this man." Alternatively, "anatthatto" means "anatthado" (one who gives harm). The rest is clear.

In the verses beginning with "puthusaddo," "puthusaddo" means one who has a great sound (loud-voiced). "Samajano" means similar people, people who are the same. It means that all these people who engage in quarreling have a great sound by emitting noise from all around, and they are also similar to one another. "Na bālo koci maññatha" means that among them, not even a single person thought, "I am a fool"; all of them indeed considered themselves wise. "Nāññaṃ bhiyyo amaññaruṃ" means that not only did no one think "I am a fool," but even while the Saṅgha was splitting, they did not even realize this cause: "The Saṅgha is splitting because of me."

"Parimuṭṭhā" means those who are forgetful (unmindful). "Vācāgocarabhāṇino" means (the letter 'ā' is shortened); they are those who speak by dwelling only in the range of words, not in the range of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and so on. How do they speak? As much as they wish to open their mouths, they open them that much and speak; the meaning is that not even one person restrains his mouth out of respect for the Saṅgha. "Yena nītā" means by which quarrel they were led to this shameless state. "Na taṃ vidū" means they do not know it, thinking, "This quarrel has such a danger."

"Ye ca taṃ upanayhanti" means those who harbor a grudge in such a manner as "He abused me, he struck me," etc. "Sananatano" means ancient (tradition).

"Pare" means those others who engage in quarreling, excluding the wise. While they are quarreling in the midst of the Saṅgha, they do not realize, "We are passing away, we are constantly and continuously approaching the presence of death." "Ye ca tattha vijānanti" means the wise ones there who do realize, "We are going to the presence of death."
434:
Because they know this, quarrels are stilled. Indeed, knowing this, they arouse wise reflection and practice for the pacification of quarrels.

This verse beginning with 'Aṭṭhicchinnā' is spoken with reference to King Brahmadatta and Prince Dīghāvu. Even they achieved reconciliation; why can it not be so for you, whose parents' bones have not been broken, whose lives have not been taken, and whose cattle, horses, and wealth have not been seized?

The verse beginning with 'Sace labhetha' is spoken to show the praise and blame of wise and foolish companions. 'Abhibhuyya sabbāni parissayānīti' means overcoming manifest dangers such as lions, leopards, and tigers, as well as hidden dangers such as lust and hatred, one should wander joyfully and mindfully with that wise companion.

'Rājāva raṭṭhaṃ vijitaṃ' means that just as King Mahājanaka and King Arindama abandoned their conquered kingdoms and wandered alone, so should one wander alone. 'Mātaṅgaraññeva nāgo' means like a noble elephant in the forest. 'Mātaṅga' refers to an elephant; 'Nāga' is a designation for greatness. Just as the Mātaṅga elephant who cared for his mother wandered alone in the forest and did no evil, and like the Pālileyyaka elephant, so should one wander alone and do no evil.

## The Story of Going to Pālileyyaka

'Pālileyyake viharati rakkhitavanasaṇḍe' means he stayed in the Rakkhita forest grove depending on Pālileyyaka village. 'Hatthināgo' refers to a great elephant. 'Hatthikalabhehi' means with young elephants. 'Hatthicchāpehi' means with very young, milk-drinking calves. 'Chinnaggāni' means he eats the grass stubs resembling stumps, left after the young elephants walking ahead had bitten off the tips. 'Obhaggobhaggaṃ' refers to the branches broken off and dropped from high places by that great elephant. 'Assa sākhābhaṅgaṃ' means those young elephants eat the broken branches belonging to him. 'Āvilāni' means he drinks the muddy water mixed with silt, stirred up by those young elephants who entered and drank first. 'Ogāhā' means from the landing place.

'Nāgassa nāgena' means the mind of the great elephant is equal to the mind of the Buddha-Nāga. 'Īsādantassa' refers to the elephant with tusks like chariot poles. 'Yadeko ramatī vane' means that just as the Buddha-Nāga delights alone in the forest in seclusion, this great elephant also delights alone in the forest; therefore, his mind is equal to the Buddha-Nāga's mind in delighting in solitude.
435:
The mind of the great elephant is equal to the mind of the Buddha-Nāga; it means they are identical in delighting in solitude.

'Having stayed as long as he liked' means it should be understood that the Blessed One stayed there for the three months of the rainy season. During that time, the report spread everywhere that the Blessed One, harassed by the monks of Kosambī, had entered the forest and stayed there for three months.

'Then the lay followers of Kosambī' means the lay followers residing in Kosambī, upon hearing this report.

## The Story of the Eighteen Grounds

I shall explain the eighteen grounds for schism, such as declaring non-Dhamma as Dhamma, in the Saṅghabhedaka Khandhaka.

'Having reinstated that suspended monk' means taking him, going to the boundary, making him confess the offense, and reinstating him by a formal act (kammavācā). 'Performing the Uposatha at that very moment' means the Harmony Uposatha should be performed on that very day according to the method stated in the Uposatha Khandhaka.

'Without reaching the root from the root' means not reaching the source from the source, implying staying without deciding the matter. 'Upāli, this concord of the Saṅgha is said to be devoid of meaning and merely nominal' means that while there is no concord in actual meaning, it merely possesses the name 'Saṅghasāmaggī'.

'In the affairs of the Saṅgha' means when the duties of the Saṅgha arise. 'In consultations' means in Vinaya consultations. 'When meanings arise' means when Vinaya meanings arise. 'In decisions' means in the decisions of those very meanings. 'Mahatthika' means of great benefit. 'Paggahāraha' means worthy of being supported.

'First not to be blamed for virtue' means first of all, one who is not to be reproached regarding virtue. 'Avekkhitācāra' means one whose conduct is observed. It refers to one whose conduct is investigated through the method of acting with clear comprehension in looking ahead and looking aside, etc. In the Commentaries, however, it is stated as 'one whose conduct is not concealed'.
436:
"Visayha" means having overcome (subdued). "Anuyuttaṃ bhaṇanti" means speaking words that are permitted and consistent with reason. For that monk speaks what is permitted; he does not speak words devoid of reason due to envy or following a wrong course (agati). Therefore, he does not diminish the benefit. However, a monk who speaks out of envy or following a wrong course diminishes the benefit and cannot provide a reason; therefore, when he enters an assembly, he trembles and is agitated. A monk who is not like this (not having envy or bias) is shown as "one worthy of exaltation" (paggahāraho).

Furthermore, regarding the verse beginning with "Tatheva pañhaṃ," the meaning is: just as one speaking permitted words does not diminish the benefit, likewise, when questioned in the midst of an assembly, he neither broods nor becomes dejected. Indeed, one who does not know the meaning broods. One who is unable to speak becomes dejected. But one who knows the meaning and is able to speak neither broods nor becomes dejected. "Kālāgataṃ" refers to words that have arrived at the proper time for speaking. "Byākaraṇārahaṃ" refers to words worthy of being answered in accordance with the meaning of the question. "Vaco" means while speaking, or when speaking such words. "Rañjeti" means he pleases. "Viññūparisaṃ" refers to the assembly of the wise.

"Ācerakamhi ca sake" means in the doctrine of one's own teacher. "Alaṃ pametuṃ" means being capable of investigating and weighing various matters with wisdom. "Paguṇo" means having familiarity or practice through repeated association. "Kathetave" means in what is to be spoken. "Viraddhikovido" means being skilled in matters of failure or mistakes.

The verse beginning with "Paccatthikā yena vajanti" is stated to show in what kind of speech he is proficient. The meaning here is: by such speech, opponents are subdued, and the great multitude attains understanding and realization. A monk who, while speaking, does not diminish his own teacher's doctrine and answers the question in accordance with the legal issue (adhikaraṇa) that has arisen without causing harm to others, is one proficient in what is to be spoken.

"Dūteyyakammesu alaṃ" means being capable in the duties of a messenger for the Saṅgha because of being endowed with the eight qualities of a messenger. "Samuggaho" means taking up well. This is the meaning. Alternatively, just as one well receives the alms food to be offered, likewise, with a heart full of joy and satisfaction, he is one who well undertakes the duties of the Saṅgha, a recipient of various tasks among the Saṅgha's affairs. He is one who carries out instructions, and because of carrying out such instructions, he does not indulge in conceit or excessive pride, thinking, "I am doing this, I am bearing the burden of the Saṅgha."
437:
Just as they well receive the alms food and offerings brought for worship, likewise, with a mind born of joy and satisfaction, he well undertakes the duties of the Saṅgha; the meaning is that he is the recipient of various tasks among the Saṅgha's affairs. "Karaṃ vaco" means being one who carries out instructions. "Na tena maññati" means that because of carrying out those instructions, he does not speak with conceit or excessive pride, saying, "I am doing this, I am fulfilling the Saṅgha's burden."

"Āpajjati yāvatakesu vatthūsu" means the number of grounds through which he falls into an offense. "Hoti yathā ca vuṭṭhiti" means the manner in which emergence from that offense occurs. "Ete vibhaṅgā" means these Vibhaṅgas (analyses) which illuminate these meanings: the grounds for falling into an offense and the manner of emergence. "Ubhayassa" means for that monk, there are the two Vibhaṅgas. "Svāgatā" means they are well-come (well-mastered by heart). "Āpattivuṭṭhānapaddassa kovido" means being skilled in the causes for emergence from an offense.

"Yāni cācaranti" means a monk who practices the causes of disputes and so forth reaches expulsion (nissāraṇa) by way of acts such as the act of rebuke (tajjaniya-kamma). "Osāraṇaṃ taṃvusitassa jantuno" means he also knows the rehabilitation (osāraṇa) that should be performed for a person who has completed that penance. The meaning of the remaining words is clear in all respects.
